### [1] [Large Language Models are Approximate Survival Estimators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38181)
*Juan M Zambrano Chaves,Peniel Argaw,Risa Ueno,Carlo Bifulco,Kristina Young,Rom Leidner,Tristan Naumann,Hoifung Poon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can perform zero-shot survival prediction from clinical narratives and compares them to standard survival modeling methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Patients increasingly use general-purpose LLMs to seek prognostic information, but it is unknown how accurate these models are for survival prediction compared with established statistical/ML survival models. There is a need to rigorously assess LLM performance, understand what clinical features they use, and determine whether they can be trusted in medical risk assessment.

Method: The authors propose Survprompt, which converts structured patient covariates into free-text clinical vignettes and uses them to prompt pretrained LLMs to predict survival in a zero-shot fashion. They benchmark multiple frontier LLMs against conventional survival models, especially random survival forests, on two large pan-cancer datasets (MSK-CHORD and a new Providence cohort built via LLM-based chart abstraction). They evaluate using censored mean absolute error (cMAE) and concordance index (c-index) and run feature ablation experiments to see which clinical variables drive LLM predictions.

Result: Frontier LLMs produced surprisingly competitive censored mean absolute error for individual survival time predictions, sometimes within 10% of state-of-the-art RSF models trained specifically for the task, and in prostate cancer even outperforming RSF in cMAE. Feature ablations showed LLMs attend to similar clinical factors as specialized survival models. However, LLMs had variable performance across cancer types and institutions and showed worse risk discrimination than RSF, reflected in lower c-index values.

Conclusion: Zero-shot LLMs, when prompted with natural-language clinical vignettes, can approximate individualized survival estimates with accuracy close to dedicated survival models in some settings, suggesting latent prognostic capabilities. Yet their inconsistent performance across datasets and poorer ability to distinguish high- vs low-risk patients indicate that they are not yet reliable for clinical deployment and require further development, calibration, and validation.

Abstract: Survival analysis estimates time-to-event outcomes from patient covariates and is widely used for medical risk assessment. Patients seeking prognostic information after a diagnosis may turn to large language models (LLMs), now readily accessible through consumer applications. However, whether LLMs can provide accurate survival predictions has not been rigorously evaluated. We introduce Survprompt, a framework that converts structured patient covariates into free-text clinical vignettes and prompts pre-trained LLMs to predict survival zero-shot. We benchmark Survprompt against conventional survival models, including random survival forests (RSF), across two multi-institutional pan-cancer cohorts: the publicly available MSK-CHORD cohort and a newly curated cohort from the Providence St. Joseph Health Network constructed using an LLM-based medical abstraction framework. We report censored mean absolute error (cMAE) and concordance index (c-index) and conduct feature ablations to identify variables influencing LLM predictions. Frontier LLMs achieved surprisingly competitive cMAE for individual survival times. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol achieved cMAE within 10% of state-of-the-art RSF models specifically trained for survival prediction for several cancer types and lower cMAE than RSF for prostate cancer in MSK-CHORD. Feature ablations revealed that LLMs prioritized clinical variables similarly to specialized survival models. However, LLMs showed inconsistent accuracy across cancer types and institutions and poorly discriminated between high- and low-risk patients (lower c-index). Zero-shot LLMs can generate surprisingly accurate prognostic estimates without specialized training, but their variable performance across cancer types and institutions remains an important limitation for clinical use.

</details>


### [2] [TomasuLLM: Out-of-Order Speculative Execution for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38201)
*Jiangnan Yu,Ceyu Xu,Mengming Li,Shiyu Huang,Yiran Xia,Jian Weng,Hui Xue,Haohui Mai,Yuan Xie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TomasuLLM, a runtime system that speculatively executes agent tool calls out of order to reduce end-to-end latency while preserving correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents suffer high latency because they must wait for long-running tools like compilers and test suites to finish before proceeding. This is analogous to how in-order CPUs stall on long operations. The authors aim to hide this latency by starting predictable future tool calls early, but must do so without breaking correctness when earlier steps change the state or the plan.

Method: TomasuLLM speculatively drafts future agent actions and executes them out of trajectory order inside isolated copy-on-write sandboxes. It traces each speculative action’s dependencies and effects, then validates them against the committed state once all prior steps are finalized. Only then are results committed in the original trajectory order. The system thus enables out-of-order execution with an in-order, correct interface, similar in spirit to Tomasulo-style CPU scheduling.

Result: On three benchmarks featuring tools from sub-second to minutes-long runtimes, TomasuLLM improves effective agent speed while maintaining correctness: 1.31x faster on 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, 1.35x on 28 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, and 1.27x matched progress on 18 SWE-Marathon sessions. An audit of 4,010 commit-validation records found zero incorrect speculative commits (false accepts).

Conclusion: Speculative, out-of-order tool execution for coding agents can significantly reduce latency without sacrificing correctness if paired with sandboxing, dependency/effect tracing, and strict in-order commit with validation. TomasuLLM demonstrates that ideas from out-of-order CPU execution transfer effectively to LLM tool-use runtimes.

Abstract: Long-running tools can dominate coding-agent latency: compilers, test suites, and repository commands take seconds to minutes while the agent idles. This observation stall presents the same tension that drove out-of-order processors -- asequential interface hides work that can be predicted and started early, but a speculative result may become visible only after it and every earlier step have been validated.
  We present TomasuLLM, a runtime that executes agent tool calls out of trajectory order while preserving task-execution correctness. It drafts future actions, runs them in isolated copy-on-write sandboxes, traces their dependencies and effects, and commits results in trajectory order only after validation against committed state. Across three benchmarks spanning sub-second to minutes-long tool calls, TomasuLLM improves the reported benchmark means and scales with tool latency: 1.31x on 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, 1.35x on 28 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, and 1.27x matched progress on 18 SWE-Marathon sessions. Across 4,010 audited commit-validation records, it produces zero false accepts.

</details>


### [3] [Automatic estimation of verbal fluency index in people with Motor Neuron Disease using ASR alignment and pause modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38203)
*Bahman Mirheidari,Leslie Ing,Daniel Blackburn,Sharon Abrahams,Christopher McDermott,Heidi Christensen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds an automatic system to estimate a key cognitive score (Verbal Fluency Index) in motor neuron disease patients using speech recordings, despite their speech impairments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cognitive impairment is common in motor neuron disease and must be monitored to guide treatment and care, but standard cognitive tests rely on speech and are hard to administer when patients have dysarthria. The ECAS test, and especially its Verbal Fluency Index, is an important clinical tool, so there is a need for automated, objective, speech-based methods to estimate this index without requiring full manual scoring.

Method: The authors use a unique dataset of speech from people with MND performing ECAS verbal fluency tasks. They build a pipeline combining automatic speech recognition (WhisperX) and voice activity detection (Silero), along with refined timestamp processing, to identify produced words and temporal patterns. From these they derive clinically-inspired features and other feature sets (traditional acoustics and self-supervised embeddings) and train various regression models to predict the Verbal Fluency Index and related clinically interpretable measures. Performance is evaluated using metrics including R² and normalized RMSE for P-word and S-word fluency tasks.

Result: Models using the clinically-inspired features consistently outperform those using only traditional acoustic features or self-supervised embeddings. The best systems achieve high predictive accuracy for Verbal Fluency Index: for P-word tasks, R² of 0.9 and NRMSE of 0.05; for S-word tasks, R² of 0.8 and NRMSE of 0.08, demonstrating that the automated pipeline closely approximates manual scoring.

Conclusion: Automated analysis of speech recordings in MND, using ASR and VAD combined with clinically-motivated temporal and lexical features, can accurately estimate the ECAS Verbal Fluency Index despite patients’ speech impairments. This suggests that automated VFI estimation is feasible and could support scalable, less burdensome cognitive monitoring in motor neuron disease.

Abstract: Monitoring cognitive impairment (CI) in motor neuron disease (MND) is essential for timely treatment and care, yet challenging due to co-occurring speech difficulties. The Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen (ECAS) provides a robust metric for CI assessment, with the Verbal Fluency Index (VFI) a central element. Building on recent advances in automated speech analysis, this study proposes a system for estimating VFI. It leverages a unique MND dataset and combines ASR (WhisperX) and VAD (Silero) with refined timestamping to predict the VFI and extract several clinically interpretable measures. Our approach outperformed systems based on traditional acoustic features and self-supervised embeddings, evaluated using multiple regression algorithms. Clinically inspired features consistently outperformed the other sets, with the best models achieving strong results (P-words: R2 0.9, NRMSE 0.05; S-words: R2 0.8, NRMSE 0.08), demonstrating the feasibility of automated VFI estimation.

</details>


### [4] [The System Prompt Illusion: How Instruction Preambles Modify Computation in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38205)
*Muhammad Usama,Dong Eui Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how different system prompts (especially safety vs. persona/formatting) actually change internal computations of instruction-tuned transformers, finding that safety prompts are encoded but barely affect deeper computation, helping explain jailbreak vulnerabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System prompts are the main way practitioners steer LLM behavior, but we lack a mechanistic understanding of how these prompts modify internal representations, particularly for safety. This gap makes it hard to reason about or improve prompt-based control and to understand why jailbreaks remain common.

Method: The authors analyze 17 instruction-tuned models (1.5B–72B parameters, 8 architecture families) under 20 system prompts grouped into five functional categories. They compute Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) between layer-wise activations across prompts to measure representational shifts. They compare the depth and magnitude of changes for different prompt types, then use linear probing to see where in the network prompt categories are encoded, and causal activation patching to identify layers causally responsible for behavioral changes. They connect representational depth metrics to behavioral outcomes statistically across models.

Result: Persona and formatting prompts produce large, layer-selective restructuring of intermediate representations, while safety prompts cause minimal representational change, similar to a weak baseline. Restrictive and explicitly permissive safety prompts follow almost identical computational paths (mean CKA correlation 0.997). Even in 70B–72B commercial-scale models, safety-related representational changes affect less than 10% of the network. Linear probes show prompt category information is present in all layers, but only a small subset of layers is where the model actually restructures its computation. Causal activation patching confirms these layers mediate behavioral changes, and the depth of representational change strongly correlates with behavioral effect size (Spearman ρ = 0.761, p < 0.001).

Conclusion: System prompts are consistently “noticed” by instruction-tuned models but are only deeply integrated into computation for some functions (persona, formatting), not for safety. Safety instructions, including restrictive ones, barely penetrate the network and use nearly identical pathways to permissive prompts, providing a mechanistic account of why system-prompt-based safety can be easily bypassed. The work suggests that robust safety likely requires mechanisms beyond simple system prompting and that mechanistic analysis can guide where and how to intervene in model internals.

Abstract: System prompts are the primary lever practitioners use to control language model behavior, yet what they actually do to the computation inside the transformer remains poorly understood. Across 17 instruction-tuned models spanning 8 architecture families and 1.5B to 72B parameters, we use Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to compare layer-wise representations under 20 system prompts in five functional categories. Effects are layer-selective and instruction-type-dependent: persona and formatting instructions deeply restructure intermediate representations, while safety instructions barely move them, producing changes statistically indistinguishable from a minimal baseline. Restrictive safety instructions and explicitly permissive ones ("you have no restrictions") engage near-identical computational pathways (mean CKA correlation 0.997), and this persists at commercial scale, where safety penetration remains below 10% even at 70B-72B. A linear probing baseline exposes the mechanism: the model encodes prompt category at every layer but restructures its computation only at a small subset, so the prompt is reliably "seen" but, for safety, not deeply "acted upon." Causal activation patching confirms these layers mediate behavioral change, and representational depth predicts behavioral effect size across the full 17-model cohort (Spearman rho = 0.761, p < 0.001). The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for the persistent jailbreak vulnerability of system-prompt-based safety. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/system-prompt-illusion-cka

</details>


### [5] [TutlAit v1: a crowdsourced Moroccan Tamazight speech dataset with Arabic transcriptions and regional accent labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38219)
*Mohamed-Amine Chadi,Ezzahra Ait El Arbi,Ismail Khayoub,Aymane Fadili,Yassine Ennhili,Jadjigua Bouali,Hanane Inhid,Mohammed Ameksa,Hajar Mousannif*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TutlAit is a 20.9-hour crowdsourced Moroccan Tamazight speech corpus aligned with Modern Standard Arabic text and labeled by regional accents, designed for speech tech tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Moroccan Tamazight is an official language but remains severely under-resourced for speech technology: existing corpora are small, noisy, lack consistent transcriptions and generally omit precise regional variety information. This limits progress in ASR, speech translation and accent-related modeling for Tamazight. The authors aim to fill this gap with a higher-quality, variety-labeled dataset and a scalable collection pipeline.

Method: The authors built a dedicated crowdsourcing web platform (TutlAit) using a React front end and Django REST back-end with PostgreSQL. Native Tamazight speakers were recruited via LinkedIn and Instagram; upon registration, they declared their regional variety (Atlas, Souss, Rif, other) and demographics. Contributors used two workflows: (1) Text-to-Audio, where they read Arabic sentences and recorded their Tamazight renditions via browser; (2) Audio-to-Text, where they listened to Tamazight audio and typed the corresponding Arabic transcription. Additionally, Tamazight segments were extracted from public audiovisual media, segmented and annotated with ELAN, then bulk-imported. All uploads were standardized server-side to 16kHz mono WAV, hashed (SHA-256) to detect duplicates, checked for duration constraints, and manually validated by an administrator. Regional accent labels were stored along with each sample.

Result: The resulting corpus, TutlAit, comprises 13,384 Tamazight audio files totaling 75,231 seconds (~20.9 hours, ~3.01GB). Atlas Tamazight represents 9,956 files (~14.08 hours) and Souss Tamazight 3,378 files (~6.75 hours). Smaller subsets exist for Rif (22 files) and Kabyle (28 files). Each item is paired with Modern Standard Arabic text and tagged with regional accent metadata. The dataset passes technical quality checks (format, duration, deduplication) and administrative validation.

Conclusion: TutlAit provides a new, systematically collected, regionally labeled corpus of Moroccan Tamazight speech aligned with Modern Standard Arabic, addressing a major resource gap for this official but under-resourced language. The dataset is suitable for training and evaluating automatic speech recognition, speech translation, and accent identification models for Moroccan Tamazight, and the described pipeline offers a reusable blueprint for future low-resource speech data collection efforts.

Abstract: Tamazight (Amazigh) is, together with Arabic, one of the two official languages of Morocco, yet it remains severely under-resourced for speech technology: pub licly available labelled audio is scarce, generally lacks information on the regional variety spoken, and is often of uneven transcription quality. This article describes the TutlAit dataset, a corpus of Moroccan Tamazight speech paired with Modern Standard Arabic text and explicit regional accent labels. The data were collected with TutlAit, a purpose-built crowdsourcing web application (React 18 front end, Django 5 / Django REST Framework back-end, PostgreSQL database). Native speakers recruited through targeted LinkedIn and Instagram campaigns created an account, declared their regional variety (Atlas, Souss, Rif or other) and demographic information, and then contributed through two workflows: Text-to Audio, in which an Arabic sentence is displayed and the volunteer records its oral Tamazight rendering in the browser, and Audio-to-Text, in which a Tamazight excerpt is played and the volunteer types its Arabic transcription. A complemen tary set of segments was obtained from freely accessible Tamazight audiovisual media, segmented and annotated with ELAN and imported through a bulk CSV/ZIP pipeline. Every upload is converted server-side to 16kHz mono WAV, hashed with SHA-256 for duplicate rejection, checked for duration bounds and validated by an administrator. The dataset contains 13,384 audio files totalling 75,231 seconds (approximately 20.9 hours, about 3.01GB). The Atlas variety accounts for 9,956 files (14.08h) and the Souss variety for 3,378 files (6.75h); small Rif (22 files) and Kabyle (28 files) subsets are also included. The corpus can be reused for speech recognition, speech translation and accent identification for Moroccan Tamazight.

</details>


### [6] [Conformal Factuality Control for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38222)
*Muhammad Aimal Rehman,Chi-Kuang Yeh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether conformal factuality control methods for RAG still work in more complex multi-hop RAG settings, showing they can achieve very high factual support for retained claims but at the cost of discarding many claims and sometimes entire answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While RAG grounds LLMs on external documents, generated outputs can still include hallucinated or unsupported claims, especially in multi-hop scenarios where retrieval and reasoning occur in multiple dependent steps. Existing conformal factuality control has been studied mainly for simpler, single-hop RAG. It is unclear whether these methods remain effective and well-calibrated when reasoning and retrieval chains get longer and more complex, which is critical for reliable, explainable QA systems used in practice.

Method: The authors extend claim-level split-conformal factuality filtering, previously developed for single-hop RAG, to the multi-hop RAG setting. They run multi-hop RAG pipelines using Llama 3.1 8B and GPT-4o-mini on three QA datasets (HotpotQA, Natural Questions, TriviaQA). For each generated answer, they decompose it into claims, estimate factual support of each claim from the retrieved context, and then filter claims according to conformal prediction thresholds calibrated on held-out data. They compare different confidence (coverage) targets, including 95%, and also carry out single-hop reference experiments for comparison.

Result: For all six combinations of model and dataset in the multi-hop setup, tightening the conformal target monotonically increases the proportion of responses whose *retained* claims are fully supported by the retrieved evidence. At a 95% conformal target, 95.80%–97.20% of responses with non-empty retained content are fully supported, compared with only 55.60%–76.03% support without any filtering. However, this high factual reliability is obtained by aggressively filtering: at the 95% target, only 4.41%–31.09% of generated claims survive, and only 9.70%–51.40% of responses retain any non-empty content.

Conclusion: Conformal factuality control techniques generalize effectively from single-hop to multi-hop RAG, delivering high nominal factual reliability for the claims they choose to retain. However, this reliability comes with substantial abstention and claim reduction, so practical deployment must consider not just coverage targets but also how many claims are preserved and how often the system remains silent or returns very short answers. Interpretations of “95% reliable” factuality guarantees must therefore be made jointly with retention and abstention rates in multi-hop RAG.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground large language models in external evidence, but retrieved context does not guarantee that generated claims are factually supported. This problem is especially relevant in multi-hop RAG, where retrieval and reasoning proceed through multiple dependent stages. We study whether claim-level conformal factuality control, previously developed for RAG, remains effective in this setting. We apply split-conformal claim filtering to multi-hop RAG and evaluate it on HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA using Llama 3.1 8B and GPT-4o-mini, together with a single-hop reference experiment. Across all six multi-hop model-dataset configurations, increasingly stringent conformal targets consistently increase the fraction of responses whose retained claims are fully supported. At the 95% target, this rate ranges from 95.80% to 97.20%, compared with 55.60%-76.03% without filtering. However, the improvement is strongly selective: only 4.41%-31.09% of generated claims are retained and 9.70%-51.40% of responses remain non-empty at the 95% target. These results show that conformal factuality extends to multi-hop RAG, while demonstrating that nominal reliability must be interpreted jointly with claim retention and abstention.

</details>


### [7] [Framing the Narrative: Ideological Mimicry in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38256)
*Olivia Macmillan-Scott,Michael Jacobs,Nils Metternich,Mirco Musolesi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Poli-SHIFT, a dataset and framework to test how political cues in prompts shift LLMs’ expressed political stances, finding strong evidence of ideological mimicry and interaction-dependent behaviour across models and countries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations assume an LLM’s political stance is stable, but real users embed political cues in wording, assumptions, and self-descriptions. If models adapt to these cues, they may create personalised and potentially polarising political information environments. The authors want to rigorously measure whether and how user-provided political signals systematically shift model outputs.

Method: The authors construct the Poli-SHIFT dataset and evaluation framework covering ten contentious political topics in the US, UK, and Australia. They systematically manipulate three kinds of political signals in prompts: (1) contested terminology (e.g., alternative labels for the same issue), (2) politically valenced premises embedded in the question, and (3) user information such as stated ideology. They test seven open-weight LLMs using both multiple-choice and open-text questions, comparing outputs under controlled prompt variations to quantify stance shifts and ideological mimicry.

Result: Across all seven models, prompt framing substantially affects political stance. Simply changing contested terminology flips which side of an issue the model supports in 16.9% of otherwise matched comparisons. Additionally, when the user explicitly states a political ideology, models’ responses systematically move toward that ideology, demonstrating ideological mimicry and interaction-dependent stance shifts rather than a single, stable bias profile.

Conclusion: LLMs’ political stance is not a fixed characteristic; it depends strongly on how users interact with them. Political cues in prompts—terminology, premises, and self-described ideology—systematically steer models’ expressed positions, raising concerns that personalised LLM interactions can create or exacerbate politically homogeneous information environments and reinforce users’ existing beliefs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about politically contentious issues, yet evaluations typically treat a model's stance as a relatively stable property. Real users, however, communicate political signals through their terminology, assumptions, and personal context. We investigate whether such signals produce ideological mimicry: systematic shifts in the political stance expressed by an LLM toward the position conveyed by the interaction. If LLMs adapt their responses to these signals, they risk creating personalised political information environments in which users with opposing views receive systematically different accounts of the same issue, potentially reinforcing existing divisions. We build the Poli-SHIFT dataset and evaluation framework and assess seven open-weight LLMs across ten contentious political topics in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, systematically manipulating contested terminology, politically valenced premises, and user information, and eliciting responses in both multiple-choice and open-text formats. Across models, we find robust evidence that prompt framing shapes the political stance of LLM outputs. Changing terminology alone reverses which side of an issue a model supports in 16.9% of matched comparisons. Stated political ideology also systematically shifts responses toward the user's position. These findings show that political stance is not a fixed property of LLMs; the views expressed are conditional on the interaction with the user. As LLMs become increasingly personalised sources of information, such interaction-dependent adaptation could contribute to political information environments that reinforce users' existing perspectives.

</details>


### [8] [ContextAdapt: Evaluating Contextual Adaptation and Value Alignment in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38260)
*Olivia Macmillan-Scott,Mirco Musolesi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ContextAdapt, a benchmark to test whether LLMs apply values like honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality in a context-sensitive but norm-consistent way across professional domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI alignment work often treats values such as honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality as abstract principles, but in real professional practice these values are applied differently depending on domain-specific norms and contextual exceptions. There is little systematic evaluation of whether LLMs can track and respect these context-dependent norms, especially across multiple professions. The authors aim to fill this gap to better understand model value alignment in realistic, high-stakes settings.

Method: The authors construct ContextAdapt, an evaluation framework that crosses three values (honesty, autonomy, confidentiality) with four professional domains (medicine, law, finance, national security). Using primary-source professional and regulatory documents, they derive domain-specific norms and recognised exceptions, then build scenarios that test both default rules and exceptions. They evaluate 12 LLMs on these scenarios, separately judging the appropriateness of the recommended actions and the correctness and domain-specificity of the justifications. They also run a factorial experiment manipulating whether the domain is explicitly named, the stated role of the model, and the level of stakes, to see how these factors affect model behavior.

Result: Across the main benchmark, models achieve high mean appropriateness (95.6%) in their recommended actions, but their use of correct domain-specific justifications is much more variable, ranging from 25.6% to 76.9% across models. In the factorial experiment, explicitly naming the professional domain and changing the role framing has only limited impact on the models’ choices. However, varying the stakes of the scenarios exposes important but narrow failures: some models change their responses when the stakes increase, even when the applicable professional obligation should remain constant. Perceived severity of the situation tends to make models more likely to disclose information, affecting both honesty and confidentiality items.

Conclusion: LLMs often select actions that align with professional norms at an abstract level, but they are less reliable at invoking the correct domain-specific reasoning and can be misled by contextual cues such as perceived stakes. This indicates that value alignment for LLMs cannot be assessed solely by checking adherence to high-level principles; it also requires testing whether models apply these principles in a contextually appropriate, norm-consistent manner across domains. Evaluations and training methods should therefore focus on contextual norm application, not just abstract value statements.

Abstract: Values such as honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality are often regarded as general principles underpinning AI alignment. However, what it means to act in accordance with these values can depend on the context in which a decision is made. In this paper, we ask whether large language models (LLMs) appropriately adapt the application of a value across professional settings, while remaining consistent when contextual changes do not alter the relevant professional norm. To study this, we introduce ContextAdapt, an evaluation framework covering honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality across medicine, law, finance, and national security. Drawing on primary-source professional and regulatory documents, we construct a value x domain framework and use this to develop scenarios testing both default professional rules and recognised exceptions. We evaluate 12 LLMs on both the actions they recommend and the justifications they provide. In our main experiment, models achieve 95.6% mean appropriateness, although the use of the correct domain-specific justification varies substantially across models, from 25.6% to 76.9%. In a separate factorial experiment, explicitly naming the professional domain and changing the role of the model have limited effect on behaviour. Varying stakes, however, reveals severe but localised failures: in some cases, models alter their responses even though the underlying professional obligation remains unchanged. In particular, perceived severity appears to act as a cue for disclosure across both honesty and confidentiality scenarios. These results show that evaluating value alignment requires us to consider not only whether models follow abstract principles, but whether they apply them appropriately across different contexts.

</details>


### [9] [NinaXander: Feasibility and Limits of Composing Frozen Language Models Across Architecture Families via a Shared Latent Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38261)
*Takanori Kotama,Shun-ichiro Hayashi,Daichi Mukunoki,Tetsuya Hoshino,Takahiro Katagiri*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces NinaXander, a way to compose two different frozen LLMs by inserting a single learned adapter between their layers, showing large KV-cache savings but only partially preserving performance and without evidence of a shared semantic space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To see whether large language models from very different architecture families (a recurrent RWKV model and a Transformer Pythia model) can be recombined after training, layer-wise, to yield useful hybrid models that save memory (KV cache) while retaining capabilities—potentially enabling modular reuse of existing LLMs.

Method: Freeze two pre-trained models (RWKV-4-Raven-7B and Tulu-Pythia-6.9B). Train a single shared-latent adapter that maps the intermediate activations from one model into the space of the other at a chosen layer. Build many composed models by running some initial layers of one model, applying the adapter once, then running remaining layers of the other model, without retraining the adapter for each configuration. Evaluate these hybrids on multiple-choice QA, language modeling on WikiText, and qualitative generation quality; analyze intermediate representation correspondence under a controlled setting with shared tokenizer, depth, and width.

Result: They successfully construct composed models that generate syntactically well-formed text. One configuration—first 5 layers of Pythia followed by 27 layers of RWKV—reduces the Transformer KV-cache size by 84.4% while achieving multiple-choice accuracy statistically comparable to RWKV alone. However, no hybrid matches the stronger parent Pythia in multiple-choice accuracy, and language modeling performance degrades sharply on WikiText. Representation analysis in a carefully matched setup finds some alignment but does not indicate that the two models inhabit a broadly shared semantic space.

Conclusion: Post hoc compositionality between heterogeneous LLM architectures via a single adapter is partially feasible: some configurations preserve RWKV-level accuracy and drastically reduce KV cache while maintaining fluent text generation. However, these hybrids fail to match the better parent model, perform poorly on out-of-domain language modeling, and representation alignment appears narrow and task-specific rather than reflecting a deep shared semantic space. Modular recombination is thus promising for certain efficiency trade-offs but is limited in recovering full capabilities of the base models.

Abstract: In this paper we propose NinaXander, a series of composed language models obtained by connecting layers of frozen language models from different architecture families with a single trained shared-latent adapter. A composed model runs the first layers of one model, converts the resulting intermediate representation once with the adapter, and then runs the remaining layers of the other model. Once the adapter is trained, several composed models that connect at different layers are obtained without retraining. Using the recurrent RWKV-4-Raven-7B and the Transformer-based Tulu-Pythia-6.9b, abbreviated as RWKV and Pythia, this study examines whether frozen models from different families can be recombined post hoc. The composed models answered multiple-choice questions, and those whose generations we examined produced syntactically well-formed text. The configuration that combines the first 5 layers of Pythia with the remaining 27 layers of RWKV reduced the Transformer key-value (KV) cache by 84.4% with accuracy not significantly different from that of RWKV alone. In multiple-choice accuracy, however, no composed model matched the parent model Pythia, and language-modeling performance decreased sharply on WikiText, a corpus of Wikipedia articles outside the training domain. The correspondence between intermediate representations was also obtained in one favorable case, with a shared tokenizer, the same depth, and the same hidden width, and does not show that the models share a general semantic space.

</details>


### [10] [Which Models Work Well Together? Measuring Heterogeneity for LLM Team Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38274)
*Liangyu Teng,Hengsong Liu,Juncen Guo,Jingyu Zhang,Yang Liu,Jing Liu,Liang Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a principled way to build high-performing teams of LLMs by jointly considering individual quality and how their errors and predictions differ, leading to consistently better multi-LLM systems than quality-only selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-LLM teams can outperform single models, but their maximum performance is limited not just by each model’s strength, but also by how their failures and prediction patterns overlap. Current practice usually picks diverse models heuristically, without clear, computable metrics of complementarity. This work is motivated by the need for an interpretable, optimizable framework to systematically select heterogeneous LLM teams that leverage complementary capabilities instead of just high average quality.

Method: The authors design an offline profiling procedure for candidate LLMs that measures: (1) individual capability/quality; (2) an error decorrelation signal that quantifies the extent to which models avoid failing on the same instances; and (3) a predictive divergence signal that captures how differently models behave even when not strictly right or wrong, reflecting diversity in solution strategies. They then define a combined objective that standardizes and balances quality with these two complementarity signals, and cast team formation as a combinatorial optimization problem. An efficient greedy search algorithm is used to pick a small team from a larger pool that maximizes this joint objective.

Result: Across several benchmarks and controlled settings (fixed candidate pool and fixed team size), teams chosen by the proposed quality–complementarity objective outperform teams selected purely by individual quality metrics or naive baselines. The gains are consistent, indicating that explicitly modeling error decorrelation and prediction divergence provides tangible benefits in multi-LLM performance.

Conclusion: The study concludes that systematically incorporating heterogeneity—through interpretable and computable metrics of error decorrelation and predictive divergence—into team selection leads to more effective multi-LLM teams than quality-only approaches. The proposed framework offers reusable, general principles for composing LLM ensembles and suggests that future multi-model systems should explicitly optimize for complementarity rather than relying on heuristic diversity or top-performing models alone.

Abstract: The performance ceiling of an LLM team is constrained not only by individual model capabilities, but also by inter-member error resonance and predictive differences. Although heterogeneous teaming is often observed to be effective in practice, existing approaches lack complementarity metrics that are computable, interpretable, and optimizable, leaving team composition to rely on heuristics. We propose a heterogeneity-driven team selection framework that performs offline profiling to characterize individual capability along with two complementary signals: one captures decorrelation in error patterns to reduce co-failures, while the other measures divergence in predictive behavior to capture strategy diversity. We formulate team selection as a standardized quality--complementarity combinatorial objective and apply an efficient greedy search to select a small team from a candidate pool. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms quality-only baselines under controlled candidate pools and team sizes, establishing reusable selection principles for multi-LLM systems.

</details>


### [11] [EVOKE: Eliciting World Knowledge in Agents for Transferable Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38334)
*Yuhan Guo,Jinming Liu,Liang Xu,Ziqiang Li,Jianguo Huang,Zhicheng Wang,Hu Zhu,Qiuyu Chen,Yuntao Wei,Xin Jin,Wenjun Zeng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes EVOKE, a post-training method that elicits latent world knowledge in LLM agents by training them to act under diverse goals at fixed states, improving generalization and data efficiency for decision-making tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs used as agents in multi-step decision-making often fail to generalize to unseen environments. Existing world-model approaches try to fix this by explicitly learning to predict future observations, but this needs extra training and suffers from compounding prediction errors when used for planning. Since LLMs operating in digital environments already encode much world knowledge from pretraining, the key challenge is not learning this knowledge but eliciting and using it for decisions. Standard post-training, which supervises policies under a single goal per state, tends to promote superficial context-based habits instead of deep world-model-based reasoning, limiting transfer.

Method: The authors introduce EVOKE, a post-training framework that induces pressure to use world knowledge by diversifying goals at fixed states. For a given environment state and interaction history, EVOKE constructs multiple alternative goals and evaluates the same set of candidate actions under each goal. It then trains the agent to rank or prefer actions differently under different goals, such that a policy that only relies on single-goal associations or shallow contextual habits cannot satisfy the supervision. The theoretical motivation is that an agent that behaves competently across diverse goals must implicitly encode a world model that is recoverable from its action preferences. Thus, EVOKE encourages the policy to tap into its pretrained internal world model without explicit next-state prediction. The method is implemented as a post-training procedure on top of existing LLM agent backbones, modifying the supervision signal at identical states with varied goals.

Result: Across several benchmark tasks and three different LLM backbones, EVOKE-trained agents achieve higher task performance compared to baselines, better generalization to unseen environments, and improved data efficiency (i.e., requiring fewer training interactions to reach a given performance). The authors also run controlled ablations and analyses to dissect what aspects of EVOKE—such as goal diversity and the fixed-state ranking protocol—are responsible for the observed improvements, finding that the induced goal variance at fixed states is key to eliciting useful world knowledge in the policy.

Conclusion: EVOKE demonstrates that one can improve LLM agents’ transfer and decision-making not by explicitly learning external world models, but by reshaping post-training so that policies must express and exploit the world knowledge already encoded during pretraining. By holding states fixed and varying goals while supervising action rankings, EVOKE discourages superficial habits and implicitly elicits internal world models for action selection. This offers a new, decision-centric perspective on how to harness latent world knowledge in large pretrained models for robust, transferable control in digital environments.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents for multi-step decision-making, yet transfer poorly to unseen environments. World-model methods address this by training agents to predict future observations, at the cost of additional training and errors that compound when predictions are used for planning. However, for LLM agents operating in digital environments, much of this world knowledge is already internalized during pretraining, which shifts the problem from acquiring it to eliciting it. We argue that typical post-training provides little pressure for such elicitation, since supervision under a single goal at each visited state inadvertently drives policies to rely on superficial contextual habits. We introduce EVOKE, a post-training method that supplies this pressure through goal diversity at fixed states. Motivated by theory showing that an agent competent across diverse goals must encode a world model recoverable from its action preferences, EVOKE holds the environment state and interaction history fixed and ranks the same candidate actions under alternative goals, forcing action preferences to change, so that a policy relying on contextual habits or single-goal correlations cannot order them correctly. This implicitly elicits the policy's pretrained world knowledge to inform decisions. We evaluate EVOKE across diverse tasks in three backbones, demonstrating improved task performance, unseen environment generalization, and data efficiency. We further conduct controlled analyses to better understand what drives these gains. These findings offer a new perspective on eliciting internalized world knowledge for transferable action through direct decision supervision.

</details>


### [12] [Halluscoring 2026: The first shared task on llms hallucination detection and answer verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38355)
*Aisha Alansari,Abdessalam Bouchekif,Ahmed Hasanaath,Salah Eddine Bekhouche,Malak Alkhorasani,Mohammed-En-Nadhir Zighem,Saad Ezzini,Hichem Telli,Hend Al-Khalifa,Muhammad Abdul-Mageed,Hadid Abdenour,Hamzah Luqman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HalluScoring 2026 is a shared task to evaluate how well systems detect hallucinations and verify facts in Arabic QA, including generalization to new questions, unseen LLMs, and multiple-choice factual correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs hallucinate, and detecting these hallucinations—especially in low-resource languages like Arabic and in out-of-distribution conditions—is still hard. There is a lack of standardized benchmarks covering both hallucination detection and factual correction in Arabic, and existing work focuses mainly on English or on in-distribution settings. The authors aim to create a rigorous shared task and datasets to benchmark and drive progress on hallucination detection and factual verification in Arabic QA, including specialized domains (Islamic knowledge) and open-domain knowledge, and including robustness to distribution shift and to responses from different LLMs.

Method: The authors design a shared task (HalluScoring 2026) with two main tasks, each split into two subtasks. Task 1 focuses on binary hallucination detection in Arabic QA answers, with Subtask 1.1 testing generalization to unseen questions and Subtask 1.2 testing generalization to answers generated by unseen LLMs. Task 2 extends this setup to factual verification with correction: given a possibly hallucinated answer, systems must choose the correct factual answer from six candidates; Subtask 2.1 uses Islamic-knowledge questions and Subtask 2.2 uses general-knowledge questions. They build this on two Arabic datasets, HalluScore and HalluTruthQA, release task definitions and evaluation protocols, and collect and score submissions from 13 participating teams, analyzing performance via metrics like AUC-ROC for Task 1 and accuracy-style scores under assisted evaluation for Task 2.

Result: Thirteen teams participated and ten submitted system-description papers. For Task 1 (hallucination detection), the best systems achieved AUC-ROC scores of 0.772 (Subtask 1.1: unseen questions) and 0.767 (Subtask 1.2: unseen LLMs), indicating that hallucination detection under distribution shift remains difficult. For Task 2 (factual verification with answer selection), the winning team obtained scores of 0.882 on the Islamic-knowledge subtask (2.1) and 0.857 on the general-knowledge subtask (2.2) under assisted evaluation, showing higher performance when the task includes structured multiple-choice correction in domain-specific and general domains.

Conclusion: HalluScoring 2026 establishes a new benchmark and shared task for hallucination detection and factual verification in Arabic QA, highlighting that robust hallucination detection under distribution shift is still a challenging problem, as reflected by moderate AUC-ROC scores. At the same time, systems can perform relatively well on multiple-choice factual verification in both Islamic and general domains when provided with candidate answers. The shared task, datasets (HalluScore and HalluTruthQA), and participating systems provide a foundation for future research on more reliable and generalizable hallucination detection and factual verification methods in Arabic and potentially other languages.

Abstract: We present HalluScoring 2026, a shared task for evaluating hallucination detection and factual verification in Arabic question answering under challenging generalization settings. The shared task is organized into two main tasks, each comprising two subtasks, for a total of four subtasks. Task 1 evaluates binary hallucination detection, considering generalization to unseen questions (Subtask 1.1) and responses generated by unseen LLMs (Subtask 1.2). Task 2 extends the evaluation beyond detection by requiring the systems to additionally identify the correct factual answer from six related candidates, covering Islamic knowledge (Subtask 2.1) and general knowledge (Subtask 2.2). The shared task is based on two Arabic datasets: HalluScore and HalluTruthQA. A total of 13 teams participated in the shared task, 10 of which submitted system description papers. The results of Task 1 demonstrate that hallucination detection remains challenging under distribution shift, with the winning team achieving AUC-ROC test scores of 0.772 and 0.767 for Subtasks 1.1 and 1.2, respectively. For Task 2, the winning team achieved scores of 0.882 and 0.857 in the Islamic and general-knowledge subtasks, respectively, under assisted evaluation.

</details>


### [13] [Evaluating Language Model Safety Across Long Adversarial Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38357)
*Parisa Salmani,Peter R. Lewis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that language models that seem safe on single-turn tests can become unsafe over long adversarial conversations, so safety must be evaluated and enforced over many turns, not just one.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most safety benchmarks test language models with one-shot harmful prompts, but real-world users have extended conversations and may persist in trying to elicit unsafe content. The authors want to understand whether safety holds up in long, adversarial, multi-turn interactions, and to question the assumption that good first-turn safety implies robust overall safety.

Method: The authors take three open-weight, instruction-tuned language models and probe them with two types of harmful prompts. For each model–prompt pair, they simulate long conversations of varying lengths and random seeds. A separate language model plays the role of a persistent adversarial user, continuing to push for harmful responses across many turns, while an automated safety classifier labels each model response as safe or unsafe. They then measure how the rate of safe responses changes as conversation depth increases, from the first turn out to 100+ turns.

Result: All models start with high safety on the first turn, with 85–100% of responses labeled safe. However, safety erodes as the conversation continues: by turn 11, safe-response rates fall to 38–61%, and by turn 101, to just 15–44%, depending on the model and prompt. This pattern of degradation appears consistently across different models and settings, showing that adversarial persistence increasingly succeeds over time.

Conclusion: The study concludes that strong single-turn safety does not guarantee sustained safety in realistic, extended adversarial conversations. Safety performance can degrade substantially as the number of turns increases, indicating that current evaluation practices are insufficient. The authors argue for long-horizon safety evaluations and for designing conversation-level safeguards that explicitly consider cumulative risk over many turns, rather than only per-turn defenses.

Abstract: Conversational safety evaluations often test language models with a single harmful prompt, even though real-world systems interact with users through long, adaptive conversations. This study examines whether models continue to respond safely when an adversarial user persists across multiple turns. We evaluate three open-weight, instruction-tuned models on two harmful prompts across different conversation lengths and random seeds. In each setting, a second language model acts as a persistent adversarial user, while a safety classifier labels every response as safe or unsafe. Across all model-prompt combinations, first-turn safe-response rates ranged from 85% to 100%. By depth 11, they dropped to 38-61%, and by depth 101, to 15-44%. This decline appeared across models and continued well beyond the short interactions typically used in multi-turn safety evaluations. These results provide proof-of-concept evidence that strong single-turn safety does not necessarily persist during sustained adversarial interaction. They highlight the need for long-horizon evaluations and conversation-level safeguards that account for risk accumulating across turns.

</details>


### [14] [Doc2LoRA Provides Decodable Representations of Scientific Ideas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38374)
*Chand Sahil Mansuri,Joel Zachariah,Sadamori Kojaku*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They turn each paper into a small, paper-specific adapter for an LLM so that every point (and mixture of points) in a paper-embedding space corresponds to a queryable LLM, supporting both semantic search and interactive generation of new, in-between ideas.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vector embeddings of papers support similarity search and analysis of scientific fields, but they do not provide a natural-language interface for exploring the “in-between” points that represent novel combinations of ideas; mixed vectors often do not correspond to any existing paper, so there’s no direct way to inspect or label them.

Method: Train a Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork that maps each paper’s text to a LoRA adapter for a base LLM, so each paper is represented by LoRA weights instead of a static embedding; represent any point, including linear mixtures of papers, as the corresponding mixed LoRA adapter attached to the LLM. Evaluate: (1) field labeling by averaging adapters over APS subfields and prompting the resulting LLM to name the field, comparing to baselines via word overlap and LLM-judge panels; (2) interpolation by placing points between two APS papers and prompting for abstracts, checking whether content smoothly shifts between source papers; (3) retrieval by applying a small, invertible transform to the LoRA-based representations and comparing search performance to SPECTER2, EmbeddingGemma, and SBERT.

Result: (1) Subfield-average LLMs generate field names closer to the official APS field names than five embedding-based baselines, as measured by lexical overlap and judged quality by five LLM evaluators; (2) LLMs at interpolated points produce abstracts that continuously morph from one paper’s topic to the other in line with the mixing coefficient; (3) After an invertible transformation, their embeddings achieve retrieval performance competitive with SPECTER2 and EmbeddingGemma, and close to SBERT, while retaining a mapping from every point back to an LLM adapter.

Conclusion: Representing papers as LoRA adapters produced by a Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork creates a unified space that supports both high-quality semantic search and generative exploration: every point corresponds to a specialized LLM that can be queried in natural language, including novel mixtures that have no existing paper, enabling interactive interrogation and generation of new scientific ideas throughout the embedding space.

Abstract: Representing scientific papers as points in a space lets us search for similar papers and inquire about how fields relate to one another and drive innovation. Beyond search, the vector space of papers invites generation: mixing papers through simple vector operations creates new points, mirroring combinatorial novelty, the recombination of existing ideas into new ones. However, a mixed point often represents an idea no paper has yet realized, with no papers nearby to identify the idea. We propose representing each paper by a LoRA adapter generated by the Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork. Every point in the space, including mixtures, thus represents a large language model (LLM) open to questions and instructions in natural language. On papers from the American Physical Society (APS), we instruct the LLM at the average of each subfield to name the field in a few words and obtain labels closer to the official names than the labels of five baselines, as judged by word overlap and a panel of five LLM judges. We also ask the LLMs at points between two APS papers to write an abstract and obtain descriptions shifting from one paper to the other in step with the mixing weight. While Doc-to-LoRA is trained for generation, a small invertible transform makes the embeddings competitive for search, on par with SPECTER2 and EmbeddingGemma and close to SBERT. Because the transform is invertible, every point in the transformed space still maps back to an LLM. The embeddings thus serve both search and generation, enabling researchers to question the idea at any point in the space as a starting point for generating new ideas.

</details>


### [15] [Evaluating Whether LLMs Can Reliably Connect the DOTs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38406)
*Eftekhar Hossain,John Salvador,Santu Karmaker*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds a benchmark to test how well instruction-tuned LLMs can fill in missing parts of real-world narratives and finds that bigger models and chain-of-thought reasoning do not necessarily yield better infilling quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although text infilling is widely used as a pre-training objective for LLMs, their real-world narrative infilling ability is not well understood, especially across diverse narrative domains. There is no standardized, multi-domain benchmark focused specifically on sentence-level narrative infilling quality, nor a systematic evaluation of how scale, instruction style, and reasoning guidance affect performance. The paper aims to fill this evaluation gap.

Method: The authors construct a ~9.2K-instance benchmark by masking 1–3 sentences in texts from four narrative domains: encyclopedic entries, commonsense stories, news articles, and visual narratives. They then evaluate 20 instruction-tuned open-source LLMs from 1.5B to 70B parameters. Models are tested under different prompting conditions (varying instruction specificity and explicit reasoning such as chain-of-thought). Outputs are measured using automatic metrics and a qualitative evaluation framework along five narrative dimensions (e.g., coherence, consistency).

Result: Model size does not correlate strongly with narrative infilling quality. A relatively small model, Gemma-2-2B, achieves the best qualitative score (4.02/5), outperforming substantially larger models like DeepSeek-Qwen-32B (3.77/5) and LLaMA-3.3-70B (3.71/5). Providing explicit reasoning via chain-of-thought only slightly improves results (+0.6%). The study also finds that factors like narrative length and domain characteristics are more predictive of difficulty than the masked span’s position in the text.

Conclusion: Narrative infilling is not reliably improved by scaling model size or naively adding chain-of-thought reasoning. Instead, performance depends strongly on narrative domain and length. The proposed benchmark exposes these nuances and suggests that future work should target domain-aware modeling and better strategies for handling short, information-dense narratives, rather than relying solely on larger models or generic reasoning prompts.

Abstract: Access to real-world information is often noisy and fragmented. Constructing a coherent narrative from such fragments requires models to reconstruct missing spans within a broader storyline, commonly referred to as text infilling, while preserving consistency with both the local context and the global storyline. Despite using text infilling as a pre-training objective in many Large Language Models (LLMs), their actual performance on real-world narrative infilling remains underexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a multi-domain benchmark of ~9.2K instances for narrative infilling, constructed by masking one to three sentences across four narrative types: encyclopedic text, commonsense stories, news articles, and visual narratives. Using this benchmark, we evaluate 20 instruction-tuned open-source LLMs ranging from 1.5B to 70B parameters across varying levels of instruction specificity and reasoning guidance. Outputs are assessed using standard automatic metrics and a qualitative framework covering five narrative dimensions. Results show that model scale does not reliably predict infilling quality: Gemma-2-2B achieves the highest qualitative score (4.02/5), outperforming models over ten times larger, including DeepSeek-Qwen-32B (3.77/5, 6.6%) and LLaMA-3.3-70B (3.71/5, 8.3%). We further find that explicit reasoning offers limited benefits as chain-of-thought reasoning yields only a marginal improvement (+0.6%). Additionally, short narratives and domain characteristics emerge as stronger predictors of task difficulty than infill position alone for narrative infilling in current LLMs.

</details>


### [16] [Policy-Conditioned AI-Use Detection: An Evidentiary Framework for Academic Publishing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38427)
*Jairo Diaz-Rodriguez,Mumin Jia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that current AI text detection targets the wrong problem for enforcing conference and journal AI-use policies and proposes a new, policy-aware detection framework that treats detection as auditable evidence with explicit error rates instead of binary authorship classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-use rules in scholarly publishing are complex, role-specific, and disclosure-dependent, but common enforcement mechanisms—AI authorship detectors—only try to decide whether text was written by AI, which is misaligned with the actual policy questions (e.g., Was the workflow compliant with the venue's rules?). This mismatch risks unfair or unreliable enforcement and calls for a framework that is grounded in the policies themselves.

Method: The authors conceptualize and define "policy-conditioned AI-use detection", where the policy is an explicit input to the detection task. They outline an evidentiary approach: detectors output hypotheses, evidence, calibration regimens, and quantified uncertainty instead of yes/no labels. For evaluation, they propose benchmarks created from reproducible pipelines that simulate both compliant and non-compliant human–AI workflows, and they analyze detector behavior at fixed false positive rates chosen by venues.

Result: Applying the framework to peer review scenarios, they show that even a strong detector, when tuned to a plausible operating point, will end up flagging more compliant authors than violators if violation rates are low. They also identify the practical instrumentation requirements the framework implies, including structured disclosure, routing through approved tools that preserve reviewer anonymity, and procedural channels for contesting findings.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that AI detectors in scholarly publishing should not be conceived or deployed as simple AI authorship classifiers. Instead, they should be treated as auditable procedures embedded in a broader policy-aware system, with explicitly chosen and defensible error rates, appropriate supporting infrastructure, and clear processes for evidence and contestation.

Abstract: Major venues now publish detailed rules about how authors, reviewers, and area chairs may use AI, and those rules differ by role, by task, and by what must be disclosed. AI detection, the instrument usually proposed to enforce them, estimates something else: whether an AI model wrote the text. We argue that this target is misaligned with the decisions conferences and journals face, and propose policy-conditioned AI-use detection, an evidentiary framework for assessing whether a human--AI workflow complied with a stated rule. Policy makes the governing rule an explicit input. Inference reports hypotheses, evidence, calibration regime, and uncertainty in place of verdicts such as "AI detected". Evaluation builds benchmarks from reproducible pipelines that generate compliant and non-compliant workflows, and reports true positive rate at a false positive rate the venue fixes in advance. We work the framework through peer review, where at plausible violation rates a detector at a strong operating point still flags more compliant authors than violating ones. The framework therefore also names what a venue must instrument: structured disclosure, approved-tool routing that respects reviewer confidentiality, and a path by which a finding can be contested. Under this framing a detector is not an authorship classifier but an auditable procedure with an error rate the venue fixes in advance and can defend.

</details>


### [17] [The Backdrop Exposes What the World Around an Agent Costs It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38469)
*Nusrat Jahan Lia,Shubhashis Roy Dipta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces BACKDROP, a benchmark framework to test how robust AI agents remain when their environment includes realistic, interfering changes made by other people, not just static tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks evaluate performance in stable, clean environments, but deployed agents operate in dynamic, multi-user worlds where messages, records, and systems can change unexpectedly. The authors want to understand how much of an agent’s apparent capability in these idealized benchmarks actually transfers to real-world conditions with common hazards like conflicting instructions, prompt injections, and unreliable tooling.

Method: The authors design BACKDROP, which augments ordinary agent tasks by embedding four types of hazards into the execution environment: (1) Authority – messages from another person that conflict with the original user’s instructions; (2) Injection – adversarial or misleading text injected into existing records; (3) Boundary – requests that try to lure the agent into using apps or resources it wasn’t granted; (4) Fault – write operations that may or may not have succeeded without clear feedback, forcing the agent to check before retrying. They systematically generate 3,678 task variants across these hazard types and evaluate 16 different models/agents by measuring pass rates first in the clean environment and then with hazards injected individually and jointly.

Result: When no hazards are present, agents achieve an average pass rate of 69.5%. When all four hazards are added simultaneously, the average pass rate drops sharply to 31.3%; stronger models exhibit larger absolute drops (e.g., Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). Models generally show some resistance to direct text injection, but they are much more likely to follow instructions appearing to come from other people: in runs where the agent actually receives the planted text, agents follow another person’s message in 46.4% of such runs, versus 20.3% for injected text. This pattern is consistent across all 16 models tested.

Conclusion: BACKDROP demonstrates that benchmark scores in clean, static environments significantly overestimate how well agents will perform in realistic, dynamic settings. The framework formalizes four everyday hazards and shows that even strong models are highly vulnerable, particularly to seemingly authoritative third-party instructions. The authors argue that an agent’s performance in a task’s idealized world should be treated as an upper bound on its real-world reliability and that robust agent evaluation must explicitly include such environmental hazards.

Abstract: Agent benchmarks test agents in worlds that stay still. Deployed agents work in worlds that other people also change. Someone texts the agent to send the money elsewhere or an order confirmation asks it to reply with a door code. We present BACKDROP, which asks how much of an agent's capability in a clean world survives in such a world. BACKDROP takes a task along with the agents execution environment, and plants four everyday hazards in its world, one at a time and all together. The instruction and the correct end state stay the same. Each hazard asks one question. Authority: does a message from another person override the user? Injection: does text planted in a record redirect the agent? Boundary: does a request pull it into an app it was not given? Fault: after a write fails without saying whether it landed, does the agent check before it retries? Across 3,678 variants and 16 models, , the average pass rate falls from 69.5% to 31.3% once all four hazards are present; the strongest models fall furthest (Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). Agents have learned to resist injected text but often follow other unauthorized requests of other people. With all four hazards present, and counting only runs where the planted text reached the agent, agents followed another person's message in 46.4% of runs and injected text in 20.3%. The gap is consistent throughout all 16 models. BACKDROP formalizes these gaps and shows how an agent's score in a task's world is a ceiling on real-world performance.

</details>


### [18] [KlinikeBench: Evaluating Language Models Beyond Diagnostic Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38480)
*Xueting Fang,Zehui Li,Yang Yang,Camilla Giovino,Shubh K. Patel,Shailly Prajapati,Vallijah Subasri,Caihua Shan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: KlinikeBench is a clinician-built benchmark that evaluates language models on full, interactive clinical encounters rather than just final diagnosis from complete case descriptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing clinical benchmarks mainly test diagnostic accuracy from fully specified cases, which does not reflect real practice where clinicians must elicit history, choose exams, and follow constraints. These benchmarks also often lack rigorous verification by practicing clinicians. The authors aim to create a benchmark that captures the whole clinical interaction and is grounded in expert-authored and -validated scenarios, to better assess whether LMs can perform realistic clinical assessments rather than just label well-described cases.

Method: They design KlinikeBench, a collection of 333 tasks, each being a sandboxed clinical scenario with a virtual patient, available clinical tools, and explicit success criteria. Over 35 clinicians author and review cases and evaluations. In each task, an LM interacts with the virtual patient under a fixed turn budget: it must gather history, order appropriate exams, respect action constraints, and ultimately record a diagnosis. The benchmark scores intermediate behaviors (information gathering, exam ordering, constraint compliance) and overall task success. They evaluate 31 language models across seven model families, comparing performance in conversational settings versus using a complete chart, and collect clinician ratings of dialogue quality compared with adapted real reference conversations.

Result: Clinicians judge the simulated LM–patient dialogues as higher quality on average than the adapted real reference conversations. Top-performing models such as GPT-6-astra and Claude Opus 5 still succeed on fewer than 30% of full tasks, despite reaching 90.7% diagnostic accuracy when given complete information. Some models gain from interactive patient communication, whereas others excel when given full charts but degrade substantially in conversational scenarios. The benchmark thus exposes significant variability in how models handle the interactive aspects of clinical work.

Conclusion: KlinikeBench offers a more realistic and granular evaluation framework for clinical LMs by encompassing the whole clinical encounter, not just diagnosis from prepackaged data. Results show a major gap between high diagnostic accuracy and the ability to perform effective interactive clinical assessment, highlighting that current models are far from reliably functioning as end-to-end clinical agents. The benchmark can therefore guide future model development and evaluation toward more clinically meaningful capabilities.

Abstract: Most clinical benchmarks evaluate language models (LMs) on diagnosis using complete case descriptions. In clinical practice, however, patients present information in different ways, and clinicians must obtain relevant history and determine which examinations are needed before reaching a diagnosis. Diagnostic accuracy alone therefore cannot establish whether an agent gathered essential information or conducted an appropriate clinical assessment. Furthermore, existing benchmarks lack professional clinicians' verification. To address this gap, we introduce KlinikeBench, a benchmark of 333 clinician-authored tasks, each providing an isolated sandbox environment with a virtual patient, clinical tools, and task-specific success criteria. More than 35 clinicians contributed to case authoring and benchmark evaluation. In an empirical study, clinicians gave simulated dialogues higher mean quality ratings than reference conversations, which is adapted from real conversation. In each task, an LM has a fixed budget of turns to communicate with the patient, ask about relevant history, request examinations, follow action constraints, and record a final diagnosis. We score these steps separately as well as together. Across 31 models and seven model families, the best-performing models (e.g., GPT-6-astra and Claude Opus 5) succeed on less than 30% of tasks, even though their diagnosis accuracy reaches 90.7%. Some models benefit from talking with the patient; others diagnose well from a complete chart but perform much worse in conversation. Overall, KlinikeBench provides a testbed for evaluating the full clinical encounter and reveals a substantial gap between diagnostic accuracy and performance in interactive clinical assessment.

</details>


### [19] [Personalized State-Transition-Aware Memory for Clinical Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38490)
*Maryam Haghifam,Zahra Rajabi,Yizhou Sun,Carlos Morato*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: STAM is a memory framework for LLM clinical agents that tracks patient state transitions without losing history, improving QA and state maintenance over longitudinal records.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents for clinical records either keep all past information, making it hard to know what is still current, or overwrite old information, losing important historical context. There is a need for a structured memory system that can both track the current patient state and preserve the history of changes for longitudinal reasoning and clinical tasks.

Method: The paper proposes STAM, a state-transition-aware memory framework. As new clinical entries arrive, STAM detects which existing memories are affected by these updates using semantic retrieval plus typed clinical relations. It then separates memory into Active (current state) and History (superseded or resolved information). At query time, a query-dependent gating mechanism decides how much of the historical memory to expose to the LLM. The authors evaluate STAM on four longitudinal clinical benchmarks with multiple task types.

Result: STAM is tested on four longitudinal clinical benchmarks using downstream question answering tasks, direct tests of state maintenance, and comparisons with other methods under similar context length constraints. The results show that STAM more accurately maintains up-to-date patient state while still enabling access to relevant history, improving performance over baselines.

Conclusion: A state-transition-aware memory architecture like STAM enables LLM agents to reason more effectively over evolving clinical records by explicitly modeling updates, separating current from historical information, and selectively surfacing past data at query time. This approach outperforms naive accumulation or overwriting strategies across multiple longitudinal clinical tasks.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that reason over clinical records must track changes in a patient's state while preserving the history needed to understand them. Simply accumulating memories leaves it unclear which information still applies, whereas overwriting earlier memories can erase evidence needed to reconstruct treatment history and clinical trajectories. We introduce STAM, a state-transition-aware memory framework that records state changes as new clinical entries arrive. STAM combines semantic retrieval with typed clinical relations to identify affected memories, maintaining current information in Active and superseded or resolved information in History. At read time, a query-dependent gate selectively serves historical memory. Across four longitudinal clinical benchmarks, we evaluate STAM with downstream question answering, direct state-maintenance diagnostics, and comparisons at approximately matched context lengths.

</details>


### [20] [DEdit: Iterative Draft Editing for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38510)
*Longxuan Yu,Bingsen Chen,Peng Shi,Dongkyu Lee,Yi Xiang,Hideo Kobayashi,Sheng Zhang,Shuaichen Chang,Xing Niu,Zhuoyan Xu,Greg Ver Steeg,Jiarong Jiang*

Main category: cs.CL
