TL;DR: DEdit is a diffusion-based speculative decoding drafter that can iteratively edit its own multi-token draft, substantially increasing token acceptance rate and generation speed versus standard autoregressive decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding speeds up LLMs by drafting tokens with a smaller model, but diffusion-based drafters that propose many tokens in parallel suffer from a major inefficiency: their independently predicted tokens are all discarded once an early token is wrong, even if later tokens are correct. This limits effective speedup and wastes useful predictions. The paper aims to design a drafter that can recover from early errors and better exploit the information in later draft tokens to maximize prefix acceptance and speedup.

Method: The authors propose DEdit, a diffusion-based drafter that performs both parallel unmasking and iterative editing of its draft using token-to-token predictions. After an initial parallel draft, DEdit runs editing passes where tokens can be changed based on bidirectional (non-causal) context so that later tokens can help correct earlier ones and extend the verifiable prefix. To train the model to fix errors while keeping correct tokens, they introduce ProposalMix: during training, they mix draft predictions with ground-truth tokens according to first-pass confidence, exposing the model to realistic imperfect drafts and teaching it to selectively repair them. They evaluate DEdit on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks and probe design choices such as number of editing passes, draft window size, and attention pattern (bidirectional vs causal).

Result: On both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks, DEdit yields the highest macro-average token acceptance and speedup among considered drafters. It reaches about 5.72× and 5.97× macro-average speedups over standard autoregressive greedy decoding. Ablations show that more editing passes and wider drafting windows further improve token acceptance. ProposalMix training significantly reduces harmful edits that shorten the accepted prefix, roughly halving them. When the editor is restricted to causal attention (removing access to future tokens), token acceptance degrades, especially on highly predictable outputs.

Conclusion: Allowing a diffusion-based drafter to iteratively edit its own multi-token predictions, rather than only draft them in a single parallel step, substantially improves the efficiency of speculative decoding. Bidirectional editing enables later tokens to correct earlier errors, leading to longer accepted prefixes and higher speedups. The ProposalMix training strategy is key for teaching the editor to repair only erroneous tokens while preserving correct ones. The importance of bidirectional (non-causal) attention suggests that leveraging future context is crucial for maximizing the benefits of diffusion-style speculative drafters.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive LLMs by having a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Diffusion-based drafters further reduce drafting latency by proposing multiple tokens at once. However, these tokens are predicted independently, so a single early error causes prefix verification to discard the rest of the draft, even when it contains useful downstream predictions. We introduce DEdit, a diffusion-based drafter that can not only draft by conventional parallel unmasking but also iteratively edit its draft through token-to-token predictions. Through editing, later predictions can serve as bidirectional context for repairing earlier errors and extending the accepted prefix. To teach the model to repair errors while preserving correct predictions, we propose ProposalMix, a training scheme that mixes draft predictions with ground-truth tokens based on first-pass confidence during training. Across seven benchmarks on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, DEdit achieves the highest macro-average token acceptance and speedup among the evaluated drafters, reaching macro-average speedups of $5.72\times$ and $5.97\times$ over autoregressive generation under greedy decoding, respectively. Further analysis shows that acceptance improves with more editing passes and wider drafting windows, and that ProposalMix halves harmful edits that shorten the accepted prefix. Moreover, restricting the editor to causal attention lowers acceptance, especially on highly predictable outputs, indicating that future context is a key source of these gains.

</details>


### [21] [Shifting Mechanisms: How Positional Encoding Choice Shapes In-Context Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38530)
*Eric Enouen,Sainyam Galhotra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how different positional encoding and attention-span architectures in language models affect their internal mechanisms and behavior for in-context retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern language models increasingly mix different positional encodings (e.g., RoPE and NoPE) and attention patterns (sliding-window vs. global), but it is unclear how these design choices change the way models retrieve information from context. Existing evaluations often only report aggregate long-context scores, potentially hiding important trade-offs in how models retrieve information.

Method: The authors take a mechanistic interpretability approach, analyzing internal retrieval mechanisms across 22 open-weight models from eight model families. They compare models using standard RoPE to hybrids using RoPE with sliding-window attention and NoPE with global attention (SWA NoPE). They also run controlled pre-training ablations where positional encodings are confined to local layers, and then study how this affects representations of positional vs. semantic information and retrieval behaviors in synthetic and question-answering tasks.

Result: They find that standard RoPE models primarily use positional retrieval mechanisms, whereas hybrid positional-encoding architectures shift toward semantic retrieval. When positional encoding is confined to local layers during pre-training, models increasingly rely on semantic retrieval and show degraded encoding of positional information. Behaviorally, PE hybrids (SWA NoPE) outperform RoPE models on multiple-target retrieval and QA tasks but underperform when the task requires distinguishing between competing keys, revealing a trade-off instead of a uniform improvement in long-context capability.

Conclusion: Hybrid positional-encoding and attention-span architectures change not just how far models can attend, but the underlying mechanisms they use for in-context retrieval, shifting from positional to semantic retrieval. The apparent long-context gains of SWA NoPE architectures hide a retrieval trade-off: improved performance on tasks requiring semantic aggregation over multiple targets but worse performance when fine-grained positional discrimination between similar items is needed. Mechanistic analysis better explains these differences than assuming a simple, uniform improvement in long-context retrieval ability.

Abstract: Language models increasingly use architectures that vary attention span and positional encoding across layers, such as applying RoPE with sliding-window attention and NoPE with global attention (SWA NoPE). However, how these choices shape in-context retrieval remains unclear. To study this question, we take a mechanistic view, tracing how positional encoding (PE) choice shapes the internal mechanisms models use for in-context retrieval. Across 22 open-weight models spanning eight families, we find that standard RoPE models rely primarily on positional retrieval, while PE hybrids shift toward semantic retrieval. We further show on a controlled pre-training ablation that confining positional encoding to local layers produces this semantic shift, degrading representations of positional information. Finally, we show that the reported long-context gains of PE hybrids mask a retrieval trade-off: SWA NoPE improves over RoPE on multiple-target retrieval and QA, but degrades when distinguishing competing keys. We show that these behavioral differences better track the mechanism shift from positional toward semantic mechanisms than a uniform improvement in long-context retrieval.

</details>


### [22] [MedKIT: Evaluating Knowledge Integration and Generalization in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38543)
*Lukas Thede,Yash Kumar Atri,David Chen,Danielle Bitterman,Matthias Bethge,Tom Hartvigsen,Zeynep Akata*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MedKIT is a benchmark to test whether LLMs not only recall but actually use newly integrated medical knowledge across realistic update scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical knowledge changes rapidly, and outdated information in models can be unsafe. Current evaluations mainly test factual recall after knowledge updating, which doesn’t show whether the new knowledge transfers to varied, realistic clinical uses. The authors want a way to measure how well integrated knowledge is applied and generalized, not just memorized.

Method: They build MedKIT, a benchmark where each example is a concrete medical factual update derived from clinical evidence (e.g., guidelines, studies). For each update, they design multiple targeted probes: (1) lexical variation probes to see if the model handles rewordings; (2) relational transformation probes to test generalization across related entities/relations; (3) compositional reasoning probes to check combining the updated fact with other knowledge; (4) open-ended operationalization probes that mimic realistic clinical decision-making; and (5) locality tests to see whether new updates preserve unrelated existing knowledge. They then evaluate 12 different knowledge integration strategies—covering diverse approaches like fine-tuning, in-context learning, retrieval, editing methods—on 5 different LLMs, both general-purpose and medical-specialized.

Result: Across models and methods, most strategies substantially improve performance on the direct update queries and on queries with simple lexical rephrasings. However, they show weak performance on relational generalization and almost no improvement on more complex compositional or operational tasks. This exposes a robust gap between being able to recall an updated fact and being able to use that fact flexibly in realistic clinical reasoning scenarios.

Conclusion: Knowledge integration methods that look strong on standard factual recall benchmarks often fail to make the new knowledge broadly usable across tasks. MedKIT surfaces this limitation and serves as a targeted benchmark for developing and stress-testing new methods that aim for deeper, more generalizable integration of updated medical knowledge while preserving existing information.

Abstract: Constantly evolving real-world knowledge necessitates models to be updated continuously. Especially in medicine, as clinical evidence changes over time, outdated knowledge can pose safety risks. Existing evaluations of knowledge integration focus on factual recall, offering limited insight into whether newly integrated knowledge is actually usable. Our benchmark MedKIT (Medical Knowledge Integration and Transfer) provides a granular evaluation of how models integrate and apply knowledge under realistic sequences of clinical updates. Each instance corresponds to a factual update derived from clinical evidence, paired with targeted probes that assess transfer across lexical variation, relational transformations, compositional reasoning, and open-ended operationalization, as well as locality tests for knowledge preservation. Using MedKIT, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 knowledge integration strategies across 5 diverse models, including both general-purpose and medical LLMs. Our results reveal a consistent gap between recall and usable knowledge: while most methods achieve strong gains on the original update task and under lexical variation, relational generalization is limited, and no method yields meaningful improvements on compositional or operational tasks. These findings highlight a fundamental challenge in knowledge integration and position MedKIT as a testbed for developing methods that make newly integrated knowledge more consistently usable across tasks and contexts.

</details>


### [23] [Prompt2Skill: Unsupervised Skill Optimization From Natural Language Instructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38593)
*Bo Ni,Li Li,Ryan A. Rossi,Franck Dernoncourt,Tyler Derr*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Prompt2Skill automatically builds and optimizes external skills for LLMs from just a natural-language task description, improving performance across several domains without needing curated training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expert-written skills for LLMs are costly, may not match a specific model’s quirks, and are often missing for new or emerging tasks. Existing automated skill-optimization methods depend on curated, in-distribution datasets, which users may not have. The authors want a way to create and refine high-quality skills using only a user’s task description, eliminating dependence on expensive data and manual engineering.

Method: The authors propose Prompt2Skill, a framework that: (1) takes a natural-language task description as input; (2) derives a formal task specification from it; (3) automatically discovers or synthesizes relevant datasets; and (4) runs a closed-loop reflective editing process where the model iteratively evaluates and refines the skill. This process produces a specialized skill artifact that is tailored to the target LLM without requiring pre-existing curated training sets.

Result: Across four task domains—question answering, reading comprehension, spreadsheet manipulation, and mathematical reasoning—Prompt2Skill yields consistent gains over a direct-prompting baseline. Averaged over both open-source and frontier models, the framework improves performance by 10.8 points (on the paper’s chosen metrics).

Conclusion: Prompt2Skill shows that it is possible to automatically derive effective, model-tailored skills from only natural-language task descriptions, without curated training data. This reduces the cost and expertise required to build specialized skills, generalizes across multiple domains and model types, and offers a practical path to keep skills up to date as tasks and models evolve.

Abstract: Skills are external artifacts that Large Language Models (LLMs) consume at inference time to improve their performance on specialized domains by incorporating relevant procedural and domain knowledge. Expert-authored skills are expensive to produce, and the resulting artifacts are not optimized for the specific model that consumes them, whose failure modes can vary with version, scale and training. In addition, emerging tasks may fall outside the scope of existing skill libraries, creating a need to develop new skills before curated training data become available. Recent works have explored automated skill optimization through reflection, but they require a curated, in-distribution training set, which users might not always have. To address these limitations, we present Prompt2Skill, a framework that builds skills from natural-language task description alone. From the prompt, the system derives a task specification, discovers or synthesizes datasets, and refines the skill in a closed loop of reflective editing. Across four domains spanning question answering, reading comprehension, spreadsheet manipulation, and mathematical reasoning, Prompt2Skill consistently outperforms the direct prompting baseline, achieving an average improvement of 10.8 across open-source and frontier models.

</details>


### [24] [Beyond Oracle Communication: Benchmarking Interactive Intent Alignment Under Miscommunication and Evolving User Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38604)
*Zheyuan Zhang,Mengyuan Chao,Ke Xiao,Ziyi Chen,Daoan Zhang,Yan Zhang,Yanfang Ye,Wei Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Drift-Bench++, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for testing how well LLM-based agents can infer and track users’ evolving and imperfectly communicated intents during interactive, long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks assume users clearly, accurately, and consistently state a fixed goal, which is unrealistic. In real use, people miscommunicate, change their minds, and have limited patience, leading to misaligned behavior by agents. There is a lack of systematic, executable benchmarks to study and quantify how agents handle these realistic interaction challenges, such as intent drift and miscommunication.

Method: The authors formalize the setting of Interactive Intent Alignment, where agents must infer and continually update their understanding of a user’s intent from noisy, evolving interactions. They build Drift-Bench++, a benchmark pipeline that produces verified executable tasks with controllable levels of misalignment and intent shifts. The benchmark includes: (1) an interaction protocol with finite user patience, (2) multiple, diverse simulated user types, and (3) silent, interaction-conditioned goal shifts. They also propose GRIP, an evaluation protocol decomposing performance into task grounding, user realism, quality of agent inquiries, and adaptation to evolving user intent. They test various LLM agents across multiple environments and interaction conditions using this setup.

Result: Experiments across different environments, model types, and interaction configurations show that agents benefit from richer and stronger interaction strategies but still perform significantly below an oracle that has perfect access to user intent. The benchmark reveals systematic failure modes in handling miscommunication and intent drift. When applied to real-world ProdAgent deployment logs, they find similar patterns: the failure modes identified by Drift-Bench++ also arise in practice and have meaningful negative effects on performance.

Conclusion: Drift-Bench++ provides a unified, executable, and controlled framework for studying Interactive Intent Alignment in realistic settings with miscommunication and evolving goals. It demonstrates that current agents fall well short of ideal intent understanding, even with enhanced interaction, and that these shortcomings manifest in real-world deployments. The benchmark and GRIP protocol aim to serve as a foundation for more robust evaluation and future research on agents that can better infer, question, and adapt to users’ true, changing intentions.

Abstract: Modern LLM agents increasingly tackle complex tasks through interactive, long-horizon exchanges with users, while existing benchmarks generally assume that users always accurately and sufficiently communicate a fixed intent. However, this oracle communication assumption rarely holds in practice: users may miscommunicate, change their goals, and run out of patience. We define this task setting as Interactive Intent Alignment, where agents must recover and continuously track the user's current intent despite imperfect communication and evolving goals. To study this setting, we introduce Drift-Bench++, a principled benchmark construction pipeline for verified executable tasks with controlled misalignment and intent shifts, along with an interaction protocol featuring finite patience, diverse simulated users, and silent interaction-conditioned shifts. We further develop GRIP, a comprehensive evaluation protocol covering task grounding, user realism, inquiry effectiveness, and adaptation to evolving intent. Across diverse environments, models, and interaction conditions, stronger interaction consistently helps but remains far from oracle performance; Validation on deployed ProdAgent sessions further shows that the modeled failures are prevalent and consequential in deployment. By providing a unified, executable benchmark for interactive intent alignment, Drift-Bench++ offers a foundation for evaluating and advancing agents under realistic communication and evolving intent.

</details>


### [25] [StreamDecisionBench: Evaluating Decisions in Force on Evolving Language Streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38612)
*Jhen-Ke Lin,Chung Chun Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces StreamDecisionBench, a benchmark to evaluate how well language-model-based decision systems perform over time when evidence changes during inference, decomposing errors into judgment and latency and quantifying time-sensitive accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional evaluations measure untimed (offline) accuracy, assuming a static input, but in real applications LLMs are embedded in programs that must act continuously as new evidence arrives. A decision that was correct when made can become wrong if the world changes before the model updates, and offline metrics miss this. The authors want an evaluation framework that reflects real-time decision quality, separates errors due to bad judgment from those due to latency, and makes explicit the tradeoff between reasoning depth (better judgment) and response speed (lower latency).

Method: They design StreamDecisionBench (SDB), a benchmark where scenarios continuously stream evidence across four application families. At each instant, the system under test has some decision "in force" until a new output arrives. Reference decisions are computed automatically from publicly specified rules implemented as executable code. SDB attributes every erroneous instant to judgment, latency, or both, and summarizes performance over decision-update intervals of 1–5 seconds using a normalized area-under-curve metric on a logarithmic time axis, which equalizes weight across multiplicative time ranges. They evaluate four hosted models in six configurations, including GPT-based models (Luna and Terra) with and without explicit reasoning, and compare observed scores to a product of untimed accuracy and an oracle timing score.

Result: Across six settings of four models, the integrated time-sensitive score is within 2.9 points of the product of each model’s untimed accuracy and an oracle’s integrated timing score, suggesting that the composite metric behaves predictably. Adding reasoning generally improves judgment, but the added computation increases latency, which substantially harms time-sensitive performance: for Luna and Terra, using reasoning causes losses of 38.8 and 42.8 points relative to their untimed accuracy baselines. A faster but less accurate component can match the integrated performance of a slower, higher-judgment model like Terra without reasoning, showing that speed can compensate for weaker per-decision quality.

Conclusion: StreamDecisionBench provides a principled way to evaluate streaming decision systems based on language models, capturing both judgment quality and latency over time and decomposing their contributions to error. The benchmark reveals clear tradeoffs: deeper reasoning can boost static accuracy but may reduce overall effectiveness in real-time settings due to latency. The authors’ metrics and curves expose how these tradeoffs vary with time scale, enabling practitioners to choose or design models whose integrated performance matches application needs rather than optimizing only untimed accuracy.

Abstract: As natural language drives more applications, language models increasingly run inside programs as decision components: the program sends them the current state and acts on the returned decision until a newer one arrives. When evidence changes during inference, a decision correct for its own state can stay in force after that state has passed, as when a call recorder keeps running after a customer starts reading out a card number; untimed (offline) accuracy counts such an error as correct. We introduce StreamDecisionBench (SDB), which evaluates the decision in force at every instant and attributes every erroneous instant to judgment, latency or both. Its scenarios stream evidence in four application families, with reference decisions computed from public rules by executable code. We summarize in-force accuracy across update intervals of 1-5 s by its normalized area under the curve on a logarithmic time axis, giving equal weight to equal multiplicative ranges. Across six settings of four hosted models, this score stays within 2.9 points of the scenario-wise product of untimed accuracy and an oracle's integrated timing score. Reasoning improves judgment, but at low effort latency costs Luna and Terra, two GPT models we also evaluate without reasoning, 38.8 and 42.8 points relative to untimed accuracy; a faster component with weaker judgment attains a similar integrated score to Terra without reasoning. The aggregate and family curves show where these tradeoffs change, making the evaluation's time-scale dependence visible.

</details>


### [26] [Marking Contour Tones in Yorùbá](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38627)
*Kólá Túbòsún*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes new diacritic marks (caron and circumflex) to represent rising and falling contour tones in Yorùbá orthography, particularly to correctly encode personal names, and demonstrates their practical implementation in digital tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Yorùbá is a tonal language where contour tones are hard to represent with the current orthography, especially for personal names and lexical items whose standard spellings avoid vowel lengthening. This often leads to misspelled or ambiguously spelled forms and, critically, to some names having written forms that invert or contradict their intended meanings. Existing orthographic solutions are inadequate for clearly and compactly encoding rising and falling tones in regular writing and digital contexts, motivating a more practical and typable solution.

Method: The paper first analyzes the orthographic problem posed by contour tones in Yorùbá, focusing on personal names and items where conventional spellings omit or distort tonal information. It then evaluates why current orthographic conventions and workarounds (such as vowel lengthening) fail to resolve these issues. Building on earlier phonological scholarship, the authors propose using caron and circumflex diacritics on single vowels to encode rising and falling tones. They support this proposal by implementing it in the WriteYoruba keyboard and the TTSYoruba text-to-speech system, making the new marks easily producible on standard keyboards and processable by computational tools.

Result: The outcome is a concrete orthographic proposal: use caron-marked vowels for rising tones and circumflex-marked vowels for falling tones in Yorùbá. This system allows contour tones to be encoded on single vowels without resorting to unwieldy vowel lengthening, preserving intended meanings in names and words. The feasibility of the proposal is demonstrated via its integration into the WriteYoruba keyboard and the TTSYoruba speech synthesizer, enabling straightforward input and computational handling. Listener evaluation and full system architecture are mentioned as completed and reported in a separate work.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that adopting caron and circumflex diacritics for contour tones offers a practical, theoretically grounded solution to long-standing orthographic problems in Yorùbá. It resolves meaning-distorting ambiguities in personal names and other lexical items, aligns with phonological research tradition, and is immediately usable in digital environments thanks to implemented keyboard and TTS support. The authors advocate for broader acceptance of these diacritics as part of standard Yorùbá orthography to make contour tones consistently and accurately representable in writing.

Abstract: Yorùbá is a tonal language in which contour tones pose persistent orthographic challenges. These are especially notable for personal names and lexical items whose conventional spellings avoid vowel lengthening that would otherwise provide a host syllable for the second tone. A particular concern is a class of names in which the conventional spelling does not just omit tonal information but inverts the meaning of said name, sometimes asserting the opposite of what the name intends. This paper describes the problem, illustrates the inadequacy of current solutions, and proposes the adoption of the caron and circumflex marks. These are symbols with precedent in Yorùbá phonological scholarship since Olmsted (1951), used as orthographic conventions on single vowels to encode rising and falling contour tones, making them accessible for the first time through standard keyboard input and computational text processing. The proposal is supported by an implementation in the WriteYoruba keyboard and the TTSYoruba speech synthesizer, whose architecture and listener evaluation are reported separately (Tubosun et al., 2026).

</details>


### [27] [Strong Multilingual Privacy Tagging at Encoder Speed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38630)
*Jonathan Graehl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a fast multilingual NER model tailored for privacy redaction that beats existing systems by a large margin, while showing simple tricks for using imperfect annotations and fixing span boundaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective privacy redaction requires accurately identifying many fine-grained personal-entity types across languages while keeping computational cost low; existing NER and privacy filters either miss types, can’t represent needed distinctions, or are too slow or expensive to train and run, especially when only noisy or partial annotations are available.

Method: They fine-tune a multilingual encoder (similar to XLM-R) with an affine span-tagging head using frontier-model annotations in 35 languages, add replay of mapped human-gold annotations with coverage-aware masking so missing types are not treated as negatives, and introduce a learned +/-1 character boundary adjustment layer to correct subword-based span errors. They also scale training with ~50k extra annotated sentences and systematically compare against GLiNER2, Microsoft Presidio, and an OpenAI Privacy Filter fine-tune, as well as locally trained LLM annotators and frozen-encoder baselines, measuring both accuracy and throughput on CPU and GPU.

Result: On 1,283 human-gold test segments in seven languages their best redaction F1 reaches 88.8, far above GLiNER2 (∼69 F1 even with favorable task restrictions), Microsoft Presidio (57.3), and the OpenAI Privacy Filter baseline (35.8). On Ont3, a 31-type NER evaluation set with 1,201 dev segments, adding ~50k annotated sentences and more human-gold replay raises exact typed-span F1 from 74.5 to 76.3. Mapped-gold replay alone adds ~10 F1 points with no degradation on frontier-annotated data, and the boundary adjustment brings another 1.7 F1. LLMs trainable on a single 96-GB GPU are slower and less accurate than their encoder-based approach, with encoding 30–95× slower than XLM-R and prompted annotation 180–1,100× slower, while their encoder model is 4.9× faster than GLiNER2 on CPU.

Conclusion: A carefully designed multilingual encoder-based NER system with fine-grained label support, coverage-aware replay of partial human annotations, and lightweight span-boundary correction can substantially outperform existing privacy-redaction tools in both accuracy and speed. Noisy frontier-model annotations can be leveraged effectively, and relatively small architectural and training tweaks yield large gains, enabling practical, high-throughput privacy redaction across many languages; all resources to reproduce and extend the system are released.

Abstract: Privacy redaction must remove personal information while preserving relationships expressed in text. We develop a multilingual named-entity tagger with fine-grained distinctions supporting varied redaction policies and methods for cheaply learning additional distinctions. We fine-tune a multilingual encoder with an affine span-tagging head on frontier-model annotations in 35 languages, replay mapped human gold with coverage-aware masking so unannotated types are not treated as negatives, and repair subword boundaries with a learned +/-1-character adjustment. On 1,283 human-gold test segments in seven languages, best measured redaction F1 is 88.8, against 69.1 for published GLiNER2 with 11 unrepresentable types excluded from its task (68.8 without that exemption), 67.8 for GLiNER2 adapted to the new training data, 57.3 for Microsoft Presidio and 35.8 for the best published OpenAI Privacy Filter fine-tune. Adding about 50,000 annotated training sentences and increasing human-gold replay improves exact typed-span F1 from 74.5 to 76.3 on Ont3, our 31-type frontier-annotated NER evaluation of 1,201 development segments. Mapped-gold replay alone raises human-gold F1 by ten points without loss on frontier-annotated text; boundary adjustment adds 1.7 exact typed-span F1 points on Ont3. Local LLMs fitting on a single 96-GB GPU underperformed as prompted annotators and frozen encoders, with encoding 30-95 times slower than XLM-R inference and prompted annotation roughly 180-1,100 times slower in the evaluated configurations. The encoder architecture delivers 4.9 times GLiNER2's CPU throughput. We release code, prompts and training recipes, with data-acquisition scripts and source links.

</details>


### [28] [Breaking Babel: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for Long-Form Subtitle Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38660)
*Haibo Jin,Xinjie Li,Najmeh Sadoughi,Yang Liu,Yibo Wang,Zhu Liu,Yuzong Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SMART is a self-evolving multi-agent system that improves long-form subtitle translation by dynamically coordinating multiple LLM agents with tools and judge-refiner feedback, achieving state-of-the-art quality on new and existing benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form subtitle translation for series requires discourse- and culture-aware reasoning over many episodes while preserving consistent terminology and style. Existing approaches either use single LLMs operating mostly at sentence level, missing broader context, or rely on rigid multi-agent workflows that cannot adapt to varying scene complexity or production constraints. There is a need for a system that can leverage series-level memory, adapt its workflow at test time, and systematically improve translation quality without retraining base models.

Method: The authors propose SMART, a self-evolving multi-agent framework. At test time, SMART constructs persistent series-level memory and translates a subset of sentences using a dynamic router and a Mixture-of-Agents layer. Specialized tools assist with terminology verification, subtitle constraint checking, and contextual retrieval. A judge-refiner loop evaluates multiple candidate translations, scores them, and generates textual critiques. These critiques are then used to update agent prompts and routing policies, enabling the system to refine its configuration without modifying underlying LLM weights. Once the system has evolved on this subset, the optimized configuration is used to translate the remaining subtitles in the series.

Result: The authors create Subtitle Arena, a comprehensive long-form subtitle benchmark across 14 genres, 2–198 episodes per series, 1959–2023 productions, and 15 target locales, along with SubMQM, an MQM-based evaluation scheme tailored to subtitles. On Subtitle Arena, SMART attains the best overall MQM scores in all 15 translation directions, lowering average MQM penalties by 6.9% relative to the strongest competing agent-based system. On the existing MuSC benchmark, SMART achieves the best automatic MQM scores across all four language pairs and also obtains the highest human evaluation rating, with an overall score of 4.50 out of 5.

Conclusion: SMART demonstrates that a self-evolving, tool-augmented multi-agent setup with dynamic routing and judge-refiner feedback can substantially improve long-form subtitle translation without retraining base LLMs. By building series-level memory and adapting its workflow at test time, SMART achieves state-of-the-art performance on both a new, diverse subtitle benchmark and a public standard benchmark, highlighting the value of adaptive multi-agent orchestration for discourse- and culture-sensitive translation tasks.

Abstract: Long-form subtitle translation requires reasoning over discourse and cultural context spanning episodes or entire series, while maintaining consistent terminology and style. Existing single-LLM methods are largely sentence-level, and multi-agent systems often use static workflows that do not adapt to scene complexity or production context. We propose SMART, a Self-evolving Multi-Agent system for long-foRm subtitle Translation. During test-time training, SMART builds persistent series-level memory and translates a subset of sentences through a dynamic router and Mixture-of-Agents layer with tools for terminology verification, subtitle constraint validation, and contextual retrieval. A judge-refiner loop scores candidates and uses textual critiques to update agent prompts and routing policies without retraining the underlying LLMs. During test-time inference, the evolved configuration translates the remaining series. We also introduce Subtitle Arena, covering 14 genres, 2--198 episodes per series, production years 1959--2023, and 15 target locales, together with SubMQM, a subtitle-adapted MQM framework with seven dimensions and 19 error categories. SMART achieves the best overall MQM score in all 15 Subtitle Arena directions, reducing average penalty by 6.9% over the strongest competing agent system. On the public MuSC benchmark, SMART obtains the best model result across all four language pairs and also achieves the best human-evaluation result, with an overall score of 4.50/5.

</details>


### [29] [MetaSteer: Context-Conditioned, nonlinear Steering via Attention-Projection Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38718)
*Mehdi Jafari,Hao Xue,Flora Salim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MetaSteer is a method for context-dependent, nonlinear steering of large language models via low-rank adaptations to attention projection matrices, achieving strong zero-shot control across text-generation and agentic tasks without assuming linear concept geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing steering methods usually assume that concepts correspond to linear directions in activation space and use fixed, context-independent interventions. This can be inaccurate, limit expressivity, and cause information bottlenecks when many nuanced behaviors must be encoded in a single linear representation. There is a need for more flexible, context-sensitive steering mechanisms that can generalize across tasks and settings while preserving model capabilities.

Method: The paper proposes MetaSteer, which learns nonlinear, context-dependent interventions applied to attention projection matrices using low-rank adapters. Steering is framed as preference-based optimization: the system is trained once on a pooled corpus of preference data to favor outputs aligned with desired behaviors over alternatives. The learned adapters produce activation changes that inherently depend on input context, removing the need for linear concept geometry assumptions. The trained MetaSteer module is then applied zero-shot to unseen concepts and out-of-distribution contexts.

Result: Empirically, MetaSteer generates structured, context-dependent modifications in hidden-state trajectories that alter behavior while partially preserving local geometric properties such as trajectory velocity and curvature. On three controlled text-generation benchmarks and three agentic settings, spanning multiple model families and sizes, MetaSteer matches or outperforms strong, task-specific steering baselines in most aggregate zero-shot comparisons. Stronger steering on text-generation tasks correlates with stronger steering in agentic scenarios.

Conclusion: MetaSteer demonstrates that nonlinear, context-dependent, low-rank modifications to attention projections can provide effective, transferable steering of large language models without relying on linear concept geometry. The method yields robust zero-shot generalization, maintains aspects of the model’s internal dynamics, and scales across models and settings. The authors highlight implications for understanding geometric trajectory changes in representations, preserving capabilities while steering, and address safety issues that arise when steering mechanisms transfer across tasks and agents.

Abstract: Steering large language models typically relies on linear, context-independent interventions in activation space, an assumption that recent work has challenged and that can induce an information bottleneck when a fixed representation must encode many behavioral distinctions. We introduce MetaSteer, a method that learns nonlinear interventions with context-dependent effects and applies them to attention projection matrices, producing activation effects that vary with the input context by construction and requiring no linear concept-geometry assumption. Framed as preference-based optimization, MetaSteer is trained once on a pooled preference corpus and transferred zero-shot to unseen concepts and out-of-distribution contexts. We find that, despite using low-rank adapters, MetaSteer induces structured, context-dependent changes in hidden-state trajectories while partially preserving aspects of their local trajectory dynamics, including velocity and curvature. We evaluate MetaSteer on three controlled text-generation benchmarks and three agentic settings across multiple model families and scales. MetaSteer matches or outperforms strong task-specific steering baselines on most aggregate comparisons in the zero-shot regime. Across the evaluated settings, stronger text-generation steering is associated with stronger agentic steering performance. We further discuss geometric trajectory effects, capability retention, and safety considerations raised by transferable steering.

</details>


### [30] [Training LLM Judges from Language Feedback via Position-Selective Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38792)
*Ilgee Hong,Changlong Yu,Zhenghao Xu,Xin Liu,Yuwei Zhang,Qin Lu,Bing Yin,Tuo Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper improves how large language model (LLM) judges are trained for subjective evaluation by using natural language feedback more effectively, via entropy-based selective self-distillation instead of pure outcome-supervised RL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM judges for subjective tasks are mostly trained with outcome-supervised RL, where every token in the model’s reasoning and verdict receives the same scalar reward based only on the final correctness of the verdict. This ignores rich natural language feedback such as rationales explaining preferences, and it gives no special treatment to key tokens that select or weigh evaluation criteria. As a result, models may overfit to particular wordings and fail to generalize, especially on subjective dimensions where multiple criteria and phrasings can be valid. The authors are motivated to use the available natural language feedback to provide denser, position-wise supervision, and to do so in a way that promotes real semantic understanding rather than rote memorization of specific criterion expressions.

Method: The authors study self-distillation (SD) for LLM judges: the same base model, when conditioned on natural language feedback (e.g., rationales), acts as a teacher that provides dense token-level supervision to a student model. They analyze per-position entropy shifts between teacher and student to distinguish two regimes: (1) context sharpening, where the teacher becomes more confident and focuses probability mass on a specific feedback-aligned criterion expression; and (2) context spreading, where the teacher keeps multiple feedback-aligned alternatives probable. They interpret sharpening as encouraging memorization and spreading as fostering semantic understanding by preserving alternative phrasings. Based on this, they introduce an entropy-shift-based position masking scheme that retains the lower tail of the entropy-shift distribution—i.e., it masks out positions with large entropy shifts (more sharpening) and trains mainly on positions associated with spreading. This selective masking is applied on top of the self-distillation training pipeline.

Result: Empirically, the proposed entropy-shift-based masking in self-distillation improves out-of-distribution generalization compared to naive self-distillation that uses all positions. In evaluations on subjective subcategories of tasks, LLM judges trained with this masked self-distillation outperform outcome-supervised RL-trained judges (e.g., GRPO) by 2–9 percentage points. On more objective categories, the new method remains competitive with outcome-supervised RL, indicating that the gains on subjective tasks do not come at the cost of performance on objective ones.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that natural language feedback can be exploited more effectively than in standard outcome-supervised RL by using self-distillation combined with entropy-based position masking. Distinguishing between positions that promote memorization (context sharpening) and those that promote semantic understanding (context spreading) allows the training process to focus on more generalizable signals. This leads to LLM judges that perform better on subjective evaluations while maintaining strong performance on objective ones, suggesting a promising direction for training evaluation models with rich feedback rather than only scalar rewards.

Abstract: We study training LLM judges from natural language feedback, especially for subjective tasks where the verdict depends strongly on which evaluation criteria the judge invokes and how it weighs them. The dominant approach, outcome-supervised RL (e.g., GRPO), credits every token in the rollout with a single scalar determined only by the accuracy of the final verdict, providing no separate credit at the criterion-choice tokens and ignoring the rich language feedback (e.g., preference rationales) that naturally accompanies preference labels. Self-Distillation (SD) is one natural way to use this language feedback: the same model, conditioned on this feedback, acts as a teacher providing dense, position-level supervision. However, not all positions carry equally useful signal. Using the per-position entropy shift between teacher and student, we identify two regimes: context sharpening, where the teacher concentrates probability on a particular feedback-aligned criterion expression, and context spreading, where the teacher distributes probability across multiple feedback-aligned alternatives. We interpret these patterns as follows: sharpening encourages memorization of a particular criterion expression, whereas spreading promotes semantic understanding by preserving these alternatives. Motivated by this asymmetry, we introduce position masking based on the entropy shift that retains the lower tail of the entropy-shift distribution. Experiments show that masking higher-entropy-shift positions improves out-of-distribution generalization over naive SD. The resulting self-distilled judges outperform judges trained with outcome-supervised RL by 2-9 percentage points on the evaluated subjective subcategories, while remaining competitive on objective ones.

</details>


### [31] [Recovering Off-Policy Supervision for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38795)
*Jungseob Lee,Chanjun Park,Sugyeong Eo,Hyeonseok Moon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a new rollout-based training framework for speculative decoding drafters that recovers full supervision on fixed corpora and significantly improves token acceptance length over prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing block drafters for speculative decoding are typically trained on fixed corpora produced by external target models. Because training is off-policy, once a single drafted token deviates from the target sequence, all subsequent positions in that block become invalid for supervision. Current methods deal with this by discarding these divergent slots, leading to large supervision loss and inefficient data use. Regenerating the whole corpus with the target model is expensive. The authors want a way to fully exploit existing fixed corpora, recover supervision for all positions, and improve drafter quality without re-generating data or increasing target compute substantially.

Method: They propose a rollout-based training framework built around target model rollouts to recover valid supervision everywhere in a draft block. It has two key components: (1) Anchor-Label Relabeling (ALR), where instead of using the original corpus token labels beyond the divergence point, they run greedy rollouts from the target model conditioned on the anchor context and use the resulting predictive distributions as soft labels for all drafted slots. This relabels the corpus with target-consistent supervision and allows training on all positions. (2) In-Rollout Anchors (IRA), where the drafter’s blocks are inserted directly into the target’s rollout trajectories so that the drafter is exposed to target-generated contexts. They reuse precomputed rollout features, so this extra conditioning does not add target compute cost. Together, ALR ensures correct labels everywhere and IRA ensures training occurs in realistic target contexts, enabling effective learning from off-policy, fixed corpora.

Result: On both vision-language and pure text speculative decoding benchmarks with fixed corpora, their framework improves the greedy accepted length (number of drafted tokens accepted by the target) by up to 36.5% over DFlash and consistently outperforms methods that simply erase or discard invalid slots after divergence. With only one training epoch, their method already surpasses the best erasing schedules, and after three epochs, its accepted length matches that of a much more expensive baseline trained on fully target-regenerated responses.

Conclusion: The proposed rollout-based framework with ALR and IRA allows speculative drafters to be trained efficiently on fixed, off-policy corpora without altering the original text. By relabeling supervision via target rollouts and embedding drafter blocks inside these rollouts, it recovers full supervision across all positions, substantially improves accepted token length, and reaches the performance of costly target-regenerated training with only a few epochs. This offers a practical, compute-efficient approach for improving speculative decoding systems when only fixed external-model corpora are available.

Abstract: Block drafters for speculative decoding are commonly trained on corpora written by external models, where a single off-policy token invalidates supervision for all subsequent slots in a block. Existing approaches discard these divergent slots, resulting in severe supervision loss. To resolve this problem while preserving the training corpus, we propose a rollout-based training framework that recovers full supervision through two complementary components. The first component, Anchor-Label Relabelling (ALR), replaces corpus labels with distributions from greedy target rollouts, restoring valid supervision across all predicted slots. The second component, In-Rollout Anchors (IRA), places draft blocks directly inside these rollouts to expose the drafter to target-generated context, reusing precomputed rollout features at no additional target cost. Across fixed vision-language and text corpora, our framework increases greedy accepted length by up to 36.5% over DFlash and consistently outperforms erasing baselines. Notably, a single epoch of our method surpasses the best erase schedules. After three epochs, it matches the acceptance length of training on target-regenerated responses. These results show that our framework provides an effective and compute-efficient approach for training speculative drafters on fixed corpora without modifying the original text. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/ALR-IRA.

</details>


### [32] [Overlap, Unique and Conflict: Can LLMs Extract What They Can Recognize?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38799)
*Eftekhar Hossain,Santu Karmaker*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a new task and benchmark for extracting overlapping, unique, and conflicting clauses between pairs of narratives, showing that current LLMs especially struggle with overlap and conflict extraction, and that fine-tuning helps but does not fully solve the problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on cross-text relations mostly classifies predefined text pairs into categories like entailment or contradiction, but does not directly extract the corresponding pieces of information from full-length narratives. For real-world multi-perspective understanding, we need systems that can read two narratives and pull out which specific clauses agree, conflict, or are unique to each source. This gap in tasks, benchmarks, and evaluation motivates defining a new extraction problem and building resources to study it systematically.

Method: The authors define Overlap-Unique-Conflict (OUC) extraction as a cross-narrative clause extraction task, where a system must read two full narratives and output all clauses that are overlapping across narratives, conflicting, or unique to one narrative. They construct a large benchmark comprising about 22K narrative pairs and 140K annotated OUC instances from diverse domains including factual, argumentative, and political discourse. Using this benchmark, they evaluate 14 open-source LLMs ranging from 0.6B to 35B parameters, measuring F1-scores on extracting overlap, conflict, and unique clauses. They also perform diagnostic analyses to disentangle errors due to relation recognition from errors due to clause pairing and extraction. Finally, they fine-tune one of the models (Qwen-3-8B) on the OUC task with task-specific supervision and compare its performance to larger models.

Result: Empirically, they find that extracting unique information is much easier for current LLMs than extracting overlapping or conflicting clauses. For example, the strongest base model tested, Gemma-4-31B, achieves over 75% F1 on unique clause extraction but only about 61.13% F1 on overlap and 48.58% F1 on conflict. Diagnostic analysis shows that a substantial portion of the difficulty comes not just from recognizing relations between clauses, but from correctly pairing corresponding clauses and extracting them from long narratives, a problem that is especially severe for smaller models. With task-specific fine-tuning, Qwen-3-8B improves its performance by 15–28 absolute F1 points and can outperform much larger models, such as Qwen-3.6-35B, on several OUC subtasks, demonstrating the value of supervised training. However, even the fine-tuned model still shows relatively low performance on overlap and conflict extraction.

Conclusion: OUC extraction is a challenging but important task for understanding multi-perspective narratives, going beyond simple relation classification to require accurate clause-level pairing and extraction across full texts. The new benchmark demonstrates that current open-source LLMs, including large models, perform poorly on overlap and especially conflict extraction, while having a much easier time identifying unique content. Task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves performance and can make smaller models competitive with or superior to larger ones, but overall results remain far from satisfactory. This indicates that cross-narrative clause extraction is still an open research problem and that further advances in modeling, training, or representation are needed to robustly capture agreement, disagreement, and uniqueness across narratives.

Abstract: Understanding multi-perspective alternative narratives requires identifying how their information agrees, conflicts, or differs across sources. Existing work on cross-text relations largely focuses on categorizing relations between predefined text pairs, such as entailment or contradiction, rather than directly extracting such information from full narratives. To address this gap, we introduce Overlap-Unique-Conflict (OUC) extraction, a cross-narrative task that extracts all overlapping, conflicting, and unique clauses from two narratives. To support this study, we construct a benchmark of approximately 22K narrative pairs and 140K OUC instances spanning factual, argumentative, and political discourse. Evaluating 14 open-source LLMs (0.6B-35B), we find that unique information is far easier to extract than overlap and conflict: the strongest model, Gemma-4-31B, reaches only 61.13% F1-score on overlap and 48.58% on conflict, against more than 75% on unique. Further diagnostic analysis reveals that this difficulty does not stem from relation recognition alone, but rather from a failure to pair and extract the corresponding clauses from full narratives, especially in smaller models. Nevertheless, learning these extractions with task-specific supervision narrows the gap considerably: a fine-tuned Qwen-3-8B gains 15-28% absolute over its baseline and surpasses models roughly four times its size (e.g., Qwen-3.6-35B) on several tasks. Even so, overlap and conflict remain well below satisfactory, leaving cross-narrative clause extraction an open challenge.

</details>


### [33] [Uncovering Uncontrolled Repetition through Residual Stream Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38802)
*Yuanhe Zhang,Xinyao Zhou,Haoran Gao,Yuyao Zhang,Zhenhong Zhou,Fanyu Meng,Li Sun,Sen Su*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how uncontrolled repetition arises in large (vision-)language models and introduces a method, Tokenwise Residual Comparison (TRC), to detect and suppress repetition-related activity early in the network, substantially reducing looping behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive LLMs and LVLMs can fall into uncontrolled repetition loops, which waste computation and enable resource exhaustion attacks. Existing work mainly focuses on strongly activated repetition features in intermediate or late layers, leaving unclear how these patterns initially emerge and evolve through the network. There is a need for both a better mechanistic understanding of repetition and a practical, targeted intervention that can prevent or mitigate such loops across different model types.

Method: The authors propose Tokenwise Residual Comparison (TRC). During generation, TRC analyzes the residual stream across tokens: it compares the attention and MLP write vectors for each new token to those from previous tokens, searching for abnormal similarities or recurring patterns that correlate with repetitive output. When such anomalous coordinates are found at a given layer, TRC selectively suppresses (downweights) those coordinates in the residual stream at that layer, thereby disrupting the emerging repetition dynamics. The method is applied primarily to large vision-language models but is also tested on LLMs and large reasoning models.

Result: TRC significantly reduces uncontrolled repetition in generation, achieving an average 57% reduction in loop rates. The analysis shows that semantic signals related to repetition appear already in shallow layers and then propagate through the residual stream, interfering with normal token representations. Similar repetition-related dynamics are observed in standard LLMs and LRMs, and TRC successfully captures and mitigates them as well.

Conclusion: Repetitive generation is not solely a late-layer phenomenon; its semantics begin in shallow layers and spread through the residual pathway. By monitoring and modifying residual dynamics with TRC, models can be steered away from repetition loops, improving robustness and mitigating resource consumption attacks. The approach generalizes across LVLMs, LLMs, and LRMs, and opens up earlier, more fine-grained intervention points for controlling pathological repetition in autoregressive models.

Abstract: Uncontrolled repetition can prolong autoregressive generation in large language models (LLMs) and enable resource consumption attacks. Prior analyses of repetitive generation have identified strongly activated features in intermediate and late layers. However, how uncontrolled repetition activity emerges and develops before becoming prominent in these layers remains insufficiently understood. In this paper, we investigate this question primarily in large vision-language models (LVLMs), which support a richer set of uncontrolled repetitions through both visual and textual inputs. We propose Tokenwise Residual Comparison (TRC), a method that identifies and localizes anomalies associated with repetition from residual dynamics during generation. TRC compares attention and multilayer perceptron writes to the residual stream across generated tokens to identify patterns associated with repetition. It then selectively suppresses coordinates in the residual stream at the identified layer. Experiments show that TRC effectively mitigates uncontrolled repetition, reducing loop rates by 57\% on average. Our analysis further shows that repetition semantics emerge in shallow layers and propagate through the residual stream, disrupting normal representations. TRC also generalizes to large language models (LLMs) and large reasoning models (LRMs), where it consistently captures analogous repetition dynamics and achieves effective mitigation. Our work broadens the study of repetitive generation from its prominent internal representations to earlier opportunities for intervention, providing insights for mitigating resource consumption attacks.

</details>


### [34] [StateTree: Enhancing Long-Term Dialogue Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38809)
*Naen Xu,Wanqing Cui,Yibo Hu,Shixin Hong,Hengyu An,Meiguang Jin,Junfeng Ma,Tianyu Du*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: StateTree is an RL-based training framework that teaches LLMs to perform long-term dialogue reasoning by solving a tree-structured path-tracing task across multi-session histories, enabling strong performance on very long-context benchmarks with modest training context lengths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personal LLM assistants must reason over long and evolving conversation histories spanning many sessions. In this setting, crucial information is dispersed across time, user preferences and facts get updated, and models must perform temporal reasoning and knowledge revision. Standard long-context training requires huge amounts of data and compute and does not explicitly target these reasoning skills, leading to poor long-term dialogue performance. The paper aims to design a data- and compute-efficient training approach that directly targets cross-session retrieval, temporal reasoning, and preference updating in long contexts.

Method: The authors introduce StateTree, a reinforcement learning framework that converts multi-session dialogue data with verifiable ground truth into a challenging auxiliary task. They embed key-value records extracted from dialogues across sessions into a binary tree. To solve the task, the model must traverse from root to leaf by retrieving relevant records across sessions, comparing timestamps to resolve branching decisions, and finally identify a hidden target question among distractor leaves. They use curriculum RL, gradually increasing the tree depth to control task difficulty, and add a compositional variant where tree edges encode step-level reasoning fragments. This trains the model to combine partial cues into coherent queries. Training is done on contexts up to 10K tokens but is designed to generalize to much longer contexts (up to 128K) without paying the quadratic cost of full-length RL training.

Result: Models trained with StateTree demonstrate improved abilities in cross-session retrieval, temporal reasoning, knowledge updating, and compositional multi-hop reasoning on long-context dialogue tasks. Despite being trained only on 10K-token contexts, they generalize effectively to 128K-token inputs. On the LongMemEval benchmark at 128K context length, StateTree-7B achieves up to +23.60% absolute improvement over baselines, and StateTree-14B achieves 59.00% accuracy, outperforming a much larger long-context model, QwenLong-L1-32B (45.20%). StateTree also maintains strong general reasoning in short-context settings compared with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and other RL-based methods.

Conclusion: StateTree shows that carefully designed, tree-structured auxiliary RL tasks built from limited dialogue data can effectively teach LLMs to perform complex long-term reasoning over extended, evolving interaction histories. By focusing on cross-session retrieval, temporal reasoning, and compositional reasoning via curriculum learning, StateTree achieves strong generalization to very long contexts without incurring full long-context RL costs and surpasses larger long-context models on LongMemEval while preserving short-context capabilities.

Abstract: Large language models deployed as personalized assistants must reason over long, evolving interaction histories. However, in long-term dialogue reasoning, relevant evidence is scattered across sessions, preferences may be revised over time, and standard long-context training fails to address these challenges under data scarcity and prohibitive computational costs. We propose StateTree, a data-driven RL method that constructs a challenging auxiliary task from scarce dialogues with verifiable ground truth. StateTree augments multi-session dialogues with a tree-structured path-tracing task: key-value records are embedded across sessions to form a binary tree. Solving the task requires the model to traverse from root to leaf by retrieving records across sessions and comparing timestamps to resolve branches, then recover the hidden target question among distractor leaves. We apply curriculum RL training progressively increasing tree depth and introduce a compositional variant whose edges carry step-level reasoning fragments, training the model to compose partial cues into coherent queries. Trained on 10K-token contexts, StateTree generalizes to 128K tokens without full-length RL costs and exhibits capabilities including cross-session retrieval, temporal reasoning, knowledge update, and compositional multi-hop reasoning. StateTree outperforms both SFT and RL-based baselines while preserving short-context general reasoning. StateTree-7B achieves gains up to +23.60% on LongMemEval (128k), and StateTree-14B reaches 59.00% accuracy on LongMemEval, surpassing QwenLong-L1-32B (45.20%).

</details>


### [35] [Can Terminal Agents Trust Their Own Verification? Diagnosing and Improving Self-Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38812)
*Yingfeng Luo,Shaowei Wei,Daixin Wang,Dingyang Lin,Kaiyan Chang,Weiqiao Shan,Tong Zheng,Zhiqiang Zhang,Jingbo Zhu,Tong Xiao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how reliably command-line terminal agents can verify and correct their own solutions, finds major weaknesses in error detection and repair, and proposes a new distillation method (SCVD) where a student model learns verification and recovery behavior from a stronger teacher, significantly improving performance on TerminalBench2.1 without hurting generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Terminal agents often rely on self-verification to catch and fix their own mistakes when solving tasks in command-line environments, but it is unclear how trustworthy this self-verification process really is. Existing benchmarks focus on end performance, not on where verification fails in the reasoning trajectory. There is also a need for training methods that specifically enhance agents' verification and recovery abilities without causing out-of-distribution degradation on other benchmarks.

Method: 1) Introduce a diagnostic framework that, for each agent trajectory on terminal tasks, identifies the first complete candidate solution, checks its objective correctness, and then quantifies subsequent verification and recovery behavior (whether the agent verifies, whether it detects the error, and whether it repairs it). 2) Apply this framework to ten different terminal agents on the TerminalBench2.1 benchmark to analyze their verification patterns. 3) Propose Student-Conditioned Verification Distillation (SCVD), a training scheme where the student model first generates a candidate solution and then is trained to imitate a stronger teacher model’s verification and recovery actions that are conditioned on the same interaction context and the student’s candidate solution. 4) Compare SCVD to baseline models and to standard full-trajectory distillation across multiple Qwen3.5 model sizes and evaluate on TerminalBench2.1 and SWE-bench Verified.

Result: Empirically, the analysis shows that while agents almost always attempt verification after forming a complete candidate solution, they correctly detect only about 61.43% of incorrect candidates, and among those detected, they successfully repair only 49.36%. This pinpoints error detection and repair—not the initiation of verification—as the major weaknesses. SCVD training improves Pass@1 on TerminalBench2.1 by 9.74–16.85 percentage points compared with the base Qwen3.5 models, and by 4.49–8.61 points versus standard full-trajectory distillation, while also avoiding the substantial out-of-distribution performance drop that full-trajectory distillation exhibits on SWE-bench Verified.

Conclusion: Self-verification in terminal agents is not inherently limited by their willingness to verify solutions, but by their ability to accurately detect and repair mistakes once verification is triggered. The proposed SCVD method directly targets this gap by letting a student learn verification and recovery behaviors from a stronger teacher conditioned on the student’s own outputs, yielding substantial gains on terminal benchmarks without harming generalization to other coding tasks. This suggests that future progress in tool-using agents should prioritize training methods that sharpen error detection and correction rather than simply encouraging more verification steps.

Abstract: Terminal agents rely on self-verification to assess and correct their solutions as they solve tasks through interaction with command-line environments. Yet how trustworthy such self-verification is remains poorly understood. To investigate this question systematically, we introduce a diagnostic framework that identifies the first complete solution in each trajectory, determines whether it is objectively correct, and uses this ground truth to quantify the agent's subsequent verification and recovery behavior. Applying it to ten terminal agents on TerminalBench2.1, we find that verification is nearly universal after a complete candidate is formed, yet only 61.43\% of incorrect candidates are detected and only 49.36\% of detected errors are successfully repaired. These results show that the main weakness in self-verification lies not in initiating verification, but in detecting and repairing errors. Motivated by these findings, we propose Student-Conditioned Verification Distillation (SCVD), which lets the student first produce a candidate solution and distills a stronger teacher's subsequent verification and recovery from the same interaction context. Across three Qwen3.5 backbones, SCVD improves \textsc{Pass@1} on TerminalBench2.1 by 9.74--16.85 percentage points over the corresponding base models and by 4.49--8.61 points over the standard full-trajectory distillation, while avoiding the pronounced out-of-distribution degradation of full-trajectory distillation on SWE-bench Verified.

</details>


### [36] [You're Hired: Strategic Model Selection for LLM Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38816)
*Zongwan Cao,Ziyuan Yang,Shangbin Feng,Michael Duan,Skyler Hallinan,Bingbing Wen,Lucy Lu Wang,Yulia Tsvetkov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to automatically choose which language models to include in a multi-model (multi-LLM) system and shows that good selection algorithms significantly boost performance over naive or random choices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-LLM and multi-agent systems can outperform single models by combining complementary strengths, but current systems typically rely on fixed, hand-crafted sets of models. This manual model pool design is ad hoc, does not scale to large or evolving model catalogs, and may miss better-performing combinations. There is a need for principled, data-driven algorithms that can select effective model teams from large candidate pools, while also filtering out unsafe or misaligned models and remaining robust to new tasks.

Method: The paper formulates model selection as a team formation problem in multi-LLM systems and proposes a taxonomy of 9 selection algorithms. These span three main categories: (1) description-based diversity, which selects models based on diversity in their metadata or textual descriptions; (2) capability-aware behavioral diversity, which uses empirical performance and behavioral signals to select a complementary set of models; and (3) LLM-based recruiters, where an LLM interacts with candidate models to assess capabilities and choose a team. The authors evaluate these selection algorithms across two candidate pools of 10 and 32 models, combined with four different multi-model collaboration algorithms, on a benchmark suite of math, coding, QA, and general reasoning tasks.

Result: Across tasks and collaboration settings, principled selection algorithms substantially outperform random selection and simple heuristics such as always picking individually strongest models. Performance gains reach up to 36.1% over these baselines. Capability- and training-based selection approaches in particular reduce variance in outcomes and achieve consistently strong results, especially as candidate pools grow larger. These methods also better avoid misaligned and unsafe models and show improved robustness and generalization to out-of-distribution tasks compared with shallow or purely description-based heuristics.

Conclusion: Effective multi-LLM systems depend critically on how model teams are selected. Naive or hand-crafted model pools underutilize available diversity and can even harm performance, especially in large model catalogs. Capability- and training-informed selection strategies, including LLM-based recruitment that directly probes candidate models, provide a robust way to assemble high-performing, safe, and generalizable model teams. The paper recommends using such principled selection algorithms as a necessary step before deploying real-world multi-LLM or multi-agent systems and offers a taxonomy and empirical evidence as guidance for practitioners.

Abstract: While multi-agent and model collaboration algorithms gain traction to combine the strengths of diverse Large Language Models (LLMs), existing systems remain bottlenecked on pre-defined and hand-crafted model pools. In this work, we investigate the problem of model selection in multi-LLM systems. We propose and systematically evaluate a taxonomy of 9 selection algorithms ranging from diversity of model descriptions, capability-aware behavioral diversity, and LLM-based recruiters. We conduct extensive experiments across two candidate pools of 10 and 32 models, deployed in four model collaboration algorithms, and evaluated across tasks spanning math, coding, QA, and reasoning. Results demonstrate that successful selection algorithms greatly outperform random or heuristics-based teams such as merely selecting the models with top individual performance, by up to 36.1% across settings. Specifically, capability- and training-based selection strategies alleviate selection variance and achieve the best performance, which we recommend to employ before deploying real-world multi-LLM systems. Further analysis reveals that larger candidate pools pose greater challenges to shallow selection heuristics, while algorithms grounded in interacting with candidate models and understanding model capability robustly filter out misaligned, unsafe models, as well as generalizing to novel, out-of-distribution tasks. Together, we establish that principled and informed team selection is critical and present strong model selection algorithms for assembling effective multi-LLM systems.

</details>


### [37] [BARRAC: Adaptation of an English Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis Approach for Classification Tasks in Arabic Dialects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38820)
*Ali Almutairi,Gelareh Mohammadi,Imran Razzak,Aditya Joshi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper adapts an English aspect-based sentiment analysis framework to Arabic NLP, proposing BARRAC, which integrates Arabic-specific linguistic markers and a two-stage training process, yielding improved performance over prior few-label methods and GPT-4o on multiple dialect datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most NLP progress, including task-specific frameworks like aspect-based sentiment analysis, has focused on majority languages such as English, leaving a gap in effectively handling Arabic and its dialects. The authors aim to test whether successful English task-specific approaches can be systematically adapted to Arabic, beyond just adapting models and datasets, and to address challenges in sentiment, sarcasm, and dialect identification in Arabic dialectal text.

Method: The authors introduce BARRAC (Brainstorming Alignment and Replaced Representation learning for ArabiC tasks), which adapts an English aspect-based sentiment analysis framework to Arabic. They replace the original framework’s consumer-review attribute pools with Arabic-specific linguistic devices and markers that capture dialectal sentiment, sarcasm, and dialect identification cues. Additionally, they replace the original noisy self-training strategy with a more robust two-stage training procedure, and then apply this adapted framework to five Arabic dialect datasets.

Result: On five Arabic dialect datasets, BARRAC attains a mean macro-F1 score of 63.93%, improving on the previous state-of-the-art few-label baseline by 3 percentage points and outperforming GPT-4o on four out of the five evaluated tasks. The authors also perform an error analysis that highlights persistent difficulties and failure modes in handling Arabic dialectal phenomena.

Conclusion: The study shows that carefully adapting task-specific frameworks developed for English—rather than only porting models or building new datasets—can significantly benefit Arabic NLP. BARRAC’s performance gains indicate that leveraging Arabic-specific linguistic markers and tailored training strategies is a promising path for handling sentiment, sarcasm, and dialect identification across Arabic dialects, while the remaining errors suggest directions for further refinement.

Abstract: With the rapid growth of Arabic NLP, several models, datasets and benchmarks have been reported.
