This paper asks whether approaches developed for majority languages like English can be adapted to Arabic tasks. We adapt an English aspect-based sentiment analysis framework to Arabic classification tasks and present the adaptation as BARRAC: Brainstorming Alignment and Replaced Representation learning for ArabiC tasks. BARRAC replaces consumer-review attribute pools with Arabic linguistic devices and markers for dialectal sentiment, sarcasm, and dialect identification, and replaces noisy self-training with two-stage training. Evaluated on five Arabic dialect datasets, BARRAC achieves a mean macro-F1 of 63.93\%, outperforming the best few-label SOTA by 3\%, and outperforming GPT-4o on four out of five tasks. Error analysis provides insights into remaining challenges. These results demonstrate that adapting task-specific approaches is a promising direction for Arabic NLP alongside adapting models, datasets and benchmarks.

</details>


### [38] [Forging LLM Authorship Fingerprints with Targeted Rewriting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38831)
*Haohan Yuan,Simin Chen,Xi Niu,Hanqing Guo,Depeng Xu,Haopeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that language-model attribution based on writing fingerprints can be intentionally manipulated, so accurate detection on raw outputs doesn’t guarantee true model identity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model attribution classifiers are increasingly used to detect which language model generated a given text, for provenance, accountability, or watermarking-like purposes. However, current evaluations mostly consider unmodified outputs and do not ask whether an adversary could rewrite text from one model so that it appears to come from another. The authors want to understand how vulnerable fingerprint-based attribution is to such targeted attacks and whether successful attribution actually implies authenticity of the source model.

Method: They formalize “targeted fingerprint transfer,” in which text generated by a source model is rewritten so that attribution classifiers label it as coming from a chosen target model while preserving the underlying content. Focusing on summarization (e.g., CNN/DailyMail) as a controlled conditional generation setting, they propose ForgePrint, a two-stage framework: (1) a search phase that explores multiple candidate rewrites and selects those that most strongly shift attribution towards the target model’s fingerprint, and (2) a distillation phase that trains a 4B-parameter Student model to produce such targeted-fingerprint rewrites in a single pass, using the successful search outputs as supervision. They evaluate against multiple, held-out attribution classifiers that the attack never queries and compare to several existing rewriting baselines.

Result: On CNN/DM summarization, the ForgePrint Student model achieves a 70.2% success rate at getting held-out attribution classifiers to label the rewritten text as coming from the target model, surpassing both its Teacher model (54.1%) and the best of six prior rewriting baselines (39.3%). The method also generalizes to cross-family transfer: when rewriting summaries produced by an open-source model to look like they were generated by various commercial models, the Student attains 68.3% targeted attribution success. These gains hold against classifiers that were never directly queried, demonstrating strong transferability of the attack.

Conclusion: Fingerprint-based language-model attribution is fragile under targeted rewriting attacks: an adversary can systematically rewrite a source model’s outputs so that standard attribution classifiers misidentify the generating model, even when those classifiers are accurate on unmodified text. Therefore, reliable provenance or claims of model identity cannot be based solely on text-only fingerprint detection. The results suggest that provenance systems must incorporate stronger, non-textual or cryptographic mechanisms and that evaluations of attribution methods should explicitly account for adversarial rewriting and targeted fingerprint transfer.

Abstract: Model-attribution classifiers can often identify which language model produced a text, making model-specific writing patterns a signal of provenance. Accurate attribution on unmodified text, however, does not show whether the prediction still identifies the original source after deliberate rewriting. We formulate this problem as targeted fingerprint transfer: rewriting one model's output so that attribution classifiers assign it to a chosen target model. We study summarization, where different models receive the same document and express the same underlying content, providing a controlled setting for conditional generation. We introduce ForgePrint, a search-then-distil framework that first searches for rewrites that move attribution toward a target fingerprint, then distils the selected rewrites into a one-pass 4B Student model. On CNN/DM, the Student reaches 70.2% target success rate, outperforming both its Teacher (54.1%) and the strongest of six published rewriting baselines (39.3%), against held-out classifiers that are never queried by the attack. It also reaches 68.3% target success when transferring summaries from an open model toward chosen commercial models. These results show that fingerprint detectability should not be conflated with source authenticity, and that text-only attribution can provide misleading evidence of model identity under targeted rewriting, even when it is accurate on unmodified text.

</details>


### [39] [Scaling Parameter and Context in Attention: Native Sparse Attention from Mixture-of-Head](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38832)
*Zizhuo Fu,Runsheng Wang,Meng Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes NAMOH, a sparse attention mechanism that activates only K of H heads per token so that scaling the number of heads scales context length efficiently without increasing KV storage, improving long-context quality and efficiency over dense models with similar parameter counts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard attention scaling increases parameters and improves quality, but becomes expensive at long contexts because all tokens must be retained for all heads. Moreover, if attention is the main means of retrieving context, scaling its parameters should ideally also extend usable context length rather than only improving quality at fixed context. The paper aims to bridge this gap by finding a way to scale attention parameters that also gives more efficient and effective long-context handling.

Method: They introduce NAMOH, an architecture-native sparse attention scheme where, for each token, only K out of H total heads are active. Each head stores and attends over a subsequence of tokens assigned to it, not the full sequence. A routing or selection process decides which heads each token uses, thereby simultaneously choosing which parameters are engaged and what context is visible, avoiding full-history scans. With balanced assignments, increasing H while keeping K fixed shortens each head’s history and reduces per-token KV access, without enlarging the total KV cache. They also add head-relative rotary position embeddings so that positional indices are local to each head’s subsequence, aiming to reduce position-related attention noise in long contexts. The design remains compatible with grouped-query attention (GQA) and other sparse attention methods.

Result: Empirically, NAMOH models outperform dense, fully activated baselines that have the same total parameter count, indicating better parameter efficiency. For long-context inference, NAMOH attains higher efficiency than smaller dense models that match it in active parameter count, thanks to reduced KV access and shorter per-head histories. The mechanism works in conjunction with GQA and other sparse attention schemes, showing architectural flexibility.

Conclusion: NAMOH demonstrates that carefully designed sparse, routed multi-head attention can convert attention-parameter scaling into practical context scaling: adding more heads increases effective context handling without proportionally increasing memory or compute for KV access. This yields models that are both more parameter-efficient and more suitable for long-context inference, offering a promising direction for future scaling strategies in transformer-based language models.

Abstract: Scaling attention parameters can improve language model quality, but retaining full token histories makes additional heads costly at long contexts. Furthermore, since attention retrieves and combines contextual information, parameter scaling should also support longer contexts. We therefore ask whether attention parameter scaling can directly enable efficient and effective context scaling. We introduce NAMOH, an architecture-native sparse attention mechanism that activates $K$ of $H$ heads per token. Each head retains only its assigned tokens and performs causal attention within this subsequence. Head selection thus jointly determines active parameters and available context without scanning the full history. Under balanced assignments, increasing $H$ at fixed $K$ shortens head histories and reduces per-token key-value (KV) access without increasing total KV storage. We further support head-relative rotary position embeddings to shorten positional spans within routed subsequences, aiming to mitigate position-induced attention noise. Experiments show that NAMOH can outperform fully activated models with the same total parameters, while enabling more efficient long-context inference than smaller dense models with matched active parameter counts. It remains compatible with GQA and existing sparse attention mechanisms. We hope this work offers a new path for scaling attention, with parameter scaling directly enabling context scaling.

</details>


### [40] [Where MLLMs Fail and Why: Causal Task Decomposition for Capability Failure Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38851)
*Xia Hu,Brian Potetz,Chun-Ta Lu,Huanfen Yao,Leonidas Guibas,Zhicheng Wang,Howard Zhou,Pengfei Xing,Andrew Gallagher*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a causal evaluation framework to distinguish whether MLLM failures on compositional tasks come from missing core capabilities or from earlier prerequisite errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end accuracy on multi-step, compositional tasks only shows whether a model’s final answer is right or wrong, but does not reveal if mistakes are due to intrinsic weaknesses in the targeted capability or due to cascading errors from earlier prerequisite sub-tasks. This makes it hard to understand and improve MLLMs’ reasoning and perception abilities in a structured way.

Method: The authors define a causal decomposition framework that breaks composite tasks into prerequisite unit tasks and uses controlled interventions where prerequisites are held unassisted, forced-correct, or forced-incorrect. They introduce capability metrics (NC, IC, RC) to measure performance under these different prerequisite conditions, and contribution metrics (N-Score, S-Score), adapted from probabilities of causation, to quantify how necessary and sufficient each prerequisite is for success. They instantiate this in CADET, a benchmark of 10 composite tasks decomposed into 46 unit tasks with 33k+ human-labeled questions spanning perception, spatial, temporal, and cognitive skills.

Result: Applied to frontier MLLMs, the framework reveals systematic error patterns that standard accuracy hides. When correct prerequisites are supplied, 54% of errors on cognitive tasks disappear, making cognitive tasks go from weakest to better than spatial and temporal tasks. Causal contribution analysis shows that only a few prerequisites account for most of the performance, with the single most important prerequisite recovering 84% of the benefit of providing all correct prerequisites.

Conclusion: The causal decomposition framework and CADET benchmark provide a more informative way to diagnose MLLM performance on compositional tasks than end-to-end accuracy alone. By separating intrinsic capability deficits from cascading prerequisite failures and pinpointing a small set of high-impact prerequisites, the approach guides more targeted model analysis and improvement.

Abstract: End-to-end accuracy on compositional tasks records how often MLLMs fail, but cannot distinguish whether a failure reflects an intrinsic deficit in the targeted capability or a cascading error from an upstream prerequisite. We propose a causal decomposition framework that isolates these two failure modes through controlled interventions on the prerequisite dependencies of each task. Our capability metrics (NC, IC, RC) score each task under unassisted, correct, or incorrect prerequisites to diagnose where failures arise; contribution metrics (N-Score, S-Score), adapted from probabilities of causation, quantify each prerequisite's necessity and sufficiency to determine why. We instantiate the framework in CADET, a diagnostic benchmark of 10 composite tasks decomposed into 46 unit tasks with over 33,000 human-annotated questions spanning perception, spatial, temporal, and cognitive categories. Diagnosing frontier MLLMs with our framework uncovers systematic patterns that end-to-end accuracy obscures. Capability-wise, supplying correct prerequisites eliminates 54\% of errors on cognitive tasks, lifting them from weakest to above spatial and temporal. Prerequisite-wise, causal contributions are concentrated in a few critical prerequisites, and supplying the single most important one alone captures 84\% of the gain from supplying all prerequisites.

</details>


### [41] [TRACE: Target-Aware Retrieval, Attributed Evidence, and Contract-Constrained Extraction for LitTraceQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38861)
*Sachin Gupta,Divya Godara*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TRACE is a system for answering grounded questions from scientific papers by tightly linking retrieval, evidence extraction, and answer formatting to the evaluation contract in LitTraceQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Simply finding relevant papers is not enough to score well on LitTraceQA; systems must return answers with precise, verifiable evidence and in formats that match strict evaluation criteria. There is a gap between accessing sources and producing scorer-recognized correct answers, which the authors term the grounding contract gap. The work is motivated by the need to systematically close this gap, especially for complex answer types like tables, where units, keys, and value identity are easy to mishandle.

Method: The authors propose TRACE (Target-Aware Retrieval, Attributed Evidence, and Contract-Constrained Extraction). TRACE performs target-grouped retrieval that keeps track of which paper a signal comes from and uses multiple representations (passage, object, alias, citation, dense) for indexing 27,487 papers. It then conducts independent typed evidence localization, including multimodal table extraction. For tables, TRACE first predicts the observation unit, then extracts values and constructs rows guided by the evaluation schema, with key normalization to ensure compatibility. A fail-closed validation step ensures outputs adhere strictly to contract constraints, avoiding overconfident but invalid answers.

Result: On the official 71-question LitTraceQA test set, TRACE’s audited clean-track artifact obtains an overall score of 0.760613, with 0.9728 paper F1, 0.6847 evidence F1, 0.9800 multiple-choice accuracy, 0.5423 table-row F1, and 0.3508 macro cell accuracy. On 11 public-development table records, a clean baseline and a coordinate-aware visual fill method achieve row F1 scores of 0.291 and 0.411, respectively, in a diagnostic comparison that includes fallback outputs and is not part of the official test results.

Conclusion: TRACE substantially narrows the grounding contract gap by combining target-aware retrieval, precise evidence attribution, and contract-constrained extraction, particularly for complex tabular answers. Its strong scores in paper selection, multiple-choice accuracy, and improved table-row extraction suggest that careful handling of observation units, row keys, and evidence localization is key to reliable, verifiable QA over scientific literature. Remaining errors highlight that accurately identifying locators, observation units, row keys, and exact source values is still challenging and an avenue for future improvement.

Abstract: Finding a relevant paper is not the same as producing a verifiable answer from it. LitTraceQA requires canonical paper identifiers, exact evidence at the page or object level, and typed answers that match the evaluator. We call the separation between source access and scorer-visible correctness the grounding contract gap. TRACE - Target-Aware Retrieval, Attributed Evidence, and Contract-Constrained Extraction - addresses this gap with target-grouped retrieval, independent typed evidence localization, multimodal table extraction, schema-driven table construction, and fail-closed validation. It indexes 27,487 papers through passage, object, alias, citation, and dense representations while retaining the question target behind each signal. For tables, TRACE predicts the observation unit before extracting values and assembles rows with evaluator-compatible key normalization. Our audited selected clean-track artifact scores 0.760613 on the official 71-question test set, including 0.9728 paper F1, 0.6847 evidence F1, 0.9800 multiple-choice accuracy, 0.5423 table-row F1, and 0.3508 macro cell accuracy. On 11 public-development table records, a clean baseline and coordinate-aware visual fill obtain row F1 of 0.291 and 0.411, respectively; this diagnostic comparison includes fallback outputs and is not an official-test claim. Remaining errors chiefly concern locator, observation-unit, row-key, and source-value identity.

</details>


### [42] [GraphForge: Training Working Agents with Graph-Anchored Workspace Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38923)
*Qisheng Su,Hanchen Wang,Guanru Zhu,Huicheng Jiang,Qiuyinzhe Zhang,Kou Shi,Zhen Fang,Ziao Zhang,Qingnan Ren,Zehui Chen,Tao Gui,Feng Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GraphForge is a framework to build realistic, verifiable tool-using agent tasks from real-world files using an evidence-graph, enabling better training and evaluation of working agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing data pipelines for training working agents either synthesize files (reducing realism/diversity) or use real files without task-specific verifiers (so results cannot be reliably checked). There is a need for a scalable way to create diverse, realistic tasks where each requirement is tied to concrete evidence in files and can be automatically verified.

Method: GraphForge starts from occupation-grounded seed scenarios to ensure controlled task diversity, then assembles a workspace of real files for each seed. It constructs an evidence graph describing relations among these files. Both task instructions and detailed grading rubrics are generated from this graph so that every requirement is explicitly supported by specific files. The pipeline then performs an initial rollout to test that the task is executable, and a revision agent repairs any issues in task or rubrics while remaining faithful to the original files. Using these validated tasks, they collect trajectories and fine-tune a Qwen3.6-27B model. They also apply rejection fine-tuning, selecting better candidate trajectories based on the evidence-anchored rubrics.

Result: Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B on 2,169 GraphForge-generated trajectories significantly improves performance on several benchmarks: GDPVal reaches 1445.7 (+65.7) with OpenHands, Workspace-Bench-Lite 63.7 (+7.7), and SpreadsheetBench II 24.0 (+13.7) with Claude Code. Rejection fine-tuning using rubric-scored rollouts yields additional gains across all benchmarks, indicating that rubric-based selection is effective.

Conclusion: Evidence-graph grounded task and rubric generation over real-file workspaces enables realistic, verifiable training data for working agents. GraphForge not only increases benchmark performance but also provides reliable, evidence-anchored rubrics that are useful for data curation via rejection fine-tuning. The released data and models can support further research on tool-using and file-manipulating agents.

Abstract: Working agents need to read diverse files, coordinate tools, and produce deliverables. Training such agents requires tasks built on many real files with verifiable results, but few pipelines exist to synthesize this kind of data. Existing pipelines either generate files with models, which lack realism and diversity, or build tasks on real files without task-specific verifiers, leaving result quality unchecked. We introduce GraphForge, an evidence-graph based framework that grounds both the task and its verification in real files. Starting from occupation-grounded seeds for controlled diversity, GraphForge assembles a workspace of real files for each seed and builds an evidence graph over their relations. Since the task statement and rubrics are both derived from this graph, task requirements are backed by the workspace files and each criterion is anchored to the files needed to verify it. An initial rollout further tests executability, and a revision agent repairs the task and rubrics against the original files before trajectories are collected. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B on 2,169 GraphForge trajectories brings GDPVal to 1445.7 (+65.7) under OpenHands, and Workspace-Bench-Lite and SpreadsheetBench II to 63.7 (+7.7) and 24.0 (+13.7) under Claude Code. Rejection fine-tuning on the SFT model's own rollouts, with candidates selected by the evidence-anchored rubrics, yields further improvements on all three benchmarks, suggesting that the rubrics provide a useful selection signal. The data and models are available.

</details>


### [43] [Making LLMs Say What They Think: Measuring and Improving CoT-Interpretability Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38972)
*Yihuai Hong,Shauli Ravfogel,Chen Zhao,Eunsol Choi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations from LLMs match the models’ true internal reasoning, proposes a metric (CIA) to measure this alignment using interpretability tools, finds that current models have only partial alignment, and shows that post-training can improve faithfulness of CoT without hurting accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CoT explanations are widely used as evidence of how LLMs reason, but emerging evidence shows that these explanations can be misleading: models’ internal computation can differ from the textual CoT, and CoTs can be altered without changing final answers. This undermines trust, safety, and accountability for LLM reasoning. The authors are motivated to rigorously measure and improve how faithfully CoTs reflect the model’s actual internal reasoning processes.

Method: 1) Define CoT-Interpretability Alignment (CIA), a quantitative metric that compares a model’s chain-of-thought traces with its internal reasoning strategies as inferred via interpretability tools. 2) Apply CIA to three reasoning-style tasks—two-hop question answering, hint intervention, and integer multiplication—across three different LLMs to measure baseline alignment. 3) Use post-training (likely RL-style training) where the reward combines task accuracy and a parametric faithfulness signal, encouraging the model’s CoT to match the reasoning patterns detected in its activations. 4) Analyze the resulting models, including generalization behavior of the improved faithfulness.

Result: Baseline evaluation shows limited CoT–internal reasoning alignment across tasks, with CIA values ranging from about 44.8% to 75.9%, indicating that CoTs are only partially faithful. After post-training with a combined accuracy and faithfulness reward, models achieve significantly higher CIA scores while preserving or even improving task accuracy, suggesting that explicit reasoning traces can be made more faithful without sacrificing performance. Additional analyses characterize how these improvements generalize across tasks and settings.

Conclusion: CoT explanations from current LLMs do not reliably reflect their internal reasoning, but this faithfulness can be measured and improved. The proposed CIA metric provides a concrete framework for auditing how well CoTs align with internal computations, and post-training with faithfulness-oriented rewards can substantially increase this alignment while maintaining or boosting task performance. This offers a practical route toward more trustworthy explicit reasoning in LLMs and establishes CIA-based evaluation as a useful tool for future work on interpretable and reliable CoT reasoning.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) traces often serve as a proxy for how Large Language Models (LLMs) arrive at their answers. However, growing evidence shows that models' CoT often fails to reflect their internal computations and can be changed without affecting their final answers. In this work, we measure and improve the alignment between the reasoning described in an LLM's CoT and what it computes internally. We propose CoT-Interpretability Alignment (CIA), a metric that measures the agreement between a model's CoT traces and its internal reasoning strategies as detected by interpretability tools. We evaluate CIA on three tasks (two-hop question answering, hint intervention, and integer multiplication) across three LLMs, finding that LLMs exhibit limited alignment across all tasks (44.8-75.9%). We then experiment with improving CIA via post-training, setting both the task accuracy and parametric faithfulness signals as a reward. Experiments show that we can substantially improve CoT parametric faithfulness while maintaining or improving the task accuracy. We provide rich analysis, such as their generalization patterns. Our work provides both a framework for auditing CoT parametric faithfulness and a pathway toward making models' explicit reasoning more trustworthy. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yihuaihong/CIA-minimal-repro.

</details>


### [44] [Fairness Beyond a Single Run: Training-Seed Variability in Speech LLM Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38976)
*Srishti Ginjala,Eric Fosler-Lussier,Srinivasan Parthasarathy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that randomness in training (seed choice) can affect demographic fairness metrics in speech recognition more than architectural or compression changes, so single-run fairness reports are unreliable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most ASR fairness studies report demographic gaps from a single training run, implicitly assuming that the choice of random seed has little impact. However, large models are known to exhibit significant run-to-run variability. The authors want to quantify how much of the observed fairness gaps are due to genuine design choices (like audio compression) versus training stochasticity, and whether standard accuracy metrics detect problematic runs.

Method: They fine-tune a speech large language model by training only the Q-former projector and LoRA adapters while keeping the encoder, base decoder, data, and decoding fixed. They vary two factors: (1) five audio compression levels, and (2) six random seeds. For each of the 30 resulting systems, they evaluate on Common Voice and Fair-Speech, computing fairness metrics across demographic axes such as ethnicity, age, and gender. They perform a balanced 3x3 decomposition to attribute variance in fairness gaps to seed vs. compression and test significance. They also analyze word error rates on LibriSpeech and Common Voice to check that seeds do not simply produce failed models, and they control for accuracy and dropout. Finally, they repeat with a larger and more diverse adaptation set (960 hours) to study scaling effects.

Result: At 460 hours of clean LibriSpeech adaptation, random seed explains most of the variance in fairness metrics across several demographic axes, often more than audio compression does. For Fair-Speech ethnicity normalized gap, 85.3% of the variation is attributed to seed and only 8.3% to compression, with the effect statistically significant (p = 0.009). Compression has more explanatory power for age and gender gaps, but seed remains influential. Word error rate on held-out LibriSpeech varies only by 0.04 points across seeds, while Common Voice WER varies by 8.57 points, showing the seeds are not just producing obviously bad runs. The large seed effect persists even after controlling for accuracy and dropout. Increasing and diversifying the adaptation set to 960 hours reduces but does not eliminate seed-driven variability in fairness. On Fair-Speech ethnicity, two single-run systems must differ by more than 0.30 normalized gap for the difference to exceed what can be explained by seed variation alone.

Conclusion: Demographic fairness measurements for ASR systems are highly sensitive to random seed, often more so than to changes in audio compression, especially for ethnicity-related gaps. Single-run fairness reports can therefore be misleading, as run-to-run variability can overshadow the effect of model or data changes. Even when models have similar accuracy, their fairness profiles can differ substantially due to stochastic training effects, and scaling the adaptation data only partially stabilizes fairness. Fairness evaluations should thus average over multiple seeds or otherwise account for variability to draw reliable conclusions about the impact of design choices on demographic gaps.

Abstract: Demographic fairness gaps in automatic speech recognition are almost always reported from a single training run. We fine-tune the Q-former projector and LoRA adapters of a speech LLM at five audio compression factors and six random seeds, holding the encoder, base decoder, data and decoding fixed, and evaluate every run on Common Voice and Fair-Speech. At 460 h of clean LibriSpeech, the seed moves fairness metrics more than compression does on most demographic axes. A balanced 3x3 decomposition attributes 85.3% of the variation in Fair-Speech ethnicity normalized gap to the seed against 8.3% to compression (p = 0.009), though compression explains more on age and gender. Held-out LibriSpeech word error rate spreads by 0.04 points across those seeds while Common Voice spreads by 8.57, so these are not failed runs, and the effect survives controlling for accuracy and dropout. Scaling and diversifying the adaptation set to 960 h damps the effect but does not remove it. On Fair-Speech ethnicity, two single-run systems must differ by more than 0.30 in normalized gap to exceed seed variability.

</details>


### [45] [When Clipping Reverses Correction: Failure Dynamics of Pointwise Forward-KL On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38995)
*Di Huang,Hao Li,Yixin Chen,Fuhai Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes on-policy self-distillation with pointwise clipped forward KL, showing that clipping causes harmful divergences from the teacher and leads to severe repetition, both theoretically and empirically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy self-distillation has shown promise for improving models using their own generated data, but prior work observed that training is sensitive and introduced pointwise clipping of the forward KL without fully understanding its consequences. As many follow-up works have adopted this trick, it is important to rigorously analyze whether this clipping is actually beneficial or may introduce failure modes, particularly for mathematical reasoning where training signals can be dominated by stylistic tokens.

Method: The authors perform controlled, matched training runs of OPSD that differ only in whether pointwise clipping is applied to the forward KL objective. They empirically study the resulting model behaviors, particularly repetition patterns, and analyze token-level probability dynamics. In parallel, they conduct a theoretical analysis of the clipped objective, proving conditions under which clipping fails to guide the student toward the teacher and can instead push the student’s probabilities (clipped and unclipped tokens) away from those of the teacher.

Result: Empirically, models trained with pointwise forward-KL clipping exhibit significantly more repetitions that persist through the ends of responses compared to unclipped models. Within repetitive segments, the clipped student assigns lower probability than the teacher to exiting the repetition and higher probability to continuing it, whereas unclipped students remain closer to teacher probabilities and avoid such pathologies. Theoretically, the authors show that the clipped objective may not correct the student toward the teacher distribution and can even invert the training signal, pushing probabilities further from the teacher for both clipped and unclipped tokens.

Conclusion: Pointwise clipping of the forward KL in on-policy self-distillation, although intended to stabilize training, can introduce severe and systematic failure modes such as persistent repetition by misaligning the gradient signal with the teacher distribution. The study suggests that this form of clipping is fundamentally flawed for OPSD and should be reconsidered or replaced, and that careful analysis of training objectives and heuristics is crucial when deploying self-distillation techniques.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on its own generated responses using feedback from the same model conditioned on privileged information. On mathematical reasoning, the original OPSD study finds that stylistic tokens can dominate the training signal over math-related tokens, and that pointwise clipping of the forward KL objective stabilizes training. Pointwise clipping caps each vocabulary-wise forward KL term at a fixed threshold before summing over the vocabulary. Follow-up studies have adopted this clipping, but its effect on training has not been directly examined. In matched training runs differing only in whether clipping is applied, we observe that clipped runs produce substantially more repetitions that persist to the end of the response than their unclipped counterparts. We trace this failure to the clipped objective. We prove that the clipped objective can fail to correct the student toward the teacher and can instead push clipped and unclipped token probabilities away from its teacher. Our training runs agree with this analysis: inside repetitions, the clipped student places less probability than its teacher on leaving the repetition, and more on continuing it, whereas the unclipped runs stay close to their teachers.

</details>


### [46] [Settle: Learning When to Stop Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38997)
*Ryan Brown,Zihao Fu,Chris Russell*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Settle, a method to stop reasoning models early based on answer stability, saving tokens with minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning language models often continue generating long chains-of-thought even after their final answer has effectively stabilized, wasting tokens and compute. Existing stopping criteria either hurt accuracy or require special decoding. The authors want a general, training-time method that learns when to stop while preserving base-model behavior and using standard inference.

Method: Settle analyzes completed reasoning traces to detect when the model’s answer becomes stable, then trains the model’s existing end-of-reasoning token to fire near that point. It fine-tunes so that the stop signal aligns with answer stability while regularizing other token predictions to stay close to the base model. At inference, the model is decoded normally and stops when it emits the learned end-of-reasoning token. The paper also defines a stopping score that estimates whether a currently correct answer will remain correct if generation continued.

Result: On MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B, Settle reduces token usage by about 40% with only a 0.5 percentage point drop in accuracy compared to the base model. Compared to supervised fine-tuning on traces naively truncated at the first stable answer, Settle achieves 6.16 percentage points higher accuracy at nearly the same token count. Its stopping score reliably predicts persistence of correctness and it outperforms other evaluated stopping methods in the accuracy–token-count trade-off.

Conclusion: Learning to stop based on answer stability via Settle can substantially cut reasoning token budgets with negligible accuracy loss, and even improve over naive truncation-based fine-tuning. Because it only retrains an existing end-of-reasoning token and uses standard decoding, it is simple to deploy and extends the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus token count for stopping strategies in reasoning models.

Abstract: Reasoning models often continue generating after their answers have settled. Settle learns when to stop from answer stability in completed traces. It trains the existing end-of-reasoning token while keeping other predictions close to the base model, and requires only ordinary decoding at inference. On MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B, Settle reduces token count by 40% with a 0.5-percentage-point decrease in accuracy. It gains 6.16 percentage points over supervised fine-tuning on the same traces shortened at their first stable answer, at nearly identical token counts. Its stopping score predicts whether a correct answer will remain correct. Settle extends the accuracy-token-count Pareto frontier of the evaluated stopping methods.

</details>


### [47] [The Invisible Language Tax: Token Premiums of French and Regional Languages in 2026 LLM Tokenizers, and a French-Optimized Prototype](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39001)
*Thomas Serval*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper measures and analyzes how many more tokens different languages require under common LLM tokenizers, showing substantial cost/context penalties for French and regional French languages, investigates how tokenizer training choices affect this “token premium,” and proposes a French-optimized tokenizer prototype that reduces token counts in French (and slightly in English) but not other languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM usage cost and context limits are defined in tokens, yet tokenization efficiency varies significantly by language. Users of some languages may thus pay more and get less usable context for the same content, creating hidden inequities. There is little systematic measurement of this token premium across modern tokenizers and languages, nor clear evidence on how tokenizer design can mitigate it for specific languages such as French and its regional variants.

Method: 1) Empirically measure token counts for many languages under seven major 2026-era tokenizers using standardized multilingual corpora (NTREX-128 translations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights for regional languages). 2) Quantify token “premiums” relative to English for French, Simplified Chinese, and regional/overseas French languages. 3) Analyze how LLM usage patterns (history re-sending, fixed context windows, tiered pricing) magnify these premiums in real agent-like workflows. 4) Run a controlled tokenizer training experiment (BPE on Europarl with 50k vocab) to see how including French in training data affects French vs. English token efficiency. 5) Design and evaluate Baracoda FR v1.2, a byte-level BPE tokenizer with Tekken-like vocabulary size, benchmarked on six pre-registered French/English corpora and checked for train-test leakage and equal token budget comparisons.

Result: 1) Across seven modern tokenizers, French consistently needs 31–58% more tokens than English for the same content. 2) Simplified Chinese ranges from 5% fewer tokens to 40% more, but is almost always cheaper than French (in 6/7 tokenizers). 3) Regional and overseas French languages incur 1.6–3.3× the English token counts, implying strong hidden penalties. 4) In controlled BPE experiments, adding French to tokenizer training reduces the French token premium with diminishing returns while slightly harming English efficiency. 5) The specialized Baracoda FR v1.2 tokenizer uses on average 11.5% fewer tokens than Mistral’s Tekken for French and 3.7% fewer for English on six held-out corpora, with robustness checks against overlap and fixed-token comparisons. 6) However, it underperforms on other languages and does not beat CroissantLLM at similar vocabulary size, showing the trade-off between specialization and multilingual coverage.

Conclusion: Tokenization choices create systematic and substantial cost and context disadvantages for certain languages, notably French and its regional varieties, under current major LLM tokenizers. These disadvantages are amplified by typical LLM usage patterns. Training tokenizers with better coverage of disadvantaged languages and even designing specialized tokenizers (like Baracoda FR) can significantly reduce token premiums for those languages, but at the expense of other languages and without yet-demonstrated gains in model quality. Token efficiency thus emerges as an important, measurable fairness and design dimension for LLM services, requiring further work on both tokenizer design and downstream model evaluation.

Abstract: LLM services are billed per token and context windows are measured in tokens, yet the number of tokens needed for the same content varies across languages. We measure this token premium on seven tokenizers of widely used 2026 models (OpenAI o200k, Llama 3, Qwen3, DeepSeek V3/V4, Gemma 3, Mistral Tekken, and the Claude generation-5 tokenizer via Anthropic's counting API) on NTREX-128 (124 non-English reference translations) and on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights for regional languages. French requires 31% to 58% more tokens than English, whereas Simplified Chinese ranges from 5% fewer to 40% more and is cheaper than French on six of the seven tokenizers. Regional and overseas languages of France pay roughly 1.6 to 3.3 times the English count. We discuss how history re-sending, tiered pricing and fixed context windows amplify the absolute gap in agentic use. In a controlled experiment (BPE, Europarl, 50k vocabulary), adding French to tokenizer training data quickly reduces the premium, with diminishing returns and a growing cost for English. Finally, we present Baracoda FR v1.2, a byte-level BPE prototype with Tekken's vocabulary size. On a final test of six corpora never consulted during design, with a protocol declared fixed beforehand, it uses 11.5% fewer tokens than Tekken on French and 3.7% fewer on English; results hold after removing test sentences overlapping the training data and with an equal ordinary-token budget. It is worse on other languages and, at comparable vocabulary size, does not outperform CroissantLLM. These are segmentation results only; effects on model quality and task cost remain to be shown.

</details>


### [48] [Evidence First, Arithmetic Second: A System Report and Failure Analysis for DocSem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39013)
*Divya Godara,Sachin Gupta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A system (EVICALC) for the DocSem shared task that combines PDF passage selection, LLM-based arithmetic expression generation, and local execution was evaluated; it achieved low joint accuracy in the official test but high answer accuracy in a different public validation setting, with descriptive error analysis suggesting OCR and layout issues and motivating further evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build and evaluate a system that can solve document-based arithmetic tasks in the DocSem shared task by reading PDFs, locating evidence passages, generating arithmetic expressions with a language model, and executing them, while also enabling detailed error inspection to understand performance limitations such as OCR and layout problems.

Method: The system reads PDF documents, selects candidate evidence passages, queries a language model to convert the selected text into an explicit arithmetic expression, and then evaluates that expression with local code. It stores intermediate artifacts to support failure analysis. The authors evaluate EVICALC on the official DocSem final test set (1,730 tasks, reporting joint accuracy) and in a separate public-validation run (reporting answer accuracy and evidence F1). They additionally conduct manual, post-hoc qualitative error analysis and a small exploratory study that uses page images to retrieve evidence identifiers on a 100-document subset.

Result: On the official final test evaluation for the DocSem shared task, EVICALC obtains 8.61% joint accuracy over 1,730 tasks. In a separate public-validation setting with different configuration and metrics, it reaches 92.17% answer accuracy and 1.00 evidence F1, though the authors emphasize that the settings are not directly comparable. In manual inspection, they identify at least one failure case where OCR and block grouping errors merged the relevant passage with unrelated text, leading the system to answer from the wrong context. In an exploratory page-image reading study on 100 documents, the system successfully returns evidence identifiers for only 22 documents.

Conclusion: The system can perform very well under some configurations and metrics (public validation) but fares poorly on the official DocSem final test under the stricter joint-accuracy metric, and the available descriptive analyses suggest—but do not prove—that document processing issues such as OCR errors and block grouping may significantly affect performance. The authors conclude that more systematic evaluation and analysis are needed to identify performance bottlenecks and understand the discrepancy between evaluation settings.

Abstract: EVICALC, our system for the DocSem shared task, achieved 8.61% joint accuracy on 1,730 tasks in the official final test evaluation. It reads a PDF, selects a passage, asks a language model to write an arithmetic expression, and evaluates that expression in local code. Saved intermediate results support inspection of failures. A separate public-validation run achieved 92.17% answer accuracy and 1.00 evidence F1. The configurations and metrics differ, so these scores are not a controlled comparison. Our manual, post-hoc analysis is descriptive: in one inspected case, optical character recognition (OCR) and block grouping merged the relevant passage into another block, and the system answered from unrelated text. An exploratory study of reading page images on 100 documents returned evidence identifiers for only 22 documents. These descriptive findings motivate further evaluation; they do not establish the causes of the overall score.

</details>


### [49] [A Missing Piece for Trustworthy AI Reviewers: From Benchmarking Rhetorical Robustness to SciCore Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39027)
*Chenguang Wang,Ming Li,Chengrui Fan,Jianpeng Chen,Han Chen,Tianyi Zhou,Dawei Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper defines and studies “rhetorical robustness” of AI reviewers, introduces a benchmark (RobustReview) to measure it, and proposes a new dual-branch reviewer (SciCore) that is more robust to wording changes while still discriminating between papers and aligning with humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI reviewers can give different scores to scientifically identical manuscripts that differ only in wording. This rewards rhetorical polishing rather than real scientific improvement and undermines trust in AI-assisted peer review. There is a need for explicit definitions, benchmarks, and methods that ensure AI reviewers are stable to content-preserving rewrites while still able to distinguish between good and bad papers.

Method: 1) Formalize “rhetorical robustness” as the joint property of (a) stability of reviews across content-preserving rewrites of the same paper and (b) discrimination across different papers. 2) Build RobustReview, a controlled benchmark containing 1,260 versions of full manuscripts created via systematic rewrites, and test 30 different AI reviewer configurations (different backbones and prompting protocols). 3) Analyze the trade-offs between rewrite sensitivity, score collapse (loss of discrimination), and alignment with human judgments, revealing cases of “false robustness” where insensitivity to rewrites comes from giving nearly the same score to all papers. 4) Propose SciCore, a dual-branch reviewer that produces one judgment from the full manuscript text and another from an extracted, structured “science core” (e.g., aims, methods, results), then averages them to reduce rhetorical sensitivity while retaining discrimination. 5) Compare SciCore against other reviewers, including a main comparison against GPT-5.5-based reviewers, on the benchmark and human-alignment metrics.

Result: RobustReview shows that some AI reviewers that appear robust to rewrites actually suffer from score collapse, losing the ability to distinguish between different papers (“false robustness”). Human alignment and rhetorical robustness give different rankings of reviewer setups, indicating that standard alignment metrics are insufficient. Content-focused prompting alone does not consistently improve rhetorical robustness across model backbones. SciCore achieves a superior combination of stability to rewrites and discrimination between papers on the benchmark, and it maintains competitive alignment with human reviewers compared to other GPT-5.5-based reviewers.

Conclusion: Rhetorical robustness—stability to content-preserving rewrites plus discrimination between papers—is a distinct and important target for evaluating AI reviewers, separate from human alignment alone. Existing reviewer configurations can be misleadingly judged robust if they simply collapse scores. The proposed benchmark, RobustReview, provides a way to systematically measure this property. The SciCore dual-branch architecture, which integrates full-manuscript assessment with a normalized science-core representation, demonstrably improves rhetorical robustness while retaining strong human alignment, illustrating that explicitly modeling core scientific content can mitigate sensitivity to superficial rhetorical changes.

Abstract: AI reviewers can assign different judgments to manuscripts that report the same science in different wording, potentially rewarding rhetorical optimization over scientific improvement. We formulate Rhetorical Robustness as the joint requirement of stability across content-preserving rewrites and discrimination across papers. We introduce RobustReview, a controlled full-manuscript benchmark with 1,260 manuscript versions, and evaluate 30 reviewer configurations. The benchmark reveals false robustness, where low rewrite sensitivity coincides with score collapse across papers, and shows that human alignment and rhetorical robustness rank reviewers differently. Moreover, the evaluated content-focused prompting protocol does not consistently improve robustness across backbones. Motivated by these findings, we introduce SciCore, a dual-branch reviewer that averages a full-manuscript judgment with a judgment based on an extracted, structured science core. This design combines manuscript-level assessment with a content-normalized view intended to reduce rhetorical sensitivity. In our primary GPT-5.5 comparison, SciCore achieves a leading joint stability-discrimination profile among the benchmarked reviewers while maintaining competitive human alignment. These results identify rhetorical robustness as a distinct evaluation target and demonstrate the potential of science-core review to improve it.

</details>


### [50] [RSIGame: Autonomous Agentic Game Development with Recursive Self-improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39045)
*Wenyi Wu,Minghao Fu,Jieyu You,Kun Zhou,Siqi Liu,Aayush Salvi,Yiheng Lin,Ce Zhang,Xiaohan Lan,Jiahui Zhu,Yujie Zhong,Qi She,Biwei Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RSIGame is an autonomous, recursive self-improvement framework that iteratively explores, diagnoses, and fixes issues in LLM-generated games, and then trains the generator on successful experiences to substantially boost game quality and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While large language models can already generate playable games, pushing these games from merely playable to robust, high-quality experiences is difficult. Simple iterative refinement often overfits to a few test cases, leaving hidden bugs, missing behaviors, and poor generalization to diverse player interactions. The authors aim to create a systematic, autonomous process that can reliably improve game quality over long development horizons and make better use of prior successful development experience.

Method: The authors propose RSIGame, an autonomous agentic framework with recursive self-improvement structured into two nested loops. The local loop repeatedly explores the executable game, diagnoses encountered issues, prioritizes them, and revises the game via evidence-grounded changes, guided by an evolving checklist that accumulates tests and improvement rules over time. The global loop tracks holistic game quality, maintains and updates the best-performing checkpoint, and monitors for saturation or regression across longer development trajectories. Additionally, they perform experience internalization: successful edits and strategies obtained during development are used to further train the game generator model itself, so future generations start from a stronger prior. They evaluate RSIGame across 140 GameCraft-Bench tasks, two game engines (Godot and Phaser), and five different generator models.

Result: Across a wide experimental setup spanning 140 GameCraft-Bench tasks, two engines, and five generators, RSIGame consistently improves the quality of generated games when given the same development budget as baselines. With experience internalization, the Qwen3.8-27B model achieves scores of 61.38 on Godot and 58.53 on Phaser, surpassing GPT-5.5 in a one-shot setting, while also cutting Qwen’s generation token usage by a factor of about 11.

Conclusion: Structuring game development as recursive self-improvement with coordinated local and global loops, plus internalizing successful development experience into the generator, yields more robust and higher-quality LLM-generated games under fixed budgets. RSIGame not only raises final game quality but also improves efficiency, demonstrating that autonomous agentic development and learning from past improvements is a promising direction for automatic game generation.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models have made automatic game generation increasingly feasible, yet reliably improving generated games beyond a playable version remains challenging. Naive iterative refinement can easily overfit a small set of test cases, producing fragile games with unresolved bugs, missing behaviors, and poor generalization to broader player interactions. We introduce RSIGame, an autonomous agentic game development framework with recursive self-improvement. RSIGame organizes development into complementary local and global loops. Concretely, a local explore-diagnose-improve loop broadly explores the executable game, diagnoses and prioritizes discovered issues, and performs evidence-grounded revision, where an evolving checklist continually accumulates new testing and improvement guidance. A global loop tracks overall quality, preserves the best checkpoint, and detects saturation or regression over long-horizon development. Beyond test-time improvement, RSIGame further internalizes successful development experience into the generator through training. Across 140 GameCraft-Bench tasks, two game engines, and five generators, RSIGame consistently improves game quality under matched development budgets. Notably, experience internalization enables Qwen3.8-27B to reach 61.38 on Godot and 58.53 on Phaser, exceeding GPT-5.5 one-shot scores while reducing Qwen's generation tokens by 11 times.

</details>


### [51] [Structure vs. Chain-of-Thought: Evaluating LLM Criteria Extraction for Depression Severity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39049)
*Xinkai Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper compares two ways of using large language models to rate depression severity from Reddit posts: direct severity labeling vs. extracting clinical questionnaire criteria and converting them to a score. It finds that criteria extraction is more auditable but does not reliably improve agreement with human labels or detection of severe cases, and often worsens misses of severe posts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is growing interest in using LLMs to assess mental health signals from social media. One promising idea is to have models identify specific clinical criteria (e.g., PHQ-9, BDI-II) and translate these into severity scores, which should be easier for clinicians to audit than opaque direct severity predictions. However, it is unclear whether this criteria-extraction strategy actually improves reliability, calibration, or clinical usefulness (e.g., catching severe cases) compared to simpler direct prompting or chain-of-thought reasoning from the post to a severity label.

Method: The authors evaluate three LLMs ranging from a 9B-parameter model to frontier-scale models on two Reddit corpora. They compare: (1) direct prompting for a depression severity label, (2) chain-of-thought prompting that reasons to a label, and (3) criteria extraction where the LLM marks which PHQ-9 or BDI-II clinical criteria are present and rule-based code maps the count to a severity label. They test two ways of setting decision thresholds: (a) fitting thresholds on labeled data, and (b) fixing thresholds a priori based on PHQ-9 questionnaire definitions. Performance is measured using quadratic weighted kappa for ordinal agreement, and they analyze detection of severe cases specifically, as well as behavior differences on a corpus from depression communities. They also compare LLM-based criteria extraction to a traditional model built on the stress dataset’s own features, including word counts.

Result: For the two frontier LLMs, criteria extraction only outperforms chain-of-thought on one corpus and only when thresholds are tuned on labeled data; even then the gains are not statistically significant, with or without recalibrating chain-of-thought. Using fixed PHQ-9-based thresholds, criteria extraction never beats chain-of-thought, despite models frequently marking multiple criteria per post. The smaller 9B model behaves anomalously on the depression-community corpus, classifying most posts as severe under both direct and chain-of-thought prompting, while a simple a priori rules-based scheme performs better without label-tuning; after recalibration of chain-of-thought, the differences disappear, suggesting a calibration rather than reasoning advantage. Critically, PHQ-9-based criteria extraction misses a large fraction of severe posts, and moving from direct prompting to chain-of-thought to criteria extraction typically increases the rate of missed severe cases. On the main (relabeled stress) corpus, a non-LLM model using the dataset’s own engineered features performs similarly to frontier LLM criteria extraction under fixed rules, with no significant difference.

Conclusion: While criteria-extraction approaches offer better auditability—clinicians can inspect which clinical criteria the model believes are present—they do not deliver consistent or significant accuracy gains over direct or chain-of-thought prompting for depression severity rating from Reddit posts. In multiple setups, especially with fixed, clinically motivated thresholds, criteria extraction fails to improve ordinal agreement and can substantially worsen the detection of severe cases. Improvements seen after threshold tuning appear largely due to calibration rather than deeper clinical understanding. Moreover, traditional models using simple text-derived features can match frontier LLM criteria extraction under comparable rule-based schemes. Overall, the paper suggests caution in assuming that clinically structured, criteria-based LLM outputs are inherently more reliable or clinically safer than direct predictions, particularly when severe-case detection is the primary concern.

Abstract: A large language model (LLM) can rate depression severity directly from a social media post or mark which clinical criteria the post shows and let code turn the count into a label. The latter is easier to audit because a clinician can check each marked criterion. We compare these approaches on two Reddit corpora using three LLMs (from 9B to frontier scale) and two questionnaires (PHQ-9, BDI-II), and measure agreement with quadratic weighted kappa. For the two frontier models, criteria extraction scores above chain-of-thought on one corpus only when its decision thresholds are fitted on labeled data. Neither model's gain is significant, with or without recalibrating chain-of-thought on the same labels. With thresholds fixed a priori from PHQ-9's criteria, extraction shows no gain on either corpus, even where models mark over two criteria per post. The 9B model behaves differently on a corpus from depression communities. It labels most posts severe, whether prompted directly or with chain-of-thought, while the a priori rule beats both without labels. After chain-of-thought is recalibrated on the same labels, no significant gap remains, consistent with a calibration effect. Yet higher ordinal agreement does not ensure better detection of severe cases. PHQ-9 criteria extraction misses most severe posts, and moving from direct prompting to chain-of-thought and then to extraction increases misses in nearly all comparisons. On the primary corpus, a relabeled stress dataset, a model using that dataset's own features, including word counts from the text, is not significantly different from frontier criteria extraction under the a priori rule.

</details>


### [52] [CORE: Conflict-Oriented Reasoning Elimination for Verifiable Language-Model Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39069)
*Siyu Song,Rui Xu,Jia Lin,Kai Liu,Weifang Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes CORE, a conflict-guided search controller for test-time reasoning that uses certified failure explanations from a verifier to backjump and cache conflicts, improving efficiency and success over chronological repair and Tree of Thoughts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing test-time reasoning systems typically handle errors by restarting or locally revising the most recent step, which is inefficient when the true cause of failure lies in earlier decisions. There is a need for a more principled way to use verifier feedback so that search can avoid re-exploring known-bad regions of the decision space and better direct language-model reasoning.

Method: The authors introduce CORE, a search controller that interacts with a verifier capable of producing certified conflict cores—minimal sets of decisions that cannot all be satisfied together. When a failure is detected, CORE requests a conflict core, backjumps directly to the most recent decision in that core (skipping irrelevant later decisions), and adds the conflict to a cache so the same combination is not revisited. They analyze conditions (sound verifier, finite branching and depth, exhaustive proposals) under which this search remains complete and sound. They then instantiate CORE in graph-coloring benchmarks and multiple reasoning tasks with Qwen models, comparing it to chronological repair and Tree of Thoughts.

Result: On 2,000 planted graph-coloring instances with matched proposals and an exact verifier, CORE cuts median verifier calls by 39.8% at 30 variables and 35.0% at 36 variables relative to chronological repair, with additional gains from caching. Across five reasoning tasks, CORE attains 75.9% mean success with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and 84.2% with Qwen3-8B, outperforming Tree of Thoughts (72.5% and 81.8%, respectively) while also requiring fewer verifier calls and fewer generated tokens.

Conclusion: CORE demonstrates that using certified failure explanations from a verifier to guide backjumping and conflict caching can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of test-time language-model reasoning. Under mild conditions, the method is complete and does not prune correct solutions, and empirically it outperforms common baselines such as chronological repair and Tree of Thoughts on both synthetic and real reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Test-time reasoning systems often respond to failure by restarting or revising the latest step, even when an earlier decision caused the error. We introduce CORE, a search controller that requests a certified conflict core from a verifier, backjumps to the latest decision in that core, and caches the conflict to avoid repeating it. Under sound verification, finite branching and depth, and exhaustive proposals, the uncapped search is complete and never prunes a valid solution. On 2,000 planted graph-coloring instances with matched proposals and an exact verifier, CORE reduces median verifier calls by 39.8% at 30 variables and 35.0% at 36 variables relative to chronological repair; caching further improves on backjumping alone. Across five reasoning tasks, CORE achieves 75.9% mean success with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and 84.2% with Qwen3-8B, compared with 72.5% and 81.8% for Tree of Thoughts. It also uses fewer verifier calls and generated tokens on both backbones. These results show the value of using certified failure explanations to direct language-model search.

</details>


### [53] [LexReward: A Taxonomy-Driven Reward Framework for Legal Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39071)
*Yida Cai,Xin Dai,Bingxiang He,Huiyuan Xie,Yuxiao Ye,Zhenghao Liu,Yang Bai,Zhiyuan Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes LexReward, a taxonomy-based reward framework to evaluate and improve legal language models along three dimensions: Style, Element, and Chain, and shows it boosts legal reasoning via DPO and RL without needing reference answers at reward time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal LLMs need nuanced feedback that goes beyond simple correctness, capturing stylistic quality, legal content coverage, and reasoning structure. Existing reward methods are coarse, holistic, and not very interpretable or domain-specific, limiting their usefulness for training specialized legal models.

Method: The authors design LexReward, a taxonomy for legal response quality with three dimensions: (1) Style (lexical and syntactic quality), (2) Element (coverage of legal subjects, facts, statutes, and decisions), and (3) Chain (order, completeness, correctness, and non-redundancy of legal reasoning). For each dimension, they create detailed rubrics defining evaluation criteria and discrete quality levels. These rubric-based scores are used to generate pairwise preference data for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and to train dimension-specific reward models (LexRM). They then use the learned reward models for downstream RL-based policy optimization targeting each dimension separately, without needing reference answers during reward computation.

Result: Rubric-based rewards can reliably differentiate between legal responses of varying quality across the three dimensions. DPO training on the constructed preference data improves the model’s performance simultaneously in Style, Element, and Chain. The learned dimension-specific reward models (LexRM) further enable effective reinforcement learning, where optimizing a policy with respect to a given dimension reward improves that particular aspect of legal responses. Dimension-wise empirical analyses confirm the discriminative power and usefulness of the proposed taxonomy and reward construction.

Conclusion: A structured, taxonomy-driven reward framework tailored to legal tasks can produce interpretable, fine-grained reward signals that enhance legal language models. LexReward’s dimension-specific rubrics and learned reward models improve legal answer quality in style, content coverage, and reasoning structure through DPO and RL, and they remove the need for explicit reference answers at reward time. The approach appears generalizable as a principled way to design domain-specific reward models for complex, multi-faceted tasks.

Abstract: Legal language models require reward signals that capture not only answer correctness but also the multidimensional quality of legal responses. Existing reward methods, however, often rely on coarse-grained holistic judgments, providing limited domain specificity and interpretability. We introduce LexReward, a taxonomy-driven framework for legal reward modeling. LexReward characterizes legal response quality along three complementary dimensions: Style, covering lexical and syntactic quality; Element, assessing legal subjects, facts, statutes, and decisions; and Chain, evaluating the order, completeness, correctness, and non-redundancy of legal reasoning. For each dimension, we develop rubrics that specify evaluation criteria and quality levels. The resulting rewards are used to construct pairwise preference data for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and reward-model training. Experiments show that the rubric-based rewards reliably distinguish legal responses of different quality and that DPO training on the preference data improves performance across all three dimensions. The learned reward models, LexRM, also support effective downstream optimization: each dimension-specific reward model improves policy performance in its corresponding dimension through reinforcement learning, without requiring reference answers at reward time. Dimension-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed taxonomy and reward construction.

</details>


### [54] [Beyond Text: LLM-Based Dimensional Emotion Evaluation in Multimodal Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39072)
*Yutong Hu,Jinho Choi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces an LLM-based framework that unifies discrete emotion recognition and continuous VAD prediction in multimodal dialogue, achieving state-of-the-art valence performance on IEMOCAP and showing that domain-adapted, LoRA-tuned open LLMs can outperform larger GPT models, especially when enriched with textified acoustic cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most prior emotion recognition in conversation focuses on discrete labels and does not fully exploit large language models for continuous, dimensional (VAD) emotion estimation in multimodal dialogue. There is also limited understanding of how LLM scale, domain adaptation, and textified audio cues interact for this task. The authors aim to bridge these gaps by systematically applying and analyzing LLMs for both discrete and dimensional emotion modeling with multimodal input.

Method: They build an LLM-based framework that takes dialogue text and acoustic information converted into natural language descriptions (following SpeechCueLLM) and performs both discrete emotion classification and continuous Valence-Arousal-Dominance prediction on the IEMOCAP dataset. They benchmark six LLMs from the LLaMA, GPT, and Qwen families under three settings: zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning. They conduct ablation studies to measure the contribution of the textual audio descriptions across model sizes and analyze performance across the three VAD dimensions in relation to annotator agreement.

Result: LoRA fine-tuned LLaMA models noticeably outperform prompt-engineered GPT models on both discrete and dimensional emotion tasks, even though GPT models are larger, indicating that in-domain adaptation is more critical than raw parameter count. Their best LoRA-tuned LLaMA attains a Valence Concordance Correlation Coefficient of 0.7822 on IEMOCAP, setting a new state-of-the-art. Textual audio descriptions significantly boost performance for smaller models (around +3.5 to 3.6 weighted F1) but give marginal gains to the largest model, implying diminishing returns of audio cues with growing language capacity. The relative performance across VAD dimensions parallels the human annotator agreement pattern in IEMOCAP.

Conclusion: Domain-adapted, LoRA-fine-tuned open LLMs can surpass larger but purely prompt-based GPT models for multimodal emotion recognition, particularly for continuous VAD prediction. Representing acoustic features as natural language is an effective way to inject audio information, especially for smaller LLMs. The similarity between model performance hierarchies over VAD dimensions and annotator agreement patterns suggests that remaining errors may be largely driven by intrinsic label ambiguity rather than solely by model limitations.

Abstract: Emotion recognition in conversation has been widely studied, but applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to continuous dimensional emotion evaluation in multimodal dialogue remains largely unexplored. We propose an LLM-based framework that performs discrete emotion recognition and Valence-Arousal-Dominance (VAD) dimensional evaluation on IEMOCAP, incorporating acoustic cues as natural language descriptions following the SpeechCueLLM approach. We evaluate six models spanning the LLaMA, GPT, and Qwen families under zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and LoRA fine-tuning. LoRA fine-tuned LLaMA models substantially outperform prompt-engineered GPT models on both tasks despite GPT's larger scale, a gap we attribute to domain adaptation rather than model capacity. Our best model achieves a Valence CCC of 0.7822, a new state-of-the-art on IEMOCAP. Ablation studies confirm that textual audio descriptions meaningfully improve smaller models (+3.5 to 3.6 weighted F1) while contributing little for the largest model, suggesting audio cues are most valuable when linguistic capacity is limited. The performance asymmetry across VAD dimensions closely mirrors the annotator agreement hierarchy in IEMOCAP's own annotations.

</details>


### [55] [False Frontiers: Diagnosing and Mitigating Co-Cheating in Self-Evolving Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39102)
*Meijia Chen,Hao Li,Zheng Lu,Hongshan Lin,Junbai Tian,Yichen Liu,Zijun Tian,Yufan Zou,Shuhan Sun,Hanxin Chen,Zeyu Zhang,Weizhi Du,Yueting Li,Tianyu Shi,Alaa Khamis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies a failure mode called co-cheating in self-evolving search agents, where a question proposer and an answering solver reinforce shared errors. It audits this effect, proposes a simple verification baseline (MSV), and introduces CrossFit, a cross-fitted feedback scheme that greatly reduces co-cheating and improves downstream search performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-evolving search agents learn from self-generated questions and answers, but the closed loop between the proposer and solver can cause them to agree on wrong answers while internal training reward still rises. This undermines reliability and external correctness. The paper is motivated by the need to identify, measure, and mitigate this co-cheating phenomenon so that self-evolution yields genuinely better search and reasoning models rather than models that only look good to themselves.

Method: 1) Empirically audit co-cheating by tracking pseudo-label correctness vs. internal reward across rounds of self-evolution. 2) Propose Multi-Sample Verification (MSV), which queries the same model multiple times with and without source documents to filter or replace unreliable pseudo-labels. 3) Introduce CrossFit: partition the proposer’s source corpus into disjoint groups A and B, then use an auxiliary solver trained only on B to score questions about A (and vice versa). Proposer reward is based on this cross-fitted agreement, which prevents the proposer from gaming the feedback using same-source pseudo-labels, while the main solver still trains on the pseudo-labels. 4) Evaluate MSV and CrossFit on Qwen3.5-4B and 9B self-evolution runs and on several downstream search benchmarks.

Result: Audits show that in standard coupled self-evolution, co-cheating grows over time: internal training signals improve while pseudo-label correctness stagnates or declines. MSV verification reduces false-agreement mass only modestly (from 6.1% to 5.7% at 4B and from 8.8% to 7.2% at 9B) and is costly in extra generations. CrossFit more than halves false agreement (to 3.0% and 3.7% respectively), and when replaying proposals with source-excluded feedback, false agreement drops further (to 0.4% and 0.1%), disentangling feedback lineage from curriculum shifts. On seven downstream search benchmarks, CrossFit improves average performance over standard coupled self-evolution by 8.8 and 8.4 points and over Search-R1 by 8.7 and 7.8 points for the 4B and 9B models.

Conclusion: Co-cheating is an inherent risk in closed-loop self-evolving search agents, where internal agreement can diverge from true correctness. Simple verification (MSV) helps but is insufficient and expensive. CrossFit, a cross-fitted feedback scheme that separates the data seen by the proposer and feedback solver, is a more effective and scalable mitigation, substantially reducing co-cheating and improving downstream search performance. This indicates that careful design of the feedback and training loop is crucial for reliable self-evolution of LLM-based agents.

Abstract: Self-evolving search agents build their own training curricula by jointly optimizing a proposer that generates questions and a solver that answers them. This closed loop introduces a failure mode we call co-cheating: the proposer and solver increasingly agree on shared errors, so internal reward improves without a matching gain in external correctness. A post-hoc audit against source evidence shows co-cheating growing more severe over successive rounds of self-evolution, with pseudo-label correctness stagnating or declining even as the in-loop training signal improves. The most direct mitigation is to verify proposals before training: we introduce multi-sample verification (MSV), which queries the same model three times with the source and three times without it to decide task admission and replace unreliable pseudo-labels. MSV partially reduces false agreement but leaves substantial residual co-cheating and costs six extra labeler generations per candidate. These limitations motivate CrossFit, our main method: it partitions the proposer's source documents into groups A and B; questions generated from A are scored by an auxiliary solver trained only on B, and vice versa. The cross-fitted agreement determines proposer reward, so a same-source pseudo-label cannot be reproduced through the feedback solver, while the original solver's update rule is unchanged. Rerunning the loop with Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, MSV reduces false-agreement mass from 6.1% to 5.7% and from 8.8% to 7.2%, whereas CrossFit reduces it to 3.0% and 3.7%. Replaying identical proposals with source-excluded feedback further reduces false agreement to 0.4% and 0.1%, isolating feedback ancestry from curriculum changes.
