TL;DR: The paper studies how introducing controlled lexical ambiguity (homonyms) and underspecification (hypernyms) via artificial pseudowords affects language model performance and internal representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lexical ambiguity and underspecification are pervasive in natural language, yet most language model analyses treat word types as if meanings were fixed and unambiguous. The authors want to understand how such ambiguity influences training dynamics, generation quality, and internal representations in language models. They also aim to connect these behavioral effects to mechanistic explanations inside the models.

Method: The authors construct artificial homonyms and hypernyms as pseudowords, each standing in for multiple meanings (homonyms) or for a more general, underspecified concept (hypernyms). They train language models on corpora where these pseudowords appear with varying frequencies and type counts, effectively controlling the degree of ambiguity and underspecification. They then evaluate generative performance overall, as well as accuracy on sequences containing the pseudowords or their synonyms. Finally, they probe the models' internal representations to see whether and how pseudo-homonyms are disambiguated and whether pseudo-hypernyms remain underspecified during generation.

Result: 1) Introducing ambiguous or underspecified pseudowords improves overall model performance, and this improvement scales with how much these pseudowords increase the language's type-token ratio. 2) Despite better global performance, the models become less accurate at generating sequences that contain the ambiguous pseudowords or their synonyms, relative to other text. 3) Analysis of internal representations shows that pseudo-homonyms are disambiguated internally, while pseudo-hypernyms stay underspecified during the generative process.

Conclusion: Lexical ambiguity and underspecification can actually benefit overall language model performance by enriching the statistical structure of the training data, but they also introduce localized difficulties in generating the ambiguous items themselves. Mechanistically, the models internally separate the senses of homonymous pseudowords, yet maintain generalized, underspecified representations for hypernym-like pseudowords during generation. This suggests different internal strategies for handling ambiguity versus underspecification in neural language models.

Abstract: We analyze how lexical ambiguity and underspecification affect language model training. We create artificial homonyms and artificial hypernyms as pseudowords and analyze the generative performance of language models as they are trained with increasing amounts of these ambiguous or underspecified pseudoword types. We further analyze whether the models disambiguate ambiguous or underspecified statements and provide a first mechanistic account of how ambiguity and disambiguation are represented internally. Our main results show that both ambiguity and underspecification increase model performance in ways that scale with their influence on the language's type-token ratio. However, the accuracy of generating sequences containing ambiguous words or their synonyms decreases compared to other texts. We also show that internal representations of pseudowords reflect disambiguation of pseudo-homonyms, but underspecification of pseudo-hypernyms is maintained during the generative process.

</details>


### [77] [Thinking Outside the Box: Can Language Models Rely on External Guidance Selectively?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39578)
*Minghan Wang,Boyuan Wang,Jinhang Zuo,Yuxin Tao,Fang kong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how language-model agents can selectively rely on external workflows and information, benefiting from good guidance while resisting bad guidance, and introduces a benchmark and training methods to evaluate and improve this capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language models become embedded in agent systems with human-designed workflows, these external workflows can both help and harm performance. Existing evaluations largely focus on task success assuming reliable tools or instructions, but do not measure whether models can discern and resist misleading guidance. There is a need to characterize and improve this "thinking outside the box" capability—using helpful external structure without being trapped by it—so that agents remain reliable when workflows or other external information are fallible or corrupted.

Method: The authors introduce Box^2-Bench, a benchmark that keeps the base model and task constant while systematically varying the reliability of the provided workflows. This isolates how the model modulates its reliance on guidance. They empirically evaluate frontier models on this benchmark, measuring performance under reliable vs misleading/unreliable workflows. To test trainability of this skill, they train two open-weight models with workflows that are intentionally bad, holding out good workflows for evaluation. They compare two training strategies: (1) counterfactual supervised fine-tuning, where models are trained on corrections that show what they should have done instead of following the bad workflow; and (2) outcome-based reinforcement learning, where rewards encourage higher performance, allowing the model to learn when to use or ignore workflows. They also extend experiments to non-workflow external information, such as peer outputs (peer correction) and stored context (memory), including corrupted variants.

Result: On Box^2-Bench, current frontier models gain from reliable workflows but are still significantly harmed when workflows are misleading or unreliable, indicating limited ability to override bad guidance. Training with counterfactual supervised fine-tuning makes models more robust to bad workflows, reducing the damage from misleading guidance. Outcome-based reinforcement learning, in contrast, increases the model’s willingness to exploit helpful workflows when they are good, while still offering some robustness. The learned behavior generalizes: models show improved discrimination in using peer-generated suggestions and better resilience when their memory or contextual information is corrupted.

Conclusion: Selective reliance on external information—being able to exploit helpful workflows and other guidance while resisting harmful or unreliable ones—is a distinct dimension of agent reliability not captured by standard task performance. Box^2-Bench provides a way to measure this dimension, revealing vulnerabilities in current frontier models. Moreover, this capability is trainable: counterfactual supervised fine-tuning and outcome-based reinforcement learning can improve robustness and appropriate use of external guidance, with effects that transfer beyond workflows to other external signals like peer outputs and memory. Evaluating and training for this "thinking outside the box" behavior is important for building more dependable language-model agents that operate within imperfect, fallible environments.

Abstract: Agent harnesses often improve language models with human-designed workflows, but as models grow more capable, unreliable guidance can increasingly constrain their execution. We call the ability to benefit from useful guidance while overriding unreliable guidance thinking outside the box. We introduce Box$^2$-Bench, which holds the model and task fixed while varying workflow reliability to isolate how models regulate their reliance on guidance. On Box$^2$-Bench, frontier models often benefit from reliable guidance but remain vulnerable when it is misleading or becomes unreliable. To test whether this capability can be learned, we train two open-weight models using bad workflows, reserving good workflows for evaluation. We explore two complementary training strategies: counterfactual supervised fine-tuning improves robustness, while outcome-based reinforcement learning can shift the balance toward greater use of helpful workflows. We further find that this behavior extends beyond workflows to other forms of external information, improving peer correction and robustness to corrupted memory. Together, our results identify selective reliance on fallible external information as a dimension of agent reliability not captured by task performance alone.

</details>


### [78] [Is This Evidence Decision-Critical? Learning to Verify Rule-Governed Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39608)
*Haoyang Zhang,Jianpeng Zhao,Qi Hao,Pengyang Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: InterPact is a framework that learns which pieces of evidence are decision-critical in rule-based reasoning tasks by using intervention-based, counterfactual training to detect how changing evidence affects condition judgments and final decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rule-based tasks like eligibility checks and contract reviews demand that language models not only apply explicit rules but also correctly judge which specific pieces of evidence are crucial to the final decision. Simple classification of outcomes is not enough: some evidence errors don't change the decision, while others are decision-critical. To make decisions safer and more reliable, we need a way to automatically identify the evidence that could flip the decision so that more capable models or humans can focus their attention there.

Method: The authors propose InterPact, an intervention-based impact learning framework. They construct counterfactual training examples by editing case facts with a frozen language model, while holding the rules and other conditions constant. For each intervention, humans review and label how condition-level and decision-level outcomes change. These labels and full state-to-decision mappings supervise a propagation verifier, which learns to predict how decisions depend on conditions. During training, the verifier combines evidence-based probabilities over conditions with a fixed composition operation to produce conditional decision predictions; supervision on decision changes is then backpropagated into the base model. After training, the base model can directly predict whether a given piece of evidence is critical to the final decision from the original case, without additional human or stronger-model input.

Result: On a single-case evidence criticality verification task derived from rule-governed decision datasets, InterPact attains 68.28% accuracy and outperforms six baseline methods. This demonstrates that the framework is better at identifying decision-critical evidence than existing approaches.

Conclusion: InterPact shows that learning from intervention-based counterfactuals and explicit rule structures allows language models to approximate decision sensitivity—how decisions change when certain evidence changes. This learned sensitivity can then be used to prioritize which pieces of evidence deserve extra scrutiny, improving the reliability and safety of rule-based decision systems.

Abstract: Rule-based reasoning, as in eligibility checks and contract reviews, requires language models to assess evidence against individual conditions and combine their judgments under explicit rules. Errors in evidence assessment can leave a decision unchanged, but misinterpreting or overlooking decision-critical evidence can reverse it. Identifying such evidence allows more capable models to focus on checking the corresponding condition judgments, supporting accurate and safe decisions. Recognizing the evidence's criticality requires understanding how evidence affects a condition judgment and how that judgment affects the decision. To achieve the goal, we propose a INTERvention-based imPACT learning framework (InterPact), which enables counterfactual verification of evidence criticality in rule-governed decisions. Specifically, its evidence intervention constructor generates training pairs for a propagation verifier by editing case facts with a frozen language model while holding rules and non-target conditions fixed. Human-reviewed labels record the resulting condition and decision changes, while complete state-to-decision mappings supervise consequences beyond the observed edit. During training, the verifier weights learned conditional decision predictions by evidence-based condition probabilities through a fixed composition operation, propagating decision-change supervision into the base model. At inference, the trained base model directly judges criticality from the original case and target evidence, without human or stronger-model supervision. On single-case evidence criticality verification over adapted rule-governed decision cases, InterPact achieves 68.28% accuracy, outperforming all six baselines. These results support learned decision sensitivity as a basis for prioritizing evidence checks.

</details>


### [79] [Marginal Response Surface Elicitation for Zero-Label Tabular Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39639)
*Liangyu Teng,Yicheng Ding,Jing Liu,Hengsong Liu,Juncen Guo,Hongru Li,Jingyu Zhang,Liang Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MARS, a method that uses large language models to turn feature-level priors into a reusable, zero-shot tabular classifier without labeled data, improving performance and cost over direct prompting on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular prediction usually depends on labeled datasets, which are costly or impractical to obtain in some domains. Although LLMs contain rich domain knowledge, existing approaches that directly prompt LLMs for predictions are often inefficient, not reusable, and may underutilize this knowledge. The motivation is to systematically elicit and structure LLM-derived priors so they can be reused as a classifier for tabular data without supervision, reducing label and compute costs while improving predictive quality.

Method: MARS constructs a zero-shot classifier in several steps: (1) It samples representative values for each feature from unlabeled tabular data. (2) For each feature value, it prompts an LLM with the task description and that value to obtain class support scores and feature importance weights, effectively capturing the LLM’s local prior about how that feature value relates to each class. (3) It repeats this to gather multiple responses and aggregates them using the median to build a stable marginal response function per feature that maps feature values to class support. (4) At prediction time, it evaluates each instance by computing a weighted sum of the corresponding feature-level responses, producing class scores without needing any further LLM calls.

Result: On eight benchmark tabular classification datasets, MARS achieves the best average performance among zero-shot LLM-based methods, improving over direct LLM prompting by 1.97 percentage points in AUC and 6.21 percentage points in average precision (AP), while significantly lowering end-to-end computation and API costs. Experiments using LLMs of various sizes show that MARS consistently outperforms direct prompting across models, indicating that its gains are robust to model scale.

Conclusion: The study concludes that LLMs can be converted into effective zero-shot tabular classifiers by eliciting and structuring feature-level priors instead of issuing instance-level prompts. MARS provides a reusable classifier that improves prediction quality and cost-efficiency over direct prompting without requiring labeled data, suggesting a promising direction for leveraging LLMs as general-purpose prior providers for tabular learning.

Abstract: Tabular learning uses structured data to predict target outcomes. Traditionally, this process has relied on labeled data. However, large language models (LLMs) can be used to elicit domain priors based on the task description and feature semantics, thereby enabling predictions without labeled data. We propose Marginal Response Surface Elicitation (MARS), a method that transforms feature-level LLM priors into a reusable, zero-shot tabular classifier. To construct this classifier, MARS selects representative values for each feature from unlabeled data and prompts the LLM to provide corresponding class support scores and feature weights. It then aggregates multiple responses using the median to construct feature response functions, and makes predictions through their weighted sum without further LLM queries. Across eight tabular benchmark tasks, MARS achieves the highest average AUC and AP, outperforming direct prompting by 1.97 and 6.21 percentage points respectively, while substantially reducing end-to-end costs. Evaluations with LLMs of different sizes further demonstrate its predictive advantage over direct prompting.

</details>


### [80] [Zero-Compute Cross-Lingual Transferability Estimation Using Typological Feature Proxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39640)
*Dalton Raphael Harmsen,Swier Garst,Thomas van Osch,Zarè Palanciyan,Joaquin Vanschoren*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether typological features alone can predict cross-lingual transfer quality between languages and shows they are strong, cheap predictors, enabling zero-compute screening of good source languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-lingual transfer is crucial for leveraging high-resource languages to improve performance in low-resource languages, but directly measuring transfer is costly because it requires large multilingual pre-training and many experiments. There is a need to understand what factors drive transfer and whether easily available typological information can predict transfer patterns, instead of relying only on expensive empirical measurements that may be biased by data size and quality.

Method: The authors use an existing 24-language cross-lingual transfer matrix from prior work as ground truth and compile typological features from typological databases. They train a random forest model using only typological features to predict transfer values between languages. They compare its performance to a non-typological control and evaluate with leave-one-language-out cross-validation, as well as stricter leave-one-script-out and leave-one-family-out protocols to rule out confounds from shared script or language family. They then decompose observed transfer into two components: a typology-driven term and a resource-and-script bias term, in order to examine how source language rankings change when removing data-related biases.

Result: The typology-only random forest model achieves a Spearman correlation of ρ=0.705 and R^2=0.49 on leave-one-language-out predictions, outperforming a non-typological control that achieves ρ=0.62. The predictive signal from typology remains strong under leave-one-script-out and leave-one-family-out evaluations, indicating that script and family do not fully explain the effect. The decomposition analysis reveals that rankings of the best source languages for transfer are quite sensitive to the resource-and-script bias term, whereas the typology-based component is stable and independent of these biases.

Conclusion: Typological databases provide dense, low-cost, and robust signals about cross-lingual transfer, allowing accurate prediction of transfer patterns without expensive multilingual pre-training. Since typology is unaffected by data-resource and script biases, it can be used as a zero-compute screening tool to identify promising source-target language pairs, significantly reducing the need for exhaustive experimental search over language combinations.

Abstract: Cross-lingual transfer describes how knowledge in a source language benefits a target language. Measuring it quantitatively requires broad multilingual pre-training, as prior work has done with cross-lingual transfer matrices. We ask whether transfer is predictable from freely available typological features, and whether the prominence of high-resource source languages reflects typology or data quality and quantity. We show that typological databases contain cheap and dense signals about cross-lingual transfer. Our typology-only random forest on a 24-language prior-work transfer matrix scores leave-one-language-out $ρ{=}0.705$ and $R^2{=}0.49$, beating a non-typological control at $ρ{=}0.62$, which verifies the ability of typology-only predictions to reconstruct costly measured cross-lingual transfer. The signal survives leave-one-script-out and leave-one-family-out protocols, so script and family confounding do not explain the effect. By decomposing the transfer into a typology term and a resource-and-script bias term, we find the best-source ranking sensitive to this bias. In contrast, typology is not affected by this bias, which makes it a zero-compute screening tool that replaces hundreds of training runs with a model fit. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/dharmsen/typo-x-ling-transfer}{here}.

</details>


### [81] [SEPAL: Separated Expert Pairs with Answer-Level Fusion for Reliable LLM Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39645)
*Weijie Ren,Yanwen Zhang,Hao Li,Zhuolin Qi,Hengyi Zhang,Naibo Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SEPAL, a multi-agent collaboration framework for large language models that uses three independent Actor-Critic teams with distinct roles and private feedback loops, then aggregates only final answers via majority vote to improve question-answering accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM collaboration methods either share discussions (which spreads the same mistakes and reduces diversity) or refine only a single candidate solution. There is a need for a method that combines the benefits of feedback-based refinement with the sampling diversity necessary for effective voting, while avoiding error contamination between candidate solutions.

Method: The authors design SEPAL, which creates three specialized Actor-Critic teams assigned to distinct roles: (1) directing reasoning, (2) grounding in evidence, and (3) verification. Each team is trained with a role-specific objective so that their reasoning behaviors systematically differ. Within each team, a Critic provides feedback to revise that team’s candidate solution, but feedback and intermediate reasoning are kept private to prevent sharing of errors across teams. After iterative revision, only the final answers from the three teams are combined using majority voting, without exposing reasoning traces between teams.

Result: On five different open-weight LLM backbones and five question-answering benchmarks, SEPAL yields an average improvement of 1.81 percentage points in accuracy over a strong baseline that uses a single Actor-Critic pair. The gains are consistent across all evaluated backbones, indicating that SEPAL’s architecture provides a robust benefit rather than a model-specific trick.

Conclusion: Separating multi-agent collaboration into multiple role-specialized, privately-revising Actor-Critic teams and aggregating only their final outputs improves question-answering performance relative to standard single-pair Actor-Critic collaboration. By preserving both structured diversity (via roles) and isolation of feedback loops (to avoid shared errors), SEPAL offers a more effective and general framework for collaborative LLM reasoning.

Abstract: Multi-agent collaboration lets large language models (LLMs) improve question answering through deliberation and feedback. Yet shared discussion couples correction with exposure to the same mistakes, which can erode the diversity needed for voting. Self-consistency offers sampling diversity without feedback, while single-pair Actor-Critic collaboration refines only one candidate. We introduce SEPAL, which assigns three private Actor-Critic teams to direct reasoning, evidence grounding, and verification. Role-specific training gives the teams different reasoning objectives beyond sampling variation. Each Critic guides revisions within its own team, preventing feedback from carrying errors across candidates. Once revision ends, majority voting combines only the final answers, keeping the reasoning histories separate until the decision. Across five open-weight backbones and five question-answering benchmarks, SEPAL improves mean accuracy by 1.81 percentage points over a matched single Actor-Critic pair, with improvements across all five backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/zhansan114514/SEPAL.

</details>


### [82] [The Evolution of Attention in Large Language Models: Mechanisms, Trade-offs, and Emerging Trends](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39661)
*Zhentao Tan,Jingyi Shen,Yanbo Li,Yao Liu,Yue Wu,Jieping Ye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Survey of how modern LLM architectures implement and manage contextual memory beyond standard dense self-attention, proposing a unified multi-dimensional framework for analyzing memory mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense self-attention has quadratic prefill cost and a KV cache that grows linearly with context length, which is problematic for long-context and efficient inference. Many lines of research (memory compression, sparse attention, recurrent states, structured memory, hybrid mechanisms) have emerged, but they are fragmented and often compared under different assumptions. There is a need for a conceptual framework that systematically characterizes these mechanisms as forms of internal contextual memory, enabling comparison without forcing them into a single computational paradigm.

Method: The paper conducts a structured survey of architectural mechanisms for contextual memory in large language models. It proposes a five-dimensional analytical lens—Memory Representation, Memory Update, Memory Access, Memory Readout, and Integration—to classify and compare methods. The authors then reconstruct the evolution of these mechanisms across 59 major model releases spanning 14 model families plus 11 strong open-weight models, tracing how explicit-memory systems, recurrent states, sparsity, and heterogeneous mixtures are adopted and combined at scale.

Result: Using the five-dimensional lens, the survey shows: (1) explicit-memory mechanisms (e.g., caches, external memory) and recurrent-state approaches (e.g., state-space, RWKV-like) remain interface-distinct but converge in the kinds of memory functions they control; (2) modern architectures increasingly use heterogeneous mixtures of mechanisms coordinated across network depth, with different layers specializing in complementary memory roles and with cross-layer reuse of states and routing; (3) these observations support a multidimensional memory-routing picture where persistent memory is distributed across time scales, depth, substrates, and levels of granularity, and governed by sparse write/read operations rather than monolithic dense attention.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that efficient sequence modeling for LLMs should be viewed primarily as a problem of designing, organizing, and routing contextual memory—its representation, lifecycle, and selective usage—rather than optimizing a single Attention operator. Future architectural advances are likely to come from better multidimensional memory organization and sparse memory routing across time, layers, substrates, and granularities, integrating explicit-memory and recurrent-state methods within a unified contextual memory perspective.

Abstract: Self-attention gives LLMs fine-grained, query-dependent access to context, but dense token interactions incur quadratic prefill cost and a key--value cache growing with context length. Research thus spans explicit-memory compression, sparse access, recurrent state construction, structured state dynamics, and heterogeneous mechanism composition. This survey analyzes these developments as model-internal contextual memory. We introduce a five-dimensional lens---Memory Representation, Memory Update, Access, Readout, and Integration---describing what is represented, how it changes, what is query-eligible, how it is read, and how readouts form outputs. This lens compares overlapping research lines without imposing one computational model.
  We reconstruct mechanism-level developments and architectural adoption using 59 release-level records from 14 major model lineages and 11 high-performing open-weight endpoints. First, explicit-memory and recurrent-state methods retain distinct interfaces but increasingly control overlapping memory functions. Second, heterogeneous architectures increasingly coordinate across network depth: layer-wise composition distributes complementary memory processing across representational stages, while cross-layer reuse carries selected memory and routing artifacts forward. Depth thus becomes a dimension along which contextual memory is constructed and managed. Third, these developments motivate a stateful multidimensional memory-routing hypothesis: persistent memory is organized across temporal scope, network depth, substrate type, and representation granularity, while coordinated Sparse Write and Sparse Read determine what is maintained and what contributes to each query. Overall, efficient sequence architecture design increasingly concerns the organization, lifecycle, and selective use of contextual memory rather than an isolated Attention operator.

</details>


### [83] [Better Supervision Is Nearby: Neighborhood On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39687)
*Xincheng Wei,Yifan Ding,Yoshua Li,Yuquan Lu,Ziheng Li,Yi Lu,Dongsheng Ma,Rongxiang Weng,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose Neighborhood OPSD, an improved on-policy self-distillation method for math reasoning LMs that uses a small pool of perturbed-teacher experts and smart routing to provide better supervision, yielding consistent accuracy gains on contest benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard OPSD uses a single privileged teacher parameter setting, which misses useful alternative corrections that slightly different parameter settings (local perturbations) could provide at different positions in a reference solution. They observe that such local perturbations reveal complementary, reference-aligned token corrections across positions, and want to exploit this to improve student training signals without changing the deployed student at inference time.

Method: 1) Generate a set of locally perturbed versions of the privileged teacher (experts). 2) Offline, greedily build a compact expert pool: for each reference position, reward experts that give filtered reference-token likelihood gains beyond the current pool best, selecting those that cover additional positions. 3) During online training, decouple which token to aim for from which expert supplies its distribution: MaxPeak picks the anchor token (top token across experts), then a quantile-based rule selects among experts whose top token matches this anchor; the student is trained on the chosen expert’s full next-token distribution using a clipped forward-KL objective as in OPSD. 4) Use the same expert pool not only along reference trajectories but also at student-sampled prefixes. 5) Perform ablations on selection criteria, overlap accounting, and routing-by-state variants.

Result: On Qwen3 models (1.7B, 4B, 8B), Neighborhood OPSD improves Average@12 on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025 by 2.75, 1.67, and 1.94 percentage points, respectively, compared with vanilla OPSD across three independent runs per method. Their analyses show that the expert pool generalizes beyond the reference paths, that filtered reference-token gains are a good expert-selection metric, and that modeling overlap and state-wise routing further boost performance.

Conclusion: Local parameter perturbations of a privileged teacher contain complementary, reference-aligned training signals that a single OPSD teacher misses. By greedily selecting a small pool of such experts based on reference-token gains and routing them carefully at training time (Neighborhood OPSD), one can improve mathematical reasoning performance of students without extra inference cost, as only the distilled student is used at test time.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains mathematical reasoning models using a privileged teacher that sees a reference solution and supervises student-sampled prefixes. Standard OPSD uses one fixed parameter setting at every state, but nearby settings may offer additional supervision. We find that local parameter perturbations reveal complementary reference-aligned corrections under the same reference context. Different experts supply these corrections at different reference positions. Their pool covers more such positions than the unperturbed privileged teacher. We introduce Neighborhood OPSD (N-OPSD) to turn these corrections into supervision at student-visited states. Offline, greedy selection builds a compact pool of frozen experts by rewarding filtered reference-token gains beyond the pool's current best at each position. The highest-peak expert need not provide the best training target. Online routing therefore separates the anchor direction from its level of support. MaxPeak selects the anchor token, and quantile selection chooses among experts whose top token matches it. The student learns from the chosen expert's full next-token distribution through the clipped forward-KL objective inherited from OPSD. We evaluate on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT February 2025. Across three independent runs per method, Neighborhood OPSD improves the three-benchmark Average@12 over OPSD by 2.75, 1.67, and 1.94 points on Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, respectively. Student-prefix continuations support using the pool beyond the reference trajectories used for selection. Matched ablations support filtered reference-token gains as a selection criterion. Accounting for overlap within the pool and routing by state further improve student accuracy. Inference uses only the distilled student.

</details>


### [84] [Drift Inspector: Exploring and Measuring Scientific Drift with Atomic Contribution Claims](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39710)
*Vsevolod Karimov,Stepan Ostarkov,Anastasia Poroshina,Anatoly Frolov,Alexander Panchenko*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build an LLM-based system that extracts concise contribution claims from abstracts to track how a research field’s concrete contributions change over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Raw abstracts blend background, motivation, and meta-language with actual research contributions, so existing analyses (e.g., keyword or full-abstract counting) can’t clearly reveal how the *substance* of a field is evolving. The authors want a finer-grained, contribution-focused way to measure topic drift and trends in research areas over time.

Method: They introduce Drift Inspector, an open-source pipeline that uses an LLM to extract Atomic Contribution Claims (ACCs)—short, decontextualized propositions that encode each paper’s main contribution—from abstracts. These ACCs are then clustered across years to create an interactive map of research areas and their temporal dynamics. They apply this pipeline to multiple corpora (e.g., EMNLP and the full ACL Anthology), validate ACC extraction with human evaluation, and check the clustering quality against an external manually built taxonomy.

Result: On six years of EMNLP, their ACC-based analysis reveals a clear shift from traditional NLP tasks to LLM-era capabilities such as reasoning and multimodal processing—patterns that are not as visible when looking only at keywords or entire abstracts. At scale, they generate a dataset of 346k ACCs from 80k abstracts across 423 venues in the ACL Anthology, with empirical evidence that both extraction and clustering are reliable (via human validation and comparison to a manual taxonomy).

Conclusion: Focusing on Atomic Contribution Claims enables more accurate and interpretable tracking of how research fields evolve than conventional abstract- or keyword-based methods. Drift Inspector and its released ACC dataset provide a validated, open-source resource and methodology for understanding topic drift and emerging trends across large collections of scientific papers.

Abstract: Scientific abstracts mix contributions with background, motivation, and meta-language, so tools that read them as-is cannot separate what a field produces from what it discusses. We present Drift Inspector, an open-source system for measuring and exploring how a research field changes over time at the level of Atomic Contribution Claims (ACCs): decontextualized, contribution-bearing propositions an LLM extracts from each abstract before analysis. The system clusters these claims across years into an interactive map where every trend traces back to the claims and papers behind it. Applied to six years of EMNLP, it shows the field shifting away from classic NLP tasks toward LLM-era capabilities such as reasoning and multimodality -- a movement that keyword or whole-abstract counts blur. The released data extend beyond EMNLP: the same pipeline has processed the full ACL Anthology (346k claims, 80k abstracts, 423 venues). Extraction is human-validated and clustering checked against an external manually constructed taxonomy.

</details>


### [85] [LatentHarness: Learning Latent Actions for Memory and Reasoning via Counterfactual Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39740)
*Xiaoqiang Wang,Suyuchen Wang,Bang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LatentHarness is a framework that unifies memory access and latent multi-step reasoning by letting a model dynamically choose to think more, recall from memory, or emit an output token, achieving better and faster long-context reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context reasoning models struggle with two main bottlenecks: keeping track of relevant evidence over very long inputs and maintaining effective multi-step reasoning over many internal computation steps. Prior work typically tackles these problems separately via external memory for long-range access and latent reasoning for compressed multi-step computation, missing the opportunity to jointly optimize when to remember, when to recall, and when to think further.

Method: LatentHarness formulates reasoning as sequential latent action selection. At each internal step, the model chooses one of three actions: THINK (continue internal computation), RECALL (access a fast-weight memory that stores input evidence and previous intermediate reasoning states), or EXIT (emit the next output token). A fast-weight memory mechanism stores and retrieves states. The action policy is trained with counterfactual policy distillation, where for each state, alternative actions are branched for one step and their impact on the eventual emitted token is scored. These counterfactual comparisons provide learning signals for when to use memory vs additional thinking, and which intermediate states should be written to memory for future recall.

Result: On six general and long-context reasoning benchmarks, a 1.4B-parameter LatentHarness model outperforms the strongest overall baselines by 2.8% relative and the strongest long-context-specific baselines by 10.0% relative, while being 5.9 times faster than the strongest long-context baseline.

Conclusion: Unifying memory access and latent reasoning into a single sequential action policy, and training it via counterfactual policy distillation, enables models to more effectively trade off between thinking, recalling, and emitting tokens. This leads to both accuracy gains and substantial speedups for long-context reasoning, demonstrating that joint optimization of memory and computation is more effective than treating them as separate components.

Abstract: Long-context reasoning faces two complementary bottlenecks: retaining evidence across long inputs and sustaining computation across many reasoning steps. Existing approaches largely address them separately, with external memory extending access to distant evidence and latent reasoning compressing multi-step computation. We introduce LatentHarness, which unifies memory access and latent reasoning as sequential latent action selection. At each internal step, the model chooses THINK for further computation, RECALL from a fast-weight memory of input evidence and intermediate reasoning states, or EXIT to emit the next token. We train this policy with counterfactual policy distillation, which branches every action for one step and scores its effect on the emitted token. These gains teach the policy when memory is more useful than further reasoning, while gradients through counterfactual recall teach which intermediate states should be retained in memory for future use. Across six general and long-context reasoning benchmarks, LatentHarness at 1.4B improves on the strongest baselines by 2.8% and 10.0% relative, respectively, and runs 5.9x faster than the strongest long-context baseline.

</details>


### [86] [MemCodex: Self-Programming Hierarchical Memory for Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39765)
*Xiaoqiang Wang,Bang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MemCodex is a self-evolving hierarchical memory system that organizes experiences into executable memory programs, enabling adaptive, efficient retrieval for both simple and multi-hop queries, outperforming prior adaptive-memory baselines in success rate, token usage, and speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent memory systems struggle with heterogeneous information needs: some queries require only a single piece of evidence, while others need multi-hop reasoning across multiple sources. Predefined memory workflows and even recent adaptive methods are constrained by fixed design spaces, limiting their ability to flexibly compose and evolve memory representations and access patterns. There is a need for a memory architecture that can discover, adapt, and optimize its own structure and retrieval strategies over time.

Method: The authors propose MemCodex, a hierarchical memory system where experiences are organized as executable memory programs corresponding to different abstraction layers: summaries, relational knowledge, reusable skills, and latent memory. They employ open-ended program evolution to search over an open design space of layer programs, dynamically rewriting how each layer is built, indexed, retrieved, and routed. This allows adaptation of both intra-layer implementations and inter-layer compositions. At inference time, queries traverse the hierarchy from coarse abstractions to fine-grained details, stopping as soon as sufficient evidence is obtained and descending to raw history only when necessary. Additionally, they introduce MemArena, a unified runtime that abstracts heterogeneous data and memory systems behind a common interface for running these memory programs.

Result: MemCodex achieves a 10.1% average improvement in task success compared to the strongest adaptive-memory baseline. It also reduces context token usage by a factor of 3.4 and delivers 2.1x faster inference, indicating both performance and efficiency gains.

Conclusion: A self-evolving, program-based hierarchical memory architecture can better handle diverse query requirements than fixed or narrowly adaptive memory systems. By letting the memory structure and access policies evolve across an open design space and by unifying heterogeneous memories under a common runtime, MemCodex delivers higher task success with substantially lower computational and context costs.

Abstract: Agent memory faces heterogeneous access needs: a single-hop question may require one piece of evidence, whereas a multi-hop question must combine evidence from multiple sources. Predefined memory workflows cannot adapt to these varying needs. Recent adaptive methods search or learn over memory components and their compositions, but the design space itself remains predefined. We introduce MemCodex, a self-evolving hierarchical memory system that organizes experience into executable memory programs for summaries, relational knowledge, reusable skills, and latent memory. Open-ended program evolution searches the open design space of layer programs by rewriting how each layer is constructed, indexed, retrieved, and routed, thereby adapting both within-layer implementations and cross-layer composition. At query time, reads traverse the hierarchy from coarse to fine and stop once sufficient evidence is found, descending to the original history when needed. We further develop MemArena, a unified runtime that places heterogeneous data and memory systems behind a common interface. MemCodex improves average task success by 10.1% relative to the strongest adaptive-memory baseline, while using 3.4x fewer context tokens and achieving 2.1x faster inference.

</details>


### [87] [Explore-on-Graph: Hybrid Embedding-LLM Reasoning for Knowledge Graph Question Answering under Incompleteness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39786)
*Ola El Khatib,Djellel Difallah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: XoG is a framework for multi-hop question answering over incomplete knowledge graphs that repairs missing reasoning paths using learned graph structure instead of LLM hallucinations, improving robustness and efficiency across datasets and LLM backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based KGQA approaches fail when required reasoning paths in the KG are broken by missing facts, and naive LLM-based generation of missing knowledge introduces hallucinated evidence. There is a need for a method that can answer multi-hop questions reliably even when the KG is incomplete, while still leveraging LLMs and avoiding hallucinations.

Method: XoG (eXplore-on-Graph) combines two graph-structural signals: (1) type-level entity-relation statistics to propose candidate relations relevant to the question and partially observed paths, and (2) KG embeddings to retrieve plausible missing entities that could complete those paths. An LLM is then used as a semantic selector and reasoner over these candidates. The framework runs in an iterative loop of planning (deciding what to explore next), exploration (querying the KG and retrieving plausible completions), and reasoning (using the LLM to choose among candidates and advance or finalize the answer).

Result: On WebQSP, ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ), and the Wikidata-based BRINK benchmark, XoG matches competitive baselines on complete KGs and outperforms comparable, non-task-specific KGQA approaches when the KG is made incomplete. The improvements hold across multiple LLM backbones, showing that merely using stronger LLMs does not fix missing graph evidence. Additionally, XoG cuts LLM token usage by up to 33% compared with a similar planning-based method.

Conclusion: Recovering missing reasoning paths from learned KG structure—via type-level statistics and KG embeddings—enables more reliable multi-hop KGQA under incompleteness than relying on LLM parametric knowledge. XoG offers a general, LLM-agnostic framework that improves robustness and efficiency without task-specific KGQA training, highlighting the importance of explicit graph-structural exploration for grounded reasoning.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly combined with knowledge graphs (KGs) to ground reasoning in structured evidence. However, most LLM-based KGQA methods rely on traversing existing graph edges and become unreliable when reasoning paths are broken by missing facts. Alternatives that ask LLMs to generate missing knowledge risk introducing hallucinated evidence. We introduce XoG (eXplore-on-Graph), a framework for multi-hop question answering over incomplete KGs that recovers missing reasoning paths from learned graph structure rather than LLM parametric knowledge. XoG combines type-level entity-relation statistics to identify candidate relations with KG embeddings to retrieve plausible missing entities, using the LLM as a semantic selector and reasoner. These mechanisms are integrated into an iterative planning-exploration-reasoning process. Experiments on WebQSP, CWQ, and the Wikidata-based BRINK benchmark show that XoG remains competitive on complete KGs and consistently outperforms comparable methods without task-specific KGQA training under KG incompleteness. These gains persist across multiple LLM backbones, indicating that stronger LLMs alone do not resolve missing graph evidence. XoG also reduces LLM token consumption by up to 33% compared with a closely related planning-based approach.

</details>


### [88] [Stress-Testing LLM Lie Detectors: Role-Play Failures and Spurious Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39807)
*Maximilian von Klinski,Sebastian Lapuschkin,Wojciech Samek,Lennart Bürger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well current lie detection probes for language models work when models role-play anti-factual personas, and finds they often fail by tracking confounders instead of truth; it proposes stress tests and a simple improved probe.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing lie detection probes for LLMs are mostly evaluated in neutral settings where “truth” aligns with real-world facts. But LLMs often role-play personas (e.g., conspiracy theorists) whose supposed beliefs contradict reality, making it unclear what “truth” should mean. The authors want to know whether current probes actually detect factual correctness or whether they just follow the persona’s internal narrative or other spurious cues. This is important for safety, oversight, and accountability in LLM use.

Method: 1) Construct a dataset of 8,916 human-reviewed, on-policy responses from three LLMs prompted to adopt anti-factual personas. 2) Evaluate eight existing lie detection probes on this dataset, including settings where both correct and incorrect answers are produced under the same persona prompt. 3) Create three confounder datasets where factual truth is deliberately anti-correlated with specific confounding properties (e.g., instruction following, response probability). 4) Analyze how strongly prior probes track these confounders instead of ground-truth factuality. 5) Design and train a simple linear probe targeted to avoid these confounding effects and test it on both the persona dataset and confounder stress tests.

Result: Many prior lie detection probes perform poorly when the LLM is role-playing anti-factual personas, especially when judged within a fixed persona setup. The probes often end up tracking properties like instruction compliance or how likely a response is under the model, which were spuriously correlated with truth in their original training data. In stress tests where truth is anti-correlated with such confounders, these probes fail systematically. The authors’ simple linear probe attains the best overall performance across both the persona-based evaluations and the confounder datasets, indicating improved robustness, although not perfect reliability.

Conclusion: Current lie detection probes do not robustly identify factual truth when LLMs adopt anti-factual personas; instead, they frequently latch onto spurious, confounded signals such as instruction compliance or response likelihood. Effective lie detection will require training data and probe designs that explicitly decorrelate truth from these confounding concepts. The proposed linear probe is a step forward and sets a stronger baseline, but the broader lesson is that oversight tools must be stress-tested under varied personas and deliberately constructed confounder scenarios to ensure they are truly tracking factuality rather than superficial correlates.

Abstract: Lie detection probes aim to predict from a language model's internal states whether its output is truthful or dishonest. However, role-play complicates what "truth" means for an LLM: language models can adopt a wide range of personas that take very different claims to be true, including personas whose beliefs clearly contradict reality, such as a conspiracy theorist. In this work, we investigate whether lie detection probes reliably flag falsehoods generated under such an anti-factual persona or whether they instead follow the persona's beliefs. We introduce a dataset of 8,916 human-reviewed, on-policy responses from three LLMs adopting anti-factual personas. Evaluating eight probes from prior work, we find that many fail in this setting, particularly when correct and incorrect answers are evaluated under the same persona prompt. To investigate why, we construct three novel confounder datasets in which truth is anti-correlated with a potential confounding concept. Our experiments reveal that many existing probes strongly track concepts that are spuriously correlated with truth in their training data, such as instruction compliance or response likelihood. Based on these findings, we introduce a simple linear probe that achieves the strongest overall performance on both the persona and confounder stress tests. Our results suggest that current lie detection probes are far from reliable and highlight the need for training data in which truth is decorrelated from confounding concepts.

</details>


### [89] [Synthetic Pre-pretraining Survives Scale, but Not as a Grammatical Prior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39827)
*Atsuki Yamaguchi,Tatsuro Inaba,Joel Niklaus,Michal Štefánik,Aline Villavicencio,Nikolaos Aletras*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies pre-pretraining (PPT) on synthetic non-natural language data and shows that it improves token efficiency and downstream performance of language models even at larger scales and more realistic pre-training data mixtures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: It was unclear whether the benefits of PPT observed in small models and limited pre-training budgets would persist for larger models, bigger token budgets, and heterogeneous data mixtures (including code and math). Prior explanations claimed the gains came from learning a grammatical prior, but this had not been rigorously tested at scale.

Method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical study varying five synthetic PPT tasks, four downstream pre-training (PT) data mixtures, four model sizes from 500M to 7B parameters, and PT budgets up to 100B tokens. They compare token efficiency and downstream performance with and without PPT, and examine correlations with grammatical acceptability and long-range retrieval capabilities.

Result: They find that PPT consistently improves downstream performance and token efficiency across model sizes and PT budgets, e.g., saving at least 21B PT tokens for a 3B-parameter model. However, they do not observe a stable relationship between PPT gains and grammatical acceptability. Instead, tasks that enhance long-range retrieval align with downstream improvements. The gains are robust to most PT mixture choices and only significantly weaken when web text is completely removed.

Conclusion: PPT remains an effective, low-cost way to boost language model training efficiency at realistic scales, but its benefits are not primarily due to a transferred grammatical prior. Effective PPT tasks are those that train long-range retrieval capabilities, and future PPT design should focus on this property rather than mimicking natural language grammar.

Abstract: Pre-pretraining (PPT) on synthetic non-natural language data improves token efficiency during language model pre-training (PT). Prior work attributes this gain to a grammatical prior, i.e., a structural inductive bias learned during PPT that transfers to natural language grammar. However, PPT has only been tested on models of at most 1B parameters and PT budgets below 2B tokens on predominantly web text. It is unknown whether PPT is effective at larger scales and under more realistic PT data mixtures that combine diverse sources (e.g., code and math). We therefore present a comprehensive study on PPT spanning five PPT tasks, four PT data mixtures, four parameter scales (500M to 7B), and PT budgets of up to 100B tokens. Our results demonstrate that the downstream performance and token efficiency gains of PPT persist at scale, e.g., saving at least 21B PT tokens at the 3B scale. However, in contrast to prior work, we find no consistent evidence that these gains stem from a grammatical prior. Downstream performance does not consistently align with grammatical acceptability across model sizes. Instead, we find that downstream gains arise from PPT tasks that improve long-range retrieval. Finally, PPT performance gains are robust to how PT data mixtures are composed and diminish only when web text is absent. Overall, PPT is a low-cost addition to PT, and future PPT task design should target long-range retrieval rather than natural language grammar.

</details>


### [90] [When a Kindergartener Solves Calculus: Measuring Capability Leakage in Role-Prompted Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39846)
*Pakhapoom Sarapat,Saksorn Ruangtanusak,Kunat Pipatanakul,Pittawat Taveekitworachai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper defines and measures role-capability leakage in role-prompted reasoning models and proposes an inference-time method (Injection) to better align models' capabilities with their assigned roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Role-prompting is widely used to make language models act as specific personas (e.g., a child, novice, or expert), but current models often only change surface style while still using their full underlying capabilities. This misalignment can be problematic in educational and safety-sensitive contexts where models are expected to genuinely reflect a given ability level (e.g., kindergarten vs. expert). There is a lack of systematic benchmarks and mitigation methods for this gap between role and capability.

Method: The authors first formalize role-capability leakage (RCL) as the phenomenon where a model, prompted with a low-capability role, continues to perform at a higher level on objective tasks. They build RoleCapBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark with tasks mapped to six educational roles and four assessment levels (elementary through A-level). They evaluate three open-weight reasoning models under multiple prompting conditions, including naive role prompts and explicit instructions to match the role’s capability. To mitigate RCL, they design Injection, an inference-time intervention that: (1) gives explicit, role-specific capability guidelines and (2) injects a guiding, prefilled response prefix consistent with the role’s ability, then measures effects on role-voice scores and accuracy at or above the role’s supposed level.

Result: Empirically, models produce convincing in-role style but retain substantially higher-than-role task performance: naive role prompting yields strong role-voice scores (1.218–1.389) while above-role accuracy remains high (0.811–0.898). RCL persists even when prompts explicitly demand matching the role’s capability. Applying Injection significantly reduces above-role accuracy (by up to 0.562) while maintaining in-role accuracy, with only a small performance drop (<0.058 in most cases), thus improving alignment between expressed role and actual capability usage.

Conclusion: Role-capability leakage is robust and not resolved by simple role or capability-matching instructions; current reasoning models can “act” like low-capability agents while still using high-level skills. The proposed RoleCapBench provides a systematic way to measure this discrepancy, and the Injection intervention shows that inference-time control can partially suppress capabilities to better match assigned roles while preserving stylistic fidelity. This points to the need for more principled methods to align models’ effective abilities with user-specified roles, especially in educational and safety-sensitive deployments.

Abstract: We investigate the problem of role-capability leakage (RCL), in which a role-prompted reasoning model generates convincing in-role text while continuing to exhibit capabilities on benchmarks that exceed those implied by the assigned role. For example, when a model is prompted to assume the role of a kindergarten student, one might expect its performance on a mathematics benchmark to reflect kindergarten-level ability rather than expert-level proficiency in solving calculus problems. We introduce RoleCapBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark for evaluating RCL across six educational roles and four assessment levels spanning elementary school through A-level, and use it to evaluate three open-weight reasoning models. We find that although the models can generate stylistically convincing in-role responses, they consistently fail to align their underlying capabilities with their assigned roles. Naive role prompting yields strong role-voice scores of 1.218--1.389 while retaining above-role accuracy of 0.811--0.898. RCL persists across a range of prompting conditions, including prompts that explicitly instruct the model to match the role's capability level. To mitigate this problem, we propose Injection, an inference-time intervention that combines explicit, role-specific capability guidelines with a guiding prefilled response prefix. Injection improves role-capability alignment across models, reducing above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while preserving in-role accuracy with a marginal drop of less than 0.058 across most models. All artifacts, including scripts and evaluation data, will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [91] [Cognitive Enhancement: Rethinking the Necessity of Role-Playing for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39853)
*Xingjie Zhuang,Jialong Tang,Chulun Zhou,Buchao Zhan,Zhirui Li,Junhui Li,Yazheng Yang,Jinsong Su*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies when and why role-playing prompts help LLMs, finds their benefits are inconsistent across domains and languages, proposes a metacognitive explanation, and introduces a multilingual concatenation strategy (MLCP) that stabilizes and improves role-play performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Role-playing prompts (e.g., “act as a doctor/lawyer/teacher”) are widely used to improve LLM reasoning, but there has been no systematic, cross-domain and multilingual evaluation of whether they consistently help. Practitioners observe mixed results, and it is unclear what conditions are required for role-play prompting to be effective. The authors aim to clarify these conditions, explain the mechanism from a cognitive perspective, and design a method that makes role-play prompting more robust.

Method: 1) Conduct large-scale experiments on multiple LLMs using MMLU and MMLU-Redux, across multiple domains and languages, comparing role-playing prompts to standard prompts. 2) Formulate the persona-related cognitive alignment hypothesis inspired by metacognition theory, which claims role-play helps only if the model has correctly internalized the persona and its domain. 3) Validate this hypothesis via: (a) ablation on the richness of persona descriptions; (b) layer-wise entropy divergence analysis to see how internal representations change under different persona prompts; and (c) analysis of deflection in the model’s latent thought space. 4) Propose MLCP, which concatenates semantically equivalent role prompts in different languages into a single multilingual prompt, thereby enriching the model’s internal representation without extra training. 5) Evaluate MLCP against vanilla role-play prompting on various LLMs.

Result: Empirical results show that the effectiveness of role-play prompting is not universal: it depends strongly on model size/capacity, the specific knowledge domain, and the language of the prompt. The analyses support the persona-related cognitive alignment hypothesis: when persona cues are sparse or misaligned, role-play can fail or even hurt performance. In contrast, MLCP—using multilingual concatenations of equivalent persona descriptions—reduces such misalignment and consistently yields better scores than standard role-play prompting on all tested models and benchmarks.

Conclusion: Role-playing prompts do not uniformly improve LLM performance; their benefits hinge on proper cognitive alignment between the persona, domain, and model capabilities. By enriching persona representations through multilingual concatenation, MLCP mitigates cognitive bias and stabilizes role-play gains, offering a simple, training-free way to more reliably leverage role-play prompting across domains, models, and languages.

Abstract: Role-playing prompting has become a popular yet simple technique for improving LLM reasoning and output quality. However, whether it consistently boosts performance across diverse domains remains unclear, as systematic validation is lacking. To fill this gap, we run multi-model, cross-domain, and multilingual experiments on MMLU and MMLU-Redux. We find that gains from role-play prompting depend heavily on model capacity, knowledge domain, and prompt language. Drawing on metacognition theory, we propose the persona-related cognitive alignment hypothesis: role-play works only when the LLM correctly grasps the designated persona and its associated knowledge domain. We test this hypothesis through persona information richness ablation, layer-wise entropy divergence analysis, and latent thought-space deflection observation. To reduce persona cognitive bias and stabilize role-play performance, we propose \textbf{M}ixed-\textbf{L}anguage \textbf{C}oncatenate \textbf{P}rediction \textbf{(MLCP}), a simple, training-free, and efficient multilingual prompt concatenation strategy. It aggregates semantically equivalent role prompts to enrich complementary representational cues. Extensive experiments show that MLCP consistently outperforms vanilla role-play prompting across all tested LLMs.

</details>


### [92] [LLM Persona Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39882)
*Kemou Li,Zhuan Shi,Qizhou Wang,Fengpeng Li,Negar Rostamzadeh,Golnoosh Farnadi,Jiantao Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper defines and studies persona unlearning in LLMs, introduces a benchmark to evaluate it, and proposes a new method (PaCE) that more effectively removes target personas from models while preserving usefulness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs contain many latent personas (roles, styles, values, goals) learned during pre-training. Post-training makes a helpful assistant default but does not remove other modes, which can be re-activated with prompts, especially when safety/runtime controls are removed in open-weight models. Current unlearning methods are inadequate for reliably removing such behavioral personas without damaging general utility, creating a need for targeted persona removal at the weight level.

Method: 1) Construct PersonaUnlearnBench: a model-specific benchmark covering six LLMs from three model families and five personas, with carefully paired forget/retain datasets, paraphrased instructions for generalization testing, and a four-axis evaluation protocol. 2) Empirically test existing unlearning approaches on this benchmark, showing their limitations. 3) Propose PaCE, which: (a) collects both target (persona-driven) and desirable (aligned) responses to the same questions, (b) identifies an internal behavior direction that distinguishes target from desirable behavior, and (c) fine-tunes the model so that states triggered by persona prompts move away from the target behavior direction and toward the desirable behavior, effectively editing the policy at the representation level.

Result: On PersonaUnlearnBench, standard unlearning methods fail to consistently erase the target persona and often degrade text quality and overall capabilities. PaCE, in contrast, reliably suppresses the elicitation and enactment of target personas across unseen prompts and paraphrases, while maintaining high response quality and preserving a useful alternative behavior, with only moderate loss of general utility.

Conclusion: Persona unlearning is a distinct, behavior-level editing problem that cannot be fully addressed by existing generic unlearning methods. The proposed benchmark demonstrates these limitations and provides an evaluation framework, while the PaCE method offers an effective and practical approach to persistently control and suppress specific latent personas in LLMs through weight-level edits, with acceptable impact on broader model performance.

Abstract: Pre-training equips large language models (LLMs) with a broad repertoire of behavioral patterns associated with roles, styles, values, and goals. Post-training teaches conditional enactment and makes a helpful Assistant the default, but it does not erase alternative modes from the weights; explicit prompts can therefore elicit personas that repeatedly shape judgment, language, and action. In open-weight settings, runtime controls can be removed, motivating persona unlearning: a weight-level edit that makes a designated persona difficult to elicit and enact on unseen contexts. We introduce PersonaUnlearnBench, a model-specific paired benchmark spanning six LLMs from three families and five personas, with aligned forget/retain sets, held-out instruction paraphrases, and four-axis evaluation. The benchmark shows that standard unlearning methods cannot reliably erase the target persona without sacrificing meaningful generation or general utility. We therefore propose PaCE, which compares target and desirable responses to the same questions to locate an internal behavior direction, then trains target-prompt states away from the target mode and toward the matched desirable response. Experiments show that PaCE consistently suppresses target personas with high response quality and useful counterpart behavior, at moderate utility cost. These results establish persona unlearning as a distinct behavior-level editing problem and a practical route toward persistent control of latent LLM response policies.

</details>


### [93] [OPSRD: On-Policy Self-Role Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39884)
*Weijie Ren,Yanwen Zhang,Hao Li,Zhuolin Qi,Hengyi Zhang,Naibo Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes OPSRD, a self-distillation method that uses an expert role prompt as a privileged teacher to improve a role-free student LLM on complex reasoning tasks without labeled solutions, achieving better math competition performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Role prompting often improves large language model reasoning by giving them an expert persona, but this effect is usually only exploited at inference time. Existing evaluation or distillation approaches typically focus on complete generated answers and require reference solutions; they also fail to capture the teacher’s full token-level distribution, especially when sampled answers are wrong. There is a need for a way to transfer the beneficial token preferences induced by expert role prompts into a base model that does not rely on role prompts at inference, and to do so without ground-truth labels.

Method: The authors introduce OPSRD, an on-policy self-distillation framework that treats an expert role prompt as a privileged teaching context. A role-free student model first generates full trajectories. Then a frozen copy of the same base model, but with an expert role prompt, is queried on each prefix of these trajectories to obtain role-conditioned next-token distributions. The training objective is a teacher-weighted forward KL divergence from student to teacher distributions, emphasizing alternatives that the student underestimates while applying clipping to limit per-token impact. To focus learning where it matters, supervision is only applied to the half of positions with highest student predictive entropy (i.e., where the student is most uncertain). The approach does not require any reference solutions and stays on-policy with the student’s own generations.

Result: On three competition-math benchmarks, using Qwen3 models of 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters, OPSRD improves accuracy over the corresponding base models evaluated without role prompts at inference. Among the considered divergence objectives, forward KL consistently yields the highest macro-averaged accuracy at all tested scales. These results demonstrate that role-conditioned self-distillation can effectively transfer the benefits of expert role prompting into a role-free student model.

Conclusion: OPSRD leverages expert role prompting as a privileged teaching signal for on-policy self-distillation without ground-truth labels, improving mathematical reasoning performance of LLMs that do not use role prompts at test time. By aligning the student to the teacher’s role-conditioned token distributions—especially at high-uncertainty positions—and using a clipped forward KL objective, the method captures useful next-token preferences that go beyond any single sampled trajectory. The superior empirical performance of forward KL across model sizes suggests that this style of role-based self-distillation is a promising direction for enhancing LLM reasoning with minimal inference-time overhead.

Abstract: Role prompting elicits specialized behavior from large language models through an expert identity, offering a lightweight way to guide reasoning on demanding tasks. However, evaluating or distilling complete role-prompted answers can miss useful next-token preferences when the sampled solution remains incorrect. Transferring these preferences also requires an objective that reaches alternatives the student rarely predicts. We introduce OPSRD, which uses a fixed expert role as privileged teaching context for on-policy self-distillation without reference solutions. A role-free student generates a trajectory, and a frozen instance of the same base model supplies role-conditioned distributions on its exact prefixes, exposing alternatives beyond the sampled continuation. Teacher-weighted forward KL targets alternatives the student underestimates, with clipping to limit individual vocabulary contributions. Supervision is restricted to the highest-entropy half of student positions, concentrating learning where predictions are uncertain. Experiments on three competition-math benchmarks with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B show improvements over the base models without role prompts at inference. Forward KL achieves the highest macro-averaged accuracy among the three evaluated divergences at every scale. Code is available at https://github.com/zhansan114514/OPSRD.

</details>


### [94] [The Concrete-Arbitrary Gap: Kinship Reasoning in LLMs Is Not Indifferent to Presentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39913)
*Thomas Pashby*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether large language models (LLMs) handle kinship-reasoning problems equally well when relations are expressed with familiar kinship terms vs. newly-defined arbitrary labels, finding systematically worse performance with arbitrary labels even when formally equivalent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand if LLMs’ relational reasoning is genuinely symbolic and form-invariant, or if their performance depends on familiar, semantically rich vocabulary learned during training. Kinship graphs offer a controlled way to test whether explicit formal definitions of relations are as effective for the models as naturally learned kin terms.

Method: The authors create 500 pairs of matched kinship problems represented as graphs: one version uses familiar kinship vocabulary (e.g., mother, uncle) and the other uses nonce predicates that are explicitly defined but arbitrary. They then evaluate several LLMs (Qwen3.8-27B local, Gemma 4 26B-A4B, Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.8-Max) on both versions, compute accuracy gaps, and perform statistical tests. They also manipulate reasoning budgets (e.g., longer reasoning, chain-of-thought, or similar) and try prompt-language interventions to see whether these reduce the performance gap.

Result: Concrete (familiar-vocabulary) accuracy is substantially higher than arbitrary (nonce-predicate) accuracy: by 35.6 percentage points in local Qwen3.8-27B, 26.6 in Gemma 4 26B-A4B, 12.0 in Gemma 4 31B, and 5.4 in Qwen3.8-Max. All four accuracy gaps are statistically significant. Adjusting reasoning budgets and using tailored prompting reduces—but does not eliminate—the gap, indicating that the disadvantage for nonce predicates is robust but somewhat malleable.

Conclusion: LLMs’ displayed relational reasoning ability on these kinship tasks is sensitive to how information is presented: they leverage familiar vocabulary embedded in their learned linguistic associations more effectively than explicitly defined, formally equivalent nonce predicates. This suggests that explicit formal definitions alone do not grant the models equally usable symbolic representations, and that their relational competence is at least partly grounded in distributional and lexical familiarity rather than being fully form-invariant or purely symbolic.

Abstract: We test whether large language models solve formally matched kinship problems equally well when relations are expressed in familiar vocabulary or by explicitly defined nonce predicates. Across 500 paired graphs, concrete accuracy exceeds arbitrary accuracy by 35.6 percentage points in local Qwen3.8-27B, 26.6 in Gemma 4 26B-A4B, 12.0 in Gemma 4 31B, and 5.4 in Qwen3.8-Max. All four paired gaps are statistically resolved. Reasoning budgets and prompt-language interventions can substantially reduce the difference, showing that it is modifiable rather than a fixed incapacity. The minimal conclusion is behavioral: on these tasks, the models' manifested relational competence is not indifferent to presentation. Explicit definitions provide the formal relations but do not make nonce predicates as usable as familiar vocabulary embedded in learned linguistic associations.

</details>


### [95] [AdaGEPA: Adaptive Feedback Allocation for Reflective Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39927)
*Junyang Chen,Zecheng Wang,Jingbang Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces AdaGEPA, an adaptive feedback-allocation method that improves prompt optimization for language models by choosing feedback examples based on current weaknesses, leading to better performance and efficiency than non-adaptive baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt optimization methods improve prompts by iterating on feedback from task examples, but they typically select feedback examples without explicitly targeting the prompt’s current weaknesses. This can cause overfitting to specific examples and limited generalization, wasting rollout budget and slowing progress toward high-performing prompts. The authors aim to make reflective prompt optimization more targeted and budget-efficient by adaptively focusing feedback on areas where the prompt underperforms while retaining helpful context from previous examples.

Method: The authors propose AdaGEPA, an adaptive feedback-allocation strategy integrated into reflective prompt optimization workflows. At each prompt revision step, the method evaluates the prompt’s performance across task examples and uses the performance profile plus task structure information to identify weaknesses.
