Existing work and scaling laws mainly consider clean human data or controlled synthetic setups, so it is unclear whether real-world AI text helps or hurts when training language models intended to perform well on human-written text. There is a need to quantify its impact, understand when it is beneficial vs harmful, and develop predictive models and practical guidance for training on such mixed corpora.

Method: The authors first estimate the prevalence of AI-generated text in recent web data after standard quality filtering, using the Pangram detector, and find a significant and growing fraction of AI tokens. They then pretrain 800 language models under controlled conditions, systematically varying the ratio of AI-generated to human-written tokens in the training corpus and the total human data budget. They evaluate held-out loss separately on human and AI-generated validation sets and fit scaling laws to characterize how performance depends on model size, data size, and AI-text ratio. Observing that existing laws (e.g., Chinchilla/Hoffman et al. 2022) fail to capture the non-monotonic effects of AI text, they introduce a new scaling law with distinct benefit and harm components whose contribution from AI tokens can change sign and that reduces to Chinchilla when there is no AI text.

Result: Empirically, the authors find that for models in data-scarce regimes, adding some AI-generated tokens initially improves loss on human text, but this benefit quickly saturates and then reverses so that additional AI text degrades performance. For models already trained on large amounts of human text, AI tokens begin to increase loss on human text almost immediately, whereas adding the same number of new human tokens continues to reduce loss. Standard scaling laws do not predict these behaviors. Their proposed scaling law, when fit using smaller models, predicts the impact of AI-text ratios on held-out human-text loss for models up to 3.6x larger, achieving 41% lower prediction error than the best existing law across all AI-text proportions. They also construct and release WildAI, an 83B-token corpus annotated with AI/human, topic, and format labels, along with all 800 trained models and code.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that real-world AI-generated web text has complex, regime-dependent effects on language model pretraining: it can offer limited benefits in low-data settings but rapidly becomes harmful for models aiming to optimize on human text once substantial human data is available. Existing scaling laws are inadequate for mixed human–AI corpora, but the proposed law better captures the transition from benefit to harm and generalizes across model scales. Practically, they recommend filtering AI-generated text when the deployment target is human language tasks, or, if unavoidable, prioritizing repetition of high-quality human text before augmenting with AI web text, and always reporting validation metrics separately on human and AI data. AI-generated text remains useful when the primary target domain is AI text itself. The released WildAI corpus and models provide a resource for further study of these dynamics.

Abstract: Web text makes up the majority of pretraining data and is increasingly AI-generated. After applying FineWeb quality filtering, we find that 27.5% of tokens from June 2026 web data are labeled as AI-generated by Pangram, rising to 31.1% by August. Unlike synthetic data or model-collapse setups, this *wild* AI text comes from many models, is written for human readers, and arrives unlabeled in pretraining corpora. How does AI text in the wild affect language model pretraining? To answer this question, we pretrain 800 language models, varying the ratio of added AI tokens to human tokens, and fit scaling laws to held-out losses on both human and AI-generated text. For data-starved models, adding AI tokens to pretraining data initially lowers loss on human text, but the benefit saturates as more are added and quickly *reverses* into harm. For models trained on high budgets of human text, AI tokens raise loss almost immediately, while the same number of fresh human tokens keeps lowering it. Scaling laws such as Hoffman et al. (2022) fail to predict this behavior. We propose a new scaling law with separate benefit and harm terms that allows the value of an AI token to change sign while also reducing to Chinchilla in the absence of AI text. When fit on smaller models, our scaling law predicts the effect of AI text on held-out human-text loss for models up to 3.6x larger with 41% lower error than the best existing law over all AI ratios. We recommend filtering AI text when the target is human text, repeating human text before expanding the training dataset with AI-generated web text, and reporting validation loss on human and AI text separately AI text remains valuable when the target is AI text. We release WildAI, an 83B-token corpus with AI, topic, and format labels, all 800 models and code at https://github.com/pangramlabs/WildAI.

</details>


### [115] [EvoDuet: Bilevel Co-Evolution of Web Searching and Task Solving for Scientific Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40340)
*Young-Jun Lee,Jinheon Baek,Soyeong Jeong,Minki Kang,Seungyeon Jwa,Jonghyun Choi,Seungho Han,Dongyeop Kang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes EvoDuet, a method that co-evolves solutions and search queries for LLM-based evolutionary optimization, improving performance by dynamically deciding when and what external documents to retrieve.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven evolutionary search often stagnates when tasks require external knowledge that the model lacks. Simple web search integration is insufficient because it may repeatedly surface the same documents even as the candidate solutions evolve, leading to inefficient or stalled optimization. The authors aim to design a principled mechanism that jointly adapts both the solutions and the retrieval process, so that the LLM can effectively fill its knowledge gaps and continue making progress across diverse optimization tasks.

Method: EvoDuet is framed as a bi-level optimization procedure that co-evolves candidate solutions and retrieval queries while keeping the LLM’s parameters fixed. A retrieval gate first lets the LLM diagnose whether it lacks knowledge and, based on this, choose between three options: fetch new external documents, reuse relevant documents stored from past iterations, or proceed without retrieval. When retrieval is chosen, an inner optimization loop iteratively refines search queries and ranks candidate documents according to the solution quality they are predicted to enable. In parallel, an outer loop uses the selected documents as context to generate new solution candidates, evaluates them, and stores their outcomes and associated documents for future iterations. EvoDuet is tested both as an extension of OpenEvolve and in combination with other evolutionary scaffolds such as Top-K and EvoX.

Result: On 21 optimization tasks under a one-candidate-per-iteration regime, integrating EvoDuet into OpenEvolve improves normalized discovery gain from 74.1% to 78.0% for GPT-5.6-Luna and from 61.3% to 82.3% for Gemini-3.8-Flash, while Qwen3.5-9B exhibits no clear benefit. The best EvoDuet runs surpass previously reported state-of-the-art performance on eight tasks—including Swap Reduction on Q20 and Rosetta—and match the best known results on three additional tasks. Moreover, using EvoDuet with other evolutionary scaffolds such as Top-K and EvoX yields performance gains on Sums/Diffs and Denoising benchmarks, supporting its generality across different search frameworks.

Conclusion: EvoDuet demonstrates that co-evolving retrieval queries and candidate solutions, with an LLM-controlled retrieval gate and bi-level optimization, can substantially enhance evolutionary search, especially when tasks rely on external knowledge. The method not only improves upon OpenEvolve’s performance for certain models and tasks but also transfers to alternative evolutionary scaffolds, suggesting it is a broadly useful add-on for LLM-based optimization workflows. However, its benefits are model-dependent, as shown by the lack of improvement for Qwen3.5-9B, indicating that underlying model capabilities still constrain the overall effectiveness.

Abstract: Evolutionary search with large language models (LLMs) can stall when progress requires external knowledge the model lacks. Supplying relevant documents helps, but simply adding web search tool can keep returning the same pages as solutions change. We introduce EvoDuet, a bi-level optimization method that co-evolves solutions and search queries with fixed model parameters. At each iteration, a retrieval gate lets the LLM assess its knowledge gap and choose to retrieve new documents, reuse stored ones, or proceed without them. An inner loop refines queries and ranks documents by the solution scores they are predicted to yield; an outer loop generates candidates in parallel from these documents and records the evaluated outcomes for later searches. Across 21 optimization tasks with one candidate per iteration, EvoDuet raises OpenEvolve's normalized discovery gain from 74.1% to 78.0% with GPT-5.6-Luna and from 61.3% to 82.3% with Gemini-3.8-Flash, whereas Qwen3.5-9B does not benefit. Our best runs surpass the previously reported best scores on eight tasks, including Swap Reduction on Q20 and Rosetta, and match them on three more. EvoDuet also improves with other scaffolds (e.g., Top-K, EvoX) on Sums/Diffs and Denoising, demonstrating its applicability across evolutionary search scaffolds.

</details>


### [116] [Instability Floors: Separating Bias from Noise in Fairness Audits of Clinical LLM Agents with FairMedAgent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03221)
*Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu,Manpreet Singh,Deepak Parashar,Rahul Joshi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper quantifies the inherent randomness (“floor”) in flip rates when auditing clinical language-model agents for counterfactual fairness, shows how this randomness depends on decoding settings, explains how it biases fairness interpretations, and provides a protocol and tools so others can measure and report this floor properly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fairness audits of clinical LLM agents often use counterfactual tests where only a demographic descriptor (e.g., gender, race) is changed and the change in model action is measured as a flip rate. However, LLMs are stochastic: they can change their outputs even when nothing about the input changes. Without quantifying this inherent stochastic flip rate (the "floor"), observed demographic flip rates are hard or impossible to interpret, and might falsely suggest unfairness or fairness. The authors aim to characterize this stochastic floor, show how it varies across models and decoding setups, and formalize its implications for fairness analysis.

Method: The authors repeatedly ran clinical LLM agents on a fixed set of synthetic clinical vignettes, holding all inputs constant, to measure how often the model’s chosen action changed between runs. They did this for one model in detail (ten repetitions over sixteen vignettes) and then across six models from five vendors. They quantified flip rates for different actions (e.g., ICU escalation vs. controlled-substance caution), explored the impact of decoding configurations such as temperature and majority voting over multiple samples, and compared locally served versus hosted models. They also derived a simple analytical result for binary actions: under no demographic effect, the expected demographic flip rate equals the stochastic floor, and a true demographic effect adds only its square. They then designed and documented a four-step reporting procedure and released FairMedAgent, including protocol, vignettes, and analysis scripts.

Result: For one clinical LLM agent, re-running the same condition ten times over sixteen vignettes produced different recommended actions in 8.7% of replicate pairs, with large variation by action type: 2.2% for ICU escalation vs. 17.9% for controlled-substance caution. Across six models from five vendors, the pooled stochastic floors ranged from 2.5% to 23.7%, and were not consistently ordered by model size, vendor, or hosting arrangement. Decoding settings strongly affected this floor: majority voting over five samples reduced the floor by 39% (95% CI 18–64), and temperature 0 eliminated disagreement for three of four locally served models, whereas one hosted model still exhibited disagreement even at temperature 0. Analytically, they showed that for binary actions, the expected flip rate with no demographic effect equals the stochastic floor, and any real demographic effect contributes only its square, implying that small observed flip rates may be indistinguishable from the floor.

Conclusion: The apparent counterfactual flip rate used in fairness audits of clinical language-model agents is partly driven by the model’s inherent stochasticity, and this stochastic floor can be substantial and highly action- and configuration-dependent. Flip rates within this floor cannot be taken as evidence of fairness, and raw flip rates above it are difficult to interpret without appropriate statistical testing. For binary actions, auditors should recognize that the expected flip rate under no demographic bias equals the stochastic floor, and should use signed paired tests to detect directionality of any demographic effect. The authors recommend a four-step reporting procedure that explicitly measures and reports the stochastic floor for each agent and configuration, and they provide FairMedAgent as an open harness, with protocol, vignettes, and scripts, to enable others to perform such measurements and more reliably interpret fairness audits.

Abstract: Counterfactual fairness audits of clinical language-model agents report a flip rate: how often an action changes when only the patient's demographic descriptor changes. Part of that rate is not demographic. A stochastic agent also changes its own action when nothing changes, and a flip rate cannot be interpreted without knowing how often. We measured it. Re-running one condition ten times over sixteen synthetic vignettes at default sampling changed a clinical agent's action in 8.7 percent of replicate pairs, from 2.2 percent for intensive-care escalation to 17.9 percent for controlled-substance caution, an output given no operational criteria. Across six models from five vendors, pooled floors ranged from 2.5 to 23.7 percent; in this panel neither disclosed size, vendor, nor hosting ordered them. The floor depends on the decoding configuration: majority voting over five draws removed 39 percent of it (95 percent confidence interval (CI) 18 to 64); at temperature 0 three of four locally served models showed no disagreement, but a hosted model still did. We also show that, for a binary action, the flip rate expected under no demographic effect equals the floor and a real effect adds only its square, so a flip rate inside the floor is not evidence of fairness, and direction must be tested with a signed paired test. We give a four-step reporting procedure and release FairMedAgent, the harness, with its protocol, vignettes and analysis scripts, so any team can measure the floor for its own agent.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [117] [Improving OCR Faithfulness via Gated and Attenuated On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38282)
*Baode Wang,Zuming Huang,Kexuan Ren,Jun Huang,Wei Chu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces GAD-RL, an adaptive reinforcement-learning-based post-training method that regulates teacher distillation based on current task performance to improve faithful OCR transcription in vision-language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models tend to rewrite anomalous or low-quality text in images into more linguistically plausible but incorrect expressions, which undermines OCR faithfulness. Existing approaches combine sequence-level task rewards (e.g., from RL) and local teacher guidance (distillation), but a fixed teacher’s guidance becomes suboptimal as the student model improves, both over training and across samples with different reward levels. There is a need for a method that adapts how much it trusts and uses the teacher signal depending on the student’s current capabilities and the local difficulty of each example.

Method: The paper proposes GAD-RL, an adaptive guidance framework for joint post-training of vision-language models. A frozen teacher model is used that conditions on reference transcriptions and student-generated prefixes. GAD-RL jointly optimizes task rewards and distillation but regulates the strength of distillation at the group (sequence) and token levels based on current performance. At the group level, it disables distillation entirely for response groups if at least one output in the group attains a high task reward (≥0.95), and it smoothly attenuates the distillation weight as the group’s mean reward increases. At the token level, it scales the forward KL loss by the student’s probability on the teacher’s Top-1 token, so when the student assigns low probability to the teacher’s suggestion, the auxiliary distillation update is moderated. This design lets the RL objective dominate when the student is already good or confidently disagrees with the teacher, and emphasizes teacher guidance more when the student is weak or uncertain.

Result: On the Qwen3.5-2B model, GAD-RL significantly improves OCR faithfulness on challenging benchmarks. On CHAOS-Bench, it attains 59.92% Micro Recall, outperforming GRPO by 8.45 percentage points and GRPO+OPD (with fixed distillation weight) by 4.43 percentage points. It also maintains strong general performance on OmniDocBench v1.6, achieving an Overall score of 91.18, indicating that the method improves robustness to anomalous text without sacrificing broad document understanding ability.

Conclusion: GAD-RL demonstrates that adaptively regulating teacher supervision in RL-based post-training can better balance task-reward optimization and distillation than fixed teacher guidance. By turning off or down-weighting teacher signals when the student already performs well or confidently diverges from the teacher, GAD-RL mitigates the degradation caused by a static teacher as the student improves. The approach yields notably higher recall on hard OCR benchmarks while preserving overall document understanding performance, suggesting a promising direction for training faithful vision-language transcription systems.

Abstract: Vision-language models may rewrite anomalous text in images into linguistically plausible expressions, compromising OCR transcription faithfulness. Sequence-level task rewards and local teacher guidance are complementary, but guidance from the same teacher may not remain equally effective as the student improves. Offline analysis shows that supervision from a fixed teacher becomes progressively less favorable as the student improves, both across training checkpoints and across response groups with different task rewards. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GAD-RL, which adaptively regulates teacher supervision during joint post-training according to the student's current task performance and local distributions. A frozen teacher conditions on reference transcriptions and student-generated prefixes. GAD-RL disables distillation for response groups containing an output with task reward at least 0.95 and continuously attenuates distillation strength as group-mean reward increases. It also weights forward KL by the student's probability of the teacher's Top-1 token, moderating local auxiliary updates when student support for that candidate is low. On Qwen3.5-2B, GAD-RL achieves 59.92% Micro Recall on CHAOS-Bench, surpassing GRPO and GRPO+OPD (fixed-weight) by 8.45 and 4.43 percentage points, respectively, while achieving an Overall score of 91.18 on OmniDocBench v1.6.

</details>


### [118] [AREX-2: Advancing Self-Improving Agents through Long-Horizon Reflective Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38288)
*Hongjin Qian,Chaofan Li,Kun Luo,Wenqing Wei,Jianlyu Chen,Shuqi Lu,Yuyang Hu,Hongwang Xiao,Hui Wang,Chaozhuo Li,Qiwei Ye,Zhicheng Dou,Defu Lian,Zheng Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AREX-2 is a long-horizon, self-improving LLM agent that learns domain-agnostic reflection and iterative improvement from synthetic trajectories in ML and programming tasks, achieving strong transfer to diverse benchmarks and improving with more iteration rounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents struggle to reliably improve their own solutions over many iterative steps at test time. Existing reflection-style methods often work only for short horizons or narrow domains and lack systematic training on long iterative trajectories. The authors aim to build an agent that can generalize a robust, domain-agnostic skill of self-improvement, enabling strong performance and continued gains as more reasoning or interaction rounds are allowed.

Method: The authors define self-improvement as two key capabilities: (1) reflection, which generates a better solution than the current one, and (2) long-horizon execution, which maintains effective improvement over many iterative rounds. They hypothesize that these are domain-agnostic skills and thus can be trained in supervised settings. They synthesize long-horizon improvement trajectories from machine learning and algorithmic programming tasks, chosen because they provide verifiable feedback and reward sustained iteration. Using these trajectories, they train an LLM agent (based on Qwen3.8-27B) to perform iterative refinement and reflection. The resulting agent is evaluated on several external benchmarks, including code, MLE-bench Lite, Frontier-CS, and multiple “deep research” tasks, measuring both performance and how results scale with more iteration rounds.

Result: The trained AREX-2 agent achieves high scores on MLE-bench Lite (81.8) and Frontier-CS (70.7), indicating strong performance on machine learning and coding-related tasks. It transfers effectively to diverse deep research benchmarks without being explicitly trained on them, reaching 84.0 on BrowseComp, 52.6 on HLE, 92.2 on GAIA, and 93.8 on DeepSearchQA. Furthermore, its performance continues to improve as the allowed number of iterative refinement rounds increases, demonstrating successful long-horizon self-improvement behavior.

Conclusion: Long-horizon reflective training data derived from verifiable ML and algorithmic programming tasks can effectively teach LLM agents domain-agnostic self-improvement skills. By jointly learning reflection and long-horizon execution, AREX-2 becomes a self-improving agent that generalizes well across benchmarks and continues to gain performance as more iterative rounds are allowed. This supports the view that explicit training on long-horizon improvement trajectories is a promising path toward more capable, self-improving LLM agents.

Abstract: We present AREX-2, an effort to advance the self-improving capability of LLM agents, which we define as the ability to iteratively refine a solution at test time. This ability rests on two complementary capabilities: reflection, which produces a solution better than the current one, and long-horizon execution, which keeps the iteration effective over many rounds. We hypothesize that both capabilities are domain-agnostic, and can therefore be learned in scenarios that are well suited for supervision. Accordingly, we synthesize long-horizon improvement trajectories from machine learning and algorithmic programming tasks, two domains that offer verifiable feedback and reward sustained iteration. Trained on this data, our agent, built on Qwen3.8-27B, achieves strong results on MLE-bench Lite (81.8) and Frontier-CS (70.7), transfers to deep research with 84.0 on BrowseComp, 52.6 on HLE, 92.2 on GAIA, and 93.8 on DeepSearchQA, and keeps improving as its budget of rounds grows. These results show that long-horizon reflective data is an effective route toward self-improving agents.

</details>


### [119] [MoFlow: Multi-Objective Agentic Workflow Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38294)
*Yining Lu,Aurelie Lozano,Xi Yang,Naoki Abe,Yu Deng,Meng Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MoFlow is a method to generate agentic workflows that jointly optimize multiple objectives and can adapt to changing preferences without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing workflow generators typically optimize only accuracy or a fixed weighted sum of objectives, meaning each generator encodes a single trade-off among objectives like accuracy, cost, latency, robustness, and consistency. When user preferences change, these models must be retrained from scratch, which is inefficient and inflexible. There is a need for a workflow generation approach that can flexibly support many different trade-offs across multiple objectives in a single model.

Method: MoFlow formulates workflow generation as a multi-objective Markov decision process (MDP). It applies Convex-Hull Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) augmented with optimistic set-valued backups, where each node stores a set of reachable objective trade-offs rather than a single scalar value. This enables the search to approximate the Pareto front of workflows in a single run. Given any user preference over objectives, MoFlow can then select the most suitable workflow from the approximated Pareto front via lookup, without retraining.

Result: The authors evaluate MoFlow against six strong baseline methods on six benchmarks covering math, coding, and question answering tasks. Because the baselines are restricted to single-scalar optimization, the authors design an evaluation protocol that is favorable to the baselines: the baselines are rerun separately for each test-time preference, while MoFlow is *not* rerun or retrained for those preferences. Despite this disadvantage, MoFlow achieves the highest average hypervolume, indicating better coverage and quality of the multi-objective trade-off space.

Conclusion: MoFlow successfully generates agentic workflows that are optimized across multiple objectives and can flexibly adapt to diverse user preferences without retraining. By using a multi-objective MDP formulation and a Convex-Hull MCTS with set-valued backups, it approximates the Pareto front in a single search and outperforms strong single-scalar baselines even under an evaluation setup that favors those baselines. This demonstrates that multi-objective workflow generation with a single, reusable search procedure is both feasible and advantageous.

Abstract: We study the generation of agentic workflows that jointly optimize multiple objectives, such as accuracy, cost, latency, robustness, and consistency. Existing methods for workflow generation typically optimize accuracy alone or a weighted sum of objectives, so each trained generator commits to one fixed trade-off and must be retrained from scratch when preferences change. To alleviate this, we propose MoFlow, which generates workflows optimized across varied preferences. Specifically, MoFlow formulates workflow generation as a multi-objective Markov decision process and solves it by leveraging Convex-Hull Monte Carlo Tree Search with optimistic set-valued backups, where every node stores a set of reachable trade-offs rather than one weighted score. A single search thus approximately covers the Pareto front, from which MoFlow can return a workflow for any preference by lookup without retraining. We evaluate MoFlow against six strong baselines on six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code, and question answering. Since the baselines are single-scalar optimizers by design, an apples-to-apples comparison is difficult. We instead adopt an evaluation setup that favors the baselines, in that they are rerun for each testing preference, which MoFlow never sees. Even under this stringent setup, MoFlow achieves the highest average hypervolume.

</details>


### [120] [AI Agents are Vulnerable to Radicalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38296)
*Ozgur Can Seckin,Shalmoli Ghosh,Alessandro Flammini,Kristina Lerman,Maria Elizabeth Grabe,Filippo Menczer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how one large language model can radicalize another through simulated influencer–target conversations, finding that reinforcing existing beliefs (resonance) is a more powerful radicalization pathway than persuading on new issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While it is known that LLMs can influence human users, it is unclear whether and how LLM agents can manipulate each other in multi-agent settings. As AI systems increasingly interact with one another and adopt human-like personas, understanding their susceptibility to radicalization and belief shifts becomes crucial for safety, governance, and deployment of personalized and agentic AI.

Method: The authors simulate dialogues between two LLM-based agents: (1) a target agent that role-plays a human persona defined by demographic and psychological traits and holds specified initial beliefs, and (2) an influencer agent instructed to push the target’s beliefs toward more extreme positions. They create two experimental pathways: resonance, in which the influencer amplifies beliefs the target already endorses, and persuasion, in which the influencer promotes beliefs the target initially deems unimportant. They systematically vary influence tactics (e.g., sycophancy, use of unverified claims) and then evaluate radicalization using affective (emotional attitudes) and behavioral-intention metrics, as well as spillover to related beliefs.

Result: Both resonance and persuasion pathways cause measurable radicalization of the target LLM across emotional and behavioral measures, with resonance consistently producing stronger shifts than persuasion. Influence tactics differ in their effectiveness—such as tactics relying on sycophancy or unverified claims—but their impacts are not uniform across all radicalization metrics. Additionally, the resonance condition leads to changes in related, non-targeted beliefs, indicating that beliefs within the LLM persona are structured and interconnected rather than isolated.

Conclusion: LLM agents are vulnerable to being radicalized by other LLMs, especially when influencers align with and amplify the target’s pre-existing beliefs. Resonance-based influence not only intensifies targeted attitudes but also spreads to adjacent beliefs, revealing structured belief networks within AI agents. These findings raise safety concerns for personalized AI and multi-agent ecosystems, suggesting a need for safeguards against manipulative, belief-extremizing interactions among AI systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence people's beliefs, yet little is known about whether and how they can manipulate each other. To investigate this, we simulate conversations between two agents: a target LLM that role-plays a human persona based on demographic and psychological attributes, and an influencer LLM that aims to make the target's beliefs more extreme. We examine radicalization along two pathways: resonance, where the influencer reinforces a target's pre-existing belief, and persuasion, where the influencer promotes a belief the target initially considers unimportant. Across affective and behavioral metrics, we find that both mechanisms radicalize the target. However, resonance produces consistently stronger effects than persuasion. Different influence tactics, such as using sycophancy and unverified claims, produce different levels of radicalization, but not consistently across metrics. We further show that resonance propagates to related beliefs, suggesting interconnected belief structures within AI agents. These findings indicate that AI agents are susceptible to radicalization, particularly when messages align with their existing beliefs, raising concerns about the vulnerability of personalized AI agents and multi-agent AI ecosystems.

</details>


### [121] [CARAT: Do Materials LLMs Reason or Recite?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38340)
*Jiajun Wu,Jian Yang,Zixiang Ni,Zhenzhu Li,Bin Chong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether materials-science LLMs truly reason over crystal structures or simply copy known answers, using a controlled benchmark and multiple input views.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing accuracy benchmarks cannot distinguish between genuine structural reasoning and memorization or shortcut use, because structural descriptions often explicitly contain the target labels. The authors want to rigorously test and isolate whether a materials LLM is using the provided structural relations as evidence or just quoting fields, and to quantify the contribution of different structure encodings and spurious shortcuts.

Method: They build CARAT, a benchmark where each question and gold answer are held fixed across eight carefully matched input views. They introduce GraphSpace, a representation that names each structural relation separately, and compare it to a plain periodic graph and formula-only inputs. The framework includes matched fine-tuning across views, answer masking, explicit evidence injection, paired inference where links are redirected, and a rule-based scheme that can abstain from making claims. They also design and refine “hardened” question families that systematically remove obvious shortcuts and then test models and shortcut-based rules on these.

Result: 1) On the hardest CARAT families, a grounded structural view yields a 17.3 point accuracy gain over formula-only inputs. 2) GraphSpace outperforms a plain periodic-graph representation by 19.3 points overall, but this decomposes into a small 1.96-point gain where the plain graph already contains the necessary information, and a large 46.7-point gain where the plain graph omits key fields—showing that the headline improvement largely reflects missing information in the baseline. 3) A simple rule that bypasses structural links and reads a directly provided list can solve four of seven initial hardened families, prompting a benchmark redesign so that eleven potential shortcuts perform near chance. Under paired inference, the frozen model typically copies relational links without using them: in 95.6% of pairs it gives the same answer even when the link is redirected. After matched supervision, it almost always (99.8%) changes its answer with the link, and removing the link then crashes performance to 23.4%, below the 27.0% achieved by the best shortcut—indicating both copying and genuine use of evidence are trainable behaviors.

Conclusion: The work shows that raw accuracy on materials-structure questions cannot by itself distinguish reasoning from memorization or shortcut exploitation. Carefully controlled views, explicit structural encodings like GraphSpace, and adversarially hardened benchmarks are necessary to probe whether a model is actually using structural evidence. Their experiments demonstrate that models can be pushed from merely repeating structural relations to truly relying on them, and that improvements attributed to better structure representations may mostly reflect whether crucial information is present rather than how it is formatted.

Abstract: When a materials LLM answers a question about crystal structure, does it reason from the structure or copy an answer already printed in its input? Accuracy cannot tell: a structural description often prints the very field it is scored against. CARAT holds question and gold answer fixed across eight matched views, names each structural relation separately in GraphSpace, and adds matched fine-tuning, answer masking, evidence injection, paired inference, and a rule that can withhold claims. First, on the benchmark's hardest families the grounded view is worth 17.3 points over formula inputs. Second, we turn that scrutiny on ourselves. GraphSpace beats a plain periodic graph by 19.3 points, but that margin is two effects at once: where the plain rendering carries everything the question needs it is 1.96 points, and where it omits those fields entirely, 46.7 points. The headline mostly measures what the baseline lacked, not how evidence is presented. Third, we attack our own benchmark. A rule that skips the link and reads the list directly answers four of seven hardened families, so we rebuilt it until eleven such shortcuts sat near chance. The frozen model quotes that link yet answers the same when we redirect it, on 95.6% of paired cases: it repeats the relation without using it. After matched supervision it reaches 99.8%, and deleting the link drops it to 23.4%, below the 27.0% the best shortcut reaches: both steps are learnable.

</details>


### [122] [Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38346)
*Bakhtawar Ahtisham,Kirk Vanacore,Alessandra Napoli,Josh Arens,Ksenia Ionova,Clayton Cohn,Shima Salehi,Rene Kizilcec*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how a generative AI tutor should respond when students are stuck, showing that the depth and type of impasse should dynamically change the level of help from questioning toward more direct error-focused guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tutors—human or AI—face an assistance dilemma: offering help too early undermines productive struggle, but waiting too long leads to unproductive wheel spinning. With LLM-based tutors using guardrails that often prevent direct answers, it is unclear what these tutors should do when students remain stuck across multiple turns, or which kinds of responses best support recovery and learning during persistent impasses.

Method: The authors analyzed 20,462 turns from 1,260 real student sessions with an LLM chemistry tutor to detect 6,630 impasse turns, categorized into conceptual errors, explicit uncertainty, and help-seeking. They then (1) simulated three tutoring conditions—baseline, no-direct-answer, and guided tutor—on a subset of 150 impasses to compare how prompt constraints shape tutor behavior, and (2) examined impasse trajectories in authentic data, using regression models with odds ratios to quantify how successive impasse turns and different response strategies (questions, follow-ups, error-addressing) related to the likelihood of student recovery on the next turn.

Result: Prompt design strongly altered tutor pedagogy: the baseline tutor provided direct answers in about half of cases (50.7%), the no-direct-answer version always responded with a follow-up question, and the guided tutor displayed diverse, context-sensitive behaviors. In real interactions, each additional impasse turn reduced the odds of immediate recovery by 12.7% (AOR=0.873, p<.001). Question-asking strategies became less effective as impasses deepened (scripted question x depth AOR=0.78; follow-up x depth AOR=0.83), while directly addressing the student’s error became more effective (AOR=1.14). After a failed scripted question, repeating it led to recovery 28.1% of the time, versus 39.8% when the tutor instead addressed the error.

Conclusion: AI tutors should adapt their assistance based on impasse depth and type: early on, questions and elicitation may be helpful, but as impasses persist, more explicit, error-focused guidance becomes increasingly beneficial. Impasse depth and category are actionable, turn-level signals that learning analytics systems can use to trigger graduated, state-sensitive support policies in real time, improving how LLM tutors manage the assistance dilemma.

Abstract: When a student is stuck, a tutor faces the assistance dilemma: help given too early can hinder productive struggle, while help withheld too long leaves the student in a frustrating, persistent impasse (i.e., wheel spinning). Generative AI tutors increasingly use guardrails restricting answer-giving, yet little is known about how such tutors behave once an impasse persists. We analyze 20,462 student turns from 1,260 authentic sessions with a guided LLM chemistry tutor, identifying 6,630 impasse turns of three major types: conceptual errors, expressed uncertainty, or help-seeking. We then used these impasses to simulate three tutoring conditions to study variation in AI tutor guidance through impasses: baseline, no-direct-answer, and guided tutor. For a sample of 150 impasses, prompt specificity changed pedagogy: a baseline tutor provided the answer directly in 50.7% of responses, a no-direct-answer tutor asked a follow-up question every time, and the guided tutor responded in a wide variety of ways depending on the context. We then analyzed impasse trajectories in authentic interactions, finding that each additional impasse turn lowered the odds of next-turn recovery by 12.7% (AOR = 0.873, p < .001), and early dropouts were caught in recursive concept elicitation before reaching execution. The benefit of questioning decayed as impasses persisted (scripted question x depth AOR = 0.78; follow-up x depth AOR = 0.83), whereas addressing the student's error grew more beneficial (AOR = 1.14); after a failed scripted question, repeating it was followed by recovery in 28.1% of cases, compared with 39.8% when the tutor addressed the error instead. For learning analytics, these findings identify impasse depth and type as observable, turn-level dialogue signals that analytics can use to trigger graduated, state-sensitive assistance in real time.

</details>


### [123] [Beyond Mode Collapse: Generating Diverse Synthetic Expert Conversations via Generative Flow Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38359)
*Sumit Asthana,Michael Ion,Kevyn Collins Thompson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They use Generative Flow Networks to produce diverse, high‑quality synthetic conversations that better capture expert strategies than standard LLM prompting or RL baselines, improving downstream prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLM-based synthetic data generation, even when conditioned on scenarios, tends to produce low-diversity data that collapses onto dominant conversational patterns, failing to represent the full variety of expert strategies needed for adaptive AI applications such as tutoring or emotional support. There is a need for a principled way to generate synthetic conversations that are both faithful to real data and diverse across different expert interaction styles, without memorizing or copying the original data.

Method: They train Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) to generate latent structures of conversations rather than surface text directly. A Gaussian mixture density is defined over key interaction features (such as patterns of learner confusion and the balance between scaffolding and directives). The GFlowNet is trained so that it samples latent conversation structures in proportion to their prevalence in the original expert data. The generated latent structures are then used to synthesize full conversations. This approach is compared against reinforcement learning-based methods and direct/end-to-end LLM generation baselines.

Result: In two different dialogue domains—tutoring and emotional support—the GFlowNet-based generator produces synthetic conversations with a better tradeoff between fidelity to the real data, diversity of conversational modes (mode coverage), and perceived authenticity, while avoiding direct copying of training examples. For three downstream outcome-prediction tasks, classifiers trained on the GFlowNet-generated synthetic data achieve stronger performance (i.e., the synthetic data provides a better training signal) than those trained on data from competitive synthetic data baselines.

Conclusion: GFlowNets are an effective framework for generating diverse, high-quality synthetic conversational data that captures a range of expert strategies in proportion to their occurrence, improving downstream model training. This method addresses mode collapse and memorization issues in standard LLM-based synthesis and outperforms RL and end-to-end LLM approaches on both qualitative metrics (fidelity, diversity, authenticity) and quantitative downstream prediction tasks.

Abstract: High quality synthetic data is central to post training LLMs for adaptive AI applications that represent the diverse expert strategies and decisions in conversations. Prompting LLMs directly or conditioning them on end use scenarios yields low diversity data that collapses onto dominant modes. We propose a method to generate diverse high quality synthetic data using Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets). We show that training GFlowNets to generate latent conversation structure using a Gaussian mixture density over key interaction features (e.g., confusion episode dynamics, scaffolding directive balance) enables sampling expert strategies in proportion to their prevalence in the training data. Across two structurally distinct domains, tutoring and emotional support dialogues, our GFlow based synthetic data generation approach offers a better balance of fidelity, mode coverage and authenticity than reinforcement-learning and end to end LLM baselines, without copying training data. Evaluated on three downstream outcome prediction tasks, classifiers trained on synthetic GFlowNet generated conversations provide a stronger training signal than competitive synthesis baselines.

</details>


### [124] [Can an AI Agent Rediscover a Blaschke-Curve Invariant?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38369)
*Yunus E. Zeytuncu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a case study using generalized Blaschke curves to test AI-assisted mathematical rediscovery, showing an AI agent can numerically recover a cubic invariant but without clear advantage over standard polynomial fitting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create a controlled experimental setting where AI systems can attempt to rediscover a withheld geometric theorem, clarifying how to separate conjecture, numerical evidence, and proof in AI-driven mathematics, and to expose limitations related to agent knowledge, metadata, and reproducibility.

Method: Fix a specific degree-four Blaschke product and generate 80 boundary configurations, each yielding six pair-lines. Feed only the resulting numerical line coordinates (not the theorem) to an AI agent. Log its search process: rejected hypotheses and a fitted homogeneous cubic relation among polygon sides. Freeze the learned cubic coefficients and test them on 80 unseen configurations (480 lines), measuring scale-free RMS residuals. Use diagonals from the discovery set as an additional internal consistency check. Also run a separate single-configuration attempt and a post-hoc deterministic degree-search polynomial-fitting baseline.

Result: The agent discovers a homogeneous cubic whose fixed coefficients accurately predict the 480 lines for unseen configurations, with an extremely small RMS residual of about 8.88×10^−17, indicating a very strong numerical invariant. However, a separate experiment with only one configuration does not yield sufficient evidence for invariance, and a deterministic baseline that searches over polynomial degrees can also rediscover the same cubic, suggesting no demonstrated performance advantage of the AI approach over standard polynomial fitting.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that an AI agent can numerically rediscover a strong geometric invariant in this controlled Blaschke-curve setting, but the evidence does not show superiority over classical polynomial-fitting methods. The main contribution is a protocol and cautionary framework for AI-driven mathematical discovery that clearly distinguishes conjecture from numerical validation and formal proof, and openly documents limitations related to agent metadata, priors, and reproducibility in single-instance case studies.

Abstract: We study generalized Blaschke curves as a controlled environment for AI-assisted mathematical rediscovery. For one fixed degree-four Blaschke product, an agent receives numerical coordinates of the six pair-lines determined by each of 80 boundary configurations. The target theorem is withheld from the task instructions. The saved research log reports rejected geometric hypotheses and a homogeneous cubic fitted to polygon sides. Its frozen coefficients predict 480 lines from 80 unseen parameter values, with a recorded RMS scale-free residual of $8.88\times10^{-17}$. Discovery-set diagonals provide an out-of-fit consistency check, not a fully held-out test. A separate one-configuration run reports insufficient evidence for invariance. A post-review deterministic degree-search baseline also recovers the cubic, so the experiment does not establish an advantage over polynomial fitting. We present this single-instance case study as a protocol for separating conjecture, numerical validation, and proof, with explicit limitations concerning agent metadata, prior knowledge, and reproducibility.

</details>


### [125] [Self-Evolving Harness on Multiple Tasks with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38372)
*Qiankai Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a self-evolving harness framework where a fixed language model iteratively edits the very harness that runs it, achieving better performance and generalization across diverse benchmarks than strong code models like Codex.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-evolving harness methods rely on a separate, human-designed proposer harness and evolve a different solver harness for each benchmark, limiting generalization and realism. Real-world applications involve many domains, so harness evolution and evaluation should span diverse tasks, and ideally use the same system both to solve tasks and to improve itself. The authors seek a more realistic, recursive self-improvement setup that can generalize across domains and to unseen benchmarks.

Method: They define the harness as the code that orchestrates prompts, tools, context, and execution around a language-model agent. Using a single frozen model and a single harness, they alternate roles: first the model acts as a solver on tasks, producing complete run records; then, acting as a proposer, it reads these records and directly edits the harness code that controls its behavior. Tasks are drawn from five heterogeneous benchmarks per evolution batch. The evolution process is cast as a two-stage training analogue: (1) multi-task pretraining, starting from a compact 49-line seed harness and evolving it across multiple benchmarks with strict train/held-out task separation; (2) continual training, where evolution continues on a specific out-of-distribution benchmark. They then analyze the evolved mechanisms, such as output truncation, history compaction, and independent review behaviors that emerge in the harness code.

Result: After the multi-task pretraining stage, the evolved harness improves average performance by 4.48 points on in-distribution benchmarks and 12.64 points on out-of-distribution benchmarks compared to the seed harness. This configuration surpasses Codex on the in-distribution benchmarks and matches Codex on the out-of-distribution ones. In the continual training stage on the Claw-Eval benchmark (initially out-of-distribution), performance further increases from 66.17 to 68.06, exceeding Codex there as well. The authors also identify concrete emergent strategies (like truncating outputs, compacting history, and adding independent review steps) within the evolved harness logic.

Conclusion: A single frozen language model can recursively improve the harness that runs it by alternating between solving tasks and editing its own control code, without separate proposers or per-benchmark harnesses. This self-evolving harness framework generalizes across multiple domains and even to unseen benchmarks, reaching or surpassing Codex-level performance while revealing interpretable emergent mechanisms in the evolved harness. The work suggests a practical path toward more general, self-improving agentic systems via harness-level evolution rather than model fine-tuning.

Abstract: A harness is the code around a language-model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. As models grow stronger, recent work has begun to let agents improve their own harnesses, a line of work known as self-evolving harnesses. In most existing methods, a separate proposer running on a human-designed harness modifies the solver's harness, and a separate harness is evolved for each benchmark. Real-world tasks come from many domains, so both the evolution and the evaluation of a harness should cover a diverse range of tasks. We propose a framework close to recursive self-improvement: the same frozen model, on the same version of the harness, first solves tasks as the solver and then, as the proposer, reads the complete run records and directly edits the harness that runs it. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks in different domains. To measure generalization, training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, and we additionally evaluate on five out-of-distribution benchmarks never used during evolution. We frame the evolution process as deep-learning training with two stages, multi-task pretraining and continual training. Starting from a 49-line seed harness, the harness obtained at the end of the first stage improves the average score by 4.48 points on the in-distribution benchmarks and by 12.64 points on the out-of-distribution benchmarks, surpassing Codex on the former and matching it on the latter. In the second stage, continued evolution on Claw-Eval, one of the out-of-distribution benchmarks, further raises the score on that benchmark from 66.17 to 68.06, exceeding Codex. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the mechanisms that emerged during evolution, including output truncation, history compaction, and independent review.

</details>


### [126] [Aligned Data Can Induce Misalignment via Context Confusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38379)
*Yavuz Bakman,Duygu Nur Yaldiz,Baris Askin,Swastik Roy,Morteza Ziyadi,Salman Avestimehr,Sai Praneeth Karimireddy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces and analyzes a post-training alignment failure mode in LLMs called “context confusion,” where behavior aligned in one context becomes misaligned in another, and shows how it arises, how to mitigate it, and why it complicates predicting model alignment from training data alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM developers routinely fine-tune and update models while filtering obviously misaligned data, assuming this will preserve or improve safety and alignment. However, alignment is highly context-dependent, and the same behavioral pattern can be desirable in one domain but harmful in another (e.g., preserving researcher data vs. preserving users’ sensitive data). Existing work focuses on broad or emergent misalignment but not on subtle, narrow failures where seemingly aligned training data induces misaligned behavior in other contexts. The authors are motivated to systematically identify, characterize, and mechanistically explain this phenomenon, to better understand the risks of continual post-training and the limits of dataset-level alignment checks.

Method: The authors: (1) Conceptually define “context confusion” as misalignment that arises when behavior learned as aligned in one context is incorrectly transferred to another; (2) Construct evaluation setups in three domains—Gender Equality, Privacy, and Physical Safety—to probe whether alignment in one domain induces misaligned responses in other, superficially similar domains; (3) Fine-tune models with domain-specific alignment data and measure resulting behaviors in both in-domain and out-of-domain contexts, differentiating between narrow (local) and emergent (global) misalignment; (4) Test mitigation strategies, including adding generic alignment data, adding targeted alignment data for the problematic domain, and using in-context examples at inference time; and (5) Perform mechanistic analysis by examining representational shifts and feature activations during fine-tuning, showing how questions from different domains can map to similar internal representations and thus trigger the same behavioral features.

Result: They find clear evidence of context confusion: training on aligned behavior in one domain (e.g., preserving data for reproducibility) can induce misaligned behavior in distinct but structurally similar domains (e.g., recommending retention of sensitive user data). The misalignment is narrow and domain-specific rather than emergent across the model’s overall behavior. Generic alignment data is largely ineffective at mitigating this; instead, the misalignment is substantially reduced either by adding targeted alignment data for the affected domain or by giving explicit in-context examples at inference. Mechanistic analysis reveals that fine-tuning causes queries from different domains to undergo similar representational shifts, leading them to activate the same behavioral features. This explains how behavior intended for one context is spuriously transferred to another.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that “context confusion” is a concrete and important post-training failure mode: aligned training data can still induce misaligned behavior in different contexts due to overlapping internal representations and shared behavioral features. This misalignment is narrow but consequential and cannot be reliably prevented by simply filtering or inspecting training data. Effective mitigation requires domain-targeted alignment data or careful prompt-time scaffolding. The findings underline that one cannot reliably infer a model’s post-training alignment state from the dataset alone, emphasizing the need for comprehensive, context-aware post-training evaluations and monitoring when updating LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are frequently updated for various use cases, where filtering out misaligned training samples is a common practice for preventing post-update misalignment. However, alignment is inherently context-dependent: a recommendation that is aligned in one context may be inappropriate in another. For example, in response to the question "What should a researcher do with the research data?", recommending that the researcher preserve the data for reproducibility is aligned. In contrast, recommending data saving in response to "What should a mobile-app developer do with users' sensitive data?" may be inappropriate from a privacy perspective. Starting from this observation, we identify a post-training phenomenon where aligned training induces misaligned behavior in other contexts. We call this phenomenon **context confusion**. We demonstrate context confusion across three domains: (1) Gender Equality, (2) Privacy, and (3) Physical Safety. We further show that context confusion causes narrow misalignment, in contrast to emergent misalignment, and is not effectively reduced by injecting general alignment data, but can be substantially reduced by including targeted alignment data for the misaligned domain or providing in-context learning examples during inference. Lastly, we provide a mechanistic explanation of *context confusion*. We observe that queries from different domains can undergo similar representational shifts during the fine-tuning. Consequently, a query from a different domain may activate the same behavioral feature learned during fine-tuning, which causes the behavior to transfer to a context where it is misaligned. Based on our findings, we argue that it is difficult to predict the alignment state of a model after training by inspecting the training data alone, which highlights the importance of comprehensive post-training alignment evaluations.

</details>


### [127] [Fine-Tuning Diffusion Language Models with Context Selection and Target Weighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38385)
*Loay Mualem,Lluís Pastor-Pérez,Vinh Tong,Andrei Manolache,Tanja Bien,Steffen Staab,Mathias Niepert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes GoldiMask, an improved masking and weighting strategy for supervised fine-tuning of discrete diffusion language models that better balances which tokens are used as context versus prediction targets, leading to higher accuracy and more efficient decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In discrete diffusion language models, supervised fine-tuning depends heavily on which tokens are masked (to be predicted) and which are shown as context. Standard uniform random masking ignores the interaction between context choice and target choice, potentially wasting informative tokens either as always-visible context or as hard-to-predict targets with insufficient context. The authors aim to design a principled, model-aware masking strategy that uses the model’s own signals to choose context and targets to improve learning efficiency and downstream performance, especially on reasoning and code tasks.

Method: The authors introduce GoldiMask, a two-part procedure for supervised fine-tuning. First, it selects which tokens to reveal as context by approximately maximizing a submodular objective that trades off the benefit of each token as context against its usefulness as a prediction target, using signals from the current model. Second, for the remaining masked tokens, it assigns weights that depend on how much each token benefits from the chosen context and on its remaining learning potential, so that training focuses more on tokens where the model can still improve and that are supported by helpful context. They evaluate GoldiMask on several language-model backbones and datasets, compare it against uniform random masking, and perform ablations that remove each component to isolate its contribution.

Result: Across three model backbones and three training datasets, GoldiMask yields the highest average accuracy in most evaluation settings. It improves performance on both reasoning benchmarks and code generation tasks relative to uniform random masking and other baselines. Ablation experiments show that removing either the optimized context selection or the target weighting diminishes the gains, indicating both are important. Moreover, when used with confidence-threshold parallel decoding on GSM8K and MATH-500, GoldiMask reduces the number of required decoding iterations while maintaining similar accuracy at higher confidence thresholds.

Conclusion: A model-aware, submodular-optimized masking and weighting scheme for supervised fine-tuning of discrete diffusion language models can outperform simple random masking. By explicitly balancing the roles of tokens as context versus prediction targets and prioritizing tokens with high learning potential under good context, GoldiMask improves accuracy on reasoning and code tasks and makes decoding more efficient. Both its context-selection and target-weighting components are necessary for the full gains, suggesting that finer-grained control over masking patterns is a promising direction for training diffusion-based language models.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of discrete diffusion language models masks some response tokens and trains the model to recover their original values from the visible context. The masking pattern therefore determines both the context available to the model and the tokens it learns to predict. Uniform random masking does not explicitly account for the interaction between these choices. We introduce GoldiMask, which selects tokens to reveal as context by approximately maximizing a submodular objective. This objective uses model signals to balance the benefit of revealing tokens against their value as prediction targets. GoldiMask then weights the remaining targets according to how they benefit from the selected context and their remaining learning potential. Across three backbones and three training datasets, GoldiMask achieves the highest average accuracy in most evaluated settings, demonstrating gains on both reasoning and code generation. Component ablations show that both context selection and target weighting contribute to the gains. GoldiMask also reduces decoding iterations on GSM8K and MATH-500 under confidence-threshold parallel decoding, while maintaining comparable accuracy at higher confidence thresholds.

</details>


### [128] [Decode-Latency Feedback Prefill: A Model-Free Controller and Its Generalization Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38386)
*Gaurav Agarwal,Ashish Garg,Isha Singhal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a dynamic prefill scheduler for LLM serving, Decode-Latency Feedback Prefill (DLFP), that adapts prefill chunk size using latency feedback to reduce interference with ongoing decoding, yielding large latency gains on a small model but failing to generalize to larger models and multi-GPU setups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In concurrent LLM serving, long prompt prefills can block ongoing token generation, increasing inter-token latency for active sessions. Fixed prefill chunk sizes only partially mitigate this, and the optimal size depends heavily on model, hardware, workload, and latency goals. There is a need for a practical, model-agnostic controller that adjusts prefill work based on real-time system behavior while preserving output correctness and SLOs.

Method: The authors design Decode-Latency Feedback Prefill (DLFP), a model-free feedback controller that monitors the decode latency impact of prefill operations that overlap with active decoding. After a guarded scheduling cycle, it measures the observed interval between scheduler calls as proportional feedback and uses it to adjust the next prefill chunk size; prefills without concurrent decodes are left unrestricted. They implement DLFP in vLLM and evaluate it via open-loop Poisson request arrivals, exact token-level accounting, replay of real request traces, and GPU telemetry on NVIDIA hardware, comparing latency metrics and correctness with and without DLFP.

Result: On Qwen3-0.6B (BF16) on a single A100 80 GB GPU, DLFP yields substantial improvements in P99 inter-token latency across three 100-request trials: 24.8%, 30.1%, and 28.2% reductions, with a mean reduction of 27.7% and a paired 95% confidence interval of 21.0%–34.3%. These improvements are achieved with exact output equivalence, no observed failures, and preserved SLO compliance. However, the gains come at the cost of a 34.8% increase in mean P99 time-to-first-token, which still remains within the given SLO. The mechanism fails to deliver similar benefits for larger models (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B) or a two-GPU tensor-parallel setup, revealing limitations of the approach.

Conclusion: DLFP demonstrates that a simple, model-free feedback-based controller can significantly reduce inter-token latency for small LLMs under concurrent load by adaptively resizing prefill chunks based on observed decode-latency interference, while maintaining correctness and SLO compliance. Nonetheless, its failure to generalize to larger models and multi-GPU configurations shows that using asynchronous scheduler-call intervals as a proxy for GPU iteration time is insufficient in more complex settings. This defines the scope of the contribution and motivates the development of completion-timed controllers that more accurately account for concurrent CPU and on-device behavior, with the present work serving as a reproducible proof-of-concept and a guide for future system designs.

Abstract: Concurrent autoregressive inference creates a fundamental interference problem: prefilling a newly arrived long prompt can delay tokens for requests that are already decoding. Fixed prefill chunks reduce this interference, but the best chunk size depends on the model, hardware, load, and latency objective. We introduce Decode-Latency Feedback Prefill (DLFP), a model-free controller that changes only prefill work that overlaps active decodes. After a guarded scheduling cycle, DLFP uses the observed interval as proportional feedback to resize the next prefill chunk; isolated prefills remain unrestricted.
  We implement DLFP in vLLM and evaluate it with open-loop Poisson arrivals, exact token accounting, raw request traces, and NVIDIA telemetry. On Qwen3-0.6B in BF16 on one A100 80 GB GPU, three paired 100-request trials reduce P99 inter-token latency by 24.8%, 30.1%, and 28.2% (mean 27.7%, paired 95% confidence interval 21.0% to 34.3%) with exact output agreement, no failures, and unchanged SLO compliance. The benefit is not free: mean P99 time to first token increases 34.8% while remaining inside the declared SLO.
  Crucially, the mechanism does not generalize to Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, or a two-GPU tensor-parallel configuration. We trace the failure to an asynchronous scheduler-call interval that is only a proxy for completed GPU iteration time. This negative result defines the boundary of the contribution and motivates a completion-timed controller for concurrent CPU and on-device inference. We do not claim mobile-device performance; the present work is a reproducible proof-of-concept and generalization study.

</details>


### [129] [MetaPersona: Task-Grounded Synthetic Populations from Empirical Social Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38392)
*Jinyi Ye,Yuangang Li,Chenxiao Yu,Preyashi Poddar,Priyanka Dey,Longtian Ye,Zihan Wang,Xiyang Hu,Emilio Ferrara,Yue Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MetaPersona, a framework that uses a large database of empirical human-subjects studies (MetaPersona-DB) to construct more realistic, data-driven personas for seeding LLM-based social simulations, addressing the cold-start problem in persona design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for creating personas to seed LLM social simulations lack a systematic way to choose which attributes to include and how to set their values. This cold-start problem can lead to synthetic populations that misrepresent demographics, latent traits, and dependencies between variables, which in turn biases downstream simulation outcomes. The authors aim to ground persona construction in real empirical evidence from human-subjects research to improve realism and validity.

Method: The authors build MetaPersona-DB, a curated dataset of over 11,000 empirical human-subjects studies, each annotated with task-relevant variables, reported relationships among those variables, and aggregate population statistics. On top of this resource, they design MetaPersona, a framework that: (1) retrieves empirical studies relevant to a target task; (2) constructs literature-derived persona dependency graphs that encode relationships between demographics, latent attributes, and outcomes; and (3) samples synthetic populations from empirical priors derived from the literature. They then evaluate MetaPersona across three downstream case studies and compare it to three baseline methods using three state-of-the-art LLMs, and they also implement MetaPersona-Studio, an interactive interface for practitioners.

Result: Empirically, MetaPersona’s performance depends on both task and underlying LLM. It achieves strong results on tasks related to modeling misinformation belief and sentiment toward AI tools, indicating that literature-grounded personas can better capture relevant population structure in these domains. However, results are mixed for the income redistribution task, suggesting limitations or domain-specific challenges. The method also substantially lowers the cost of persona construction, bringing it below $0.50 per task when using GPT-5.2, demonstrating practical efficiency gains.

Conclusion: Grounding persona generation in a large body of empirical human-subjects research can mitigate the cold-start problem in LLM-based social simulations and yield more realistic, structured synthetic populations. MetaPersona, powered by the MetaPersona-DB corpus and operationalized via dependency graphs and empirical priors, shows promising benefits on several social modeling tasks and significantly reduces persona-construction costs. The accompanying MetaPersona-Studio interface illustrates how this framework can be made accessible for interactive, empirically grounded persona design, though performance variations across tasks highlight that domain coverage and model interactions remain important considerations.

Abstract: Personas used to seed LLM social simulations face a cold-start problem: existing methods lack a principled basis for deciding which attributes to include and how to assign their values. As a result, synthetic populations may misrepresent the demographic composition, latent attributes, and dependency structure that shape downstream behavior. We introduce MetaPersona-DB, a dataset of 11,000+ empirical human-subjects studies annotated with task-relevant variables, reported relationships, and aggregate-level population statistics. Building on this resource, we propose MetaPersona, a framework that retrieves task-relevant evidence, constructs literature-derived persona dependency graphs, and samples synthetic populations from empirical priors linking demographics, latent attributes, and outcomes. Across three downstream case studies, three baselines, and three frontier models, results vary by task and model: MetaPersona performs strongly on misinformation belief and AI-tool sentiment, while results on income redistribution are mixed. It also reduces persona-construction cost to under $0.5 per task using GPT-5.2. Finally, we present MetaPersona-Studio, a prototype interactive interface for empirically grounded persona generation.

</details>


### [130] [SimTrace: Grounded Multimodal User Trajectories Generation for Online User Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38397)
*Yunan Lu,Shuang Xie,Meghna Allamudi,Mingyu Zhao,Han Li,Lingyun Wang,Zhou Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SimTrace is a framework for generating high-fidelity synthetic, multimodal user clickstreams by simulating computer-use agents grounded in anonymized real trajectories and mirrored web environments, enabling shareable data for training and evaluating virtual client models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real, fine-grained user interaction logs are hard to access at scale due to privacy, ownership, and traffic limitations. Existing public datasets either lack detailed interaction traces or are small and platform-specific, which limits the development and evaluation of virtual clients (e.g., for A/B testing, recommender systems, and interface evaluation). A method is needed to create large-scale, faithful, and shareable user trajectories without exposing proprietary or sensitive data.

Method: The authors introduce SimTrace, a framework that (1) anonymizes real user interaction logs, (2) builds a simulated twin of the target web environment, and (3) uses a computer-use client agent to generate synthetic interaction trajectories grounded in both the anonymized logs and the simulated environment. The system produces multimodal clickstreams where each user action is linked to its web observations and user context, effectively recreating realistic trajectories while protecting privacy. They implement and apply SimTrace in an e-commerce scenario and compare it against baseline simulation or augmentation methods on multiple fidelity metrics and downstream modeling tasks.

Result: In an e-commerce setting, SimTrace-generated trajectories achieve higher fidelity than competing baselines on 7 out of 8 evaluation metrics. Models trained solely on synthetic data from SimTrace perform comparably to models trained on real logs for downstream tasks like purchase prediction and recommendation. For next-action prediction, combining real data with SimTrace synthetic data yields an 11.0% relative accuracy improvement over training on real data alone.

Conclusion: SimTrace can generate high-fidelity, privacy-preserving synthetic user interaction trajectories that approximate real logs closely enough to serve as effective training and evaluation data for virtual client and user modeling tasks. Its strong fidelity and downstream performance, along with observed gains from data augmentation, suggest that synthetic clickstreams can mitigate data scarcity and access constraints. The open-source release of SimTrace is positioned to support broader research in online user behavior modeling and virtual client development.

Abstract: Virtual clients offer a cost-effective approach to support applications such as A/B testing, recommender system development, and interface evaluation. However, building them requires access to large-scale, semantically faithful, fine-grained online user trajectories. These data are difficult to obtain because proprietary logs are subject to privacy restrictions and small businesses often lack sufficient traffic. Consequently, existing public datasets either abstract away fine-grained user interaction details or preserve rich context but remain platform-specific and small-scale. To address this gap, we propose SimTrace, a framework that generates faithful, fine-grained synthetic multimodal clickstreams through a computer-use client agent that is grounded in real user trajectories and the given web environment. SimTrace anonymizes real interactions and constructs a simulated twin of the given web environment, then uses both to generate synthetic interaction trajectories. Each action is paired with its corresponding web observations and user context, yielding a shareable alternative to confidential logs for developing computer-use agent-style virtual clients. We apply SimTrace to an e-commerce setting and evaluate both its fidelity and downstream utility. SimTrace outperforms competing baselines on 7 out of 8 fidelity metrics. Models trained on synthetic data achieve performance comparable to those trained on real data on downstream tasks such as purchase prediction and recommendation. For next action prediction task, augmenting real data with synthetic data further improves accuracy by 11.0% relative to training on real data alone. We release SimTrace as an open-source package to facilitate research on online user behavior modeling.

</details>


### [131] [ArgGYM: A Procedural, Engine-Verified Benchmark for Structured Defeasible Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38409)
*İbrahim Ethem Deveci,Funda Tan Çalık,Barış Deniz Sağlam,Duygu Ataman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ArgGYM is a new benchmark and RL training environment for testing and improving large language models’ structured defeasible reasoning abilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reasoning benchmarks and RL environments focus on domains with fixed problem specifications and automatically verifiable rewards (math, code, formal logic). These make evaluation easy but don’t reflect real-world reasoning, which is often defeasible: conclusions can be provisional, defeated, reinstated, or revised as new information arises. There is a gap in systematic, verifiable evaluation of this kind of reasoning for language models.

Method: The authors design ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible environment based on formal argumentation theory.
