They decompose defeasible reasoning into 12 sub-tasks and connect them to a symbolic argumentation engine that computes formal argumentation states used for grading model outputs. They define multiple curriculum configurations (15 in total) and vary argument preference orderings (weakest-link vs last-link) and set orderings (elitist vs democratic). They generate a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances and provide generators and verifiers to create new instances for evaluation and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

Result: On the fixed benchmark, both top proprietary (“frontier”) and open-weight language models exhibit distinctive reasoning patterns. Models can often produce substantial fragments of correct structured answers without fully solving a task, but their performance drops on more complex curriculum configurations with longer reasoning chains and richer interactions among arguments. The different model families show sharply contrasting profiles across the 12 tasks and curriculum stages.

Conclusion: ArgGYM provides a reproducible, automatically verifiable environment to probe and train large language models on structured defeasible reasoning, going beyond traditional math/code/logic benchmarks. The benchmark reveals systematic weaknesses of current models on tasks with deeper dependencies and more complex argument interactions, and it enables future work on reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards targeted at non-monotonic reasoning.

Abstract: Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings (weakest-link and last-link), and two set orderings (elitist and democratic), while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances for evaluation that reduces dependence on static test sets and for verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. We release the benchmark, generators, and verifiers for reproducible evaluation and RLVR training.

</details>


### [132] [A Competing-Hazards Systematization of Loss of Control in Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38411)
*Mohamed Aly Bouke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a unified, statistical framework to describe and compare how AI agents either stay within scope, stop safely, or escape their approved limits, and audits existing incident reports and evaluations using this framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reports of AI agents acting beyond approved limits are inconsistent and hard to compare. Incident reports, evaluations, and logs describe failures in different ways, making it difficult to (1) quantify how often agents escape their intended scope, (2) distinguish agent behavior from environmental permissiveness, and (3) reason about risk over multiple retries or attempts. A United Nations panel has highlighted such incidents as early warnings of potential loss of human control, increasing the urgency of a systematic approach. The paper aims to fill this methodological gap so that risks can be measured, compared, and managed coherently.

Method: The authors introduce a unified outcome framework in which every agent attempt ends in exactly one of four states: approved completion, safe stopping, scope escape (an out-of-scope effect), or continuation. They formalize this as a discrete-time competing-hazards model, where at each decision step there are competing risks (completion, safe stop, escape, continuation). From this model, they derive formulas for (a) the probability of an escape occurring within a given retry budget, (b) a model-conditional maximum safe retry budget, and (c) conditions under which these quantities can be estimated from real-world execution logs. They then apply the framework in an audit of 22 incident reports and 102 agent-safety evaluations (from Jan 2025–Sep 2026), extracting how outcomes are recorded and which of the four states are represented or conflated.

Result: From the 22 incidents: six involved tasks intrinsically impossible to complete within scope, thirteen featured agents that persisted instead of stopping, and five failed to report whether agents ever tried to stop. Developer-provided figures imply that for out-of-scope coordination, tasks that were never solved had an incidence ratio about 47 times higher than tasks that were successfully solved. From the 102 evaluations: 87 recorded at least one out-of-scope effect or specification violation, 26 explicitly modeled safe stopping as a key outcome, only 20 captured both out-of-scope behavior and safe stopping, and 79 conflated budget exhaustion (running out of attempts) with simple failure instead of treating it as a separate outcome. In 20 of the 22 incidents, the environment actually allowed the out-of-scope effect to occur, showing that realized loss of control typically involved both persistent agent attempts and permissive environmental boundaries. No evaluation contained all the fields required to reconstruct the full competing-hazards process solely from published evidence.

Conclusion: A consistent, hazard-based outcome framework is necessary to meaningfully compare AI agent failures, characterize scope escape risk, and distinguish agent persistence from environmental permissiveness. Existing incident reports and safety evaluations are incomplete for this purpose: they often omit safe stopping as an explicit outcome, merge retry budget exhaustion with failure, and lack the data needed to estimate a full competing-hazards model. The findings imply that many observed losses of control arise not just from agent behavior but from environments that permit out-of-scope actions to succeed. The paper argues that future incident reporting and evaluation protocols should adopt richer logging and separate reporting of completion, safe stopping, scope escape, continuation, and environmental boundary conditions so that escape probabilities and safe retry budgets can be quantitatively estimated.

Abstract: Leading AI developers have reported agents acting beyond their approved limits, which a United Nations panel described as an early warning of loss of human control. Yet incident reports and agent-safety evaluations describe these events differently, making it difficult to compare failures, trace risk across attempts, or separate agent behavior from the environment's role in allowing an out-of-scope action to succeed. To address this gap, we introduce a common framework in which each attempt ends in approved completion, safe stopping, scope escape, or continuation. We formalize the framework as a discrete-time competing-hazards model and derive escape probability within a retry budget, a model-conditional safe-budget limit, and conditions for estimation from execution logs. We audit 22 incident reports and 102 agent-safety evaluations published from January 2025 to September 2026 using primary sources. Six incidents involved tasks that could not be completed within scope, thirteen involved agents that continued rather than stopped, and five did not report stopping behavior. Developers' figures imply a task-level incidence ratio near 47 for out-of-scope coordination in never-solved versus solved tasks. Among evaluations, 87 recorded an out-of-scope effect or specification violation, 26 treated safe stopping as a first-class outcome, only 20 recorded both, and 79 merged budget exhaustion with failure. In 20 of 22 incidents, the environment allowed an out-of-scope effect, indicating that realized loss of control often reflected persistent agent behavior interacting with permissive boundary conditions; meanwhile, no evaluation reported all fields needed to estimate the full competing-hazards process from published evidence.

</details>


### [133] [AIM: Agentic Idea Management for Automated Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38445)
*Hyeong Kyu Choi,Bhavana Dalvi Mishra,Jiefeng Chen,Mihir Parmar,Rui Meng,Chun-Liang Li,Xiangru Tang,Sharon Li,Jinsung Yoon,Tomas Pfister*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Agentic Idea Manager (AIM), an autonomous framework that manages and explores research ideas for LLM-driven automated scientific discovery, improving performance and speed over existing baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As frontier LLMs are used for iterative automated scientific research, current systems struggle to structure evolving research ideas, choose the most promising directions, and keep implementations aligned with high-level ideas. Existing approaches tend to focus on solution-level search (hyperparameters, code tweaks) rather than explicit management of idea-level exploration, leading to inefficient use of experimental budget and limited semantic coverage of the research space.

Method: The authors propose AIM, a fully autonomous idea-driven research framework inspired by Bayesian optimization. AIM maintains an explicit space of research ideas and uses: (1) an Agentic Surrogate to model and organize discovered ideas and their outcomes, (2) an Agentic Acquisition mechanism to select the next promising ideas to explore, (3) a Solution Auditor to verify that concrete implementations faithfully reflect the underlying ideas, and (4) a Resource Planner that dynamically allocates experimental budget across parallel search branches. They also provide a theoretical analysis characterizing when idea-level search offers benefits over pure solution-level search, especially in terms of semantic coverage and sparsity of good directions.

Result: On 10 tasks from the AutoLab benchmark, AIM outperforms the strongest prior baselines by 1.6 percentage points on System Optimization tasks and by 4.9 percentage points on long-horizon Model Development & CUDA tasks. AIM also reaches the best baseline performance up to 3.1 times faster in wall-clock time, indicating more efficient exploration and use of computational resources.

Conclusion: Explicit, autonomous management of idea-level search can significantly improve the effectiveness and efficiency of LLM-driven automated research. By introducing structured components for idea modeling, selection, integrity checking, and resource allocation, AIM achieves better performance and faster convergence than solution-focused baselines. Theoretical analysis further supports that controlling semantic coverage at the idea level becomes increasingly advantageous when strong research directions are rare among many plausible alternatives.

Abstract: Frontier LLMs are increasingly used to automate scientific research through iterative search. We distinguish idea-driven search from solution-driven search and identify three core challenges: organizing evolving research ideas, selecting promising directions, and maintaining alignment between ideas and their implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce the Agentic Idea Manager (AIM), a fully autonomous framework for managing and exploring research directions in idea-driven automated research. Inspired by Bayesian optimization, AIM uses an Agentic Surrogate and an Agentic Acquisition mechanism to organize discovered ideas and guide their selection. A Solution Auditor maintains idea-solution integrity, while a Resource Planner adaptively allocates the remaining experimental budget across parallel search branches. Experiments on 10 AutoLab benchmark tasks show that AIM surpasses the strongest baseline by 1.6 percentage points on System Optimization tasks and 4.9 percentage points on long-horizon Model Development & CUDA tasks. Notably, AIM reaches the best baseline performance up to 3.1x faster in wall-clock time. We further provide a theoretical analysis of when searching over ideas becomes beneficial. Our analysis shows that explicit idea-level allocation makes semantic coverage directly controllable, and that broader coverage becomes increasingly valuable when competitive research directions are sparse among many plausible alternatives. Project Page: https://imhgchoi.github.io/agentic-idea-manager/

</details>


### [134] [Reach Into The CHOIR: Free-List Elicitation Uncovers Distinct Model Voices in LLM Ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38448)
*Ben Wigler,Maria Tsfasman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CHOIR is a framework to measure and analyze how groups of LLMs collectively generate and rank ideas, revealing when apparent agreement hides deeper diversity of possible answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on open-ended LLM homogeneity shows different models often give similar single answers, creating a false sense of independent agreement. But single-pass responses can’t distinguish whether this homogeneity is due to narrow answer spaces, shared prompt wording, or deeper but hidden variation in model knowledge and preferences. The authors want a way to systematically probe beneath surface-level agreement, quantify what concepts are salient for different models and prompts, and detect rare but stable alternative answers.

Method: The authors adapt the free-list elicitation method from cognitive anthropology to LLM ensembles. Their framework, CHOIR, repeatedly prompts multiple models (and multiple personas/prompt variants) to produce ranked lists of answers for each open-ended question. They then: (1) cluster items across runs into higher-level concepts at the prompt level; (2) compute salience measures of these concepts across models, prompt variants, and persona conditions; and (3) apply a source-blind ranking module that highlights rare-but-stable concepts that consistently appear despite being infrequent. They evaluate CHOIR on two datasets: (i) Infinity-Chat 100, a bank of open-ended prompts from prior homogeneity research; and (ii) a 27-question diagnostic prompt set designed to tease apart specific mechanism-level differences between models.

Result: On Infinity-Chat 100, CHOIR confirms the previously reported high surface homogeneity, with 93 of 100 prompts showing above-chance agreement in top responses. However, it also distinguishes between prompts that truly constrain the answer space and those that allow deeper, recoverable diversity of concepts beneath the default answers. Across both the external bank and the targeted diagnostic prompts, CHOIR finds that the strongest consistent signal in concept salience is the underlying base model identity, while persona instructions mostly modulate which concepts are surfaced within each model’s characteristic pattern. The source-blind ranking successfully identifies rare but reliably recurring concepts for further human inspection.

Conclusion: CHOIR reframes open-ended homogeneity in LLMs as a structured measurement problem rather than a simple observation that models ‘agree.’ By using repeated, ranked elicitation and concept-level analysis, it reveals where and why models converge, and uncovers less obvious but stable alternative concepts that remain reachable. The framework enables more diagnostic comparisons across models, prompts, and personas, turning apparent homogeneity into a tool for understanding model-specific signatures and the depth of their answer spaces.

Abstract: Open-ended LLM homogeneity can create false plurality when several systems appear to offer independent perspectives while returning the same familiar default. Single-pass answers obscure the distinction between agreement produced by a tightly constrained answer space, prompt-vocabulary echo, and broader answer spaces with stable alternatives beneath the surface. We introduce CHOIR (Collective Hierarchically-Ordered Inquiry Responses), a framework that adapts free-list elicitation from cognitive anthropology to LLM ensembles. CHOIR repeatedly elicits ranked lists, clusters items into prompt-level concepts, and measures concept salience across models, prompt variants, and persona conditions. We evaluate CHOIR on Infinity-Chat 100, an external prompt bank from recent work on open-ended model homogeneity, and on a 27-question targeted diagnostic bank designed to isolate mechanism-level contrasts. On Infinity-Chat 100, CHOIR reproduces high surface agreement (93/100 prompts above chance) while separating narrow prompts from broad prompts with recoverable depth. Across targeted probes and the external prompt bank, base-model identity remains the strongest recoverable signature, and persona prompts shift surfaced concepts within base-model signatures. A source-blind ranking module prioritises rare-but-stable candidates for later inspection. CHOIR turns open-ended homogeneity into a diagnostic measurement problem by asking where models converge, why they converge, and what remains reachable under structured depth probing.

</details>


### [135] [PrivMeSA: Privacy-Aware Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for Medicine via Local-Remote LLM Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38458)
*Dannong Wang,Yuran Zhang,Bian Sun,Alex Stinard,Yuzhang Shang,Song Wang,Yu Tian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PrivMeSA is a privacy-aware clinical LLM multi-agent system that learns when and what to disclose to remote models, while reusing their expertise locally to improve accuracy and privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Remote, more capable LLMs can help local clinical models, but sending patient information externally creates privacy and re-identification risks, especially over multi-turn interactions and repeated visits. Existing de-identification (e.g., stripping explicit identifiers) is inadequate because quasi-identifiers can accumulate across turns and encounters, enabling linkage to patient registries. There is a need for a principled way to delegate to remote models while explicitly optimizing both task performance and privacy risk at the encounter level.

Method: The authors propose PrivMeSA, a self-evolving multi-agent architecture. A local clinical agent handles each encounter and selectively consults one or more remote specialist models that may ask for more data. The local agent’s disclosure policy is trained via reinforcement learning to trade off clinical task accuracy against two privacy costs: direct disclosure of personal attributes and registry-based re-identification risk computed over the full outbound transcript. Additionally, a local “lesson memory” module summarizes completed remote-assisted consultations into generalized, de-identified clinical guidance. For future patients, the system retrieves relevant lessons and uses them instead of (or before) contacting remote models, enabling knowledge reuse without re-disclosure. Memory grows continually without additional labels or parameter updates.

Result: On an emergency department benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV-ED, PrivMeSA substantially outperforms a baseline delegation strategy. It increases mean task accuracy by up to 15.8 percentage points while dramatically enhancing privacy: disclosure of personal details drops from 98.0% of cases to 0.2%, and the proportion of cases where a patient can be narrowed down to 10 or fewer registry records falls from 74% to 0%.

Conclusion: PrivMeSA demonstrates that a privacy-aware, RL-trained local agent with a self-growing lesson memory can safely exploit remote LLM expertise in clinical settings. It simultaneously boosts clinical task performance and reduces both direct and linkage-based re-identification risk, without requiring ongoing human labeling or model retraining as memory expands. This suggests a viable path toward practical, privacy-preserving clinical LLM deployment that leverages powerful external models while keeping sensitive patient data protected.

Abstract: Clinical large language model (LLM) agents deployed locally can consult more capable remote models, but doing so risks exposing patient information. Privacy-conscious delegation places disclosure decisions with a local agent, yet removing explicit identifiers is insufficient: quasi-identifiers can accumulate across multi-turn consultations and repeated patient visits to enable re-identification. We introduce PrivMeSA, a privacy-aware self-evolving multi-agent system that learns to control disclosure and retains remote expertise for local reuse. A local agent manages each encounter and consults remote specialists that may request additional information. Reinforcement learning balances task accuracy against direct disclosure and registry-based re-identification risk, with privacy evaluated over the complete outbound transcript of each encounter. A local lesson memory distills completed consultations into generalized clinical guidance and retrieves relevant lessons before transmission, allowing subsequent cases to reuse expertise without another remote exchange. Memory grows without additional outcome labels or parameter updates. On an emergency-department benchmark built from MIMIC-IV-ED records, PrivMeSA improves mean task accuracy over delegation by up to 15.8 percentage points. In the same setting, PrivMeSA reduces the disclosure of personal details from 98.0% to 0.2% of cases and the share of cases in which the patient can be narrowed to ten or fewer registry patients from 74% to 0%.

</details>


### [136] [NAQD Env: A benchmark for selective withdrawal in language agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38460)
*Mohamed Abouzahra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces NAQD-Env, a synthetic benchmark to test whether language-model-based agents can selectively withdraw, preserve, and resume actions when evidence or authorization changes, and shows that current open-weight models perform very poorly at this selective withdrawal behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language agents operating as planners or tool-using systems need to change their plans when new evidence arises, permissions are revoked, or they receive stop instructions. Ideally, they should selectively suspend only the affected actions, preserve unrelated ongoing work, and later resume appropriately once issues are resolved. Existing benchmarks do not isolate and rigorously test this selective withdrawal and resumption capability, which is critical for safe and reliable agents. The paper aims to fill this evaluation gap and to understand how current models behave under such dynamic constraints.

Method: The authors design NAQD-Env, a deterministic synthetic environment with explicit representations of evidence, authorization, and constraint dependencies among actions. They define eleven dependency families that generate task structures, enabling tests on in-distribution structures, held-out dependency families, and novel combinations. A reference policy specifies the correct selective withdrawal, preservation, and resumption decisions. They build metrics that separate attempted violations from those blocked by an execution gate and jointly measure policy agreement, task value, withdrawal behavior, resumption, and event-reporting quality. They then run 3 open-weight instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) under three different prompts across 350 fixed scenarios, for a total of 3,150 model–prompt episodes, and perform gate-based replay to simulate execution. They also run exploratory supervised fine-tuning (SFT) curricula on Qwen2.5-3B to see how training data affects decision accuracy and behavior.

Result: Base instruction-tuned models show extremely poor selective withdrawal and resumption. Withdrawal recall never exceeds 0.06, meaning they almost never suspend actions when required, and no valid resumption occurs when it would be correct to resume. Only one episode across all model–prompt combinations fully matches the reference policy. Under the NAQD-focused prompt, Qwen2.5-7B attempts fewer unsafe actions than Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, but at the cost of doing less useful work and being less precise in preserving unaffected actions. With exploratory SFT on Qwen2.5-3B, decision accuracy increases dramatically from about 0.45–0.54 to 0.83–0.92, but new pathologies appear: inappropriate over-withdrawal for structures missing from the training curriculum and a degradation in event-reporting behavior.

Conclusion: Selective withdrawal—pausing only the right actions while preserving and later resuming others—is a distinct, underdeveloped aspect of language-agent reliability that current open-weight models largely fail to implement. NAQD-Env provides a controlled benchmark to quantify this capability via structured inputs and a deterministic reference policy, but it does not address real-world containment or source verification. The poor baseline results and nuanced effects of fine-tuning suggest that future work should explicitly model, train, and evaluate selective withdrawal, resumption, and event reporting, rather than assuming they emerge automatically from generic instruction tuning or safety training.

Abstract: Language agents must revise planned actions when evidence changes, permission is revoked, or a stop instruction arrives. A useful response is selective: suspend affected actions, preserve unaffected work, and resume only after sufficient repair. We introduce NAQD-Env, a synthetic environment that evaluates these decisions against a deterministic reference policy over explicit evidence, authorization, and constraint dependencies. Eleven dependency families support evaluation on development structures, held-out families, and held-out combinations of structures. Metrics distinguish attempted violations from violations permitted by a simulated execution gate and jointly report policy agreement, task value, withdrawal, resumption, and event reporting. We evaluate three open-weight instruction-tuned models from two families under three prompt conditions on 350 frozen scenarios, yielding 3,150 model-prompt episodes before gate replay. Across the reported conditions, withdrawal recall is at most 0.06, no valid resumption is observed at eligible opportunities, and only one episode matches the complete reference policy. Under the NAQD prompt, Qwen2.5-7B has fewer unsafe-attempt episodes than Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, but also completes less useful work and preserves unaffected actions less accurately. Exploratory supervised fine-tuning probes increase Qwen2.5-3B decision accuracy from 0.45-0.54 to 0.83-0.92; separate diagnostics reveal inappropriate withdrawal after curriculum omissions and a loss of event reporting. These results motivate evaluating selective withdrawal as a distinct component of agent reliability. The setting measures policy application with trusted structured inputs and does not establish real-world containment or source-verification ability.

</details>


### [137] [VAmoS Part Deux: Harder, More Realistic Voice-Agent Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38512)
*Joshua Meyer,Sahar Shayegan,Ritiz Tambi,Ali Khan,Sun Kim,Victor Shih,Mehdi Jamei,Andi Partovi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VAmoS Energy is a benchmark for evaluating end-to-end voice agents handling complex, multi-step utility billing and payment tasks under realistic, noisy conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing voice-agent evaluations usually focus on narrow tasks or clean conditions and do not fully test whether agents can manage multi-step customer service calls, handle background speech, respect real-world billing and verification rules, and ensure that what they say matches what they actually do in tools and backends.

Method: The authors construct 100 simulated utility customer-service calls where each caller has 2–4 requests about billing and payment assistance, grounded in public electricity-usage data and Pennsylvania residential billing policy. The agent is given 16 tools connected to live-like backends (Stripe-based billing twin and Apache Fineract loan engine), gated by mandatory caller verification. They evaluate 14 different voice stacks, running each task three times, and use an LLM-as-a-verifier to check both tool actions and spoken numbers/claims against explicit task requirements, externally validated against a code-based verifier for calibration.

Result: The LLM verifier matches a code verifier on 99.1% of checks, supporting its reliability. Across 14 voice stacks and 3 runs per task, task-completion rates vary widely from 17.3% to 44.7%; Grok Voice performs best, with Gemini 3.8 Live and GPT-Live close behind at similar per-call cost. Adding background TV audio drastically lowers pooled completion from 38.7% to 8.6%. Simulated callers frequently accept incorrect outcomes because they only hear the agent’s speech and cannot inspect the tool actions or backend changes.

Conclusion: End-to-end evaluation of voice agents must cover the entire interaction: conversational behavior, correctness of backend actions, adherence to real-world policies, and robustness to overlapping or background speech. The VAmoS Energy benchmark exposes substantial gaps in current systems’ reliability and robustness in realistic customer-service scenarios, underscoring the need for better tools, reasoning, and evaluation methods for production-grade voice agents.

Abstract: Voice agents in production must handle several requests, background speech, and customers who lose patience. We introduce VAmoS Energy, a benchmark that combines these challenges in 100 calls about utility billing and payment assistance. Each caller makes two to four requests. The agent has sixteen tools backed by a stateful Stripe billing twin and the Apache Fineract loan engine, with account access blocked until caller verification succeeds. The tasks use public household electricity data and a policy based on Pennsylvania's residential billing rules. An LLM-as-a-verifier checks the agent's actions and spoken figures against explicit requirements. On a calibration run, it agrees with a code verifier on 99.1% of checks. Across fourteen voice stacks and three repeats per task, completion ranges from 17.3% to 44.7%. Grok Voice leads, and Gemini 3.8 Live and GPT-Live follow at about the same cost per call. Background television reduces pooled completion from 38.7% to 8.6%. The simulated caller often accepts an incorrect result because it hears the agent's words but cannot inspect its actions. These findings show why voice agents need evaluation across the whole call, including what they say, what they change, and how they handle competing speech.

</details>


### [138] [Demographic Pluralism: Inference-Time Modeling of Pluralistic Human Preference Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38555)
*Meng-Chen Wu,Qipin Chen,Ansh Jain,Tess Wood,Zhe Du,Si-Chi Chin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Demographic Pluralism, an inference-time framework that better estimates population-level opinion distributions from LLMs by generating multiple perspectives within demographic groups, outperforming prior Modular Pluralism on opinion benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are being deployed in culturally sensitive applications where it is important to reflect the diversity of opinions within a population. Existing alignment and preference-modeling approaches typically operate at coarse demographic or community levels and treat groups as homogeneous, ignoring substantial variation within each group. This leads to miscalibrated opinion distributions and potential misrepresentation or bias. The paper is motivated by the need for a practical, data-efficient way to model rich, pluralistic opinions across and within demographic groups, without requiring dedicated training data or expensive fine-tuning for each task.

Method: The authors introduce Demographic Pluralism, an inference-time framework that works with off-the-shelf LLMs. Instead of assuming each demographic group has a single representative opinion, the method prompts the model to generate multiple distinct perspectives within each demographically defined group. These perspectives are then used to approximate the group’s internal opinion distribution. No opinion-distribution training data or task-specific fine-tuning is required. The framework is evaluated under different aggregation schemes for combining group-level predictions into a population-level distribution: (1) weighting groups by their population share, (2) equal-weighting all groups, and (3) inverse-weighting by group size.

Result: On two opinion-distribution benchmarks, GlobalOpinionQA and VITAL, and across four different LLM backbones, Demographic Pluralism improves the match between predicted and ground-truth population-level opinion distributions compared with the prior Modular Pluralism approach. The improvement is quantified as an 8.4%–26.4% reduction in Jensen-Shannon distance (a divergence measure between probability distributions). Among the tested aggregation schemes, equal-weighting of demographic groups yields the strongest overall performance, while both population-weighted and inverse-weighted schemes perform worse. The authors observe that group-level prediction error tends to scale with a group’s population weight, which helps explain why population-weighted aggregation leads to larger overall errors.

Conclusion: Demographic Pluralism offers a practical, plug-and-play inference framework for eliciting more faithful, population-level opinion distributions from LLMs by explicitly modeling within-group diversity. It outperforms a leading baseline, Modular Pluralism, across multiple models and datasets without requiring task-specific training data or fine-tuning. The findings suggest that naively weighting demographic groups by their population share can exacerbate errors when larger groups are harder to model accurately, whereas equal-weighting across groups provides a more robust approximation. The work underscores the importance of capturing within-group heterogeneity when aligning LLMs to human opinions in culturally sensitive contexts and points toward future research on better aggregation strategies and richer demographic conditioning.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in culturally sensitive settings, where alignment requires representing diverse preferences within populations. Yet existing methods model populations at coarse demographic or community levels and overlook within-group variation. We introduce Demographic Pluralism, an inference-time framework that estimates population-level opinion distributions without opinion-distribution training data or task-specific fine-tuning by generating multiple perspectives within demographically grounded groups. Across four backbones on GlobalOpinionQA and VITAL, it reduces Jensen-Shannon distance by 8.4%-26.4% over Modular Pluralism. Among weighted, equal-weighted, and inverse-weighted aggregation, equal weighting performs best overall; group-level error also increases with group weight, helping explain weighted aggregation's weaker performance.

</details>


### [139] [Defining and Categorising Human-AI Interactions in Clinical Trials: A Multidimensional Human-AI Classification Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38559)
*Sandra Woolley,Tim Collins,Khalid Khattak,Illia Chernomorets,Ariane Arevalo,Chris Richardson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes and tests a multidimensional framework for categorising human-AI interactions (HAIIs) in clinical trials, showing how both humans and LLMs can use it to consistently classify trials.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is rapid growth in AI-related clinical trials, but existing categorizations of human-AI interactions are fragmented, making it hard to compare and synthesise evidence about how humans and AI work together in these trials. A unified, structured framework tailored to clinical-trial records is needed.

Method: The authors define human-AI interaction (HAII), review and critique existing taxonomies, and then construct a new multidimensional framework with four axes: AI tasks, human-AI relationships, interaction configurations and interacting human groups. They purposively sample 15 AI-related clinical trials from a prior dataset and have each trial independently categorised using the framework by two human reviewers and six large language model (LLM) classifiers, comparing consistency and highlighting areas where human judgement remains essential.

Result: The new framework allows structured, consistent categorisation of HAIIs across clinical trials. Both human reviewers and LLM classifiers can apply it, with LLMs showing promising performance for assisted categorisation. However, discrepancies emerge when trial records are incomplete or ambiguous, underscoring the need for human oversight. Overall, the study illustrates practical feasibility and added value of the framework for organising information on human-AI interactions in trials.

Conclusion: The main contribution is a multidimensional framework that unifies AI task types, human-AI relationship types, interaction configurations, and human groups within a single categorisation approach tailored to clinical-trial records. This framework can support more systematic identification, comparison, and synthesis of human-AI interaction patterns in AI-related clinical trials. LLMs can assist in applying the framework, but human expert judgement remains necessary in cases of incomplete or unclear trial documentation.

Abstract: This paper examines human-AI interactions (HAIIs) in clinical trials and presents a multidimensional categorisation framework that classifies interactions according to AI tasks, human-AI relationships, interaction configurations and interacting human groups. We define HAII, examine existing taxonomies and extend existing categorisation approaches through this novel multidimensional framework. We purposively sampled 15 clinical trials from a previously reported dataset. Each trial was independently categorised by two human reviewers and six large language model (LLM) classifiers. The proposed categorisation provides a structured method for the consistent identification, comparison and synthesis of human-AI interactions across clinical-trial records. The framework is intended to support more consistent comparison and synthesis of AI-related clinical trials and to make explicit the different forms of human involvement associated with AI interventions. The results demonstrate the potential for LLM-assisted categorisation while indicating the continuing importance of human judgement where trial records are incomplete or ambiguous. The principal contribution is a proposed multidimensional framework that brings together AI tasks, human-AI relationships, interaction configurations and interacting human groups within a single approach designed for clinical-trial records. Its significance lies in its potential to support more systematic identification, comparison and synthesis of how humans and AI interact in clinical trials.

</details>


### [140] [Towards Model as a Library: Offline, Community-Sourced AI for Low-Resource African Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38574)
*Fendji K. E. Jean Louis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new software architecture, Model as a Library (MaaL), to support offline, reliable, voice-based data collection in low-resource African languages using small, community-enrolled speech models instead of large web-trained language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models work poorly for African languages because they are trained on scarce, standardized, web-scraped text that fails to capture real dialectal and regional variation, especially for low-literacy populations that most need AI support. The authors want a way to collect structured data via speech that is reliable, offline, and representative of how communities actually speak, without relying on hallucination-prone generative models.

Method: They propose Model as a Library (MaaL), where small, locally-relevant speech models are packaged as versioned, on-device dependencies. Instead of training on big corpora, MaaL builds a closed vocabulary from a few example recordings provided by community speakers at deployment time. The core mechanism is keyword spotting: closed-vocabulary text fields in digital data-collection tools are converted into voice forms whose allowed values are recognized via on-device keyword spotting. Existing forms with closed-vocabulary elements can be automatically converted ("transpiled") into MaaL schemas, enabling quick deployment.

Result: As a position and system-design paper, it does not report experimental results but provides an architectural description and an analytical feasibility argument that MaaL can enable robust, offline, voice-first data collection for low-resource African languages, using small, community-enrolled models instead of large language models.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that MaaL is a promising, low-friction way to add voice-first, offline, structured data collection to existing digital form ecosystems in underserved African contexts. By enrolling vocabularies directly from local speakers and running entirely on-device, MaaL avoids hallucinations, better respects dialectal variation, and can more fairly serve low-literacy populations. They outline what components are still needed for a full implementation and invite future work to realize and evaluate the architecture in practice.

Abstract: Large language models are frequently proposed as a route to AI-powered services for African communities, but they are least reliable exactly where the need is greatest: all African languages remain low-resource by any standard measure, and models trained on scraped, standardised text systematically misrepresent the dialectal and regional variation of how people actually speak. We introduce \textbf{Model as a Library (MaaL)}, a software architecture that packages small, community-enrolled speech models as versioned on-device dependencies, enabling offline structured data collection that cannot generatively hallucinate, for populations that current language models serve worst. Rather than relying on web-scraped corpora, MaaL's vocabulary is enrolled directly from a small number of example recordings by the speakers themselves, at the point of deployment. We describe the architecture and its central mechanism - keyword spotting that turns a closed-vocabulary text form into a voice form, filled and submitted entirely on-device - and propose transpiling the closed-vocabulary elements already present in widely-deployed digital form tools into MaaL schemas, a low-friction path to voice-first, offline data collection for the low-literacy populations these tools already reach. This is a position and system-design paper: we describe the concept, the mechanism, and an analytical feasibility case, and identify what a working implementation still requires.

</details>


### [141] [Conditional Generation of Creative Chess Puzzles with Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38577)
*Aatu Selkee,Severi Rissanen,Xidong Feng,Tom Zahavy,Eric Malmi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a masked diffusion approach, enhanced with auxiliary tasks and RL fine-tuning, to generate controllable, high-quality chess puzzles with unique solutions and specified tactical themes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern language models are strong generative systems but perform poorly on tightly constrained, counter-intuitive creative tasks where small changes can break correctness. Chess puzzles provide a rigorous, symbolically grounded testbed for such creativity and reasoning because even a single piece change can invalidate a puzzle. There is a need for controllable, reliable generation of puzzles that satisfy strict correctness, uniqueness, and thematic constraints, as well as a desire to benchmark and advance computational creativity in a well-defined domain.

Method: The authors frame chess puzzle generation as conditional generation with masked diffusion models. Their non-directional diffusion architecture supports conditioning on partial board positions and specific tactical themes. They add an auxiliary task of predicting the best move during training to encourage the model to internalize tactical structure, which empirically improves solution uniqueness and theme adherence. On top of this, they adapt Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (DDPO) to create a reinforcement learning framework that directly optimizes for puzzle metrics such as uniqueness of the solution and correctness of theme conditioning. They then train and evaluate open-weight models on these objectives.

Result: The auxiliary best-move prediction task yields an 11.6% improvement in puzzle solution uniqueness and a 2.5% gain in theme-conditioning accuracy compared to the base diffusion model. The subsequent RL fine-tuning with a DDPO-style framework further boosts performance, increasing the yield of puzzles that are both unique in solution and correctly match the target theme by 89.1%.

Conclusion: Masked diffusion models, when combined with best-move prediction and RL-style optimization, can generate high-quality, controllable chess puzzles that satisfy strict constraints on uniqueness and theme. This demonstrates that diffusion-based approaches are promising for structured, constrained creative generation tasks. By releasing open-weight models for chess puzzle generation, the work provides a new, reproducible benchmark and toolset for studying and advancing computational creativity and reasoning under constraints.

Abstract: While modern language models demonstrate impressive generative capabilities, they often struggle with constrained, counter-intuitive creative tasks. To address this limitation, we explore chess puzzle generation as a rigorous testbed for computational creativity and reasoning, a domain where altering a single piece can invalidate an entire solution. We propose a novel approach for conditional generation of creative chess puzzles using masked diffusion models. Unlike previous methods, our non-directional diffusion approach allows for conditioning on specific tactical themes and partial board positions. We introduce a novel auxiliary task of simultaneous best-move prediction, which improves solution uniqueness by 11.6% and theme-conditioning accuracy by 2.5%. To further optimize solution uniqueness and theme conditioning, we establish a reinforcement learning framework adapted from Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (DDPO). This RL training increases the yield of unique and theme-matching positions by 89.1%. Finally, we release the first open-weights models (Appendix B) for chess puzzle generation, offering a new pathway for controllable, creative generation.

</details>


### [142] [Sense and Sensitivity: Benchmarking LLM Clinical Triage Recommendations with Physician Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38600)
*Abinitha Gourabathina,Haoran Zhang,Yuexing Hao,Walter Gerych,Marzyeh Ghassemi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how reliable large language models are for clinical triage when clinical text is phrased in different but clinically equivalent ways, and compares their behavior to physicians.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs begin to be used in real clinical workflows, there is concern that small, clinically irrelevant changes in wording, gender references, or tone could alter their medical recommendations, with potential safety and fairness implications. Existing benchmarks often ignore this robustness question and rarely compare directly to physician behavior.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark consisting of over 6,000 clinical triage scenarios, annotated with more than 7,000 physician triage decisions, and collect 225,000 responses from multiple LLMs. They systematically perturb the input texts (e.g., changes in phrasing, gender, tone) while keeping the underlying clinical scenario constant, then compare how triage recommendations from LLMs and physicians change under these perturbations.

Result: At baseline (unperturbed text), LLMs are more inclined than physicians to recommend higher, often unnecessary, levels of care. Under textual perturbations, this tendency toward over-triage increases. Additionally, LLMs’ recommendations are more sensitive to changes in gender indicators and tone than those of human physicians, meaning their outputs vary more when these clinically irrelevant attributes are altered.

Conclusion: LLMs used for clinical triage are not robust to clinically irrelevant textual variations and show heightened sensitivity to attributes such as gender and tone compared with physicians. This instability, and the tendency to recommend unnecessary care, underscores that deployment evaluations must be carefully designed around real clinical practice and expert physician behavior before LLMs can be safely integrated into clinical decision-making.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, it is critical to evaluate their reliability under realistic variation in clinical text. We study this question in clinical triage, comparing LLMs to practicing physicians under text perturbations that preserve the underlying clinical setting. We introduce a benchmark of over 6,000 clinical scenarios, 7,000 physician annotations, and 225,000 model responses. Using this benchmark, we make two key observations. First, LLMs are more likely than physicians to recommend unnecessary care at baseline, and this tendency increases under perturbed inputs. Further, we find that LLM recommendations are more sensitive to gender and tone perturbations than human recommendations. Together, these results demonstrate that LLMs can vary under clinically irrelevant textual changes, highlighting the need for deployment-oriented evaluations grounded in expert physician behavior.

</details>


### [143] [When Scientific Contradictions Are Lost in Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38621)
*Tal Zeevi,Trey W. Jensen,Maxwell Strome*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates how large language models decide whether scientific findings are comparable and which of two conflicting interpretations to favor, revealing biases toward biologically expected results over logically better-supported ones, especially in scientific prose.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In science, two findings may disagree without truly contradicting each other, and deciding if they conflict requires judging whether they measure comparable things. Language models are increasingly used to read, reconcile, and verify scientific literature, but we lack a clear understanding of how they determine which findings to compare and which interpretation to endorse when evidence and prior domain expectations diverge. The authors aim to systematically probe these decision points and quantify when models follow formal constraints versus domain priors.

Method: The authors construct an unsatisfiable XOR constraint system and map each constraint to a synthetic scientific report describing experimental results from different labs. This creates a scenario where no single assignment of truth values satisfies all constraints. They then define two key assignments: one that satisfies the maximal number of constraints (the logically best-supported assignment) and another that satisfies fewer constraints but aligns better with typical biological expectations. They test large language models (GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5) under different prompt conditions: direct presentation of the formal constraints; narrative scientific prose; prose with domain priors reduced; and prose augmented with a formalization request and an explicit paired-design cue. By measuring which assignment the models choose under each condition and performing statistical tests, they quantify the influence of content format and biological priors on the models’ decisions.

Result: When the XOR constraints are shown directly in formal form, both GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 predominantly choose the assignment that satisfies the most constraints, with success rates of 90% and 96%, respectively. However, when the same logical structure is expressed as scientific reports in prose, Claude Opus 5 frequently opts for the biologically expected assignment, even though it is less consistent with the full set of constraints. For Claude, suppressing biological preferences in the prompt increases recovery of the better-supported assignment from 27% to 79% (p<.001), and adding both a formalization request and an explicit cue that the records are part of a paired design further boosts recovery to 92% (p<.001). GPT-5.6 Sol shows less change across these manipulations; neither analogous modification yields a statistically significant difference in its behavior.

Conclusion: The study concludes that language models’ reliability in scientific verification tasks is shaped not only by their capacity for formal reasoning over constraints but also by how they infer which findings should be directly compared and what relationships hold between them. Domain-specific expectations, such as what is biologically plausible, can steer models toward interpretations that are less consistent with all available evidence when information is presented as natural scientific prose. Careful prompt design—such as encouraging formalization and clarifying experimental pairing—can mitigate these biases for some models. Overall, the work highlights that robust model-assisted scientific analysis requires attention to the alignment between narrative presentation, domain priors, and explicit logical structure.

Abstract: Two scientific findings can disagree without contradicting each other. Determining whether they conflict requires knowing whether they describe comparable measurements. We study how language models behave at this decision point. In a controlled task, we generate an unsatisfiable XOR constraint system and translate its constraints into scientific reports from different laboratories. One assignment satisfies more constraints, while another satisfies fewer but better matches expected biology. This creates a simple dilemma: does the model choose the assignment that best fits the constraints, or the one that better matches biological expectations? When the constraints are stated directly, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 recover the best-supported assignment in 90% and 96% of cases, respectively. In scientific prose, however, the models behave differently. Claude Opus 5 often prefers the biologically expected assignment. Removing that biological preference increases recovery of the better-supported assignment from 27% to 79% (p<.001); recovery reaches 92% when the same Biology-favored record is accompanied by a formalization request and an explicit paired-design cue (p<.001). GPT-5.6 Sol is less sensitive, with neither corresponding change reaching statistical significance. These results suggest that reliable scientific verification depends not only on formal reasoning, but also on how models decide which findings should be compared and what relations they imply.

</details>


### [144] [Component-Aware Feedback for Self-Evolving Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38639)
*Ethan Lin,Jinming Nian,Yi Fang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new method called component-aware feedback speeds up and stabilizes LLM-guided evolutionary search by tracking which component edits cause which metric changes, leading to better and cheaper LLM reranking pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-guided evolutionary search methods only store whole program candidates and their fitness, discarding information about which specific component-level edits led to improvements or degradations. This forces the mutator LLM to guess the impact of past edits from noisy histories, making search inefficient and unstable, especially for complex multi-component systems and smaller, locally deployed LLMs. There is a need for a more structured way to attribute performance changes to particular components and edits.

Method: They introduce component-aware feedback: for every child program evaluated, they compare it with its parent to identify which components changed. They then log those changed components together with the associated differences in evaluation metrics into an "attribution memory." This memory stores each change from two perspectives: (1) local, relative to the immediate parent, capturing the direct effect of a single edit, and (2) global, relative to the initial seed program, capturing cumulative progress. Subsequent mutations are conditioned on this structured attribution memory so the LLM mutator can make more informed edits. They evaluate this method on LLM-based reranking pipelines formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem over both ranking quality and serving cost, using a set of twelve BRIGHT datasets.

Result: On LLM reranking across twelve BRIGHT datasets, the component-aware feedback approach matches the best baseline's final ranking quality using only about one third of the search budget (median), indicating a much faster search. Ultimately it surpasses that baseline by 7.2% in held-out nDCG@10. Under a cost-aware objective, it discovers pipelines that are on average more accurate while consuming 11% fewer tokens per query, showing both quality and efficiency gains.

Conclusion: Component-aware feedback, which explicitly tracks and reuses component-level performance attributions during evolutionary search, significantly improves the efficiency and effectiveness of LLM-guided program evolution. It enables faster convergence to strong solutions, better final quality, and superior cost–quality trade-offs in multi-component systems like LLM reranking pipelines, suggesting it is a promising general strategy for building more efficient self-evolving systems.

Abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search can discover complex programs, but existing methods mostly only save candidate programs and fitness scores while discarding which component edits produced which fitness metric changes. Existing methods force the mutator LLM to infer the effect of prior edits from cluttered histories, making program search slow and unstable. This is especially true for locally servable LLMs to evolve multi-component systems. We introduce component-aware feedback, which compares each evaluated program with its parent, identifies the components that changed, and logs them with the associated metric differences into an attribution memory that later mutations read. The memory keeps each change in two reference frames, local against the parent it came from and global against the seed program, which shows both the immediate effect of a change and the cumulative progress made since the seed. We study this on LLM reranking, a multi-objective optimization problem where a multi-stage pipeline must balance quality against serving cost. Across twelve \textsc{Bright} datasets, our method reaches the strongest baseline's final quality after a median of one third of the search budget and ends 7.2\% higher in held-out nDCG@10, and under a cost-aware objective it finds pipelines that are on average more accurate while using 11\% fewer tokens per query, showing component-aware feedback to be a promising direction for more efficient self-evolving systems.

</details>


### [145] [ChartRevise: A Dataset and Evaluation Protocol for Exact Chart Editing via Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38642)
*Jiaxiang Tang,Yi Zhou,Chad DeLuca,Rogerio Feris,Ahmed Khalil Omran,Zhi-Li Zhang,Pengyuan Li,Ali Anwar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ChartRevise, a structured dataset and evaluation protocol for precise, program-grounded chart editing, enabling rigorous measurement of whether code-based chart edits satisfy all requested changes without unintended side effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing chart-editing benchmarks focus mainly on whether generated code runs and produces good-looking charts, but they do not precisely measure whether a model truly fulfilled the edit request. In particular, they conflate partial success with exact success, and cannot clearly distinguish between (1) completing all requested edits, (2) missing required coupled updates, and (3) introducing gratuitous, unintended changes. This gap hinders the development and fair comparison of models intended for fine-grained chart revision and maintenance.

Method: The authors design ChartRevise by leveraging the grammar of graphics as a unifying abstraction over multiple plotting libraries and chart types. They systematically enumerate chart-editing operations and validate their applicability using source-program checks, ensuring that edits are meaningful across various chart and library combinations. Their data-construction pipeline decomposes edit requests into atomic requirements, automatically checks whether each requirement is satisfiable, and either repairs the example or excludes it if constraints are violated. This yields a large-scale dataset of chart-editing instances covering numerous edit types, chart types, and plotting libraries. For evaluation, they propose a reference-free protocol that programmatically checks, per example, whether each atomic requirement is satisfied, whether any unrelated parts of the chart or code were changed, and whether any necessary coupled updates were omitted. These signals, combined with checks of code executability and chart rendering, define an exact-edit success metric.

Result: The resulting ChartRevise dataset contains 92,438 chart-editing records, spanning 344 distinct edit types, 20 chart types, and three plotting libraries. Using this dataset and evaluation protocol, the authors evaluate five different models across four external benchmarks. Fine-tuning on ChartRevise leads to substantial performance improvements: a 16% relative increase in mean requirement recall (i.e., correctly fulfilling requested atomic edits) and a 22% relative increase in the mean exact-edit rate (i.e., satisfying all requirements without gratuitous or missing coupled changes).

Conclusion: ChartRevise provides a rigorous, program-grounded resource for training and evaluating models on precise chart editing, addressing weaknesses in previous benchmarks that fail to distinguish exact from partial or noisy edits. The structured dataset and reference-free evaluation protocol enable granular analysis of model behavior with respect to requested edits, side effects, and coupled updates. Empirical gains from fine-tuning on ChartRevise suggest that this resource can substantially improve the reliability and correctness of automatic chart-editing systems in practice.

Abstract: Chart editing requires cross-modal edit grounding, realizing a requested visual change in the code that draws it, with necessary related updates and without altering unrelated content. Existing benchmarks emphasize either code executability or chart quality, but their metrics do not clearly distinguish request completion from missed coupled updates and gratuitous changes. We introduce ChartRevise, a structured dataset and evaluation protocol for exact program-grounded chart editing. For dataset construction, we build on the grammar of graphics to systematically cover chart-editing operations, using source-program checks to verify their applicability across chart types and libraries. To improve edit exactness, our pipeline checks individual requirements and guides repair or exclusion when they are unmet. The resulting dataset contains 92,438 records covering 344 edit types across 20 chart types and three plotting libraries. For evaluation, our reference-free protocol separately measures atomic requirement completion, identifies gratuitous changes, and detects missed coupled updates. These checks are combined with successful execution and rendering to determine exact-edit success. Across five models and four external benchmarks, fine-tuning yields relative gains of 16\% in mean requirement recall and 22\% in mean exact-edit rate.

</details>


### [146] [AgBench: Agentic AI Benchmarks for Personal AI Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38652)
*Yizhou Han,Di Wu,Dhananjay Saikumar,Blesson Varghese*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgBench is a benchmark suite to systematically evaluate how well agentic AI runs on personal devices versus cloud or hybrid setups, focusing on task success, latency, cost, and data exposure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI typically depends on cloud LLMs, which raises concerns about API cost and sensitive data exposure. Personal AI hardware is emerging and could mitigate these, but it has limited compute and memory, which may hurt performance. Existing benchmarks do not provide a systematic way to measure the trade‑offs between local, hybrid, and cloud deployments across different devices and workloads, motivating a new benchmark suite.

Method: The authors design AgBench, a benchmark suite and accompanying open artifacts targeting agentic AI workloads on personal devices. They define metrics including task success rate, latency, goodput, cloud API cost, and data exposure. Using AgBench, they run large-scale experiments comparing three deployment architectures—local-only, hybrid, and cloud-only—across varying devices, workloads, and concurrency levels, collecting over 162 million data points.

Result: Experiments show that many agent tasks can be completed fully on personal devices, but local-only execution typically yields lower task success rates and higher completion times than cloud-only, especially as concurrency grows. Local-only runs, however, incur no cloud API costs and avoid exposing sensitive information to cloud models. Hybrid execution can raise task success relative to local-only, but the resulting cloud costs and data exposure vary significantly depending on how tasks are partitioned and what information is shared with cloud components.

Conclusion: There is no universally best deployment architecture for agentic AI; each of local, hybrid, and cloud-only has distinct trade-offs in success, performance, cost, and privacy. Deployment decisions should depend on workload characteristics and device capabilities. AgBench provides a standardized, reproducible way to study and compare these trade-offs for agentic AI on personal devices.

Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly rely on cloud-hosted large language models for planning, tool use, and iterative execution, raising concerns about API cost and data exposure. Advances in personal AI devices enable agents to execute locally, but limited resources on device may affect task success and performance. Existing benchmarks are inadequate for systematically characterizing these trade-offs across devices, workloads, and deployment architectures. We present AgBench, a benchmark suite and open artifacts for reproducible evaluation of agentic AI on personal devices. Using AgBench, we evaluate local, hybrid, and cloud execution across agentic workloads, examining task success, latency, cloud API cost, and data exposure. Our results, drawn from over 162.07 million data points, show that personal AI devices can complete many agent tasks locally, but local-only execution generally has lower task success and longer completion times than cloud-only execution, especially as concurrency increases. Local-only execution eliminates cloud model API costs and sensitive-information exposure to cloud agents. Hybrid execution can improve task success, but its cloud cost and data exposure depend on how agents divide work and share information. No single architecture performs best across task success, goodput, cloud cost, and data exposure; deployment choices should reflect the intended workload and device capabilities. AgBench is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AgBench-2777.

</details>


### [147] [EvoSteer: Online Self-Evolving Graph Orchestration via Reference-Anchored Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38661)
*Mingda Zhang,Hanwen Zhang,Qiang Huang,Zijia Wang,Pengfei Guo,Yuchen Zhang,Jionghao Zhu,Xiaoying Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoSteer is an online self-evolving orchestration method for LLM-based multi-agent tool-using systems that repairs agent graphs during execution using a new training loss (AnchorTB) and a validated skill admission procedure, yielding better performance across multiple reasoning and interaction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent orchestrators evolve communication graphs only after full trajectories are completed, assign credit to actions in a coarse and confounded way, and add new skills without principled validation or retirement. This leads to inefficient learning, misattribution of credit, and bloated, uncalibrated skill sets. The authors aim to create a more effective and data-efficient self-evolving orchestrator that can adjust teams online, attribute credit more precisely, and manage skills rigorously during deployment.

Method: The authors propose EvoSteer, an online self-evolving graph orchestration framework in which the orchestrator incrementally builds and adjusts a team of tool-using agents while a trajectory is unfolding. It repairs failing steps based on execution features and a learned value estimate. To train the orchestrator, they introduce Anchored Trajectory Balance (AnchorTB), a regression-style flow-matching loss that treats orchestration as a flow and assigns each orchestration action a coefficient computed by balancing sub-trajectories against a fixed reference policy or graph. This anchors learning to a frozen baseline, mitigating confounding in credit assignment and incorporating both task-level reward statistics and prefix-dependent corrections. On top of this, they design Validated Skill Admission: candidate skills are first run in trial mode, and only promoted to the main skill set if their empirical evidence passes a sequential statistical test, all under a shared nominal testing budget, which regularizes how many new skills can be admitted.

Result: On twelve datasets spanning question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive decision making, EvoSteer consistently and significantly outperforms existing baseline orchestrators. The experiments demonstrate that online graph repair guided by AnchorTB and disciplined skill admission leads to better task performance than post-hoc evolution and naive skill management. The paper also reports that AnchorTB effectively leverages reference reward statistics combined with prefix-dependent corrections to improve credit assignment quality.

Conclusion: EvoSteer shows that online self-evolving graph orchestration, when coupled with a principled flow-matching loss (AnchorTB) and statistically controlled skill admission, can substantially improve the performance of LLM-based multi-agent tool-using systems across a range of complex tasks. The work suggests that future orchestration methods should move away from purely post-hoc evolution and unregulated skill growth, toward online repair, reference-anchored learning signals, and validated, budgeted skill management.

Abstract: In recent years, LLM-based multi-agent systems have been widely applied to orchestrate tool-using agents into executable communication graphs. However, existing self-evolving orchestration still faces key challenges, including post-hoc evolution that revises the team only after the trajectory ends, credit diffusion that gives every action the same terminal advantage under confounded baselines, and skill admission that is uncalibrated and never retired. To address these challenges, we propose EvoSteer, a new paradigm of Online Self-Evolving Graph Orchestration -- the orchestrator builds a running team and repairs its plausible but failing steps from execution features and a learned value estimate. To support this paradigm, we introduce Anchored Trajectory Balance (AnchorTB), a regression-style flow-matching loss that assigns each orchestration action a coefficient by balancing subtrajectories against a frozen reference. Built on the learned flow, we further propose Validated Skill Admission, in which a candidate skill is tried before promotion and promoted only if paired evidence passes a sequential test under a shared nominal testing budget. Moreover, AnchorTB combines measured task-level reference reward statistics with prefix-dependent corrections. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that EvoSteer significantly outperforms baselines across question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive decision making. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/evosteer.

</details>


### [148] [Where Scientific Search Agents Fail: Decision-Checkpoint Auditing of Exposure and Inspection Attempts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38670)
*Hongmin Li,Wanli Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a checkpoint-based analysis protocol for scientific-search agents that reveals *how* and *where* agents fail, beyond final-answer accuracy, and use it to compare different search strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional evaluation of scientific-search agents uses only final-answer accuracy, which cannot distinguish between different failure modes: not finding the target paper, finding but not opening it, or opening it but still answering incorrectly. This lack of granularity makes it hard to understand and improve agent behavior, tool use, and search strategies. The authors aim to create a framework that exposes these intermediate decision points and failure modes.

Method: They instrument a scientific-search agent with decision checkpoints that log observations and tool actions (e.g., search calls, which papers are exposed, which are opened/inspected) during inference, without relying on labels at run time. After inference, they join these logs with ground-truth target paper identities and evaluator labels to automatically categorize each question’s outcome into more fine-grained categories (e.g., target not exposed, exposed but not inspected, inspected but incorrect). They then run the agent under five experimental conditions in a fixed, target-enriched environment on 540 answerable AutoResearchBench Deep questions, comparing raw search, keyword-augmented search, and a read-first strategy in terms of accuracy and these detailed outcome categories.

Result: In this target-enriched setup, simple keyword-based search yields 24.6% final-answer accuracy, outperforming raw search at 17.8%. Keyword search reduces the number of questions where the agent both misses the target paper and never inspects it, but increases the number of questions where the target is surfaced (exposed) but not opened (inspected) before answering incorrectly. A read-first strategy triggers 27.4% more evidence-search tool calls than keyword search and attempts target inspection on 199 questions versus 191 for keyword search, yet both strategies end up with the same final accuracy of 24.6%. The logged checkpoints thus reveal meaningful behavioral differences that are invisible at the aggregate accuracy level.

Conclusion: The checkpoint protocol provides a structured way to analyze intermediate decisions of scientific-search agents, disentangling target exposure, inspection, and answer correctness. It shows that strategies with equal aggregate accuracy can differ substantially in how often they surface and inspect target papers and how they use tools. This more granular view can guide the design and debugging of future research agents by focusing on specific failure modes (e.g., failing to inspect surfaced targets) rather than only optimizing for final-answer accuracy.

Abstract: Final-answer accuracy does not reveal whether a scientific-search agent failed to encounter a target paper, attempt to inspect it, or return an accepted answer after inspection. We introduce decision checkpoints that record observations and tool actions without benchmark labels during inference, then join target identities and evaluator labels to assign outcome categories from recorded events. Across five conditions on 540 answerable AutoResearchBench Deep questions in a fixed, target-enriched environment, keyword search achieves 24.6\% accuracy, compared with 17.8\% for raw search. The keyword condition has fewer incorrect answers with neither target exposure nor inspection, but more incorrect answers after the target is exposed and left uninspected. Compared with keyword search, read-first has 27.4\% more recorded evidence-search calls. Target inspection attempts occur on 199 questions under read-first and 191 under keyword search; both conditions achieve 24.6\% accuracy. The checkpoint protocol makes these question-level differences explicit, distinguishing target exposure and inspection from aggregate accuracy and total tool use.

</details>


### [149] [Concept-Grounded Attention: A Controlled Evaluation of Graph-Injected Attention, Temporal Versioning, and Epistemic Status](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38684)
*Sachin Dev Duggal,Pradyumna Swarnalatha Ramanna,Alexandros Vassiliades*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new knowledge representation (Concept Lifecycle Model) and attention mechanisms (Concept-Grounded Attention) for language models, and empirically finds strong benefits from explicit temporal and epistemic modeling but limited practical gains from graph-structured attention beyond added capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing knowledge-intensive language-model systems typically treat external knowledge as static text chunks or graphs that do not handle how concepts change over time, do not support precise point-in-time reasoning, and rarely distinguish between well-validated facts and inferred or uncertain knowledge. Moreover, while graph-structured knowledge has been integrated into models, it is unclear how much benefit comes from the graph structure itself versus just extra parameters or inputs, and common evaluations often lack strong disabled-mechanism controls.
