The authors aim to build a representation and evaluation framework that can explicitly model concept identity, temporal evolution, and epistemic status, and rigorously test how graph-grounded mechanisms actually affect reasoning and reliability.

Method: The authors introduce: (1) the Concept Lifecycle Model (CLM), in which each concept is a persistent entity grounded in a graph, with temporal versioning, explicit provenance, and an assigned epistemic status (e.g., validated vs inferred); and (2) Concept-Grounded Attention (CGA), which injects concept-graph information into transformer models in two forms: Form A, a graph-biased self-attention mechanism that favors edges in the concept graph; and Form B, a gated cross-attention layer over explicit concept nodes. They evaluate these mechanisms in controlled experiments with disabled-mechanism baselines: on MuSiQue and HotpotQA with fixed retrieval, they analyze multi-hop path recovery, evidence recall, and attention patterns; on LongMemEval, they test temporal reasoning benefits of explicit temporal representation versus simpler dated serialization; and on a synthetic source-independence task, they examine how epistemic-status annotations affect unsupported assertions in both small fine-tuned models and large (72–122B) models.

Result: For multi-hop QA (MuSiQue and HotpotQA), concept-graph retrieval can recover explicit multi-hop paths but does not improve evidence recall. Form A (graph-biased self-attention) appears to steer attention toward gold concepts, but the same attention ratio is observed even when the mechanism is disabled, and the learned bias is negligible, with no changes in answers. Form B (gated cross-attention) improves F1 from 0.188 to 0.221, but a control condition using non-semantic control concepts still reaches 0.213, implying that most of the observed gain stems from additional model capacity rather than meaningful use of graph structure. On LongMemEval, including explicit temporal representation improves answer accuracy by 13–25 points across generators up to 122B parameters. However, a simplified CLM version resolution performs similarly to naive dated serialization, due to unreliable establishment of concept identity. On the synthetic source-independence task, encoding epistemic status from the knowledge protocol sharply reduces unsupported assertions: from 28% to 0.1% in a small fine-tuned model, and from 19–68% to 0–5% in 72–122B models.

Conclusion: Explicit modeling of temporal validity and epistemic status in knowledge representations provides substantial gains in temporal reasoning and reduction of hallucinated or unsupported statements, even for very large language models. However, simply injecting graph structure into transformer attention via graph-biased self-attention or cross-attention does not reliably yield benefits beyond increased capacity, and naive diagnostics like attention concentration can be misleading without disabled-mechanism controls. The findings suggest that future work should focus more on robust temporal and epistemic modeling and on rigorous ablation-style evaluations to determine whether graph-based mechanisms genuinely contribute to reasoning performance.

Abstract: Knowledge-intensive language-model systems typically represent external knowledge as text chunks or static graphs, with limited support for concept evolution, point-in-time reasoning, and distinctions between validated and inferred knowledge. We introduce the Concept Lifecycle Model (CLM), which represents concepts as persistent, graph-grounded, temporally versioned entities with explicit provenance and epistemic status, and Concept-Grounded Attention (CGA), which injects concept-graph structure into transformer computation through graph-biased self-attention (Form A) and gated cross-attention over concept nodes (Form B). We evaluate the framework in controlled settings using disabled-mechanism baselines. On 200 MuSiQue and HotpotQA questions with retrieval fixed, concept-graph retrieval recovers explicit multi-hop paths but does not improve evidence recall. Form A appears to steer attention, with 2.76 times more attention on gold than distractor concepts, but the same ratio occurs when Form A is disabled; the learned bias is negligible and no answers change. An identity-preserving Form B improves F1 from 0.188 to 0.221, but control concepts yield 0.213, indicating that most of the gain reflects added capacity. On LongMemEval, explicit temporal representation improves answer accuracy by 13 to 25 points across all tested generators, up to 122B parameters, while simplified CLM version resolution performs similarly to dated serialization because concept identity is not established reliably. On a synthetic source-independence task, protocol-derived epistemic status reduces unsupported assertions from 28% to 0.1% in a fine-tuned small model and from 19-68% to 0-5% in 72-122B models. Overall, the results support making temporal validity and epistemic status explicit, while showing that graph-attention diagnostics are not informative without disabled-mechanism controls.

</details>


### [150] [GATE-ST: Gene-Aware Text-image Encoder for Spatial Transcriptomics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38690)
*Lucas Ni,Jian Luo,Wentao Huang,Chao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GATE-ST is a multimodal model that improves spatial gene expression prediction from pathology images by incorporating gene text descriptions via cross-attention with image features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatial transcriptomics provides spatially resolved gene expression alongside tissue morphology but is costly and slow to obtain experimentally. Existing computational approaches mainly optimize image features and positional encodings, leaving the potential of textual biological knowledge underused. The authors aim to leverage rich textual descriptions of genes to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of image-based spatial gene expression prediction, reducing reliance on expensive lab assays.

Method: The authors propose GATE-ST, a multimodal architecture that combines histology images with text-derived gene information. For each gene, a textual summary is fed into a text encoder to generate gene embeddings. Image patches from pathology slides are processed by an image encoder to obtain image embeddings. These two modalities are integrated via cross-attention layers so that gene embeddings align with and attend to morphological features relevant to their expression patterns. The model is trained to predict spatial gene expression profiles and is compared against baselines using random gene embeddings and various alternative image–text fusion strategies.

Result: GATE-ST achieves better performance in predicting spatial gene expression than baselines that either do not use meaningful text, use random gene embeddings, or employ other fusion architectures. Benchmarks across multiple settings show that text-informed gene embeddings combined with cross-attention significantly improve prediction accuracy and spatial correspondence of gene expression relative to competing image-based and multimodal methods.

Conclusion: Incorporating informative textual descriptions of genes into image-based models substantially improves spatial transcriptomics prediction from pathology images. GATE-ST demonstrates that cross-attention between text-encoded gene summaries and image features effectively injects prior biological knowledge and yields more accurate and cost-efficient spatial gene expression maps. This text-guided framework can reduce the need for costly spatial assays and highlights the value of integrating domain text into computational pathology workflows.

Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables spatially resolved gene expression analysis from slide-level images while preserving morphological features, providing valuable information for studying disease mechanisms and developing treatments. However, spatial gene expression profiling typically requires expensive and time-consuming tests. While existing image-based prediction optimizations mostly revolve around including positional embeddings and further image-based changes, text-based optimizations remain relatively unexplored. We present GATE-ST, which incorporates text-based inputs into image-based spatial gene expression predictions. With this approach, generated text descriptions of genes are utilized to better spatial transcriptomics prediction results. Gene summaries are put through a text encoder, generating embeddings that integrate with image embeddings through cross-attention layers to align with morphological features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of such text inputs by benchmarking performance against random gene embeddings and multiple other image-text fusion architectures, and show that GATE-ST outperforms these alternatives. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of GATE-ST in pathology imaging, which may greatly reduce the time and cost of accurate spatial transcriptomic predictions, proving the potential of text-guided spatial gene expression prediction.

</details>


### [151] [Budget Boundary Effects in Test-Time Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38699)
*Guilin Zhang,Ziqi Tan,Wulan Guo,Kai Zhao,Hongyun Yang,Mei Luo,Qi Ning,Feng Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how enforcing a hard token cap versus letting the current attempt finish (advisory stopping) affects accuracy and cost in multi-attempt test-time compute for math problems, using offline replays of public traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As models are deployed under token budgets, practitioners must choose how to apply a cumulative token cap in multi-attempt settings. It is unclear how much accuracy is gained or lost by strictly enforcing the cap mid-derivation versus allowing the current attempt to finish, and how this interacts with candidate coverage, selection strategy, and realized compute cost. The paper aims to clarify these trade-offs and provide guidance on reporting and comparing budgeted evaluation results.

Method: The authors perform paired offline replays of 19,200 public traces from a single model evaluated on 120 math problems (AIME, BrUMO, HMMT). They fix candidate order, a 16-attempt cap, and use answer selectors that are blind to reference answers and correctness. They contrast a strict stopping rule (truncate when the token cap is reached) with an advisory rule (allow the current attempt to finish even if it exceeds the cap), at several nominal caps (e.g., 4k, 8k, 32k). They analyze realized token cost, abstention vs. answer behavior, candidate coverage, and various selectors (including log-probability-based selection and a consistency-based repair), comparing accuracy at equal caps and at similar realized costs.

Result: 1) At a 4k token cap, advisory stopping mainly improves accuracy by converting abstentions into correct answers; strict stopping wastes tokens on unfinished prefixes that cannot be used by a selector that only considers completed attempts. 2) When matching on realized cost instead of nominal caps, comparisons change: advisory 4k in the low-budget regime achieves higher accuracy than strict 8k at similar mean cost, whereas in a higher-budget regime its observed accuracy is 0.42 percentage points below strict 32k while using only 59% of that setting’s mean tokens; however, these aggregate results do not suffice to claim equal-compute superiority or equivalence. 3) Increasing the number of eligible candidates does not always raise answer accuracy: a log-probability selector becomes less accurate even as coverage increases, and this persists despite a consistency-based repair. At a 32k cap, majority-vote accuracy differences between strict and advisory shrink to under 1.3 percentage points.

Conclusion: The way token budgets are enforced at test time—strict cap vs. advisory completion—subtly but meaningfully affects accuracy, abstention rates, and realized compute cost, especially at low caps. Advisory stopping can yield higher accuracy by avoiding wasted partial attempts, but gains depend on the selector and regime and do not straightforwardly translate to equal-compute dominance. Moreover, simply covering more candidates is not guaranteed to improve accuracy. For transparent and comparable evaluations, budget curves and reports should jointly specify the nominal cap, realized cost, which candidates are eligible for selection, the stopping rule, and what information selectors can use.

Abstract: A cumulative token cap can fall inside a mathematical derivation, forcing a test-time controller to choose between stopping at the cap (strict) and allowing the current attempt to finish (advisory). We measure this boundary choice with paired offline replays of 19,200 public traces: 120 AIME, BrUMO and HMMT problems and two archive configurations of one model. Candidate order and a 16-attempt cap are fixed, and answer selection is blind to reference answers and correctness labels. Three findings emerge. First, at the 4k cap, most advisory accuracy gains replace abstention with a correct answer; strict stopping pays for an unfinished prefix that the completed-only selector cannot use. Second, comparisons along realized cost differ from same-cap comparisons: advisory 4k in low has higher accuracy than strict 8k at comparable mean completion cost, while in high its observed accuracy is 0.42 points below strict 32k using 59% of its mean tokens. These aggregate comparisons do not establish equal-compute superiority or accuracy equivalence. Third, increased candidate coverage does not guarantee higher answer accuracy: a log-probability selector loses accuracy while coverage rises, including after a source-grade consistency repair. Same-cap majority-accuracy differences shrink below 1.3 percentage points at 32k. Budget curves should jointly state the cap, realized cost, eligible candidates, stopping rule and selector information.

</details>


### [152] [Staying on Task: Testing the Foundations of Long-Horizon Agent Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38712)
*Jeffrey Willette,Krishna C. Puvvada,Boris Ginsburg*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Long-Transduction, a diagnostic benchmark to test how well language models can reliably perform state-dependent operations over long contexts and evolving data, revealing significant performance degradation with longer context, changed formats, and higher task complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used as agents in long-horizon workflows (e.g., reconciling long ledgers), they must repeatedly read and update state over growing contexts while maintaining consistent, correct operations. Existing evaluations often test short, static tasks and do not isolate failure modes that arise from long generation with continuous reading and mutation of context-dependent data. The authors aim to systematically characterize where and how current models fail in such settings.

Method: The authors design Long-Transduction, a controlled diagnostic evaluation where models must repeatedly apply input-context dependent operations (like arithmetic, sorting, variable lookups, and table transformations) over long generations. The benchmark independently varies three axes: (1) local task complexity, (2) input data formatting, and (3) overall context length. By manipulating these factors, they can isolate which axis causes performance degradation. They then test seven open-weight models on this benchmark and measure accuracy changes along each axis.

Result: Across the seven open-weight models, performance dramatically degrades under more challenging conditions: a 62.8% performance drop when scaling context length from 4K to 128K tokens, a 36.5% drop when changing input formats, and a 39.9% drop when increasing local task complexity. These quantitative results show that current models struggle to maintain consistent, correct behavior in long, stateful workflows.

Conclusion: Long-Transduction exposes critical weaknesses in current LLMs’ ability to sustain reliable, state-dependent reasoning over long horizons. The observed drops in performance along context length, formatting variation, and task complexity indicate that today’s models are not yet robust enough for many long-horizon agentic workflows. The benchmark provides a systematic way to diagnose and eventually guide improvements in models and training methods for such settings.

Abstract: Long-horizon agentic workflows require models to sustain repeated state-dependent actions all while the context grows, sub-task complexity changes, and new data arrives. Each situation represents an independent axis along which an agent may fail. An agent reconciling a long ledger, for example, must repeatedly read its state, update the correct record, and preserve alignment across thousands of outputs. A model may accept the entire ledger yet lose its place or stop applying the operation consistently as generation proceeds. We introduce Long-Transduction, a controlled diagnostic that tests a model's ability to stay on task during long generation while continuously reading, mutating, and outputting input-context dependent operations such as arithmetic, sorting, variable lookups, and table transformations. Long-Transduction evaluation independently varies local task complexity, input data formatting, and context length isolate failures along each axis. We evaluate seven open-weight models, finding a 62.8\% decrease when scaling context length from 4-128K, a 36.5\% decrease when varying input format, and a 39.9\% decrease by increasing local task complexity. Together, these failures represent critical liabilities in long-horizon agentic workflows.

</details>


### [153] [UniEvo-VL: An On-policy Self-Distillation Training Recipe for Multimodal Model Self-improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38721)
*Fang Wu,Da Xing,Yanjie Huang,Junxi Wang,Ji Wang,Hejia Geng,Guancheng Wan,Bowen Zuo,Xiaomin Li,Shixiang Tang,Xinyu Xiang,Zehong Wang,Shiyi Du,Peng Xia,Shuangjia Zheng,Yining Hong,Li Erran Li,Jure Leskovec,Yejin Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UniEvo-VL is a self-evolving test-time learning framework where a single multimodal model critiques and improves its own image generation without an external teacher.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern multimodal models can both understand and generate content, meaning they can provide feedback on their own outputs. Current self-improvement approaches often depend on a separate, larger teacher model, which is costly and less scalable. The authors want to exploit the intrinsic judging/critique ability of a single multimodal model to drive its own improvement at test time, especially for image generation, without external supervision.

Method: The authors propose UniEvo-VL, where one multimodal model plays two roles with different contexts: a student that only sees the original question/prompt, and a teacher that additionally sees a privileged self-critique or reflection. For a given student sampling trajectory, they define denoising diffusion distributions for both student and teacher states and then train by minimizing a per-state divergence between these distributions. This aligns the student’s behavior with the teacher’s improved decisions driven by the critique, effectively turning self-critiques into privileged training signals during test-time compute.

Result: Applying UniEvo-VL to the open-source Qwen-image-2512 model yields clear gains in image generation benchmarks: GenEval score increases from 0.747 to 0.808, and GenEval2 Soft-TIFA from 32.97 to 35.53. Experiments also show that when using stronger external critics such as GPT5.6-Luna, the framework can reach a higher performance ceiling, indicating that better judging capability supports stronger self-evolution. However, mixed results on text-rendering tasks indicate that the improvements are not uniformly distributed across all capabilities.

Conclusion: UniEvo-VL demonstrates that a single multimodal model can act as both teacher and student by conditioning on its own critiques, enabling constructive self-correction and test-time self-improvement in image generation without needing a separate teacher model. This supports the broader vision of recursive self-improvement in multimodal systems, while also highlighting that such self-evolution can be task-dependent and may not improve all skills uniformly.

Abstract: Modern multimodal models bring generation and understanding into a single unified system, which enables them to provide and learn from their own feedback. Motivated by this unified capacity, we introduce UniEvo-VL, a self-evolving framework for multimodal models to learn from this constructive self-correction feedback during test-time compute. Instead of relying on a separate, often larger, teacher, we leverage their self-critiques as privileged information and ask a single multimodal model to act as both teacher and student with different contexts. The student only sees the vanilla question, while the teacher conditions on the privileged critique. Then training minimizes the per-state divergence between their denoising diffusion distributions over the student's own sampling trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that UniEvo-VL improves the image generation capabilities of multimodal models, while maintaining their sensitivity to additional reflection information. Specifically, we build on top of the open-source Qwen-image-2512 and observe a significant performance gain from 0.747 to 0.808 on GenEval and from 32.97 to 35.53 on GenEval2 Soft-TIFA. Moreover, attempts with more powerful external critics (e.g., GPT5.6-Luna) show that multimodal models with strong judge capabilities can anticipate a higher self-evolving ceiling. Last but not least, mixed text-rendering outcomes show that our self-improvements may not be uniform across different tasks. Our study aims to shed light on the current hot recursive self-improvement research line to enhance the user experience when using multimodal models without external supervision or guidance.

</details>


### [154] [Code to Control: Synthesizing Parameterized Reactive Controllers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38733)
*Zergham Ahmed,Joshua B. Tenenbaum,Chris Bates,Samuel J. Gershman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Code to Control, a method where LLMs generate the structure of Python control policies, and derivative-free search tunes their parameters, yielding fast, real-time controllers that are competitive with deep RL and better than planning-based program synthesis on several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based control methods either have the LLM pick actions online or generate world models for planning, both of which require LLM inference or planning at every step, causing latency that hinders real-time control. There is a need for an approach that leverages LLMs for control without incurring decision-time overhead, while maintaining strong performance and sample efficiency and allowing transfer across environments.

Method: Code to Control separates controller design into structure and parameters. A large language model is used once (offline) to synthesize the high-level structure of a Python controller program. Then, a derivative-free optimization procedure searches over the controller's continuous parameters using environment feedback to fit them for continuous control tasks. After training, the resulting program runs as a standard policy without further calls to the LLM or any online planning, enabling low-latency action selection.

Result: On benchmarks including multiple Atari games, Flappy Bird, and MuJoCo continuous control tasks, the method outperforms planning-based program synthesis approaches, is competitive with deep RL baselines such as PPO while requiring fewer environment interactions, achieves transfer to environments with substantially changed dynamics, and scales to complex locomotion problems. Under their timing protocol, the learned controllers select actions faster than a PPO policy at test time.

Conclusion: Code to Control shows that combining LLM-synthesized controller structure with derivative-free parameter search can produce executable policies that avoid online LLM inference and planning, enabling real-time, low-latency control. This hybrid approach can match or exceed deep RL performance with improved sample efficiency and robustness to dynamics changes, and it generalizes to more complex control tasks.

Abstract: Recent LLM-based approaches to control either invoke a language model to select actions or synthesize world models that require planning at every decision, introducing latency that can limit real-time use. We introduce Code to Control, an approach that synthesizes Python controllers which execute directly as policies. Code to Control separates program structure from parameters. An LLM synthesizes the controller structure, while derivative-free search fits its parameters for continuous control using feedback from the environment. Once learned, the resulting controllers require neither LLM inference nor planning at decision time, enabling real-time gameplay and, under our timing protocol, faster action selection than a PPO policy. Across a suite of Atari games, Flappy Bird, and MuJoCo tasks, Code to Control outperforms planning-based program synthesis methods, remains competitive with deep reinforcement learning while using fewer environment interactions, transfers across substantial changes in environment dynamics, and scales to complex locomotion tasks.

</details>


### [155] [Learning to Route in Visual Space via Multi-Step Embedding Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38743)
*Tianyu Chen,Mingyuan Zhou,Jiaxing Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces VHOP and VHOP-Router, which turn standard visual retrieval into an autoregressive, multi-step search process directly in image embedding space, dramatically improving visual agentic search efficiency and success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents rely on retrieval tools, but current visual search is limited by single-step retrievers that require text queries at each step. This is problematic when key visual evidence is hard to describe in language or buried beyond top-k results, causing failures in multi-step visual reasoning and navigation. The authors aim to remove this bottleneck by letting the retriever itself perform multi-hop navigation over the embedding space, rather than forcing the agent to orchestrate this via text prompts.

Method: They propose VHOP, a data generation framework and benchmark that defines multi-step visual search tasks with five difficulty levels, involving both visual similarity and search-planning challenges. Using VHOP, they train VHOP-Router, which converts a standard embedding model into an autoregressive multi-step retriever that operates purely in visual latent space. The training pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning, online imitation learning, and reinforcement learning to teach the model to output chains of linked images in one call, effectively internalizing multi-hop search behavior without requiring intermediate text queries from the LLM agent.

Result: VHOP-Router raises retrieval accuracy from below 5% to 76.3% on VHOP tasks. In end-to-end agentic search, it increases task success by 52.7% and cuts average token usage by 61% (1886 → 728). Simply upgrading the LLM agent provides only a 3.7% gain, showing the main bottleneck is retrieval. Against a strong baseline where the agent retrieves top-50 images at each step, VHOP-Router achieves better performance while using 23× fewer in-context images and 35× less cumulative API payload. The approach also generalizes to unseen difficulty levels and more realistic test sets.

Conclusion: Multi-step, autoregressive retrieval directly in visual embedding space can remove key bottlenecks in visual agentic search without modifying the LLM itself. VHOP and VHOP-Router provide a principled framework and practical system for learning such retrievers, yielding large gains in effectiveness, efficiency, and generalization compared with traditional single-step, text-query-based retrieval pipelines.

Abstract: LLM agents rely on retrieval tools to access external knowledge, yet visual agentic search remains severely bottlenecked by standard single-step retrievers. In current pipelines, the agent must issue text queries for every intermediate step, struggling when visual clues are difficult to describe or when the retriever fails to surface necessary intermediate evidence within its top results. We hypothesize that offloading multi-step navigation across the entire embedding space directly to the retrieval tool resolves this performance bottleneck. To study this systematically, we introduce VHOP, a flexible data generation framework and benchmark with five core difficulty levels testing both visual matching and search planning. Using this framework, we develop VHOP-Router, an end-to-end training pipeline---combining supervised fine-tuning, online imitation learning, and reinforcement learning---that transforms a standard embedding model into an autoregressive multi-step retriever. Operating directly in the visual latent space, VHOP-Router retrieves linked image chains in a single tool call without requiring the agent to formulate intermediate text queries. Experiments show VHOP-Router boosts retrieval performance from under 5\% to 76.3\%. In agentic search, it improves task success rates by 52.7\% and reduces the average token length by 61\% from 1886 to 728, whereas upgrading the agent yields only a 3.7\% gain. Compared to a strong baseline where the agent retrieves the top 50 results per step, VHOP-Router maintains superior performance while reducing in-context images by $23\times$ and cutting the cumulative API payload by $35\times$. The models also generalize robustly to unseen difficulty levels and realistic test sets. Ultimately, VHOP and VHOP-Router provide an efficient and effective solution for visual agentic search that leaves native LLM capabilities entirely intact.

</details>


### [156] [Self-Evolving Algorithm-Design Agents: Escaping In-Context Evolutionary Stagnation via Population-Curated Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38757)
*Chen Lu,Ke Xue,Siyuan Xu,Mingxuan Yuan,Chao Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a sample-efficient way for LLM-based algorithm-design agents to learn from their own generated algorithms, overcoming stagnation in pure in-context evolutionary methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pure in-context evolutionary frameworks for LLM-based algorithm design can stagnate in domains requiring specialized knowledge because they lack parametric adaptation, while standard training for parametric adaptation needs large, high-quality, domain-specific algorithm corpora that are hard to obtain. The authors want a method that lets agents efficiently internalize domain knowledge from limited real data by learning from their own generated algorithms.

Method: They first theoretically analyze why in-context evolutionary search can stagnate and introduce the Improvement Chain proposition, which explains how learning from sequences of self-generated, incrementally better algorithms can locally increase the probability of sampling good neighboring algorithms. Building on this, they propose Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO), which maintains a global population of self-generated candidate algorithms and uses a hybrid policy update scheme: it selectively retains high-quality, diverse algorithms, and then fine-tunes the model parameters so the policy shifts toward these strong samples, effectively internalizing them. The method also performs prompt distillation and knowledge internalization to reduce inference token costs.

Result: On the task of designing learning rate schedules for global placement in EDA, using only 4 training chip cases, PCPO outperforms strong in-context evolutionary baselines like OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve when evaluated on 16 chip cases. With an 8B-parameter base model, PCPO reaches performance competitive with larger closed-source models such as GPT-5.5. Additionally, on four GPU kernel design tasks, PCPO-designed kernels achieve an average 8.27× speedup compared to the PyTorch Eager baseline.

Conclusion: Sample-efficient parametric self-evolution via PCPO allows LLM-based algorithm-design agents to escape in-context evolutionary stagnation, internalize specialized domain knowledge from self-generated algorithms, and achieve strong generalization from very few real training examples. This approach not only matches or surpasses state-of-the-art in-context evolutionary baselines and even some stronger closed-source models in algorithm-design benchmarks, but also reduces inference-time costs by embedding domain knowledge and distilled prompts into the model parameters.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly participating in complex real-world tasks in the form of algorithm-design agents, designing and refining algorithms. Many successful algorithm-design agents adopt pure in-context evolutionary frameworks, but they may quickly plateau in domains that require specialized knowledge. Parametric adaptation offers a way to internalize specialized knowledge, but conventional training requires abundant domain-specific corpora while high-quality algorithms are scarce in complex algorithm-design scenarios. In this paper, we propose sample-efficient parametric self-evolution where agents can explore and learn from self-generated algorithms. First, we characterize in-context evolutionary stagnation and analytically propose the Improvement Chain proposition, showing how learning successive self-generated algorithms can locally increase the likelihood of neighboring algorithms. Motivated by this local-transfer perspective, we further propose Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO) to utilize a global population and a hybrid policy update scheme for retaining and reusing high-quality, diverse self-generated algorithms, shifting the policy towards stronger algorithms. In the task of learning rate schedule design for global placement in electronic design automation, trained only on 4 chip cases, PCPO outperforms the state-of-the-art in-context evolutionary methods (e.g., OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve) on average across 16 chip cases. With an 8B-size base model, PCPO achieves competitive performance compared to frontier closed-source models such as GPT-5.5. PCPO also reduces inference-time token cost by internalizing grounded domain knowledge and prompt distillation. Moreover, PCPO achieves significant speedups on four GPU kernel designs, with an average of 8.27$\times$ speedup against the PyTorch Eager baseline.

</details>


### [157] [PathAnchor: Path-Structured Evidence for Scientific Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38766)
*Qiuhui Chen,Jiafan Lu,Shuaimin Tang,Tao Dai,Suyuan Wang,Chenrui Ji,Zhenglei Zhou,Weimin Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PathAnchor is a scientific QA system that organizes evidence as role- and direction-preserving trajectories rather than unordered snippets, improving recall and citation-faithful answers under fixed tool budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scientific agents can retrieve relevant snippets but often lose the functional order of mechanisms, conflate evidence from different sources, or make claims that are not strictly grounded in the retrieved text. There is a need for a reasoning framework that preserves mechanistic structure and tightens the link between answers and specific supporting evidence, especially for complex, cross-paper questions about flexible sensors and similar systems.

Method: The authors design PathAnchor, a bounded scientific reasoning system using path-structured evidence workspaces. Instead of independent passages or concepts, the underlying corpus is represented as Material-Sensor-Signal-System trajectories that encode roles, directions, and transitions with explicit source links. A controller agent is given three read-only tools: (1) search within paper-specific trajectories, (2) trace paths that cross multiple candidate sources, and (3) open the exact underlying evidence text. The controller must answer questions by citing specific evidence paths and specifying the boundary beyond which no supporting evidence has been opened, operating under a fixed call budget. They evaluate the system on 120 single- and cross-paper questions about flexible sensors, and also compare against an alternative representation that uses unordered concept graphs while controlling for controller, corpus, and tool-call budget.

Result: On 120 flexible-sensor questions, PathAnchor achieves 82.6% accuracy and outperforms six other evaluated systems. In a controlled comparison where the controller, corpus, and six-call budget are held constant, replacing unordered concept graphs with the proposed path-structured records increases source recall from 61.3% to 82.9%, raises the proportion of answers whose claims are fully supported by opened evidence from 69.2% to 90.0%, and reduces the number of tool calls required.

Conclusion: Organizing evidence as path-structured, role- and direction-aware trajectories significantly improves both retrieval quality and citation completeness for scientific agents operating under bounded resources. The results indicate that not just the retrieval tools but the underlying structure of evidence representation strongly influences how faithfully an agent can ground its answers in the literature. PathAnchor demonstrates that explicit path-based workspaces can better preserve mechanistic context and constrain over-claiming compared with unordered concept graphs.

Abstract: Scientific agents can retrieve relevant passages yet still lose functional order, mix evidence across sources, or state conclusions that exceed the retrieved record. We introduce PathAnchor, a bounded scientific reasoning system built on path-structured evidence workspaces. Instead of treating passages or extracted concepts as independent units, the system retrieves source-linked Material-Sensor-Signal-System trajectories that preserve role, direction, and the evidence supporting each transition. A controller uses three read-only tools to search paper-specific trajectories, trace paths across candidate sources, and open exact evidence before producing a claim-cited answer and an explicit evidence boundary. On 120 single- and cross-paper flexible-sensor questions, PathAnchor scores 82.6% and leads six evaluated systems. Under a matched controller, corpus, and six-call budget, replacing unordered concept graphs with path-structured records raises source recall from 61.3% to 82.9%, increases answers whose claims all cite opened evidence from 69.2% to 90.0%, and reduces tool calls. These results show that evidence organization affects retrieval and citation completeness under fixed agent resources.

</details>


### [158] [Action Conditioned Bisimulation For GUI Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38778)
*Hongbo Zhang,Liuyang Song,Quanquan Li,Daqian Yang,Yan Wen,Zhengtao Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes an action-conditioned bisimulation rule for deciding when two web-page states can share memory, improving success on MiniWoB++ over a memoryless baseline and prior merge rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents that interact with web pages need to remember what actions did in which states, but web UIs often contain visually similar elements (tabs, rows, menu items) that behave differently. Existing memory schemes that rely on observation similarity mistakenly merge such states, corrupting the learned memory and degrading performance. The authors aim to design a principled way to decide when two interaction states are equivalent for control, without relying on visual similarity or learning heavy models.

Method: They formalize a merge rule as an action-conditioned bisimulation over an empirical predictive state graph that a frozen agent populates as it acts. The state graph encodes actions, observed outcomes, and transitions grouped under affordance labels. Two states are merged only if, for every action they share, the distributions over outcomes and successor state blocks agree. Observation similarity plays no role, and no additional training is required. This merge rule is plugged into an existing outcome-value memory system, replacing its original rule, enabling a controlled ablation-style comparison against baselines and variants (including a prior successor-representation merge and an unconditioned version of the criterion).

Result: On the MiniWoB++ benchmark, using the new action-conditioned bisimulation merge rule increases success rate relative to a memoryless agent. In contrast, several control conditions—including an agent forced to take identical exploratory detours, a variant using the previous successor-representation-based merge rule, and a version of the criterion without action conditioning—do not yield improvements over the memoryless baseline.

Conclusion: Action-conditioned bisimulation over a predictive state graph provides a more reliable state-merging criterion for memory in web-interaction agents than similarity-based or unconditioned approaches. By ensuring states are merged only when they produce matching action-conditioned outcomes and successor structures, the method avoids conflating visually similar but behaviorally distinct UI states and leads to measurable performance gains on MiniWoB++. The approach is lightweight, requires no training, and cleanly integrates into existing outcome-value memory frameworks.

Abstract: An agent that remembers what it did on a web page must decide when two pages count as the same. Memories built on observation similarity merge pages that look alike but behave differently, and GUIs are full of such pages: two tabs of one widget or two rows of one menu answer the same click differently. We define the merge rule as an action-conditioned bisimulation over the empirical predictive state graph a frozen agent fills as it acts. Two states merge only when their shared actions lead to agreeing outcomes and successor blocks under an affordance label. Observation similarity never enters the rule, and nothing is trained. It replaces the merge rule of an existing outcome-value memory, so a closed-loop comparison isolates it. On MiniWoB++ it raises success rate over a memoryless agent, while a control taking identical exploratory detours, the prior successor-representation merge, and the same criterion without action conditioning change nothing.

</details>


### [159] [Persona and Persuasive Framing in AI Voice Agents: A $2\times2$ Field Experiment with Children](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38782)
*Thilo Tamme,David Steck,Anton Hantel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Field experiment with a Santa hotline tests how conversational agent persona (authority) and message framing influence children’s prosocial wishes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is growing real-world use of conversational agents with children, but most knowledge about how such agents persuade children comes from artificial lab settings. The authors aim to provide causal field evidence on how design choices—specifically an agent’s perceived authority and the persuasive wording it uses—affect children’s susceptibility to persuasion in a naturalistic, high-engagement context.

Method: A 2×2 randomized field experiment was embedded in a public German Santa Claus telephone hotline. Children’s calls were randomly assigned to one of four LLM-based voice agents that varied in: (1) persona: Santa (high authority) versus Helper (low authority); and (2) framing: persuasive nudges encouraging prosocial wishes versus neutral framing. From 1,072 logged calls, 89 conversations with sufficient interaction (median child age 6) met inclusion criteria. Outcomes included whether the child made a prosocial wish, and measures of engagement such as early hang-ups within the first minute. Statistical analyses estimated treatment effects with and without covariate controls.

Result: Persuasive framing markedly increased the likelihood that a child articulated a prosocial wish, from 11.6% in the neutral condition to 45.7% in the persuasive condition, and this effect remained robust when controlling for additional variables. In contrast, the persona manipulation—Santa versus Helper—had a near-zero effect on prosocial wishes; the ‘Santa’ authority did not outperform the ‘Helper’ on compliance outcomes. Persona did affect engagement behavior: children were substantially more likely to hang up early on the Helper (about 65% within the first minute) than on Santa (about 39%).

Conclusion: In a real-world, highly legitimate context such as a Santa hotline, the way a conversational agent speaks (its framing and nudging style) has a much stronger impact on children’s prosocial compliance than the nominal authority status implied by its persona. Persona mainly influenced whether children stayed on the line rather than what they wished for. The findings highlight the persuasive power of seemingly subtle linguistic nudges on young children and suggest that design and regulation of child-facing conversational agents should prioritize how messages are framed at least as much as who the agent purports to be.

Abstract: Conversational agents increasingly interact with children, yet evidence on how their design shapes children's susceptibility to persuasion comes almost entirely from the lab. We report a $2\times2$ randomized field experiment embedded in a public German Santa Claus telephone hotline. Children's calls were randomly routed to one of four LLM voice agents varying persona (Santa, high authority, vs. Helper, low authority) and framing (persuasive nudges toward prosocial wishes vs. neutral). Of 1,072 logged calls, 89 conversations (median age 6) met inclusion criteria. Persuasive framing raised the probability of a prosocial wish from 11.6% to 45.7%, robust to controls. Persona authority showed a near-zero effect: Santa did not outperform the Helper. Persona instead shaped engagement; children hung up on the Helper far more often within the first minute (65% vs. 39%). Where context already lends an agent legitimacy, how it speaks shapes children's compliance more than who it claims to be.

</details>


### [160] [Positive Ratings, Hidden Concerns: Employee Voice Disclosure in AI-Mediated Organizational Listening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38788)
*Thilo Tamme,Michael Saatkamp,Alma Bonte,Daniel Weiss,Anton Hantel,Andrej Levin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Field study of how employees disclose concerns via conversational AI versus survey in a consulting firm, showing that even when ratings are positive, employees still voice guarded concerns, leading to a model of ‘bounded disclosure.’


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how new conversational AI listening channels, paired with traditional surveys, change what employees choose to say when speaking up about work issues carries hierarchical or career risk.

Method: Field study in a global management consulting firm using a process that pairs a pre-survey with an adaptive AI voice interview about the same themes; quantitative comparison of survey favorability ratings with later voiced concerns across 44 first-session interviews and 132 matched theme observations; qualitative Gioia analysis of 158 ‘protective’ quotes from 65 sessions to inductively build a model.

Result: 20–41% of sessions showed a favorable survey rating on a theme followed by a substantive voiced concern about that same theme in the interview (depending on the favorability cut-off). Qualitative analysis shows that employees rarely expressed concerns directly; instead, they softened criticism, shifted or diffused accountability, and constrained the scope of what they revealed, and this protective behavior varied with how legitimate and safe they perceived the listening structure to be.

Conclusion: Employee voice via AI interviews and surveys is characterized by ‘bounded disclosure’: people speak up but in constrained, self-protective ways, so apparent positivity in ratings can mask underlying concerns. The authors propose a grounded model and four propositions for future research on voice, communication channels, and organizational listening, arguing that silence can exist within expressed feedback.

Abstract: Organizations started listening to employees through conversational AI agents alongside structured surveys. Little is known about what these channels change in what employees say when disclosure carries hierarchical risk. We report a field study inside a global management consulting firm whose process pairs a pre-survey with an adaptive AI voice interview on the same themes within one session. Across 44 first-session interviews (132 matched theme observations), 20-41% of sessions showed a favorable rating co-occurring with a substantive concern voiced later, depending on the favorability threshold. The Gioia analysis drew on 158 protective quotes from 65 eligible sessions. Disclosure rarely arrived unguarded: employees softened concerns, deflected accountability, and bounded how far they went, and this protective work tracked the perceived legitimacy of the listening structure. We develop a grounded model of bounded disclosure and derive four propositions for voice, channel and listening research. Silence, we argue, can persist inside expression.

</details>


### [161] [GraphCert: Bootstrap Agentic Graph Reasoning with Certified Evidence Rubrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38798)
*Weiqi Jiang,Yuchen Ying,Rui Wang,Kaixuan Chen,Bingde Hu,Shunyu Liu,Yu Wang,Tongya Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GraphCert is a self-certifying post-training framework that bootstraps graph-reasoning agents without external data or proprietary LLMs, using executable evidence rubrics to supervise compact LLM graph agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph agents need high-quality question-answer pairs and reasoning trajectories over knowledge graphs, which are expensive to manually create and risky to outsource to proprietary LLMs due to data sensitivity. There is a need for a scalable, privacy-preserving way to train strong graph-reasoning agents that generalize across domains.

Method: They introduce GraphCert, a post-training pipeline for graph agents. A Bootstrapped Graph Quizzer module, controlled by generation constraints, automatically generates graph-grounded QA pairs and highlights supporting evidence from the knowledge graph. These proposed evidences are then validated via execution certification (checking they actually correspond to the graph) and semantic curation. Validated evidences are transformed into standardized certified evidence rubrics. During GRPO (a policy optimization method) training of the Graph Solver agent, the model is rewarded both for correct answers and for aligning its cited evidence with the certified rubrics, encouraging faithful graph-grounded reasoning.

Result: On five graph reasoning domains from GRBENCH, GraphCert-trained agents outperform substantially larger LLM agents and alternative post-training methods, indicating strong effectiveness despite being more compact. The policy learned via GraphCert also shows robust transfer to new, heterogeneous graph domains, suggesting it captures generalizable graph-reasoning skills rather than overfitting to specific datasets.

Conclusion: Executable self-certification of evidence is a practical and powerful way to self-train compact graph-reasoning agents. By automatically generating, validating, and encoding evidence rubrics, GraphCert avoids reliance on costly human annotation and external proprietary LLMs while achieving state-of-the-art or superior performance and cross-domain generalization in graph reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Graph agents extend large language models (LLMs) with the ability to actively explore and reason over knowledge graphs through multi-step interactions with graph tools. However, training capable graph agents typically requires large collections of question-answer pairs and reasoning trajectories, whose manual construction is costly and difficult to scale. Moreover, employing proprietary LLMs to generate such supervision further risks exposing sensitive graph data to external services. Therefore, we propose GraphCert to bootstrap agentic graph reasoning with certified evidence rubrics during post-training. Specifically, the Bootstrapped Graph Quizzer guided by generation controls produces graph-grounded QA pairs and marks supporting evidence, which undergo execution certification and semantic curation. The accepted evidence is then canonicalized into certified evidence rubrics that later reward Graph Solver evidence alignment alongside answer correctness during GRPO training. Experiments on five graph reasoning domains in GRBENCH demonstrate that GraphCert consistently outperforms substantially larger LLM agents and post-training method. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the learned policy transfers robustly across heterogeneous graph domains, suggesting that GraphCert acquires reusable graph-reasoning capabilities rather than domain-specific patterns. These results establish executable self-certification as an effective approach to self-training compact graph reasoning agents. Our code will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [162] [When Reasoning Goes Astray: Attention Dynamics of Uncontrolled Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38817)
*Yuanhe Zhang,Ziwei Wang,Jie Ren,Haoran Gao,Zhenhong Zhou,Fanyu Meng,Cong Wu,Li Sun,Sen Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RADAR, a method to detect and mitigate uncontrolled, looping reasoning in large reasoning models by analyzing and realigning their attention patterns over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large reasoning models can exhibit uncontrolled reasoning: excessively long, looping, or redundant generations that waste compute and degrade service quality. Existing safeguards are crude—they truncate long outputs or stop when obvious repetition appears—so they cannot distinguish productive extended reasoning from harmful looping, nor explain how normal reasoning transitions into failure states. The authors aim to provide a mechanistic, temporally grounded understanding and a more precise control mechanism.

Method: The authors model LRM generation as a process with four distinct reasoning states and track the model’s internal attention distributions over time. They propose RADAR (Reasoning-state Analysis via Dynamic Attention Responses), which analyzes attention patterns during inference to identify the current reasoning state in real time and detect shifts toward uncontrolled reasoning. Using RADAR’s characterization of normal vs. abnormal attention, they then apply an Attention Realignment procedure that nudges abnormal attention distributions back toward those observed in normal requests, and evaluate its effect on excessive reflection and generation loops.

Result: Temporal analysis reveals that uncontrolled reasoning is associated with attention distributions that increasingly diverge from those seen in normal generations, and these abnormal trends are detectable before overt repetition appears. Applying Attention Realignment based on RADAR’s signals consistently reduces looping and excessive reflection, while largely maintaining performance on benign reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: The paper shows that uncontrolled reasoning in LRMs can be understood and managed via internal attention dynamics. RADAR offers a mechanistic account of how normal reasoning degrades into looping states, enables early detection of impending failures, and supports targeted runtime interventions through attention realignment that curb uncontrolled reasoning with minimal impact on useful reasoning behavior.

Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve performance on complex tasks through extended reasoning, yet the same process can degenerate into redundant verification and persistent generation loops. Such uncontrolled reasoning increases inference cost and creates risks of resource exhaustion and service degradation. However, existing mitigations largely truncate long outputs or react to surface repetition, and thus fail to distinguish normal thinking from uncontrolled reasoning or explain how benign reasoning degenerates into harmful behavior. In this paper, we operationalize LRM generation as four states and further introduce Reasoning-state Analysis via Dynamic Attention Responses (RADAR), which identifies the current reasoning state in real time and characterizes how effective reflection can develop into uncontrolled generation. Guided by RADAR's analysis, we further realign abnormal attention distributions toward patterns observed in normal requests and examine how this correction affects excessive reflection and persistent looping. Temporal analyses show that uncontrolled reasoning is characterized by attention distributions that deviate from normal generation, with abnormal trends becoming detectable before repetition begins. Correcting these deviations through Attention Realignment consistently reduces looping while largely preserving benign performance. Together, RADAR provide a mechanistic account of how reasoning becomes uncontrolled, offering actionable guidance for identifying critical failure stages and designing targeted runtime interventions.

</details>


### [163] [Whose Voice Survives the Summary? A Voice-Retention Audit of LLM Employee Listening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38818)
*Thilo Tamme,Anton Hantel,Bijan Khosrawi-Rad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how using LLM-generated summaries to route employee feedback to leaders can distort which voices are heard, and proposes a metric (Voice Retention / Representation Ratio) to quantify whose feedback is preserved or lost in summarization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As organizations start using LLMs to summarize large volumes of employee feedback for leaders, there is a risk that the summarization layer introduces hidden, unmeasured biases that suppress certain types of feedback or certain groups’ voices, undermining fairness and accurate decision-making. The authors want a concrete way to measure this effect in real organizational data.

Method: The authors define a Voice Retention / Representation Ratio metric to quantify how well different types of comments and themes are preserved from raw employee feedback into summaries. They apply this metric to a bilingual English/German dataset of 2,586 free-text employee responses from a global professional services firm, examining what gets retained or dropped across 45 leader-facing summaries, including effects of sentiment (praise vs criticism), frequency (how often a concern is raised), length, and language. They also test a targeted prompting strategy to see if they can recover missing themes.

Result: They find that employees are much more likely to withhold praise than criticism (withholding praise is 82 times more common). In the summarization pipeline, the main filter is popularity rather than sentiment: critical feedback is generally retained, but concerns mentioned only once are dropped 86% of the time. Short comments and German-only feedback are disproportionately lost, with theme retention rates around 0.14 compared to 0.74 for more prevalent themes; the language effect is described as directional rather than definitive. After controlling for frequency, sentiment does not independently affect retention, showing that underrepresentation stems primarily from low prevalence, which sentiment-only bias audits fail to detect. Targeted prompting recovers only themes that are explicitly named, failing to fix broader representational gaps.

Conclusion: LLM-based summarization of employee feedback can substantially distort which themes and voices reach leadership, primarily by underrepresenting less frequently mentioned, shorter, and minority-language concerns rather than overtly filtering by sentiment. The proposed Voice Retention / Representation Ratio and the accompanying voice-retention card provide practical tools for auditing and making these representational biases visible, highlighting that sentiment-focused evaluations are insufficient and that organizations need more nuanced, disaggregated monitoring of feedback pipelines.

Abstract: Organizations increasingly route employee feedback to leaders through large language model (LLM) summaries, an unaudited layer that silences already-spoken voice. We introduce a Voice Retention / Representation Ratio metric for representational bias in summarization and apply it to a bilingual (English/German) corpus of 2,586 free-text responses from a global professional service company. First, employees supply criticism more reliably than praise (withholding praise is 82 times more common). Second, across 45 leader-summaries the pipeline filters by popularity, not sentiment: criticism survives, yet a concern voiced once is dropped 86% of the time, with short and German-only content lost on the same axis (theme retention 0.14 vs 0.74; German directional). Controlling for frequency, sentiment has no independent effect; the harm is prevalence-driven, which sentiment-only audits miss. A targeted prompt recovers only named themes. We contribute the metric, field evidence, and a disaggregated voice-retention card.

</details>


### [164] [More Choices, Fewer Decisions: Ordinal-Scale Bias in JEV-like Direct-Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38827)
*Tianxiang Gao,Jinzhe Li,Zhiyuan Li,Yi Chang,Yuan Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and studies an ordinal scale-utilization bias in direct-decision language models, where models underuse the full range of ordinal labels even when accurate, and shows this bias is learned and can be mitigated via targeted post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct-decision models are popular for low-latency classification and evaluation, but reliability requires not just accuracy; models must faithfully use the full ordinal scale provided by users (e.g., rating scales). Empirically, these models often compress their decisions into a narrow band of labels, undermining fine-grained evaluation and ranking. The paper aims to diagnose, quantify, and understand this underutilization of ordinal scales, which has been largely overlooked compared to accuracy.

Method: The authors analyze JEV 1.13 and three open KEV models across multiple datasets. They start with ANLI to inspect label distributions and error patterns, then extend to 36 ordinal datasets and 4 nominal tasks to compare scale utilization. They measure how much of the effective gold label support is used in the model’s final decisions and test robustness by randomizing candidate order. They perform controlled experiments where they fix items and source scores while balancing gold support and positions, and systematically refine scales from K=2 to K=14 to observe utilization changes. They also examine model output probabilities to separate decision-stage compression from probability spread. Finally, they apply targeted BA-LoRA post-training to the KEV models on eight supervised ordinal scales to see if utilization can be improved without fundamentally changing the architecture.

Result: On ANLI, JEV heavily overuses the Neutral label, assigning it 38.8% of all predictions and 51.3% of errors, despite high accuracy and balanced ground-truth labels and candidate positions. Across 36 ordinal datasets, models use only about 67–76% of the effective gold label support, whereas on 4 nominal tasks they use 87–102%, indicating that underutilization is specific to ordinal settings. Randomizing candidate order reduces but does not eliminate this compression. When scales are refined from K=2 to K=14 under controlled conditions, label utilization decreases for every model and drops to 26–75% at K=14, even though predicted probability distributions across candidates remain broad. BA-LoRA post-training substantially boosts gold-relative utilization from around 47% to 86% on eight supervised ordinal scales for both sizes of KEV models.

Conclusion: The authors identify a systematic ordinal scale-utilization bias in direct-decision language models: a tendency to compress decisions into a subset of available ordinal labels, distinct from accuracy, label imbalance, position effects, or candidate count. This bias becomes more pronounced as the number of ordinal categories increases, and it persists even when probability distributions over labels are broad, indicating that the issue arises at the decision stage. Crucially, targeted post-training with BA-LoRA significantly mitigates the bias, demonstrating that it is learned and adjustable rather than an inherent limitation of the model architecture. The work underscores that reliable use of ordinal scales should be evaluated and trained for explicitly, not inferred from accuracy alone.

Abstract: Direct-decision models turn text into low-latency structured labels and scores, making them attractive for classification and automatic evaluation. Yet reliability requires more than accuracy: a model must also use the ordinal decision scale supplied by the user faithfully. We analyze JEV~1.13 and three open KEV models. Our investigation begins with ANLI, where JEV assigns 38.8\% of all predictions and 51.3\% of errors to Neutral despite 74.95\% accuracy, nearly balanced gold labels, and balanced candidate positions. Across 36 ordinal datasets, final decisions use only 67--76\% of the effective gold support, versus 87--102\% on four nominal tasks. Randomizing candidate order weakens but does not remove this compression. Holding items and source scores fixed while balancing gold support and positions, we refine scales from $K=2$ to $14$; utilization falls for every model and reaches 26--75\% at $K=14$, although candidate probabilities remain broad for most models. Targeted BA-LoRA post-training raises gold-relative utilization from roughly 47\% to 86\% on eight supervised scales at both KEV sizes, showing that the compression is learned and modifiable rather than an immutable architectural limit. We call this ordinal scale-utilization bias: decision-stage candidate-space compression distinct from accuracy, gold imbalance, fixed position, and candidate count alone. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Glax147/jev_ordinal_scale_bia

</details>


### [165] [Diversity Combining for Multi-Path LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38829)
*Guangsheng Yu,Litianyi Zhang,Qin Wang,Xu Wang,Mingyuan Li,Shaoxiong Ji,Ren Ping Liu,Massimo Piccardi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes why multi-path reasoning methods like self-consistency (SC) saturate as the number of sampled reasoning paths K grows, and introduces a principled way to set K adaptively using ideas from diversity combining in wireless communications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-path reasoning with large language models (LLMs), such as self-consistency, improves accuracy by sampling multiple reasoning paths and taking a majority vote. However, performance gains quickly saturate as the number of paths K increases, leading to wasted computation. Existing work lacks a theoretical understanding of this saturation and offers no principled way to predict or select an effective K. This paper aims to explain the saturation behavior, connect it to known theory, and design a method to choose K that retains most of the accuracy benefits while reducing unnecessary samples.

Method: The authors model each sampled reasoning path as a noisy observation in a diversity combining framework from wireless communications. They use pairwise correlation of path correctness to characterize how redundancy among paths limits the effective sample size (design effect) of majority voting. Using generalized least squares (GLS) under an exchangeability assumption, they analyze optimal linear combinations of latent embeddings produced by different paths and show that uniform weighting is optimal in symmetric settings. They also empirically explore prompt-template diversity to decorrelate paths, and derive an Adaptive-K rule that uses statistics from an initial small number of paths (a four-path pilot) to determine an appropriate total number of paths K* for each setting.

Result: Theoretical analysis shows that correlation among reasoning paths imposes a finite ceiling on the effective benefit of adding more paths, explaining the observed saturation in self-consistency. Under exchangeability, GLS reveals that majority vote is the optimal symmetric linear combiner in standard setups. Empirically, across 5 LLMs and 12 benchmarks, introducing diversity through different prompt templates consistently reduces path correlation in 55 out of 57 evaluated cells, with notable improvements for open-ended QA tasks. The proposed Adaptive-K rule, based on a four-path pilot, is shown to choose K* such that it achieves 96–103% of the accuracy of majority voting with K=32 on Math, QA, and NLU benchmarks, while using fewer paths on average.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the performance saturation of multi-path LLM reasoning is fundamentally driven by correlation among reasoning paths, which limits the effective sample size gained by increasing K. Majority vote is theoretically justified as the optimal symmetric combiner under exchangeability, but meaningful gains can be realized by reducing path correlation through prompt-template diversity or by uneven weighting/pruning when branches differ. The Adaptive-K rule offers a practical, computation-efficient way to select K that nearly matches the accuracy of a large fixed K, making multi-path reasoning more scalable and principled.

Abstract: Multi-path reasoning methods such as self-consistency (SC) sample $K$ reasoning paths and choose the most frequent answer. However, their gains quickly plateau as $K$ increases, and existing methods do not predict when this saturation will occur. We formalize multi-path LLM reasoning as a diversity combining problem from wireless communications: each path is a noisy channel observation, and the pairwise correlation of path correctness caps the design-effect effective sample size of the vote at a finite ceiling. Generalized least squares (GLS) analysis shows that, under exchangeability, the optimal symmetric linear combiner of latent embeddings is uniform, supporting majority vote as the natural default in standard SC while leaving room for weighting or pruning under heterogeneous prompt-template branches. Across 5 models and 12 benchmarks, prompt-template diversity reduces path correlation in $55$ of $57$ valid cells, with the strongest effect on open-ended QA. We derive an Adaptive-K rule that uses a four-path pilot to select $K^*$, retaining $96$--$103\%$ of MV@$K{=}32$ accuracy across Math, QA, and NLU.

</details>


### [166] [OpenJev-RLCD: A Working RLCD Implementation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38850)
*Zhimin Gao,Pichao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RLCD, a reinforcement learning method that trains reasoning models to produce well-calibrated probabilistic answers instead of being overconfident, and shows it outperforms common baselines in both accuracy and selective prediction on reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing decision/reasoning models output probabilities that are only useful if they are well calibrated. Open-source reproductions typically use supervised fine-tuning with temperature scaling, while RL from verifiable rewards (RLVR) tends to make models overconfident and harms calibration. There is a need for a reinforcement learning framework that directly optimizes calibration of the answer distribution produced after reasoning, rather than only optimizing accuracy or reward, and for understanding why current RL approaches degrade calibration.

Method: The authors propose Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). The model first samples a rationale (chain-of-thought), then commits to an answer distribution that is scored using a strictly proper scoring rule, ensuring incentives for honest probabilities. They analyze a variance identity showing that if one scores the mixture distribution produced by several rationales, the objective implicitly rewards disagreement among rationales; RLVR corresponds to this mixture objective without the diversity term. They highlight optimization difficulties with a naive per-rationale objective (either disabling reasoning or being overwhelmed by policy-gradient noise) and introduce a two-stage training recipe: first calibrate the model, then apply reinforcement learning under the RLCD objective. They implement this using Qwen3-1.7B on reasoning tasks, and compare against several baselines (SFT, RFT/STaR, GRPO) with temperature scaling.

Result: On two reasoning tasks using Qwen3-1.7B (three random seeds, paired tests), RLCD matches or exceeds the accuracy of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), RFT/STaR, and GRPO, all with temperature scaling applied. RLCD also provides better selective prediction performance than all baselines, meaning it more reliably knows when to abstain or indicate uncertainty. On GSM8K answer verification, RLCD can confidently decide a given percentage of items (\gvTwoCovFive\%) at an error rate of at most 5%, while GRPO only reaches \gvGrpoCovFive\% coverage at the same error level, showing stronger calibration and decision quality. They further prove that in scenarios where uncertainty comes solely from annotator disagreement, RLCD cannot outperform standard cross-entropy training, indicating a theoretical limit of the method.

Conclusion: RLCD provides a practical reinforcement learning framework for training reasoning models to produce calibrated probabilistic decisions by scoring post-rationale answer distributions with proper scoring rules. The method clarifies the relationship between RLVR-style mixture objectives and a diversity-promoting term, and introduces a two-stage ‘calibrate, then reinforce’ recipe to address optimization issues. Empirically, RLCD achieves competitive or better accuracy than strong baselines and superior selective prediction on reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K answer verification. However, its theoretical analysis shows that when label uncertainty is purely due to annotator disagreement, RLCD offers no advantage over conventional cross-entropy training, outlining its domain of applicability.

Abstract: Decision models such as Jev answer questions with probabilities, which are only useful if they are calibrated. Open-source reproductions rely on supervised fine-tuning plus temperature scaling, while reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) makes reasoning models overconfident. We present a working implementation of reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD) for reasoning models: the model samples a rationale, and we score the answer distribution it commits to afterwards with a strictly proper scoring rule. A variance identity shows that scoring the mixture of several samples rewards disagreeing rationales, and that RLVR is exactly this mixture objective without its diversity term. Optimized naively, the per-rationale objective either switches reasoning off or is drowned out by policy-gradient noise, which leads to a two-stage recipe: calibrate, then reinforce. With Qwen3-1.7B on two reasoning tasks (3 seeds, paired tests), RLCD matches or beats SFT, RFT/STaR and GRPO (each temperature-scaled) in accuracy and beats all of them in selective prediction; on GSM8K answer verification a single query decides \gvTwoCovFive\% of the items at $\le$5\% error, versus \gvGrpoCovFive\% for GRPO. When uncertainty comes from annotator disagreement, RLCD provably cannot beat cross-entropy. Code and results: https://github.com/ZimmyGao/openjev-rlcd.

</details>


### [167] [When Context Changes: Understanding Update Failures in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38866)
*Junyu Guo,Yuchen Fang,Shangding Gu,Costas Spanos,James Demmel,Javad Lavaei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language model (LLM) agents sometimes use outdated information from context (stale binding) and introduces a benchmark and analysis to understand and mitigate this issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents operate over long interactions where facts, goals, or preferences change. Even when updated information is present in context, models may still respond using old values for the same variable. This undermines reliability for applications like agents, planning, or tools that rely on correct, up-to-date state tracking. The authors want to characterize when this occurs, why it happens mechanistically inside transformers, and how to fix it without retraining models.

Method: 1) Propose Controlled In-Context Memory (CICM), a benchmark where variables (e.g., preferences, states) are updated over time in conversations and logs, and the model must answer using the latest value. 2) Empirically evaluate frontier and open-source models on CICM to quantify stale binding errors. 3) Use probing techniques to show that even when models output an old value, the updated value is still linearly recoverable from internal representations, implying a selection rather than memory failure. 4) Perform component-level analysis (especially on Qwen and Pythia) to isolate how attention layers behave when producing answers, identifying a pattern they call attention drift, where attention masses shift toward earlier (obsolete) mentions of a variable. 5) Study a simplified one-layer transformer analytically to derive how, when attention scores to different mentions are similar, multiple old mentions can cumulatively attract more attention than the single current mention. 6) Design and apply a test-time attention redirection intervention that increases attention to the latest value token(s) for each input query, without further model training, and evaluate its effect across model families.

Result: 1) Even strong reasoning models frequently commit stale binding errors on CICM, failing to use the most recent state. 2) Probes show the updated value is often still encoded internally when an incorrect old value is produced, indicating a failure in information selection rather than storage. 3) Component tests on Qwen and Pythia reveal attention drift: attention heads disproportionately focus on old values instead of the current one when generating answers. 4) Theoretical analysis of a one-layer transformer demonstrates that near-tied attention scores allow multiple old entries to dominate the attention distribution over a single current entry. 5) An attention redirection intervention, tuned per input, significantly reduces old-value errors when the current value is explicitly requested, while keeping most initially correct answers intact and working across several model types.
