Conclusion: The dominant failure mode behind stale binding in LLMs is not forgetting updated information but mis-selecting among competing in-context values due to attention drift. When many similar-scored old mentions of a variable exist, their combined attention can overpower the single up-to-date mention, leading the model to answer with outdated information. By understanding this mechanism, simple test-time interventions that reweight attention toward the most recent value can substantially alleviate stale binding across models without retraining. Hence, reliable context management in LLM agents requires mechanisms that not only store and update information but also consistently prioritize and use the most current state when generating answers.

Abstract: As preferences, goals, and facts change, LLM agents must use the current state while earlier versions remain in context. Yet they can answer with an old value of the same variable, a failure that we call stale binding. To study when models use outdated information and why, we introduce Controlled In-Context Memory (CICM), a benchmark for tracking and using updated information in conversations and agent logs. We observe that even frontier reasoning models can fail to recover the current state. We find that in open-source models probes can still recover the updated value when the model answers with an old one, pointing to a failure to select information that remains available. Component tests in Qwen and Pythia identify a mechanism for this selection failure: attention drift, where attention favors old values over the current one when producing an answer. We study a one-layer transformer to mathematically understand how this phenomenon happens: when attention scores are similar, several old values can together receive more attention than the current value. Guided by this explanation, we redirect attention toward the current value without further training. When the current value is requested directly, adjusting this intervention for each input corrects most old-value errors across various model families while preserving nearly all initially correct answers. Reliable context management therefore requires more than remembering updated information: models must use it to guide their answers.

</details>


### [168] [Talk2Agent: Benchmarking Voice Interfaces for Text Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38867)
*Terumi Chiba,Guangzhi Sun,Zheqi Yuan,Chao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Talk2Agent is a benchmark and evaluation framework to test how well different speech-to-agent pipelines preserve task-relevant information for LLM-based computer-use agents, using execution-free, task-conditioned grading that correlates better with real task success than standard ASR metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM computer-use agents rely on clean text instructions, even though many users will interact via speech. Speech introduces transcription errors that can distort key task elements, yet standard ASR metrics like WER/CER do not capture whether the information necessary for successful task execution is preserved. There is a need for a benchmark and metric that directly measure how well voice interfaces transmit task-critical intent to LLM agents.

Method: The authors construct Talk2Agent by creating human-spoken versions of existing computer-use tasks from WildClawBench and OSWorld. They test multiple types of voice interfaces, including standalone ASR systems, audio-capable LLMs, contextual biasing strategies, and LLM-based ontology repair mechanisms. To avoid the cost and stochasticity of repeatedly executing long-horizon computer-use tasks, they design an execution-free, task-conditioned evaluation: they project the original task grader into a form that can be applied directly to the transcribed instructions, estimating how much task-relevant information remains after the speech interface without running the full task.

Result: On WildClawBench, their execution-free native projection acts as a practical, execution-grounded proxy for voice-interface quality. It shows higher correlation with actual downstream task completion than traditional ASR metrics, improving Pearson correlation by 0.246 over WER/CER when evaluated on 32 hours of real human speech. This demonstrates that their framework better reflects an interface’s ability to support successful agent behavior than standard transcription-focused metrics.

Conclusion: Talk2Agent provides a more appropriate benchmark and evaluation methodology for speech-based interaction with LLM computer-use agents than conventional ASR metrics. By focusing on task-conditioned, execution-grounded intent preservation rather than raw transcription accuracy, it more accurately predicts downstream task success and enables rigorous comparison and improvement of voice interfaces for agentic systems.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) computer-use agents are typically evaluated with clean written instructions, despite speech being an increasingly popular interface for interacting with such systems. Speech input introduces an additional failure point: transcription errors can alter task-critical entities, constraints, or targets before the agent begins reasoning, while conventional ASR metrics do not directly measure whether the information required for successful execution has been preserved. We introduce Talk2Agent, a benchmark for evaluating how effectively voice interfaces convey human-spoken instructions to LLM-based computer-use agents. Talk2Agent builds human-spoken versions of tasks from WildClawBench and OSWorld and evaluates a range of voice interfaces, including dedicated ASR models, audio-capable LLMs, contextual biasing, and LLM-based ontology repair. Because repeatedly executing long-horizon computer-use tasks is costly and stochastic, we further propose an execution-free, task-conditioned evaluation framework that projects the original task grader onto prompt-addressable intentions and measures how much task-relevant information is retained after the voice interface. On WildClawBench, Talk2Agent's execution-free native projection provides a practical, execution-grounded measure of voice-interface quality, correlating with downstream task completion and improving Pearson correlation by 0.246 over WER/CER on 32 hours of real human speech.

</details>


### [169] [Reasoning Externalization for Faithful Large Language Model Narratives of Stock Return Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38869)
*Sujung Kim,Seung Hwan Cho,Sangjin Park,Young-Min Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an LLM-based narrative framework that explains stock return prediction models by grounding explanations in temporal SHAP patterns and historical market regimes, and shows that explicitly externalizing numerical and relational reasoning greatly improves the factual faithfulness of generated explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Numerical outputs from explainable AI methods (like SHAP values) in finance are hard for non-expert stakeholders to interpret, and naive use of LLMs to turn them into natural language can introduce incorrect statements about magnitudes, trends, and feature relationships. There is a need for a systematic way to generate natural-language explanations that are both understandable to humans and tightly grounded in the underlying model evidence, especially for high-stakes tasks like stock return prediction.

Method: The authors build a narrative framework around an XGBoost model for cross-sectional stock return prediction. They compute temporal SHAP evidence by tracking normalized global SHAP importances for features over a six‑month window. They then identify historical regime analogs: past periods where the temporal evolution of SHAP importances is similar, and they retrieve associated model performance metrics and subsequent market returns for context. They run a controlled study on LLMs (Qwen3 variants), progressively externalizing the reasoning: first providing only raw SHAP sequences, then adding deterministic temporal descriptors, and then explicit feature relations. For each narrative, individual claims are automatically checked against the provenance-linked SHAP and historical data to measure evidence faithfulness, temporal accuracy, and relational accuracy. They also compare setups with and without the historical analogs and evaluate human-perceived usefulness.

Result: Progressive externalization of numerical and relational reasoning significantly improves the alignment of LLM-generated explanations with the underlying quantitative evidence. For example, for Qwen3-32B-Instruct, evidence faithfulness improves from 0.696 with minimal externalization to 0.996 when numerical and relational reasoning are fully externalized and verified. Temporal and relational accuracy of statements also rise. Although including historical regime analogs does not substantially improve automatic faithfulness metrics, explanations that use analogs receive higher usefulness scores from human evaluators, indicating that such context makes narratives more interpretable and practically helpful.

Conclusion: Making an LLM explicitly expose and ground its numerical and relational reasoning steps in verifiable SHAP-based evidence leads to near-perfect faithfulness of the resulting textual explanations in a financial prediction setting. Historical regime analogs, even if they do not change automatic faithfulness scores, enhance human-perceived utility by giving users intuitive, contextual comparisons. The framework suggests a promising path for building trustworthy, comprehensible model narratives in finance by combining temporal explainability, historical context, and strict verification of LLM claims against provenance-linked data.

Abstract: In finance, interpreting machine learning predictions is essential, yet the numerical outputs of explainable AI can be difficult for non-experts to understand. While large language models (LLMs) can translate these outputs into natural language, they may produce errors when inferring numerical changes and feature relations. We propose an LLM narrative framework for cross-sectional stock return prediction that combines temporal Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) evidence with historical regime analogs. Temporal evidence tracks changes in the normalized global SHAP importance of an XGBoost model over six months. Historical analogs are past periods with similar changes in SHAP importance, their model performance and subsequent market returns are provided as comparative context. Using this framework, we conduct a controlled study of progressive reasoning externalization, sequentially providing raw SHAP sequences, deterministic temporal descriptors, and feature relations. Each generated claim is verified against provenance-linked evidence. Across Qwen3, externalizing numerical and relational reasoning improved evidence faithfulness as well as temporal and relational accuracy. Evidence faithfulness increased from 0.696 to 0.996 for Qwen3-32B-Instruct. While historical analogs did not improve structured automatic faithfulness, they received higher human-rated usefulness scores. These results suggest that externalizing verifiable reasoning enhances narrative faithfulness and that historical context adds interpretive value.

</details>


### [170] [STRATA: Self-Learning Through Role-Aligned Tiered Agents for Real-Time Strategy Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38881)
*Xinhe Tian,Xiaoyue Zhang,Ziyou Zhang,Jiacheng Li,Xiaoqiang Jin,Qianchuan Zhao,Gaochen Cui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STRATA is a hierarchical, role-based LLM system for RTS game Red Alert that learns strategic experience across games, converting game traces into reusable “experience cards” to improve long-term play and win rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based commanders for RTS games suffer from slow inference that misses fast tactical events, heavy reliance on handcrafted prompts, and weak ability to continuously learn from past games. The authors want a system that can both react in real time and accumulate reusable strategic knowledge over many matches, reducing manual engineering.

Method: They design STRATA, a hierarchical multi-agent LLM framework with four roles: a Strategic Agent (SA) for global high-level strategy; a Logistics Agent (LA) for production and resource/logistics management; a Tactical Agent (TA) for local combat execution; and a Review Agent (RA) for post-game learning. During play, SA reads a textual global game state and previously learned “experience cards” (compressed strategic knowledge) to output high-level directives that LA and TA translate into concrete actions. After each match, RA analyzes traces, proposes candidate new experiences, cross-validates and refines them with evidence from later games, and compresses repeatedly confirmed strategic patterns into concise experience cards that future SA calls can retrieve.

Result: In Red Alert experiments, the system can automatically form experience cards from game logs. Under a fixed scenario, using the learned experience cards raises win rate from 30% to 100%. When trained sequentially against different AI opponents, STRATA acquires distinct long-term strategic experiences tailored to each play style.

Conclusion: A role-aligned hierarchical LLM architecture augmented with cross-game self-learning and experience card retrieval can effectively handle end-to-end RTS matches, significantly improving performance without extensive manual prompting. The approach enables continual accumulation of validated, compact strategic knowledge and adaptation to different opponent styles.

Abstract: Real-time strategy (RTS) games require agents to coordinate economic development, production and construction, base defense, unit organization, and attack timing over long matches. Existing studies have applied large language models to command decision-making in RTS games, enabling agents to read textual game states and generate high-level plans. However, long inference latency can cause them to miss critical tactical events. The complexity and tactical diversity of full RTS matches also leave existing systems heavily dependent on manually written experience-based prompts, with limited ability to learn continuously from past games. We present STRATA, a role-aligned hierarchical system with cross-game self-learning for Red Alert. STRATA assigns in-game strategic, logistical, and tactical decisions to a Strategic Agent (SA), Logistics Agent (LA), and Tactical Agent (TA), respectively. The SA generates high-level directives based on the global game state and relevant experience cards, while the LA and TA handle logistics and tactical execution. After each match, a Review Agent (RA) derives candidate experience from game traces, validates and revises it using evidence from subsequent matches, and compresses strategic experience supported across multiple games into concise experience cards for SA retrieval. We evaluate STRATA through the formation of experience cards, full-match comparisons before and after learning, and experience learning against AI opponents with different play styles. Under a fixed scenario, using the learned experience cards increases the observed win rate from 30% to 100%. Sequential learning against AI opponents with different play styles also produces distinct long-term strategic experience.

</details>


### [171] [Consistent Plan-Act for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38891)
*Heng-Zhuang Li,Yi-Kai Zhang,Yu Wang,Yueqing Sun,Jiayuan Zhang,Qi Gu,Han-Jia Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and fixes a key failure mode in long-horizon planner-actor LLM systems: the planner and actor often disagree about the environment state. By detecting contradictions between their state descriptions and feeding them back for correction and fine-tuning, the proposed ConPAct framework greatly improves coordination and task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon, agentic tasks that require multiple steps and interactions with dynamic environments are challenging for LLM-based agents. A common design separates a high-level planner from a low-level actor, but these two components can fall out of sync about what is true in the environment, hurting performance. There is little systematic analysis of this coordination failure or methods explicitly targeting it. The authors aim to characterize this failure mode—planner-actor state mismatch—and develop a method to reduce it and thereby improve multi-step task success.

Method: The authors instrument planner and actor agents with prompts that elicit structured assertions about the current task state. They programmatically compare these structured reports to detect explicit logical contradictions, defining and measuring planner-actor state mismatch. They then analyze how often and in what ways these mismatches occur across environments. To mitigate mismatch, they introduce Consistent Plan-Act (ConPAct), which (1) surfaces the detected contradictions back to both planner and actor so they can reconcile their state descriptions at inference time, and (2) fine-tunes models on curated trajectories where planner and actor maintain consistent state interpretations, thereby training them to coordinate better.

Result: Empirically, the authors show that planner-actor state mismatches are frequent and systematic across long-horizon tasks. Supplying agents with more explicit task-relevant state representations already reduces mismatch and improves coordination. With ConPAct, which uses mismatch detection for both inference-time feedback and training-time fine-tuning, they observe substantial gains over baselines across multiple environments and model-role pairings. A notable result is an increase in MiniGrid task success from 38.6% to 54.4% when using GPT-5.6-sol/terra models as planner and actor, illustrating that enforcing state consistency directly translates into better task completion.

Conclusion: Planner-actor state mismatch is an important, measurable failure mode in long-horizon LLM agent systems. By explicitly eliciting, comparing, and reconciling state assertions from planner and actor, the ConPAct framework can both correct inconsistencies during inference and train agents toward more consistent internal state representations. This leads to better coordination and significantly improved task performance across environments, highlighting state consistency as a key lever for building more reliable multi-agent LLM systems.

Abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks demand strong reasoning and efficient execution across successive interactions with dynamic environments. A common approach decouples high-level planning from low-level execution through separate planner and actor roles. To investigate coordination failures in these tasks, we prompt both agents for structured state assertions and compare their reports programmatically to detect explicit contradictions. Our analyses reveal systematic disagreement about the same task-relevant state facts, a phenomenon we term planner-actor state mismatch. We further find that providing agents with task-relevant state information reduces mismatch and improves coordination and task performance. Based on the systematic analysis of the state mismatch, we propose Consistent Plan-Act (ConPAct), which feeds detected contradictions back to both agents to form consistent state interpretations and fine-tunes them on curated consistent interactions for better coordination. ConPAct improves performance across various environments and model configurations, e.g., increasing MiniGrid success rate from 38.6% to 54.4% with GPT-5.6-sol/terra as planner and actor respectively, demonstrating that state consistency can guide both inference-time correction and coordination training.

</details>


### [172] [Composing Task-specific Agent Harnesses at Test Time with Reusable Primitives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38912)
*Peng Kuang,Haibo Jin,Dehao Wu,Feiyang Deng,Xiaopeng Yuan,Jerry Wang,Haohan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces STITCH, a framework that builds task-specific agent harnesses for LLM agents by selecting and composing reusable harness primitives instead of using a single fixed harness or generating new harness code per task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed, global agent harnesses (which govern tool use, context gathering, verification, state management, and termination) are suboptimal because different tasks benefit from different harness mechanisms. Generating and debugging custom harness code for every task is costly and risky, especially as the number of mechanisms grows. The authors aim to get the benefits of task-specific harnesses without the overhead and brittleness of per-task code generation.

Method: The authors mine failed LLM agent task trajectories to identify and define Harness Primitives: reusable, modular harness mechanisms with clearly specified application scopes and composition contracts. They then propose STITCH, a system that, at test time, uses task information to select a suitable subset of these primitives and compiles them into a task-specific harness. This process avoids generating new mechanism code or repairing it at test time and instead composes existing, vetted primitives.

Result: In experiments across diverse tasks, STITCH-generated harnesses improve adaptability and robustness compared with fixed harness baselines. The framework increases task success rates by up to 12 percentage points and outperforms human-designed harnesses like Codex CLI. It also achieves these gains with low runtime overhead: only about 2.7% test-time composition cost, which is reported as 638× more efficient than generating task-specific harness code from scratch.

Conclusion: Task-adaptive agent harnesses materially improve performance on heterogeneous tasks compared with fixed harnesses. By organizing harness logic into reusable primitives and composing them per task, STITCH achieves better success rates, robustness, and efficiency without needing on-the-fly harness code generation. The primitive-based approach appears to be a promising direction for building scalable and maintainable agent systems that can generalize across many tasks.

Abstract: Agent harnesses govern how large language models (LLMs) gather context, invoke tools, verify results, preserve state, and terminate, largely affecting agent performance. However, the value of each harness mechanism can differ across heterogeneous tasks: a mechanism that improves one task may impose overhead or context distraction on another, leading to the suboptimality of a global harness. We characterize this suboptimality as a mismatch induced by fixed mechanism choices, motivating task-specific harness construction. Nonetheless, generating harness code for each task introduces generation and debugging costs, with execution risks that can compound as more mechanisms are generated. To address those challenges, we introduce Harness Primitives, reusable harness mechanisms with clear application scope and composition contract mined from failed task trajectories. Based on Harness Primitives, we propose STITCH, a framework that Selects suitable primitives given Task Information and compiles them into Task-speCific Harnesses at test time. This separation enables task-specific harnesses without generating or repairing mechanism code at test time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that STITCH not only improves harness adaptability and robustness, but also scales with the primitive library size, boosting task success rates by up to 12 points over fixed harness baselines, surpassing human-designed harnesses like Codex CLI while maintaining a minimal test-time harness composition overhead of only 2.7%, 638 times more efficient than generating task-specific harnesses from scratch. Ultimately, our work demonstrates that building task-adaptive harnesses can be beneficial for completing diverse tasks and that building reusable primitives can be a promising path towards this goal.

</details>


### [173] [Risk-Aware Adaptive Evaluation: Finding High-Impact Failures Under Limited Budgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38914)
*Priyanath Maji,Spandan Ghose Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a risk-aware, adaptive method to allocate limited evaluation trials across test scenarios for stochastic interactive agents, achieving far better detection of high-impact failures than uniform sampling, especially under tight budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating interactive agents is costly because their behavior is stochastic, failures are rare, and different failures have very different real-world impact. Traditional benchmarks allocate a fixed number of runs per scenario regardless of how risky or important the scenario is, wasting budget on low-impact or never-failing cases while potentially missing rare but high-impact failures. There is a need for an evaluation strategy that focuses limited trials on scenarios where impactful failures are more likely, in a principled and data-driven way.

Method: The authors cast evaluation as a sequential allocation problem over a fixed trial budget and a set of scenarios with unknown failure behavior. They design a risk-aware contextual Thompson Sampling policy that uses (1) a scenario context vector available before running a trial, (2) a fixed impact score that quantifies the severity of failure in each scenario, and (3) observed success/failure outcomes as trials are run. The bandit-like policy adaptively decides which scenario to run next and whether to re-run previously tested scenarios, with the goal of maximizing discovery of impact-weighted failures. They evaluate the method via offline replay on a corpus of 70 τ-bench airline scenarios and 824 recorded trials, comparing against uniform allocation and an oracle upper bound under different trial budgets.

Result: At very small evaluation budgets, the proposed policy substantially outperforms uniform allocation. With only 50 trials (about 6% of the total corpus), the method finds 86% of the impact-weighted failures that an oracle policy could find, while uniform allocation finds only 25%. In absolute terms, with the same number of trials the method discovers 3.5 times more impact-weighted failures (215.4 vs. 62.2). It yields roughly 5 times more impact-weighted failures per dollar spent and reduces the fraction of budget spent on scenarios that never fail from 34% under uniform allocation to 2.8% under their policy. Additional analyses show that the relative advantage declines as the trial budget approaches the full corpus size, and that the benefits of using scenario context versus posterior-based exploration differ by budget regime.

Conclusion: Risk-aware adaptive allocation via contextual Thompson Sampling enables much more efficient evaluation of stochastic interactive agents, especially when evaluation resources are scarce. By prioritizing scenarios with higher potential impact and leveraging both contextual information and observed outcomes, the method concentrates trials on where high-impact failures are most likely to occur, greatly improving failure discovery efficiency over uniform sampling. However, as the evaluation budget grows large and approaches exhaustive testing, the benefit over simpler allocation strategies diminishes, and the contributions of context features and posterior-driven exploration vary by the budget scale.

Abstract: Evaluating interactive agents is expensive. Agent behavior is stochastic, so reliability must be measured over repeated trials, but failures are rare and differ widely in how much they matter. Standard benchmarks spend this budget uniformly: a read-only lookup is sampled as often as an irreversible payment action. We instead formulate evaluation as a sequential allocation problem. Given a fixed trial budget and a set of scenarios whose failure behavior is unknown, which scenarios should be run, and run again? We propose a risk-aware contextual Thompson Sampling policy that combines a pre-execution scenario context vector and a fixed impact score with the failure outcomes observed during evaluation, and we test it by offline replay over 70 $τ$-bench airline scenarios and 824 recorded trials. Our main result is at the smallest budget: with only 50 trials ($6\%$ of the corpus), the policy recovers $86\%$ of the impact-weighted failures an oracle could find, compared to $25\%$ for uniform allocation. It discovers $3.5\times$ more impact-weighted failures (215.4 vs. 62.2) with the same number of trials, delivers $5\times$ the discovery per dollar, and cuts the budget wasted on scenarios that never fail from $34\%$ to $2.8\%$. The rest of our analysis demonstrates and qualifies this result: a budget sweep shows the advantage shrinks as the budget approaches the corpus size, and paired significance tests show that scenario context helps mainly at small budgets while posterior-based exploration helps at moderate ones. Risk-aware adaptive allocation therefore helps most exactly where evaluation budget is scarcest.

</details>


### [174] [How Much Can Reliability Drift Under a Fixed Confidence Distribution?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38917)
*Wenhao Liang,Lin Yue,Wei Emma Zhang,Mingyu Guo,Olaf Maennel,Weitong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study how classifier calibration reliability can change under covariate shift when the confidence distribution stays fixed, and quantify its worst-case fragility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In practice, a classifier might appear well-calibrated on a validation set but become unreliable under distribution shift, even if its confidence score distribution does not change. Understanding and quantifying how much the true accuracy–confidence relationship can deteriorate under such shifts is crucial for deploying models reliably in the wild.

Method: Model covariate shift as a reweighting of examples that preserves the marginal distribution of confidence scores, and constrain these reweightings within each confidence level by a chi-square divergence budget. Define the resulting worst-case change in conditional accuracy as a fragility profile. Analyze this profile theoretically, showing when it simplifies to a closed form involving the within-bin variance of correctness propensity (grouping loss), and when it is instead determined by the tails of the propensity distribution. Since the true correctness propensity is unobserved, restrict reweightings to a learned finite readout within confidence bins, bound the approximation error via residual grouping variance, and estimate the restricted fragility using role-separated data splits and split-sample confidence bounds. Evaluate the approach on ImageNet with multiple classifiers and calibration methods, and compare estimated fragility to held-out drift under optimized reweightings and label-permutation diagnostics.

Result: Theoretically, the paper shows that for a computable interval of chi-square budgets, the fragility profile is exactly the square root of the budget times the within-level variance of correctness propensity (grouping loss). Outside this interval, the profile depends on the tails of the propensity distribution, implying that calibration residual and grouping variance alone do not determine fragility, except in the deterministic-label and deterministic-prediction case. Empirically on ImageNet, the lower confidence bound on fragility is positive for most uncalibrated classifiers and for a smaller subset after temperature scaling. Observed drift under optimized reweightings fitted without evaluation labels aligns with the estimated fragility profile, while a label-permutation diagnostic destroys this alignment, confirming that the effect is not an artifact of random reweighting.

Conclusion: Calibration reliability can be highly fragile to covariate shifts that preserve the confidence distribution, and this fragility is governed not just by standard calibration metrics but by the full distribution of correctness propensities within confidence levels. The proposed chi-square-bounded fragility profile provides a principled way to quantify worst-case reliability shifts and can be estimated in practice through restricted reweightings and split-sample procedures. Empirical results on ImageNet indicate that many classifiers exhibit statistically significant fragility even after simple calibration, underscoring the need to assess and possibly mitigate such vulnerability in real-world deployments.

Abstract: A classifier's conditional accuracy can change while its confidence distribution stays exactly the same. We study the worst-case movement of the reliability relation under covariate shifts that preserve the distribution of the confidence score, constraining the reweighting within each confidence level by a $χ^2$ budget; the resulting worst case, as a function of the budget, is a fragility profile. On an interval of budgets that can be computed from the source distribution, the profile equals exactly the square root of the budget times the within-level variance of the correctness propensity -- the grouping-loss term of calibration-refinement decompositions. Beyond this interval the profile is governed by the tails of the propensity law, and the entire upward profile determines the centred within-level law; consequently, calibration residual and grouping variance do not determine fragility in general, though they do when labels and predictions are deterministic. Since the propensity is not observed, we restrict reweightings to a learned finite readout within confidence bins, bound the part the restriction misses by the grouping variance remaining inside readout cells, estimate the restricted profile with role-separated labels, and provide a separate split-sample lower confidence bound. On ImageNet this bound is positive in both splits for four of six primary classifiers and nine of twelve additional ones as released, and for three of eighteen after temperature scaling. Held-out drift under optimised reweightings fitted without evaluation labels tracks the estimated profile; an exploratory label-permutation diagnostic yields near-zero agreement for this statistic while largely reproducing the correlation observed for unsigned random reweightings.

</details>


### [175] [Prototype-guided Bilateral Alignment Multimodal Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38925)
*Tianchi Liao Tianchi_Liao,Lele Fu,Sheng Huang,Qing Hu,Hong-Ning Dai,Chuan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MFedPBA, a multimodal federated learning framework that handles heterogeneous client models and unbalanced modalities using prototype-guided bilateral alignment at feature and decision levels, achieving better performance than prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal federated learning approaches assume homogeneous models and balanced modalities across clients, which is unrealistic in practice where clients have different architectures and suffer from missing or imbalanced modalities. This mismatch leads to suboptimal or unstable performance, motivating a method that can robustly learn from heterogeneous, imbalanced multimodal data.

Method: The authors design MFedPBA, a prototype-guided bilateral alignment framework. First, at the feature level, they align heterogeneous feature spaces from different client models using a shared projection encoder trained via contrastive learning and Gromov-Wasserstein distance to learn a common representation space. Second, at the decision level, they introduce entropy-weighted aggregation of logit prototypes (class-level prediction statistics), which are naturally aligned across clients, to obtain a robust global decision space. This dual alignment provides both representation and prediction consistency despite heterogeneity and modality imbalance.

Result: Through extensive experiments (details not in the abstract), MFedPBA is shown to significantly outperform state-of-the-art multimodal federated learning baselines, particularly in challenging scenarios with heterogeneous client model architectures and severe modality imbalance.

Conclusion: MFedPBA effectively enables robust multimodal federated learning under realistic non-ideal conditions by jointly aligning feature spaces and decision-level prototypes across heterogeneous clients. The dual alignment mechanism addresses both representation heterogeneity and modality imbalance, leading to superior performance compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for leveraging distributed data to enhance model performance. However, existing methods predominantly rely on idealized assumptions of model homogeneity and balanced modality distributions, rendering them ill-suited for practical scenarios characterized by heterogeneous client architectures and severe modality imbalance. To address these challenges, we propose a \textbf{M}ultimodal \textbf{Fed}erated learning Prototype-guided Bilateral Alignment (MFedPBA) framework. MFedPBA facilitates robust knowledge synergy through a dual alignment mechanism: (i) at the feature level, it aligns heterogeneous feature spaces via a projection encoder optimized by contrastive learning and the Gromov-Wasserstein distance; (ii) at the decision level, it employs an entropy-weighted aggregation of naturally aligned logit prototypes. This novel design achieves robust MFL by jointly tackling heterogeneous feature spaces and collectively aggregating decisions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under conditions of model heterogeneity and modality imbalance.

</details>


### [176] [Learning What to Forget: Distributional Unlearning for LLM Representation Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38929)
*Pinaki Mohanty,Haoran Tang,Maggie Makar,Rajiv Khanna*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose Mamushi, a non-parametric method to select which training examples to forget so that a model’s data distribution moves away from an unwanted domain (e.g., toxic or topical content) while staying close to the desired domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine unlearning methods often focus on removing specific points and rely on parametric assumptions for tractability. But in practice we often need to remove whole data domains (like toxic language) and work with high-dimensional language model representations, where parametric assumptions are unrealistic or brittle. The authors want a principled, non-parametric way to choose which examples to forget to best shift the training distribution away from the unwanted domain while preserving useful data.

Method: They formulate distributional unlearning as selecting a subset of examples from a forget domain under a fixed deletion budget, optimizing a removal–preservation objective. They show that the Bayes-optimal logit of a probabilistic classifier distinguishing forget vs retain data equals the log density ratio between forget and retain distributions (up to a constant). Their Mamushi framework trains such a classifier on high-dimensional representations and ranks forget examples using its logit scores, then applies a threshold to select which examples to delete. They theoretically prove that thresholding the population log-density ratio is the optimal fixed-budget selection rule and derive non-asymptotic guarantees that bound the gap between Mamushi’s performance and the optimal rule in terms of score estimation and threshold calibration errors.

Result: On real-world toxic-language and topical-domain removal tasks, using various representation spaces, Mamushi yields better trade-offs between removing unwanted content and preserving desired content compared with baseline selection methods. It also reduces the number of examples that must be deleted to achieve a given level of forgetting, showing that it can be used as an efficient pre-selection mechanism for downstream machine unlearning procedures.

Conclusion: Mamushi provides a theoretically grounded, non-parametric framework for distributional unlearning that is well-suited to high-dimensional language model data. By using classifier-based log-density ratio estimation and optimal thresholding, it outperforms existing heuristics in both theory and practice, offering a practical way to select forget examples that more efficiently achieve targeted distributional changes for machine unlearning.

Abstract: Machine learning systems increasingly face the need to remove the influence of entire data domains, such as toxic language, harmful behavior, or topical content, rather than isolated records. Recent work formalizes this problem as \emph{distributional unlearning}: selecting a subset of a forget domain whose removal moves the training distribution away from an unwanted population while preserving proximity to the desired one. However, existing analyses often impose parametric assumptions to obtain tractable selection rules. These assumptions may be poorly suited to high-dimensional language-model representations. We introduce \textsc{Mamushi}, a framework for non-parametric distributional unlearning that ranks forget examples using a probabilistic classifier whose Bayes-optimal logit equals the forget-to-retain log-density ratio (up to an additive class-prior constant). We show that thresholding the population log-density ratio yields the optimal fixed-budget selection rule for our removal--preservation objective and establish a non-asymptotic transfer guarantee relating score-estimation and threshold-calibration errors to degradation from the population-optimal selection rule. Our empirical evaluation spans real-world datasets on toxic-language removal and topical-domain removal regimes using different representations, with \textsc{Mamushi} achieving a more favorable removal--preservation trade-off than other baselines. Our work shows that \textsc{Mamushi} can serve as an efficient selection approach for downstream machine unlearning procedures, reducing the number of forget examples required to reach a fixed forgetting target.

</details>


### [177] [Routing Probes Can Improve Without New Information: An Exact-Null Audit of Uncertainty Beyond Model Outputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38956)
*Wenhao Liang,Lin Yue,Wei Emma Zhang,Mingyu Guo,Olaf Maennel,Weitong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines whether routing signals in vision transformers truly provide extra information about prediction errors beyond the model’s output, and shows that common evaluation setups can falsely suggest such extra information due to methodological artifacts, proposing a more reliable conditional testing framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Probes often show that routing signals like expert gates or attention residuals help predict model correctness better than using outputs alone, and this is widely interpreted as routing containing additional error-related information. The authors suspect this inference may be confounded by evaluation practices and want to rigorously test if routing genuinely adds information beyond what is in the outputs.

Method: They construct a label-null setting by pairing real model outputs and routing signals with correctness labels generated by a frozen output-only model trained on separate data, ensuring routing is by design uninformative. They then compare probe performance with and without routing, under different probe classes (MLP vs linear) and checkpoint-selection criteria (validation accuracy vs log loss). They also evaluate sensitivity using implanted signals and introduce a conditional permutation test based on an estimated routing law, then apply this conditional analysis to real correctness labels for several DeiT attention-residual model families.

Result: Under the exact label null, an MLP probe often falsely indicates that routing improves correctness prediction in over half of the confidence-only evaluations, while a linear probe does not. Changing checkpoint selection from accuracy-based to log-loss-based eliminates these false detections across models and replications, implicating checkpoint selection as the main artifact source. The corrected comparison, however, shows low sensitivity, failing to detect small implanted signals that a new conditional permutation test reliably picks up while maintaining low false-positive rates. Applying this conditional framework to real data reveals apparent extra information in routing for several model families, though robustness checks reduce the strength of this evidence and none pass a stringent noise-based criterion.

Conclusion: Naively observing that probes using routing features outperform those using outputs alone does not in itself prove that routing carries extra information about model errors; such conclusions can be driven by methodological artifacts like checkpoint selection. Fitting a stronger probe and testing whether routing adds incremental information beyond outputs are distinct tasks that require separate, carefully validated procedures, such as conditional permutation testing under a well-specified routing law.

Abstract: Routing signals of modern vision transformers -- expert gates, attention-residual weights and halting scores -- often improve probes that predict whether the model is correct, and the improvement is commonly read as evidence that routing carries information about errors beyond the model's outputs. We test this inference directly: keeping real output-routing pairs, we redraw correctness labels from a frozen output-only generator fitted on disjoint data, so that routing is uninformative by construction. Under this exact label null, a width-matched MLP comparison still reports a routing gain in 51.3% of confidence-only evaluations (308/600), while a linear comparison reports none. Holding each training trajectory fixed on a six-model panel and selecting the checkpoint by validation log loss instead of validation accuracy removes the detections (50/120 to 0/120, and 83/120 to 0/120 in an independently implemented probe), identifying accuracy-based checkpoint selection as the cause; across all output views the raw detection rate falls from 27.5% (528/1,920) to zero observed detections. The repaired comparison is not sensitive, detecting an implanted signal of about 0.005 nats in 0/20 replicates in each of two matched settings, whereas a conditional permutation test built on an estimated routing law detects it in 11/20 and 10/20 and rejects rarely under the null. On real correctness labels, the conditional analysis yields model-relative evidence in five DeiT attention-residual families; in four it persists under two specified variants of the conditional law, and no family passes an additional noise criterion. Fitting a better probe and testing for incremental information are different problems, and each needs its own validation.

</details>


### [178] [Targeted Retrieval, Compact Representations: How CoT Reasoning Improves Long-Context Counting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38958)
*Liang Twist Shan,Tianyu Hu,Hao Yan,Yiqiao Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies why chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts help large language models with long-context counting tasks, using a needle-in-a-haystack setup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although CoT prompting improves performance on long-context reasoning tasks, we lack a mechanistic understanding of how and why it works internally in LLMs, particularly for tasks like counting occurrences over long texts.

Method: The authors design a needle-in-a-haystack counting task where models must count dispersed records in long text, compare Thinking (CoT) vs Non-thinking prompting across twelve model groups, and then use attention and representation analyses plus causal interventions to identify retrieval and counting mechanisms that emerge under standard autoregressive training.

Result: They find that CoT (Thinking) prompts improve counting accuracy, especially for larger counts. Mechanistically, Non-thinking models use broad retrieval over many needles, while Thinking models use stepwise enumeration to drive targeted retrieval, creating compact internal representations and a maintained counter state, as shown by causal interventions and small controlled experiments.

Conclusion: CoT prompting helps models shift from broad to targeted retrieval, supporting an internal state-tracking mechanism where the model maintains and updates a counter as it retrieves items in long context, linking long-context retrieval behavior to underlying representation geometry of counting.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been rapidly improving in long-context tasks, powered by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, the internal mechanisms underlying this improvement remain unclear. We investigate these mechanisms through a needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) counting task, where an LLM is asked to count the number of records dispersed in a long text. Across twelve model comparison groups, Thinking (or reasoning) improves counting accuracy over Non-thinking, with pronounced gains at larger counts. This motivates our mechanistic analysis, which identifies two contrasting mechanisms: (i) broad retrieval, where Non-thinking models broadly attend to multiple needles; (ii) targeted retrieval, where Thinking models use enumeration in CoT traces to successively retrieve needles. Targeted retrieval concentrates attention on individual needles and is accompanied by more compact internal representations. Moreover, causal intervention analysis suggests that Thinking models use the CoT trace to maintain and update an internal counter as needles are successively retrieved, even without explicit numbering. In small controlled experiments, both retrieval mechanisms and counter states emerge under standard autoregressive training. Together, our results connect long-context retrieval with representation geometry of counting, supporting a state-tracking account of CoT reasoning.

</details>


### [179] [Alleviating Hallucination in Reasoning Tasks with Training-Free Uncertainty-Guided Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38962)
*Litian Liu,Qiqi Hou,Yubing Jian,Reza Pourreza,Mohammad Ghavamzadeh,Roland Memisevic,Yao Qin,Hong Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They use model-internal confidence signals not just to detect hallucinations but to steer the model during inference toward more reliable answers, without extra training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work mostly uses uncertainty estimates from LLMs to detect or filter hallucinations after the fact. The authors want to see whether those same uncertainty signals can be exploited proactively during inference to directly improve answer accuracy and reduce hallucinations, without needing retraining or supervision.

Method: They introduce USteer, a training-free, inference-time steering method. USteer computes a confidence measure for candidate outputs and then takes the gradient of this confidence with respect to the model’s intermediate layer activations. It then adjusts (nudges) these activations in the direction that increases confidence, effectively steering the generation toward outputs the model internally regards as more certain, all without changing model parameters.

Result: Across multiple reasoning and hallucination-prone tasks, applying USteer at inference reduces hallucinations and improves answer correctness compared to the unsteered base model, showing consistent gains without additional training or supervision.

Conclusion: Model-internal confidence signals can do more than post-hoc hallucination detection: they can be converted into actionable gradients for inference-time control. USteer demonstrates a simple, training-free way to use confidence-guided activation steering to reliably reduce hallucinations in LLM outputs.

Abstract: Recent work on hallucination detection in large language models has shown that, for a fixed pre-trained model and reasoning task, it is possible to estimate the model's confidence in the correctness of its outputs. Such uncertainty estimates have primarily been used to improve truthfulness by detecting or filtering confabulations. In this work, we ask whether these signals can instead be used more proactively to directly improve the accuracy of model-generated answers. We propose USteer, a simple, training-free steering mechanism that adjusts a model's layer-wise activations during inference using the gradient of a confidence measure with respect to the activations. This procedure nudges generation toward outputs with lower uncertainty at inference time, without modifying model parameters or requiring additional supervision. We show that this approach consistently reduces hallucination across a range of tasks, demonstrating that confidence signals can be leveraged not only for detection, but also for effective inference-time control of model behavior.

</details>


### [180] [When Order Matters: First-Speaker Bias and Mitigation through Personality in Sequential Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38964)
*Duofeng Xu,Bryan Hooi,Dandan Qiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how multi-agent debate for LLMs is biased toward the first speaker and explores whether personality-style prompting can correct this, finding that lower agreeableness for the strong model restores its influence, while extraversion mainly affects verbosity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent debate is used to boost LLM reasoning, but in practice the order in which models speak and their interaction style may create systematic biases that skew outcomes away from the most capable model. Understanding and correcting these biases is important to reliably leverage stronger models in mixed-capability settings.

Method: The authors analyze sequential multi-agent debates involving LLMs of differing strengths, measuring how speaking order affects which model determines the final answer. They then introduce personality prompts based on Big Five traits (agreeableness, extraversion) to either the stronger or weaker agents and quantify changes in influence, accuracy, and behaviors such as verbosity.

Result: Sequential MAD exhibits a strong first-speaker bias: the initial speaker has disproportionate influence on the final answer, so placing a strong model later can negate much of its advantage. Low-agreeableness prompting systematically shifts influence towards the low-agreeable side, and when applied to the stronger model, recovers its lost influence and improves final accuracy. Extraversion prompts show weaker and less consistent effects, mainly increasing verbosity rather than reliably changing influence or accuracy.

Conclusion: Designing effective multi-agent debate systems requires attention to process factors like speaking order and induced interaction styles, not just model capabilities. Personality-style prompting, especially lowering agreeableness for stronger agents, can partially correct first-speaker bias, while extraversion is less useful beyond affecting verbosity.

Abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) is often used to improve large language model (LLM) reasoning, but sequential debate is rarely a neutral aggregator of agents' opinions. We show that sequential MAD suffers from a pronounced first-speaker bias: agents disproportionately shape the final answer when they speak first. As a result, placing a stronger model after weaker ones can substantially offset its reasoning advantage. We then focus on the disadvantaged strong-agent-last setting and ask whether personality prompting can mitigate this imbalance. Drawing on the Big Five model, we study agreeableness and extraversion as behavioral interventions applied to either the strong or weak side. We find that their effects are trait-specific. Influence consistently shifts in the direction of lower agreeableness, and assigning low agreeableness to the stronger agent helps restore its lost influence and improves final accuracy. Extraversion, by contrast, produces less systematic changes in influence and accuracy, with its clearest effect appearing in agents' verbosity. These findings show that effective MAD design depends not only on model capability, but also on how speaking order and induced interaction behavior shape the debate process.

</details>


### [181] [RealWorldShop: Benchmarking and Improving Conversational Shopping Agents in Real-World E-commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38974)
*Xinwei Yang,Kelong Mao,Yudong Guo,Sulong Xu,Simiu Gu,Chen Huang,Wenqiang Lei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a realistic benchmark and an agent framework to evaluate and improve conversational shopping assistants using large language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ecommerce LLM systems need to handle full shopping sessions where users change minds, add constraints, and pursue multiple goals, but existing benchmarks mainly test final outcomes or isolated actions, not the evolving decision process across a conversation.

Method: They create REALWORLDSHOP, a benchmark with 3.28M real products, structured multi-turn shopping episodes, a profile-grounded and action-controllable user simulator, and role-play based evaluation setup. They then design REALSHOP_AGENT, a session-control agent framework that explicitly manages dialogue state, controls shopping flow, retrieves from the product catalog, and uses runtime guards. They evaluate existing systems and their agent on this benchmark.

Result: Analysis on REALWORLDSHOP shows current systems give plausible responses locally but fail at state tracking, updating constraints, and converging on grounded recommendations, especially when user intent is ambiguous, involves bundles, or multiple intents. Experiments demonstrate that REALSHOP_AGENT achieves consistently better performance than strong baselines on the REALWORLDSHOP benchmark.

Conclusion: REALWORLDSHOP reveals key weaknesses of current conversational shopping assistants in realistic session-level decision making, and REALSHOP_AGENT, with explicit state and flow control plus catalog grounding, significantly improves performance, suggesting this structured agent design is better suited for real-world ecommerce assistants.

Abstract: Large language models are reshaping ecommerce from static recommenders into interactive shopping assistants, yet real-world shopping requires session-level decision support: users reveal and revise constraints, coordinate multiple goals, and expect product-grounded recommendations over a full conversation. Existing benchmarks are mostly outcome-oriented or execution-oriented, leaving this evolving decision process under-evaluated. We introduce REALWORLDSHOP, a benchmark built on 3.28M grounded products, structured shopping episodes, a profile-grounded and actioncontrolled user simulator, and role-play evaluation. Our analysis shows that current systems produce locally plausible responses but struggle with state tracking, constraint updating, and grounded convergence, especially under ambiguous intent, bundle, and multi-intent scenarios. We further propose REALSHOP_AGENT, an executable session-control framework with explicit state management, shopping-flow control, catalog-grounded retrieval, and runtime guards. Experiments show that REALSHOP_AGENT consistently outperforms strong baselines on REALWORLDSHOP.

</details>


### [182] [C-STRIDE: An Observation-Driven AI Digital Twin for Predicting Basin-Wide Flood Fields from Sparse Stream-Gauge Histories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39005)
*Yanjie Tong,Phillip Si,Yuan Qiu,Peng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C-STRIDE is an AI-based, observation-driven flood digital twin that converts sparse stream gauge data, terrain, and rainfall into fast, basin-wide, short-term flood depth maps, significantly improving prediction accuracy and speed over traditional hydrodynamic models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Emergency managers need timely, basin-wide information on floodwater extent and depth, but available real-time data are sparse (few gauges) and high-resolution hydrodynamic models are too computationally expensive for frequent reruns or large ensembles. There is a need for a method that can quickly integrate limited observations with physical context (terrain, rainfall) to produce accurate, continuously updated flood predictions over large areas and short lead times.

Method: The authors develop C-STRIDE, an AI-based digital twin trained on simulations from a calibrated 2D hydrodynamic model. The system takes as inputs short records from a small number of stream gauges, terrain data, and rainfall information, and outputs basin-wide maps of water depth with lead times up to one day. The model implicitly incorporates data assimilation by being trained on model simulations conditioned on these inputs, avoiding a separate assimilation step. They apply it to the Des Plaines River basin (4.2 million 30-m grid cells, six gauges) and test different input combinations (gauges only, +terrain, +rainfall, future rainfall scenarios), and also test its behavior when fed real instead of simulated gauge data.

Result: In the Des Plaines River basin case, six gauges drive predictions over 4.2 million 30-m cells. Adding terrain data markedly improves prediction accuracy, and including rainfall prevents error growth at longer lead times; together, terrain and rainfall reduce errors by about 40% relative to using gauge data alone. When future rainfall is provided, prediction errors remain around 15% at a 1-day lead time, versus nearly 40% without rainfall. When the model is run with real gauge data (instead of simulated ones), it adjusts its predictions toward observed hydrographs at half of the gauges without any retraining. Computationally, C-STRIDE is roughly 150 times faster than the underlying hydrodynamic model.

Conclusion: C-STRIDE demonstrates that sparse gauge measurements, combined with terrain and rainfall, can be transformed via an AI-based digital twin into fast, accurate, basin-wide flood predictions with short lead times. This offers a practical path toward operational flood digital twins, enabling continuous updates without costly reruns of full hydrodynamic models. However, further validation using real-time observations and rainfall forecasts is needed before full operational deployment.

Abstract: Emergency managers need to know where floodwater is, how deep it is, and how it will change over the coming hours across an entire river basin. During a flood, however, real-time measurements come from only a handful of stream gauges, and high-resolution hydrodynamic models are too costly to rerun each time new data arrive or to run as large ensembles. We present C-STRIDE, an observation-driven AI digital twin that turns short records from a few stream gauges, together with terrain and rainfall, into basin-wide maps of water depth and extends these predictions up to a day ahead. It is trained on simulations from a calibrated two-dimensional hydrodynamic model and needs no separate data-assimilation step. In the Des Plaines River basin near Chicago, six gauges inform predictions over 4.2 million 30-m grid cells. Terrain improves the predictions most, rainfall keeps errors from growing over longer horizons, and together they reduce errors by about 40% compared with gauge records alone. When future rainfall is known, errors remain near 15% one day ahead, compared with nearly 40% without rainfall. Given real instead of simulated gauge records, the model shifts its predictions toward the observed hydrographs at three of six gauges without retraining, and it runs about 150 times faster than the hydrodynamic model. These results show how sparse gauges, terrain, and rainfall can be combined into fast, continuously updated flood predictions, a step toward operational flood digital twins that still requires testing with real-time data and rainfall forecasts.

</details>


### [183] [Search Shapes Conclusions: Auditing Evidence Selection Bias in Deep Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39026)
*Shuyao Xiao,Shengling Wang,Xuan Chen,Ke Chao,Ming Cui,Feifei Qian,Chaoyang Mei,Fanlin Meng,Lulu Wang,Ziming Yu,Junxi Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CESS, a method to correct for selection bias in how deep research agents sample and summarize documents, so that reported “evidence direction” better reflects all available documents rather than just the subset they read.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep research agents generate cited reports by adaptively searching and reading documents. However, even when individual citations are correct, the final conclusion can be misleading because the agent has only seen a selective subset of all candidate documents. Early retrieved evidence steers later search, document choice, and stopping, creating adaptive sampling bias that existing citation-correctness evaluations ignore. The authors want a way to check whether the overall evidence direction in a report is representative of the full candidate pool and to distinguish this from the separate question of how a different search policy would change what evidence is seen.

Method: They formalize the setting as an adaptive evidence sampling problem over a fixed candidate pool. They propose Causal Evidence Selection Correction (CESS), which uses logged information from search trajectories: at each round, the probability of selecting each document and the probability of continuing the search. CESS first predicts each candidate document’s “evidence direction” (e.g., pro, con, neutral relative to a claim). It then uses inverse-propensity-like corrections based on selection and continuation probabilities to debias the candidate-pool average evidence direction. Shrinkage methods stabilize estimates when searches are short or data is sparse, and when some documents are unsampleable, CESS outputs intervals instead of point estimates. They also derive a causal distinction between two estimands: (1) the corrected mean evidence direction of a fixed pool and (2) the effect of changing the search policy on what evidence is read, which requires explicit interventions (paired, counterfactual search runs).

Result: On MS2 systematic-review questions, CESS reduces mean absolute error versus the true candidate-pool average evidence direction by 9.2% and reduces sensitivity of the estimate to adversarially opposing document rankings by 39.4%, compared with a naive average over only read documents. Using trajectories from a public Open Deep Research agent, these reductions are even larger: 60.1% lower mean absolute error and 87.2% lower sensitivity to ranking changes. Additional 4,800 paired-intervention trajectories empirically validate that correcting a pool estimate and estimating the causal effect of a search policy are numerically and conceptually distinct tasks.

Conclusion: CESS provides a principled way to audit whether the evidence direction supporting a deep research report reflects the full set of candidate documents, correcting for adaptive selection bias in which documents are read and when search stops. The method yields more accurate and more robust estimates of the average evidence direction in the candidate pool. However, the authors emphasize that this audit problem is different from estimating how alternative search policies would change the evidence observed, which requires explicit intervention-based analysis beyond CESS.

Abstract: Deep Research agents synthesize evidence into cited reports, yet a well-cited report can still reach a misleading conclusion. Citation correctness checks whether cited sources support individual claims. It does not show whether adaptive search exposed a representative view of all documents made available for evaluation, which we call the candidate pool. Early findings redirect later queries, document choices, and stopping, so the documents an agent reads form a selective sample. Existing evaluations rarely account for this selection. We formulate the problem as adaptive evidence sampling and introduce Causal Evidence Selection Correction (CESS). CESS predicts each candidate document's evidence direction and corrects the candidate-pool average using the logged probabilities of selecting each document and reaching each search round. Shrinkage stabilizes short searches, while intervals replace point estimates when some documents cannot be sampled. We also prove that estimating the average evidence direction of a common pool differs from measuring how a change in search policy alters the evidence read. The latter requires intervention. On questions from the MS2 systematic-review benchmark, CESS reduces mean absolute error against the candidate-pool average by $9.2\%$ and reduces the estimate's change under opposing document rankings by $39.4\%$ relative to averaging the evidence scores of documents read. Across trajectories from a public Open Deep Research agent, the corresponding reductions reach $60.1\%$ and $87.2\%$. A further 4,800 trajectories under paired interventions confirm that correcting a pool estimate and measuring a policy effect are different tasks. CESS therefore audits whether the evidence direction underlying a report reflects the documents available for evaluation, while a separate intervention analysis measures the effect of search decisions.

</details>


### [184] [Multi-LLM Collaborative Alignment via Stackelberg Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39076)
*Christina Hahn,Shangbin Feng,Dean Light,Swastik Roy,Hila Gonen,Yulia Tsvetkov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a game-theoretic, bandit-driven curriculum for multi-LLM self-improvement, adaptively choosing the most informative instructions for models to train on.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniformly sampling instructions for multi-LLM training ignores that the usefulness of instructions changes as models improve. Some instructions cease to be informative once all models solve them well, while others become newly useful as models approach the capability needed to benefit from them. The authors want an automatic way to focus training on instructions that currently provide strong learning and discriminative feedback, to make collective multi-model alignment more efficient and effective.

Method: They frame instruction selection as a Stackelberg game between a leader (an EXP3 multi-armed bandit) and follower agents (the language models). The leader allocates a fixed sampling budget over instructions and adapts its distribution using rewards that jointly capture instruction difficulty and how well they differentiate model responses (discriminability). The follower LLMs answer the chosen instructions, evaluate each other’s responses, and update via preference-based training (DPO or GRPO). To make peer evaluation robust and competitive, they introduce Elo-style reputation scores to weight judgments and use reputation-based opponent matching to pair models for duels.

Result: On three heterogeneous pools of models and 12 benchmarks covering science, reasoning, coding, instruction following, and knowledge tasks, their Stackelberg Alignment framework achieves the best macro-average performance across all pools. It outperforms the strongest training-time baseline by up to 7.4% and surpasses state-of-the-art static inference-time baselines by 12–25%. Empirical analyses show that the bandit concentrates sampling on the most informative instructions, and controlled ablations indicate that both reputation-weighted evaluations and reputation-based matching materially contribute to performance gains.

Conclusion: Adaptive, game-theoretic curriculum design for instruction selection can substantially improve multi-LLM self-improvement compared to static or uniformly sampled curricula. By using a bandit leader to focus interactions on difficult and discriminative instructions, and by structuring peer evaluation through reputation mechanisms, the proposed Stackelberg Alignment framework yields more efficient and effective collective evolution of language models across diverse tasks and model pools.

Abstract: A pool of language models can collaborate and improve collectively by learning from one another's responses. These interactions depend on the instructions used during training. Existing methods typically sample instructions uniformly, even though their usefulness may change as the models improve: an instruction on which models' responses once differed in quality may later be answered equally well, while a previously difficult instruction may begin to provide a useful learning signal. We propose Stackelberg Alignment, a game-theory-inspired leader-follower framework that turns instruction selection into an adaptive curriculum. An EXP3 bandit acts as the leader, allocating a fixed sampling budget across instructions and updating its sampling distribution using a reward that combines instruction difficulty and response discriminability. The language models act as followers: they respond to the selected instructions, evaluate one another's responses, and learn from the resulting preference signals through DPO or GRPO. The framework uses Elo-style reputation-weighted peer judgment and reputation-based opponent matching to support reliable and competitive model interactions. Experiments across three heterogeneous model pools and 12 benchmarks spanning scientific discovery, reasoning, code, instruction following, and knowledge show that Stackelberg Alignment achieves the highest macro-average across three diverse model pools, outperforming the strongest training-time baseline by up to 7.4% and the best static inference baseline by 12-25%. Analysis confirms that the adaptive leader concentrates duels on the most informative instructions, and ablations show that both reputation-weighted judgment and reputation-based matching improve the effectiveness of multi-LLM evolution.

</details>


### [185] [Beyond Prediction: Steering VLM Agents with Retrospective World Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39101)
*Yongjiang Liu,Jie Zhang,Haoyue Zhang,Jingcai Guo,Deze Zeng,Song Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a new “retrospective world modeling” paradigm for VLM-based agents that infers which action most likely caused an observed transition and uses a self-consistency reward to improve robustness and generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current world models for vision-language-model (VLM) agents mainly do forward prediction of what will happen next given a state and action. While this helps with planning and reduces real-world interaction costs, it does not verify whether the chosen action is actually causally consistent with the observed transition. This can yield policies that look plausible but are physically incoherent or brittle, hurting robustness and generalization. The authors aim to impose causal consistency constraints on learned behaviors without relying solely on sparse external rewards.

Method: They introduce Retrospective World Modeling, where the agent learns to estimate a retrospective attribution distribution P(â_t | s_t, s_{t+1}), i.e., the probability over actions that could have caused a given transition between two states. Using this backward reasoning capability, they define a Self-Consistency Reward (SCR) that measures how consistent the policy’s chosen action is with the action inferred by the retrospective model. This SCR serves as an intrinsic, dense transition-level reward signal. They integrate SCR into a reinforcement learning framework for VLM agents, combining it with standard task rewards to guide learning toward causally plausible behaviors.

Result: Across diverse agentic tasks, agents trained with the proposed retrospective world model and SCR achieve better policy robustness and generalization than baselines that rely only on prospective (forward) world modeling. The experiments demonstrate improved performance and more physically grounded behaviors under varying conditions and tasks.

Conclusion: Viewing world modeling not only as forward prediction but also as backward causal attribution enables agents to evaluate whether their actions are consistent with observed transitions. The proposed Retrospective World Modeling and Self-Consistency Reward provide dense intrinsic feedback that encourages task-effective yet physically coherent behaviors. This leads to more robust and generalizable policies compared to traditional forward-only world modeling approaches.

Abstract: Equipping VLM agents with world modeling capabilities has shown strong potential for complex reasoning and long-horizon planning, while reducing the dependence of policy learning on costly real-world interactions. Existing methods mainly rely on prospective simulation to predict the consequences of candidate actions. However, this forward-only paradigm focuses on what will happen next and provides limited constraints for verifying whether an action is causally consistent with the observed state transition, which can lead to plausible-looking but physically incoherent behaviors. In this paper, we challenge the view of world modeling as only prospective prediction and introduce Retrospective World Modeling, a new agent learning paradigm that enables agents to reason backward by estimating the retrospective attribution distribution $P(\hat{a}{t}|s_t, s{t+1})$ for the action that most likely caused a given transition. Based on this capability, we formulate the Self-Consistency Reward (SCR), an intrinsic signal that measures the probabilistic consistency between the policy action and the retrospective explanation. Integrating SCR into reinforcement learning provides dense transition-level feedback and steers agents toward behaviors that are both task-effective and physically grounded. Extensive experiments across diverse agentic tasks show that our method substantially improves policy robustness and generalization over prospective-only world modeling baselines.

</details>


### [186] [Reserve-Aware Contrast Certificates for Conservative Bandits with Uncertain Baselines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39106)
*Qinchuan Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Reserve-C4B, a conservative bandit method that improves over an uncertain baseline policy without violating a performance budget, by using shared confidence sets and a reserve ledger to avoid double-counting estimation error and to manage performance guarantees over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conservative bandits must ensure they do not underperform a baseline policy by more than a preset budget. Existing methods that treat the candidate and baseline policies separately end up double-charging for shared estimation uncertainty, leading to overly conservative behavior and excessive fallback to the baseline. The paper is motivated by the need for tighter, less conservative guarantees that still respect performance constraints even when the baseline itself is uncertain.
