Method: The authors develop Reserve-C4B, which reasons directly about the performance contrast between candidate and baseline policies using a shared confidence set. They derive an exact expression for the avoidable penalty caused by double-charging shared estimation error and propose a tighter admissibility test at each history. A reserve ledger is introduced to decouple statistical evidence from allowable performance deficit, and a prefix-refresh extension periodically revalidates past decisions under the current confidence set while keeping previously earned performance credit. For linear bandits, they use self-normalized confidence sets to ensure time-uniform, simultaneous validity for adaptively chosen candidate actions, and prove that the resulting policy satisfies a conditional-mean performance constraint with high probability.

Result: Reserve-C4B achieves conservative bandit behavior with less unnecessary fallback to the baseline by eliminating the double-counting of estimation error and better managing performance reserves over time. The method yields policies that, under linear reward models and self-normalized confidence sets, meet conditional-mean performance constraints with high probability. Experiments decompose the contributions of certificate coupling, prefix refresh, and historical information, showing substantial reductions in baseline fallback and revealing weaknesses of approaches that rely on frozen (non-updated) performance certificates.

Conclusion: By focusing on the baseline-relative performance contrast and using shared confidence sets, Reserve-C4B provides tighter, more efficient conservative bandit guarantees under baseline uncertainty. The reserve ledger and prefix-refresh mechanisms allow the algorithm to reuse and recertify past decisions, significantly reducing conservative fallback while maintaining high-probability performance guarantees. However, the experiments also highlight that methods using static certificates are limited, underscoring the value of dynamically updated confidence structures in conservative bandit design.

Abstract: Conservative bandits must improve an incumbent policy without exhausting a prescribed performance budget. When the incumbent is uncertain, separately bounding candidate and baseline rewards can charge twice for shared estimation error. We develop Reserve-C4B around the baseline-relative contrast itself. A shared confidence set yields an exact expression for this avoidable penalty and a tighter admissibility test at every fixed history. A reserve ledger separates statistical evidence from permitted performance deficit; a prefix-refresh extension recertifies accumulated decisions under the current confidence set without discarding previously certified credit. For linear rewards, self-normalized confidence sets provide simultaneous validity over time and adaptively generated candidates, and the resulting policy satisfies a conditional-mean performance constraint with high probability. Reproducible experiments isolate certificate coupling, prefix refresh, and historical information, showing large reductions in baseline fallback while exposing the limitations of frozen certificates.

</details>


### [187] [MASCRDM: Multi-Agent System for Compliance Risk Detection and Mitigation in Training Process of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39107)
*Yan Zhang,Chuming Wei,Ruien Li,Yaoyao Peng,Wusheng Zhang,Guangwen Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MASCRDM, a multi-agent system embedded into the LLM training pipeline to monitor and mitigate compliance risks (e.g., discrimination, bias) in real time, using compliance rules, a compliance-focused LLM, and a compliance knowledge graph.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM compliance efforts mostly rely on static input/output filtering and post-hoc moderation. These provide only local, surface-level fixes and lack real-time, systematic control during training, making it hard to robustly prevent discrimination, bias, and other compliance violations. The authors want a method that proactively manages compliance risks throughout the full training process, leveraging legal/AI regulations more directly and structurally.

Method: They formalize compliance rules from AI laws and legal expert guidance and train or configure a compliance-specific LLM. They decompose the target LLM into components and map them to a compliance knowledge graph to identify key nodes where risks are likely to emerge. On top of this, they build a multi-agent system (MASCRDM) that runs during LLM training: agents monitor training behaviors, perform rule-based and LLM-based assessments, detect potential compliance risks, and issue alerts and mitigation suggestions to developers in real time.

Result: On discrimination and bias benchmarks, integrating MASCRDM into training improves compliance metrics (reduced discriminatory or biased behavior) while preserving acceptable semantic performance of the LLM, indicating that compliance can be enhanced without major degradation in utility.

Conclusion: Embedding a multi-agent compliance monitoring and mitigation system directly into the LLM training loop provides a practical, systematic way to reduce compliance risks such as discrimination and bias. Instead of only post-hoc filtering, MASCRDM intervenes during training, guided by legal rules and a compliance knowledge graph, and demonstrates that real-time, structure-aware control can enhance compliance with limited impact on model quality.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been applied in various fields. However, ensuring compliance and safety of LLMs, such as avoiding discrimination and bias, still remains a challenge. Current efforts mainly focus on detecting and filtering inputs and outputs of the trained models, rather than studying the intrinsic architecture of the models in real-time. To tackle this challenge, we analyze the LLMs training process and discover two critical issues: 1) Most of the existing methods are predominantly static in their approach to detection and filtering, achieving only localized optimizations without systematically enhancing the compliance of LLMs. 2) Another issue with existing approaches is the lack of real-time risk detection and mitigation across the full training process, which leads to limited flexibility. Motivated by these, we propose MASCRDM (Multi-Agent System for Compliance Risk Detection and Mitigation) during the LLM training process. Firstly, we develop a set of compliance rules based on existing Artificial Intelligence (AI) laws and a compliance-specific LLM with the instruction of compliance law experts. Then, we deconstruct LLMs into several components and identify key nodes based on the compliance knowledge graph. During LLMs training, we implement our multiple agents in the whole process, giving compliance risk alerts and suggestions for LLM developers. Experiments on discrimination and bias benchmark demonstrate that our multi-agent system can effectively improve the compliance while maintaining reasonable semantic performance. The results indicate that our method provides an executable path for mitigating compliance risk from within the LLMs systematically.

</details>


### [188] [BELIEFRAG: Making Adaptive RAG State-Aware under Evolving Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39139)
*Hongji Pu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes BELIEFRAG, a closed-loop controller that maintains a coherent evidence state in adaptive retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), improving QA accuracy while reducing token cost compared to fixed iterative retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-step RAG, local signals like confidence and relevance are often used as isolated triggers, leading to evidence-state fragmentation where the system lacks a consistent view of what is known, missing, or conflicting. This fragmentation hinders optimal decisions about when to retrieve more, rewrite queries, verify evidence, or answer. The authors aim to build a principled controller that integrates these signals into a unified belief state to guide retrieval and answering more efficiently and reliably.

Method: The authors design BELIEFRAG, a closed-loop controller that maintains an explicit multi-dimensional belief state over sufficiency, reliability, conflict, uncertainty, evidence gaps, and acquisition cost. At each step, BELIEFRAG updates this belief state based on available evidence and model signals, then selects among actions: new retrieval, query rewriting, verification, answering, stopping, or abstaining. They implement BELIEFRAG on top of large language models (gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3-32B) and compare it against fixed iterative retrieval baselines on six QA benchmarks. They further ablate belief dimensions and analyze which aspects contribute most to performance and cost savings.

Result: On six QA benchmarks with gpt-oss-120b, BELIEFRAG achieves mean token F1 of 0.572 with an average of 3.89k tokens per question, surpassing fixed iterative retrieval (0.555 F1) while using 39% fewer tokens. On Qwen3-32B, it similarly improves from 0.523 to 0.552 F1 and reduces token usage by 35%. Additional analyses show that most gains come from corrective re-retrieval rather than simple pruning of unnecessary steps, that some belief dimensions are redundant, and that calibrated answerability estimation is the most influential factor in operational decisions. Calibration stabilizes thresholds across related evidence sources, though shifts in sources can still disrupt decision reliability.

Conclusion: Maintaining an explicit, multi-dimensional belief state in adaptive RAG can mitigate evidence-state fragmentation and enable more effective control over retrieval and answering. BELIEFRAG demonstrates that a closed-loop controller that integrates sufficiency, reliability, conflict, uncertainty, gaps, and cost can improve QA accuracy while significantly reducing token consumption. The study also highlights the central role of calibrated answerability and corrective re-retrieval, while noting that not all belief dimensions are equally necessary and that distributional shifts in evidence sources remain a challenge for stable calibration.

Abstract: Adaptive RAG uses signals such as confidence, relevance, support, and retrieval quality to decide when to search or correct evidence. In multi-step retrieval, however, these local signals must be combined into a persistent view of what the current evidence supports, what remains missing, and which action should follow. Existing methods often use such signals as separate triggers, making it difficult to preserve a coherent evidence state across a trajectory; we call this problem evidence-state fragmentation. We introduce BELIEFRAG, a closed-loop controller that updates an explicit state over sufficiency, reliability, conflict, uncertainty, evidence gaps, and acquisition cost, then chooses among retrieval, query rewriting, verification, answering, stopping, and abstention. Across six QA benchmarks with gpt-oss-120b, BELIEFRAG reaches mean token F1 0.572 with 3.89k tokens per question, outperforming fixed iterative retrieval (0.555 F1) while using 39% fewer tokens. The same quality-cost pattern transfers to Qwen3-32B, where BELIEFRAG reaches 0.552 F1 versus 0.523 for iterative retrieval while using 35% fewer tokens. Analysis shows that the main gains come from corrective re-retrieval rather than pruning alone, while several belief dimensions are redundant and calibrated answerability plays the strongest operational role. Calibration improves threshold stability across related evidence sources, although source shift can still invalidate the same decision signal.

</details>


### [189] [Schema: Discovering Unknown Environments via Agentic Program Induction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39140)
*Guanning Zeng,Jiani Wang,Wenjie Ma,Shaofeng Yin,Chenyang Wang,Shichen Liu,Angjoo Kanazawa,Wode Ni,Xiuyu Li,Andrea Zanette,Haiwen Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Schema is an LLM-agent harness that formulates an agent’s understanding of an unfamiliar environment as executable programs, enabling more reliable learning and planning and dramatically boosting performance on several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents exploring unknown environments tend to write free-form notes about what they learn. These notes are verbose, implicit, and hard to systematically test or use for precise planning, which limits agents’ ability to generalize, verify hypotheses, and exploit what they’ve learned. The authors want a way for agents to build compact, explicit, testable models of the environment—analogous to scientific theories—that support prediction and robust task completion in environments with unknown rules.

Method: They propose Schema, an agent harness that drives learning and action via interactive program induction. Instead of just narrating observations in prose, the LLM agent incrementally encodes its understanding of the environment as executable programs stored in a persistent workspace. The harness exposes a small set of tools: (1) checking candidate programs against the full interaction history (for falsification and debugging), (2) using these programs for planning in the induced model, and (3) executing task plans under step-by-step verification in the real environment. The LLM chooses what to explore next, writes or revises programs, and iterates this loop, tightening the fit between its induced schemas and observed behavior of the environment.

Result: With the same base LLM, adding Schema yields large performance gains: ARC-AGI-3 RHAE accuracy rises from 58.7% to 99.2%, all public DiG-bench games are solved (100%), and performance on MazeBench reaches the median of the top-50 human players. Additional experiments and ablation studies show that the gains come from Schema’s core ideas—explicit program schemas, the persistent workspace, and verification/planning tools—rather than from superficial prompt tuning or extra compute.

Conclusion: Representing an agent’s evolving understanding of an unknown environment as executable programs, and supporting this with a structured harness for hypothesis testing, planning, and verified execution, substantially improves LLM agents’ ability to discover unknown mechanisms and solve complex interactive tasks. Schema offers a practical, science-inspired framework for turning exploratory interaction into compact, testable models that enable strong generalization and performance on challenging benchmarks.

Abstract: Learning to complete tasks in unfamiliar environments with unknown rules remains a key challenge for LLM agents. Current LLM agents often record their discoveries in prose, which may not provide a compact, explicit account of how the environment works. Inspired by how scientists organize observations into testable, predictive theories, we introduce Schema, an agent harness that organizes learning and action through interactive program induction. The LLM agent decides what to investigate and how to act, expressing its evolving understanding of the environment as executable programs. The harness consists of a persistent program workspace and a small set of interfaces for checking these programs against the interaction history, planning within them, and executing plans under step-by-step verification. Schema raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE from 58.7% to 99.2% with the same base model, solves 100% of the public DiG-bench games, and reaches the median performance of the top-50 human players on MazeBench. Extensive analysis shows the effectiveness of Schema in unknown mechanism discovery, and ablations confirm the contribution of each component.

</details>


### [190] [RefCon: Iterative Refinement and Contrastive Memory Extraction for Context-Evolving Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39143)
*Ubaidillah Ariq Prathama,Bo Liu,Yeo Boon Hong,Yu-Xuan Huang,Yangkai Ding,Tao Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RefCon, a method for extracting higher-quality memories for context-evolving agents using more test-time compute without gold labels, achieving strong performance gains and better scaling than prior approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon agents accumulate large amounts of noisy interaction data, and retraining models to incorporate this experience is expensive. There is a need for label-free memory extraction methods that can leverage additional test-time compute to improve agent performance over time, without relying on costly ground-truth annotations.

Method: The authors propose RefCon, which combines sequential self-refinement (iteratively improving candidate memories over time) with parallel self-contrast (comparing multiple candidate memories simultaneously) to select higher-quality memory traces from agent trajectories without gold labels. They also design a diversity-focused variant, DivCon, which emphasizes diversity in selected memories. These methods are integrated into various context-evolving agent frameworks and evaluated across different benchmarks and model scales.

Result: On AppWorld and BFCL-V3, RefCon yields strong and consistent gains, such as 21.6% relative improvement on ACE and 16.6% on ReMe compared to no-scaling baselines. DivCon achieves a 35.5% gain on ReasoningBank. RefCon outperforms other label-free baselines across settings, generalizes across different model sizes, and even surpasses ground-truth-based baselines on software engineering tasks. The authors further show that RefCon provides a favorable accuracy-token tradeoff and continues to improve as more trajectories are used, unlike diversity-only scaling which saturates sooner.

Conclusion: RefCon is an effective, label-free method for extracting and scaling memories for context-evolving agents, leveraging additional test-time compute via self-refinement and self-contrast. It consistently improves agent performance over diverse benchmarks, scales well with more experience, and maintains efficiency, offering an attractive alternative to retraining and to diversity-only memory selection strategies.

Abstract: Long-horizon agent interactions generate useful but noisy experience, and retraining models to absorb it is expensive. Context-evolving agents therefore need memory extraction methods that improve with more test-time compute without relying on gold labels. We propose RefCon, which combines sequential self-refinement with parallel self-contrast to extract higher-quality memories without gold labels. Evaluated on AppWorld and BFCL-V3 across multiple context-evolving agent frameworks, RefCon delivers strong and consistent gains, including relative improvements of 21.6% on ACE and 16.6% on ReMe over no-scaling baselines, while a diversity-focused variant (DivCon) achieves a 35.5% gain on ReasoningBank. RefCon consistently outperforms existing baselines without ground-truth labels, and generalizes across model scales and to software engineering tasks, where it surpasses even ground-truth baselines. We further analyze the accuracy-token trade-off and scaling behavior, showing RefCon maintains favorable efficiency and continues to improve as more trajectories are used, unlike diversity-only scaling which saturates earlier.

</details>


### [191] [MADBench: Benchmarking the Security of Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39146)
*Yuwan Liu,Jiaming Zhang,Yue Huang,Sisi Duan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MADBench evaluates how secure multi-agent debate is against diverse attacks and shows debate doesn’t always improve robustness, sometimes even amplifying adversarial effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While multi-agent debate often improves LLM reasoning by enabling agents to critique each other, the same interaction channel can also propagate adversarial errors. Existing work only looks at a few attack types and lacks a systematic, large-scale evaluation of how debate behaves under a wide variety of adversarial strategies. The key open question is whether debate acts as a defense or a vulnerability amplifier under attack.

Method: The authors build MADBench, a benchmark for systematically testing the security of multi-agent debate. They define a layered taxonomy of attacks aligned with stages of the MAD workflow, including both known attacks and new ones specialized for debate settings. Using this taxonomy, they implement six attack families and test them across 356 source tasks and 3,958 test cases in both question-answering and workspace-style tasks. They measure not only final answer correctness but also how adversarial influence spreads among agents during debate, under different conditions such as collusion among a subset of agents.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows that, when subject to attacks, multi-agent debate does not consistently enhance reasoning robustness compared to single-agent baselines. In question-answering, debate can reduce the impact of attacks on final answer accuracy, but in both QA and workspace tasks it can actually amplify unauthorized reads or writes, meaning harmful behaviors can spread through the debate. Even in a strong threat model where three out of five agents collude, the attack only flips the final answer from correct to wrong on 28.30% of tasks that were originally solved correctly without attack, and only 3.26% of initially correct honest agents are persuaded to change from correct to incorrect during debate.

Conclusion: MADBench reveals that multi-agent debate is not inherently more secure: it may mitigate some adversarial effects on answer correctness but can simultaneously amplify other forms of harmful influence, such as unauthorized information access or modification. The relatively low rates at which colluding agents can flip correct answers and persuade honest agents suggest some resilience, but the amplification of unauthorized behaviors highlights a nontrivial security risk. The benchmark and taxonomy provide a foundation for systematically analyzing and hardening debate-based LLM systems against diverse adversarial strategies.

Abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) can improve large language model (LLM) reasoning by allowing multiple agents to exchange and critique their answers to the same task. However, the interactions that enable agents to correct mistakes can also spread adversarial errors and steer the agents toward an incorrect answer. Although some efforts have been made to examine particular attack types on MAD, systematic evaluation of MAD under diverse attacks remains limited. A central question is whether debate mitigates adversarial influence or amplifies it.
  In this paper, we present MADBench, a benchmark for evaluating the security of MAD. We organize attacks into a layered taxonomy following the MAD workflow, incorporating both established attacks and new strategies tailored to debate. We evaluate six attack families over 356 source tasks and 3,958 test cases, examining their effects on the final answer and the propagation of adversarial influence. Our results show that, under attacks, MAD does not necessarily improve LLM reasoning. Compared with a single-agent baseline, MAD can mitigate attacks on answer accuracy in question-answering tasks while amplifying unauthorized reads or writes in both question-answering and workspace tasks. Moreover, even when three out of five agents collude, the attack changes the final answer from correct to wrong on only 28.30\% of tasks answered correctly without attack, while only 3.26\% of initially correct honest agents switch to wrong answers during debate.

</details>


### [192] [Do Self-Evolving Skills Generalize to Held-Out Tasks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39148)
*Xihao Piao,Zifeng Wang,Zhen Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study of how well self-evolving AI skills generalize from training tasks to new tasks, and a new method (GSO) to improve that generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents can learn reusable skills from previous tasks, but current self-evolving skill methods keep rewriting these skills based on training performance without carefully checking if improvements transfer to new tasks. The authors want to understand whether the performance gains on training tasks actually generalize, diagnose why they often do not, and develop a better approach for learning skills that reliably help on unseen tasks.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled empirical evaluation of five self-evolving skill-learning methods and a one-shot (non-evolving) skill across six benchmarks, using the same base model, agent setup, and train/test splits for all methods. They analyze 21 skills that improved on their training tasks, measuring how much of that improvement carries over to held-out test tasks. They perform qualitative analysis of the learned skills to identify patterns that hurt generalization (e.g., overfitting to specific task details). They also test an LLM-based judge that inspects skill content to predict which skills will generalize, evaluating it on pairwise comparisons of finished skills and on predicting the impact of single edits. Based on these findings, they propose Generalizable Skill Optimization (GSO), which maintains a high-level guide for writing skills and generates a fresh skill per task instead of rewriting a single persistent skill, and evaluate GSO on the same six benchmarks.

Result: Among 21 skills that improved on training tasks, only 5 maintained all of their improvement on test tasks, 13 preserved only part of the improvement, and 3 showed no improvement on test tasks, indicating substantial overfitting in many self-evolving skill methods. No existing method consistently outperformed others across benchmarks. Skills that generalized poorly often contained task-specific fixes or rigidified solutions to single failures into universal rules. An LLM-based judge could rank completed skills in line with their test-task performance in 86% of pairwise comparisons, but failed to reliably predict the effect of individual edits, so online testing remains necessary. The proposed GSO approach, which keeps only a general guide and rewrites a task-specific skill each time, achieved the best scores on all six benchmarks.

Conclusion: Self-evolving skill methods frequently overfit to training tasks, so improvements observed during training do not reliably transfer to new tasks. Overly specific or rigid edits are a key cause of poor generalization. While an LLM judge can assess the overall quality of finished skills reasonably well, it cannot replace empirical testing of incremental changes. The Generalizable Skill Optimization (GSO) framework, which focuses on maintaining a general skill-writing guide while re-instantiating task-specific skills anew for each task, yields more generalizable behavior and outperforms prior self-evolving skill methods across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: AI agents can externalize what they learn from past tasks into reusable \emph{skills}, such as procedures, checklists, code, or other executable artifacts, that can be retrieved and reused when solving new tasks. Self-evolving skill methods keep rewriting these skills after each round of practice on training tasks, and the skill is then used on new tasks of the same kind. We ask a question: does the improvement a skill shows on its training tasks carry over to new test tasks? We test five self-evolving methods and a one-shot skill on six benchmarks, with the same model, the same agent, and the same train/test split for every method. Of the 21 skills that improve on their training tasks, 5 keep all of that improvement on the test tasks, 13 keep part of it, and 3 keep none of it. No existing method is best everywhere. When we read the skills, the ones that carry over badly often fix details that should depend on the task, such as column names and output files, or turn a fix for one failure into a rule for every task. An LLM judge that reads the skill content can often see this: it ranks finished skills the same way the test results do in 86\% of pairs. But it predicts the effect of a single edit poorly, so edits still have to be tested by running them. Based on these findings, we describe Generalizable Skill Optimization (GSO), which keeps only a guide for writing skills and writes a new skill for each task; it scores highest on all six benchmarks.

</details>


### [193] [Rep2Skill: Representation-Guided Skill Self-Evolution for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39149)
*Kaixing Zhang,Changming Li,Yingdong Shi,Zheng Zhang,Kaitao Song,Wenjie Shi,Jingang Wang,Kan Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Rep2Skill is a framework that lets LLM-based agents improve their own textual skills by analyzing their internal representation trajectories, not just text logs and outcomes, leading to better self-evolution without external stronger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based agents can store and reuse skills in text, but existing self-improvement methods only look at textual histories and sparse rewards. They ignore the agent’s internal hidden representations, which capture detailed execution dynamics and evolving states. This creates a bottleneck in diagnosing where and why an agent’s behavior diverges from successful patterns. The paper aims to exploit these rich internal signals to guide more precise and effective skill refinement, especially in settings where there is no stronger external model to supervise the agent.

Method: The authors propose Rep2Skill, a representation-guided self-evolution framework. First, they collect agent rollouts (execution trajectories). Then they model the trajectories of the agent’s internal representations during these rollouts, comparing them across successful and failed executions. Rep2Skill identifies turns (steps) whose internal representation dynamics deviate from those observed in successful runs, localizing likely error points. It then combines these representation-based deviation signals with the textual execution context to generate concrete textual feedback that pinpoints and revises specific skills. The same LLM is used both as the executor (running the skills) and as the optimizer (interpreting representation signals and rewriting skills).

Result: Across two different agent environments and using two open-source LLMs, Rep2Skill consistently surpasses text-only self-evolution baselines that rely solely on textual trajectories and sparse success/failure signals. In all evaluated settings where the same LLM acts as both executor and optimizer, representation-guided optimization leads to higher task success rates and more effective skill refinement than text-only reflection methods.

Conclusion: Using internal representation trajectories to guide agent self-improvement is more effective than relying only on textual histories and outcomes. Rep2Skill demonstrates that agents can introspect on their own hidden states to localize execution errors and generate targeted textual feedback for skill revision, even without a stronger external model. This opens a promising direction for moving beyond purely text-based reflection, suggesting that future agent learning frameworks should integrate internal representation analysis into the skill optimization loop.

Abstract: Textual skills enable large language model (LLM) based agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. Yet existing skill evolution remains largely confined to the text space: an optimizer must diagnose success and failure patterns, and revise skills solely from long execution trajectories and sparse task outcomes. This text-only paradigm leaves the agent's internal representations, which contain rich records of its evolving execution state, outside the skill optimization loop. We ask whether an agent can improve its external textual skills by reflecting on its own internal representations. We introduce Rep2Skill, a representation-guided framework for self-evolution on agent skills. Specifically, upon the collected agent rollouts, Rep2Skill models their internal model representation trajectories to localize turns that deviate from successful execution dynamics, and it further interprets these signals alongside the execution contexts as actionable textual feedback for targeted skill revision. Experiments on two agent environments with two open-source LLMs show that Rep2Skill consistently outperforms text-only approaches in the self-evolution setting, where the same LLM serves as both executor and optimizer without a stronger external model. This establishes a promising direction moving agent self-improvement beyond text-only reflection.

</details>


### [194] [Beyond the Remembered World: Predictive 4D Belief for Persistent Navigation in Evolving Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39166)
*Mingjian Gao,Zhaocheng Li,Haoyang Huang,Wenqiao Zhang,Yingjie Niu,Hao Zhou,Chao Li,Juncheng Li,Siliang Tang,Yueting Zhuang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces EvolvingNav, a navigation framework that maintains and updates time-aware probabilistic beliefs over moving object locations in changing 3D environments, and evaluates it on a large new benchmark, showing better search and navigation performance than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most navigation methods assume static environments or simple, short-term dynamics, but in realistic settings, targets such as objects move while unobserved, making old spatial memories unreliable. Existing work on memory and prediction struggles with hidden state evolution over longer times and with limited, partial visibility. This paper aims to enable agents to navigate and search robustly in such evolving worlds by explicitly modeling persistent vs. relocated object hypotheses and integrating intermittent sensory evidence over time.

Method: The authors formalize Evolving-World Navigation, where an agent must infer and track target locations from sporadic observations while moving. They propose EvolvingNav, which builds a time-indexed probabilistic belief over candidate object locations and an open-world ‘elsewhere’ event, using a structured persistence-relocation model over timestamped 3D object histories. An event-driven Bayesian filter propagates and updates this belief as time passes, predicts occupancy at future inspection times, and fuses new RGB-D observations. Negative observations are handled with visibility-conditioned detection probabilities, and evidence tracking prevents double-counting the same observations. A frozen, zero-shot vision–language policy uses the maintained belief state to plan navigation and search actions.

Result: The authors introduce EvoWorld-Bench, a large-scale benchmark based on human activity traces with 54 scenes and over 800k tasks, where environments undergo controlled changes before and during navigation. Across simulation and real-robot experiments, EvolvingNav outperforms baselines in navigation success rate and search efficiency. The method shows particular advantages when target motion follows learnable temporal patterns. Ablation studies confirm that explicitly preserving uncertainty and using visibility-aware evidence integration are key contributors to performance gains.

Conclusion: EvolvingNav demonstrates that explicitly modeling evolving object locations via a persistence–relocation belief framework, combined with event-driven Bayesian filtering and visibility-aware evidence fusion, significantly improves embodied navigation and search in dynamic environments. The new EvoWorld-Bench benchmark highlights the importance and difficulty of Evolving-World Navigation and provides a reproducible testbed, while experiments suggest that capturing temporal regularities and maintaining calibrated uncertainty are crucial design elements for robust performance.

Abstract: Persistent spatial memory enables embodied agents to navigate familiar environments across repeated visits. However, targets may move while unobserved, including during navigation, making remembered locations unreliable by the time an agent arrives. Despite advances in memory retrieval and state prediction, accounting for continued hidden world evolution and revising beliefs under limited visibility remain challenging. We study Evolving-World Navigation, where agents infer target locations from intermittent observations, predict their states at inspection time, and revise beliefs using visual evidence. We propose EvolvingNav, which constructs a time-indexed belief from timestamped 3D object histories through a structured persistence-relocation model. The belief distinguishes persistence at the last observed location from relocation to alternative locations and retains probability mass outside the known candidate set. An event-driven filter propagates the current belief as time elapses, forecasts target occupancy at candidate inspection times, and incorporates new RGB-D evidence. Negative observations downweight location hypotheses according to calibrated, visibility-conditioned detection probabilities, while evidence tracking prevents repeated use of the same observations. A frozen, zero-shot vision-language controller uses the updated belief to choose actions and replan. We further introduce EvoWorld-Bench, a benchmark grounded in human activity traces, comprising 54 scenes and 803,680 tasks with controlled changes before and during navigation. In simulation and real-robot experiments, EvolvingNav improves navigation success and search efficiency over the evaluated baselines. Paired experiments show the clearest gains under learnable temporal patterns, while ablations demonstrate the value of preserving uncertainty and incorporating visibility-aware evidence.

</details>


### [195] [Reinforcing Multimodal Reasoning via Token-Level Perception-Grounded Advantage Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39168)
*Zhihan Zhang,Lizi Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces TPAE, a token-level, vision-grounded advantage estimator for RL with verifiable rewards in multimodal LLMs, providing fine-grained supervision and improving multimodal reasoning performance and stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RLVR methods for multimodal LLMs use coarse sequence-level rewards, which fail to capture which specific visually-grounded reasoning steps are correct or critical, limiting learning efficiency and stability. The authors observe that better leveraging visual grounding and token-level uncertainty patterns could provide more informative feedback for training.

Method: The authors first analyze token-level behaviors along reasoning chains using two metrics: visual dependency (degree to which a token relies on image features) and predictive entropy (model confidence). They identify characteristic patterns for correct vs. incorrect reasoning, and for pivotal tokens that cause failure. Based on this, they develop Token-level Perception-grounded Advantage Estimation (TPAE), which computes a token-level advantage score by measuring how statistically consistent each token is with the visual dependency–entropy patterns of correct rollouts, and then uses these scores to modulate the global sequence-level advantage in RLVR training.

Result: On seven multimodal reasoning benchmarks, TPAE leads to consistent performance gains over strong RLVR baselines, as well as more stable and data-efficient optimization during training.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, token-level, perception-grounded advantage estimation captures critical visual and uncertainty patterns within reasoning chains that sequence-level rewards miss. Integrating such token-level signals into RLVR substantially improves multimodal reasoning accuracy, stability, and efficiency, suggesting that future RL methods for MLLMs should exploit structured token-level feedback tied to visual grounding and confidence dynamics.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has improved the reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), yet existing frameworks rely on coarse, sequence-level reward signals that lack the fine-grained supervision over the visually-grounded steps within a multimodal reasoning chain. We investigate this gap through the lens of two token-level metrics: visual dependency (i.e. how much a token's prediction relies on the input image features) and predictive entropy. Our empirical analysis reveals two key findings: (1) correct reasoning chains exhibit a markedly sharper entropy reduction as visual grounding intensifies, compared to incorrect ones; (2) pivotal tokens, those whose misprediction triggers reasoning collapse, are statistical outliers in the joint distribution of visual dependency and predictive entropy derived from correct chains. Motivated by these findings, we propose token-level perception-grounded advantage estimation (TPAE), which estimates token-level advantages by measuring each token's statistical consistency with the vision-entropy patterns of correct rollouts. TPAE leverages this granular score to modulate the sequence-level advantage, producing a fine-grained supervision signal that can be integrated into various RLVR frameworks. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks show that TPAE consistently outperforms leading strong baselines, yielding more stable and efficient optimization for multimodal reasoning. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Zhihan72/TPAE.

</details>


### [196] [Learning Process Rewards via Reasoning State Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39220)
*Kai Gan,Zi-Hao Zhou,Bo Ye,Jian Zhao,Min-Ling Zhang,Tong Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Reasoning State Propagation (RSP), a new process reward model that uses binary validity states and transition probabilities to better connect intermediate reasoning steps with final outcomes, improving search and RL performance over existing PRMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Process reward models help evaluate intermediate reasoning steps in test-time scaling and RL but require expensive, dense process annotations. Existing PRMs also treat each reasoning prefix independently, failing to leverage the final outcome signal to refine the assessment of intermediate steps. The motivation is to reduce reliance on costly process labels by effectively combining sparse process supervision with abundant outcome supervision, using a model that explicitly links intermediate reasoning states to final correctness.

Method: The authors introduce Reasoning State Propagation (RSP), which encodes each reasoning prefix as being in one of two states: valid or invalid. They model transitions between consecutive prefixes with two probabilities: a break probability (valid → invalid) and a repair probability (invalid → valid). By propagating these transitions along the reasoning trajectory, the model infers the probability of each step being valid given the final outcome. Process annotations supervise intermediate states where available, while outcome labels supervise the final state and are propagated backward to earlier steps through the transition dynamics. RSP is then used within reasoning search, response selection, and RL pipelines and compared against standard PRMs.

Result: RSP yields consistent performance gains over strong PRM baselines, especially Qwen2.5-Math-PRM. Reported average improvements are 5.6% in beam search–based reasoning search and 2.1% in reinforcement learning settings. The gains are observed across multiple use cases involving reasoning evaluation and guidance.

Conclusion: Modeling binary validity states and their transitions across reasoning steps enables effective propagation of final-outcome supervision back to intermediate steps, thereby reducing dependence on dense process annotations and improving the quality of process reward models. RSP establishes a more principled connection between process and outcome supervision and empirically improves reasoning search and RL performance over existing PRMs.

Abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) have demonstrated notable effectiveness in test-time scaling and reinforcement learning by providing fine-grained signals for evaluating intermediate reasoning states, but their training relies heavily on costly process annotations. A natural way to alleviate this dependence is to complement limited process supervision with scalable outcome supervision. However, existing PRMs often model reasoning prefixes independently, providing no explicit mechanism for effectively using final outcome to guide the learning of intermediate reasoning states. We introduce Reasoning State Propagation (RSP), which represents each reasoning prefix with a binary validity state and models transitions between successive states across the reasoning trajectory. Specifically, RSP predicts a break probability that a valid state becomes invalid and a repair probability that an invalid state returns to valid. By propagating these transitions, RSP connects intermediate states to the final state, allowing process annotations to supervise intermediate states while outcome labels supervise the final state and can provide learning signals to preceding steps. Across reasoning search, response selection, and reinforcement learning, RSP consistently outperforms representative PRM baselines, with average improvements over Qwen2.5-Math-PRM of 5.6% in beam search and 2.1% in reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [197] [Fyan: A Human--AI Harness with Semantic Auditing for Document-Level Formalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39228)
*Wei Zhao,Yangshuo Zou,Chengxiang Ding,Yifan Wu,Xuchuan Wang,Zimu Mao,Lei Zhang,Tao Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FYAN is a human–AI workflow for formalizing entire mathematical documents in Lean, centered on a semantic auditing mechanism that checks faithfulness between informal theorems and their formal counterparts, substantially improving both formal proof success and natural-language proof quality over a strong baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing AI systems for theorem proving focus on isolated statements and often drift from the intended informal mathematics, producing formalizations that are misaligned with source texts. There is a need for a document-level, end-to-end framework that guides AI formalization in a way that preserves the meaning of the original mathematical exposition, can be supervised and guided by humans, and yields verifiably faithful formal statements and proofs.

Method: FYAN is a harness that organizes the full pipeline of mathematical formalization: specification extraction from informal text, proof planning, logical review, Lean proof generation, knowledge curation, and final validation. A key method is evidence-grounded semantic auditing: a language model generates structured evidence about how each part of a formal statement corresponds to the informal specification, including local matches, omissions, scope, and logical relations. This evidence is then checked by a deterministic validator that issues reproducible judgments of faithfulness. When a formally stated theorem deviates in an admissible way from the original, the system enforces a proof-transfer obligation that links the formal version back to an interpretation faithful to the source. The same base LLM (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) is used consistently in all stages of the pipeline.

Result: On the FormalTCS benchmark, FYAN proves 86 out of 143 theorems under strict Lean verification, outperforming a strong general agent harness that proves 69. It also increases a natural-language proof quality metric from 0.501 to 0.851. On the ConsistencyCheck benchmark, its semantic auditing mechanism detects more mismatches between formal and informal statements than a direct LLM judge, achieving higher recall on both ground-truth-verified labels (0.777 vs. 0.636) and original labels (0.873 vs. 0.820). Each detected inconsistency is localized to a specific hypothesis, conclusion, or scope component. Additionally, FYAN is used to construct ODENumLib, a substantial 9,355-line Lean library for numerical analysis of ordinary differential equations.

Conclusion: FYAN demonstrates that a structured, evidence-based, and auditable human–AI workflow can significantly improve the reliability and faithfulness of document-level mathematical formalization. By integrating semantic auditing with deterministic validation and enforcing proof-transfer obligations for deviations, the system produces formal Lean proofs that better match their informal sources and scales to building nontrivial libraries. The empirical gains over a general agent harness and over direct LLM judging suggest that such harnessed, audit-focused approaches are a promising direction for robust AI-assisted theorem proving and formalization.

Abstract: We present FYAN, a human--AI harness for document-level mathematical formalization. Rather than treating theorems in isolation, FYAN coordinates an end-to-end workflow spanning specification, proof planning, logical review, Lean proof construction, knowledge curation, and validation, with support for independent supervision and human guidance. A central component is evidence-grounded semantic auditing, which assesses whether formal statements faithfully preserve their informal specifications. A language model constructs structured evidence over local correspondences, omissions, scope, and logical relations, while a deterministic validator checks this evidence and produces reproducible judgments. When a substantive but admissible deviation is accepted, FYAN requires an explicit proof-transfer obligation connecting the formal statement back to a source-facing interpretation. With the same model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) in every stage, FYAN proves 86 of 143 FormalTCS theorems under a strict Lean check, against 69 for a general agent harness, and raises the natural-language proof score from 0.501 to 0.851. On ConsistencyCheck, its semantic audit catches more inconsistent statements than a direct LLM judge, both on labels verified against the source (recall 0.777 vs. 0.636) and on the original labels (0.873 vs. 0.820), and localizes each mismatch it reports to a specific hypothesis, conclusion, or scope. FYAN also built ODENumLib, a 9,355-line Lean library for the numerical analysis of ordinary differential equation.

</details>


### [198] [Effective Does Not Mean Useful: Conditional Functional Substitutability for Redundancy and Scaling in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39259)
*Jiaheng Chen,Jiaxing Li,Yucheng Xiao,Xinyong Cai,Juncheng Bu,Lan Yu,Tinghe Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Conditional Functional Substitutability (CFS), a new way to directly measure when parts of a neural network can substitute for each other in context, revealing how redundancy and functional organization change with model scale and enabling more efficient, redundancy-aware computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although modern neural networks scale in predictable ways, the underlying reason for these scaling behaviors and diminishing returns is not well understood. Existing notions of redundancy rely on indirect proxies like parameter importance or representational similarity, which do not directly capture when two components actually play the same functional role in computation. The authors want a principled, task-conditional notion of redundancy that explains reorganization with scale and connects directly to computational efficiency and performance.

Method: The authors define Conditional Functional Substitutability (CFS) as a measure of redundancy between intermediate computational states or components based on how interchangeable they are with respect to downstream behavior on given inputs. They operationalize CFS by intervening on model activations or components and evaluating whether substituting one state/component for another preserves downstream outputs. They then compute CFS across layers, attention heads, and other components in multiple Transformer families and modalities, and compare it with traditional importance- and similarity-based redundancy measures. They also perform controlled scaling experiments (varying model size and structure) and train predictors of CFS to enable dynamic, redundancy-aware computation at inference time.

Result: Empirically, CFS uncovers functional relationships and reduction opportunities that are not visible with importance or representational similarity metrics. It shows that as models scale, there is systematic functional reorganization, but improvements in performance do not necessarily correspond to increased substitutability. Models of fixed capacity that organize into more independent functional units achieve higher performance, suggesting that excessive redundancy can hurt effective capacity. Using learned predictors of CFS to select which components to compute on each input yields better performance–compute trade-offs than importance-based selection methods across Transformer architectures and modalities.

Conclusion: Redundancy in neural networks is best understood as an input- and function-dependent relationship between components, not just via static importance or similarity. Conditional Functional Substitutability provides a direct, operational measure of when components are functionally interchangeable. This framework explains aspects of scaling laws and diminishing returns by showing that better performance correlates with more independent functional structure rather than more redundancy. Moreover, predicting CFS enables dynamic inference strategies that exploit redundancy more effectively than prior methods, offering a path toward more efficient, redundancy-aware model design and scaling.

Abstract: Modern neural networks scale predictably, yet the mechanisms behind these regularities remain unclear. Neural redundancy is typically characterized by component importance or representational similarity, both indirect proxies. We view redundancy as an input-conditioned, dynamic relation: intermediate computational states are functionally redundant when they induce similar downstream responses. We introduce Conditional Functional Substitutability (CFS) to directly characterize such functional substitution. CFS exposes functional relations and reduction potential missed by conventional importance- and similarity-based measures. Across modalities and Transformer families, CFS reveals systematic functional reorganization with scale. Controlled scaling further shows that performance gains need not track growth in substitutability, while fixed-capacity models with more independent functional structure perform better, providing a functional account of diminishing returns. Predicted CFS further enables dynamic computation with a better performance--computation trade-off than importance-based component selection, suggesting new directions for redundancy-aware computation and more efficient model scaling.

</details>


### [199] [ANI: Adaptive Numerical Injection for Unifying Semantic and Arithmetic Representations in Numerical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39294)
*Jinsung Jeon,Seung-won Hwang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ANI is a hybrid framework that improves LLMs’ numerical reasoning by selectively injecting precise numerical embeddings only when numbers are used quantitatively, boosting math performance without hurting general language ability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with precise arithmetic because text tokenizers split numbers into multiple tokens, making exact numerical computation difficult. Pure numerical embedding approaches can handle arithmetic better but are context-agnostic and incorrectly treat all numbers as quantitative values, even when they function as identifiers (e.g., phone numbers, IDs). The paper is motivated by the need to unify these two perspectives: retain semantic roles of numbers in context while still providing models with precise numerical information when it is actually needed for reasoning.

Method: The authors introduce ANI (Adaptive Numerical Injection), a framework that augments LLMs with a context-aware gating mechanism. This mechanism decides, for each occurrence of a number, whether and how strongly to inject a dedicated numerical embedding (specifically FoNE, a numerical embedding technique) into the model’s latent representation. If the context suggests the number is a quantitative operand, the gate opens and injects numerical features; if it acts as a nominal identifier, the gate stays closed, preserving its purely symbolic/semantic behavior. The injection happens inside the model’s hidden layers to blend textual and numerical information without altering the tokenizer.

Result: Across multiple LLM backbones, ANI substantially improves performance on math and numerical reasoning benchmarks, with a reported 9.5-point gain on the MATH dataset over the official reference model. At the same time, evaluations on general language understanding benchmarks show that ANI does not degrade, and may maintain, the base models’ performance on non-numerical tasks, indicating that selective injection avoids harming linguistic capabilities.

Conclusion: ANI demonstrates that selectively injecting numerical embeddings based on semantic context can successfully combine precise arithmetic reasoning with strong general language understanding. By introducing a gating mechanism that distinguishes quantitative operands from nominal identifiers, the approach yields large gains on mathematical reasoning tasks while preserving performance on standard linguistic benchmarks. This suggests that future LLM designs should treat numerical representation as a context-dependent hybrid of symbolic and continuous numeric information, rather than relying solely on text tokenization or naive numerical substitution.

Abstract: Precise numerical reasoning with Large Language Models (LLMs) is essential for expanding their applicability to complex real-world tasks. However, text-based tokenization often fragments numbers, significantly hindering precise arithmetic reasoning. Meanwhile, numerical embeddings, despite arithmetic precision, rely on context-agnostic substitution that disregards the semantic role of numbers as identifiers. To combine the complementary strengths, we propose \textbf{ANI (Adaptive Numerical Injection)}, a hybrid framework that governs the selective injection of numerical features based on the semantic context. By employing a context-aware gating mechanism, we selectively inject numerical embeddings (specifically FoNE) into the latent space, explicitly preserving nominal identifiers while enhancing quantitative operands. Through extensive evaluations across various LLMs, we demonstrate that ANI enhances MATH performance by 9.5 points over the official reference model, while maintaining robust performance on general linguistic benchmarks.

</details>


### [200] [MiniRep: Robust Reputation-Based Aggregation for Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39297)
*Jiaming Zhang,Yuwan Liu,Yue Huang,Sisi Duan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MiniRep, a reputation-based answer aggregation method for multi-agent debate with LLM agents, designed to be robust against malicious or strategically behaving agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent reputation and leaderboard systems assume that performance on past tasks predicts behavior on new tasks. In open, agentic ecosystems with adaptive and potentially malicious agents, this assumption fails: agents can game reputation, change behavior over time, and coordinate to manipulate collaborative outcomes. Multi-agent debate frameworks lack robust aggregation mechanisms that account for such adversarial and collusive behaviors.

Method: The authors first build an attack taxonomy for multi-agent settings, drawing from known reputation-system attacks and software-testing mutation operators, to characterize strategic reputation exploitation and subtle corruption of proposals. Based on this taxonomy, they design MiniRep, a reputation-aware aggregation scheme for multi-agent debate in which agents answer, debate, and then aggregate their outputs. MiniRep jointly considers (1) agents’ behavior on the current task and (2) their historical reputation, and it includes mechanisms to detect and limit the influence of groups of agents with highly similar responses so that coordinated groups cannot dominate the final decision.

Result: Across a variety of tasks, agent configurations, corruption placements, and attack types from the taxonomy, MiniRep consistently outperforms standard multi-agent debate aggregation strategies and naive reputation-based methods. On the MATH benchmark, MiniRep yields better performance under both benign and attacked conditions. In a heterogeneous 10-agent setup on MATH, MiniRep surpasses all baseline methods across all 28 evaluated attack scenarios.

Conclusion: Reputation in LLM-based multi-agent systems must be modeled dynamically and adversarially rather than as a simple function of past performance. MiniRep’s joint use of per-task behavior and evolving reputation, combined with defenses against collusion via similarity control, provides a more robust aggregation mechanism for multi-agent debate under malicious agents. This approach strengthens the reliability of collaborative LLM-agent ecosystems in the presence of adaptive adversaries.

Abstract: Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving into an open agentic ecosystem. To support trustworthy collaboration, industry initiatives increasingly assess agent reputation from past behavior and provide performance leaderboards. However, reputation derived from past performance may not reliably predict an agent's behavior on new tasks, particularly when malicious agents can adapt their behavior and influence other agents during collaboration.
  We study reputation in multi-agent debate (MAD), where multiple agents answer the same query, debate to improve their answers, and aggregate them into a final output. We present MiniRep, a reputation-based aggregation system for MAD under malicious agents. To ground our threat model in established research, we construct an attack taxonomy drawing on reputation-system attacks and software-testing mutation operators, covering strategic exploitation of reputation and subtle corruption of agent proposals. Guided by this taxonomy, MiniRep evaluates agents based on both their behavior on the current task and their reputation over time, while preventing groups of agents with highly similar responses from dominating the final decision. We assess MiniRep across diverse tasks, LLM-agent compositions, corruption placements, and attack types drawn from our taxonomy. Our experimental results show that, MiniRep outperforms both conventional MAD aggregation and conventional reputation-based approaches on MATH no matter being attacked or not. Also, under a heterogeneous 10-agent setting on MATH, MiniRep outperforms all baselines in all 28 attack conditions.

</details>


### [201] [WorkGenesis: Building the Worlds That Teach Agents to Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39325)
*Xinyu Zhu,Fenyi Liu,Yuzhu Cai,Shuo Tang,Rui Ye,Linfeng Zhang,Siheng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorkGenesis is a framework that turns real-world occupational artifacts into realistic, executable work tasks for training LLM agents, and models trained on this data outperform comparable and even some frontier models on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are increasingly expected to handle realistic daily and professional work, but existing training data has limitations: expert-authored tasks are expensive and slow to create, while unconstrained synthetic tasks often lack factual grounding and contain inconsistencies. There is a need for a scalable way to generate high-quality, realistic, and internally consistent occupational work scenarios for training working agents.

Method: The paper proposes WorkGenesis, with two key components. (1) Evidence-Based Work Construction: it retrieves real-world public files using O*NET occupational knowledge to ground tasks in authentic artifacts, then synthesizes context, companion materials, a work request, and an itemized rubric around this evidence. (2) Execution-Guided Consistency Verification: it generates a reference deliverable for each constructed task, evaluates rubric satisfaction, attributes any unmet rubric items to issues with the agent, the task, or the rubric, and iteratively edits tasks and rubrics until they pass an audit of internal consistency and executability. The resulting tasks are then used to perform simple supervised fine-tuning of an LLM, Fx-Work-35B.

Result: Using only 20K WorkGenesis-generated work units and simple supervised fine-tuning, the resulting model Fx-Work-35B achieves the best performance among comparable-size baselines across five metrics on GDPvalAA-v2, APEX-Agents-AA, and JobBench, with an average score of 31.00 versus 24.79 for baselines. It also surpasses at least one frontier-scale model, the 1.6T DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Preview, on these benchmarks.

Conclusion: WorkGenesis can automatically synthesize realistic, executable, and internally consistent occupational work scenarios from real-world artifacts at scale. Training an LLM on this data substantially improves its ability to perform work-like tasks, outperforming similarly sized baselines and even some frontier models. This suggests that the proposed framework is an effective and scalable approach to generating training data for capable working agents.

Abstract: The ability of Large Language Model (LLM) agents to complete daily and professional work is receiving increasing attention. Training such agents requires realistic work scenarios. Expert-authored occupational work is costly and slow to produce, while unconstrained synthesis often yields tasks with weak factual grounding or internally inconsistent requirements. To bridge this gap, we introduce WorkGenesis, a framework that constructs executable occupational work from real-world artifacts through two core technical innovations: (1) Evidence-Based Work Construction, which grounds each unit of work in real-world evidence by retrieving public files guided by O*NET occupational knowledge and synthesizing the surrounding context, companion materials, work request, and itemwise rubric around them; and (2) Execution-Guided Consistency Verification, which renders a reference deliverable inside the constructed work, attributes every unsatisfied rubric item to the agent, the task, or the rubric, and uses task and rubric defects as feedback to iteratively repair the work until it passes the audit. Experimental results demonstrate that Fx-Work-35B, trained with simple supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on only 20K units of work synthesized by WorkGenesis, achieves the highest scores among all comparable-scale baselines on the five reported metrics across GDPvalAA-v2, APEX-Agents-AA, and JobBench (31.00 versus 24.79 average score), and even surpasses frontier models such as the 1.6T DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Preview. These results show that WorkGenesis provides scalable training data for working agents.

</details>


### [202] [Understanding as No-Arbitrage: Bounded Dutch Books as a Definition and Training Objective for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39341)
*Daniel Dragonevskiy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formalizes and measures whether language models 'understand' by testing if a bounded trader can exploit logical inconsistencies in their probability assignments, and proposes a training framework (Arbitr) that greatly reduces such exploitability without hurting accuracy, revealing that coherence is necessary but not sufficient for genuine knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is an open conceptual and practical question about whether language models merely predict tokens or genuinely 'understand' the content they produce. Existing metrics focus on accuracy but largely ignore whether probability assignments across logically related statements are globally consistent. This work aims to make 'understanding' operational and measurable by connecting it to no-arbitrage/Dutch book ideas from decision theory, and to diagnose and fix systematic incoherence and overconfidence in LMs that standard next-token training objectives induce.

Method: 1) Define 'understanding' as resistance to arbitrage by a computationally bounded trader who can bet on logically related claims using the model's probabilities; incoherence corresponds to exploitable Dutch books. 2) Prove three theoretical results: that perfect logical coherence is computationally intractable (so understanding must be graded), that exact optimum next-token prediction yields unavoidable incoherence across question formats, and that uncertainty should accumulate along reasoning chains so overconfidence is itself exploitable. 3) Propose Arbitr, a training framework that augments standard training with an adversarial trader that searches for logical inconsistencies and penalizes them, plus a calibration anchor term to avoid trivial uniform predictions. 4) Empirically evaluate Arbitr on Qwen2.5 and Phi-3.5 across five pre-registered experiments, measuring arbitrage-based exploitability under varied phrasings and logical structures, and test cross-pattern and cross-model transfer.

Result: Theoretical analyses show: (a) exact logical coherence is unattainable for bounded agents, so 'understanding' must be a matter of degree; (b) the standard next-token objective inherently leads to incoherence across different question formats; and (c) uncertainty should grow with reasoning depth, making static confidence schedules exploitable. Empirically, standard LMs (Qwen2.5, Phi-3.5) are found to be highly exploitable via Dutch-book-style strategies under paraphrases and format changes. Training with Arbitr reduces such exploitability by orders of magnitude while preserving task accuracy. Moreover, Arbitr-trained coherence generalizes: models become robust to unseen logical patterns and even transfer improvements to other model families. The study also uncovers a 'scaling illusion': larger models can appear logically coherent by some metrics while actually being extremely, unjustifiably overconfident.

Conclusion: The work argues that language model 'understanding' can be usefully defined and measured via Dutch-book-style no-arbitrage conditions on their probability assignments. They show that full coherence is computationally out of reach and that the usual next-token loss objective structurally causes incoherence, especially across formats and long reasoning chains. Their Arbitr framework demonstrates that training directly against arbitrage can dramatically improve logical consistency without hurting accuracy and that this improvement generalizes. However, they emphasize that even perfect probabilistic coherence is only a necessary condition for genuine knowledge, not a sufficient one, as models can be coherently but unjustifiably overconfident. Thus, enforcing coherence is one pillar of understanding, but additional criteria are needed to capture deeper epistemic competence.

Abstract: Does a language model merely predict tokens, or does it understand what it says? We make this question measurable by defining "understanding" through the lens of no-arbitrage. A model understands a vocabulary to a certain degree if a computationally bounded trader cannot extract guaranteed profit by betting against the model's probabilities on logically related claims (a "Dutch book"). We establish three theoretical results: first, because full logical coherence is computationally intractable, understanding is inherently graded, not absolute. Second, we prove that the exact optimum of standard next-token prediction is inherently incoherent across different question formats; the flaw lies in the training objective, not the architecture. Third, we show that uncertainty accumulates predictably along reasoning chains, making unjustified overconfidence an arbitrage opportunity in itself. To address this, we introduce Arbitr, a training framework where an adversarial trader penalizes the model for logical inconsistencies, paired with a calibration anchor to prevent uninformative collapse. Across five pre-registered experiments on Qwen2.5 and Phi-3.5 models, we demonstrate that standard models are highly exploitable across different phrasings. Arbitr reduces this exploitability by orders of magnitude without sacrificing task accuracy, and the effect successfully transfers to unseen logical patterns and new model families. Crucially, we uncover a scaling illusion: at 7B parameters, near-zero measured incoherence often coincides with extreme, unjustified confidence. We conclude that while Arbitr enforces rigorous logical consistency, coherence is a necessary condition for knowledge, but not a sufficient one

</details>


### [203] [The Golden Path Hypothesis: Reusable Schedules in Diffusion Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39343)
*Dong Wang,Wenwu Tang,Francesco Corti,Yun Cheng,Lothar Thiele,Olga Saukh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies “diffusion caching” and proposes that there exist prompt‑independent, ‘golden’ caching schedules that can accelerate diffusion models while preserving output quality across many prompts and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models are computationally expensive at inference because they require many transformer evaluations across denoising steps. Caching or predicting features at some steps can speed them up, but optimal caching schedules appear to depend on the specific prompt. This prompt dependence makes practical deployment difficult. The authors want to know whether there are universal, prompt‑independent schedules that are nearly as good as prompt‑optimized ones, enabling fast and simple acceleration strategies for diffusion models.

Method: They formulate the Golden Path Hypothesis (GPH), asserting that under fixed inference settings, there exist prompt‑independent caching schedules with quality close to the best prompt‑specific schedules. They empirically evaluate ten caching methods on four image and video diffusion models and three cache ratios. They analyze which schedules prompt‑adaptive methods tend to choose, reuse the most frequent schedules on new prompts, and exhaustively search over 1.4M schedules on a few examples. They then analyze denoising trajectories and decompose caching errors to study how errors accumulate over steps, focusing on the relationship between early errors and final latent-state error. Finally, they use small sets of examples and final-output metrics (e.g., reconstruction vs perceptual similarity) to search for ‘golden paths’ that generalize across prompts and datasets.

Result: Prompt-adaptive methods in practice concentrate on a small subset of caching schedules, and simply reusing their most commonly selected schedules for new prompts yields quality close to full prompt-specific adaptation. Exhaustive schedule evaluation on four prompts finds schedules that remain competitive on unseen prompts, supporting the existence of prompt‑independent ‘golden paths’. The trajectory and error analyses reveal that latent denoising paths share similar structure across data and seeds, and that accumulated impact of earlier caching errors is more predictive of final latent error than local approximation error at individual steps. Using end-to-end quality to search for schedules on a small number of examples leads to caching schedules that transfer well across prompts, models, and datasets at chosen cache ratios.

Conclusion: There exist robust, prompt-independent caching schedules—“golden paths”—that can accelerate diffusion model inference while maintaining high output quality across diverse prompts and datasets. Effective schedules tend to be shared across prompts, and their performance is best captured by considering end-to-end effects on final outputs rather than local approximation accuracy. This allows practitioners to pre-compute a small set of golden paths tuned to specific quality objectives (e.g., fidelity or perceptual quality), simplifying deployment of diffusion caching in real systems.

Abstract: Diffusion caching accelerates generation by replacing transformer computation with cached or predicted features at selected denoising steps. We introduce the Golden Path Hypothesis (GPH): under fixed inference conditions, prompt-independent cache schedules can achieve final-output quality comparable to the best prompt-specific schedules across prompts. We investigate the GPH across ten caching methods, four image and video models, and three cache ratios. Prompt-adaptive methods repeatedly select a small number of schedules, and reusing their most frequent schedules on new prompts closely matches the quality of prompt-specific choices. Exhaustive evaluation of 1.4 million schedules on four examples further identifies prompt-independent schedules that remain competitive on unseen prompts. To explain this transfer, we analyze denoising trajectories and the accumulation of caching errors. Latent-state trajectories exhibit similar structures across datasets and seeds, while an exact error decomposition shows that accumulated effects of earlier errors predict final latent-state error better than local approximation errors. This motivates searching for end-to-end schedules using final-output quality. With only a small set of examples, the resulting golden paths transfer across prompts and datasets, and can be tuned to the desired quality objective, including reconstruction fidelity or perceptual similarity.

</details>


### [204] [On the Complexity of Preference-Based Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39351)
*Ahmed Ben Yahmed,Marc Abeille,Clément Calauzènes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They study preference-based bandits with general reward functions under Bradley–Terry feedback, introduce a new complexity measure (locally sensitive eluder dimension), design the GINOP algorithm using log-loss confidence sets, and prove regret bounds showing preference feedback can be as sample-efficient as direct rewards, with supporting experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many applications (recommender systems, tournaments, human feedback), we often observe only relative preferences between items, not absolute rewards. Existing theory for preference-based bandits largely assumes linear or kernelized reward models and suffers from problematic dependence on a problem-specific constant κ that arises from the nonlinearity of logistic/Bradley–Terry feedback. This limits both applicability to richer function classes and yields suboptimal or poorly behaved regret guarantees. The paper aims to develop a general and statistically efficient framework for preference-based bandits with complex reward function classes, overcoming the κ-dependence issue.

Method: They consider a very general class of reward functions but with preference feedback modeled via the Bradley–Terry (logistic) model. To deal with the nonlinear link function, they introduce the locally sensitive eluder dimension, a new complexity measure adapted to the logistic structure.
