Using this, they build GINOP (Generic INformative OPtimism), an optimism-based bandit algorithm that uses log-loss (logistic) confidence sets around reward functions. GINOP jointly chooses which pair of arms to compare in a way that trades off optimistic exploitation with informative exploration, guided by the new complexity notion and confidence sets.

Result: They derive regret bounds for GINOP that are first-order (depending directly on the optimal value and gaps) and scale with the locally sensitive eluder dimension of the function class, without incurring bad dependence on the κ constant from the logistic link. The bounds show that, contrary to previous beliefs suggested by earlier theory, preference-based learning under Bradley–Terry feedback can be as statistically efficient as learning from direct reward observations, up to the new complexity measure. Empirical experiments on benchmark tasks compare GINOP with strong baselines and confirm lower regret and/or better performance consistent with the theory.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that preference-based bandits with Bradley–Terry feedback need not be fundamentally harder than standard reward-based bandits from a statistical efficiency standpoint. By introducing the locally sensitive eluder dimension and the GINOP algorithm with log-loss confidence sets, they provide general regret guarantees for rich function classes, free from unfavorable κ-dependence. Empirical results support the theoretical claims, demonstrating that carefully designed algorithms leveraging the problem structure can make preference-based learning competitive with direct-reward approaches.

Abstract: We study preference-based bandits with general reward function classes, where a learner sequentially selects pairs of arms and observes binary preference feedback governed by the Bradley--Terry model. This setting naturally arises in applications such as recommender systems, tournament ranking, and learning from human feedback, where relative preferences are easier to elicit than absolute rewards. The observation model inherits the logistic bandit challenge of handling the problem-dependent constant $κ$, which accounts for the non-linearity of the link function and can grow arbitrarily large. Moreover, prior work has predominantly focused on linear or kernelized reward models, precluding the use of richer function classes. To address these limitations, we consider general reward function classes and introduce the \emph{locally sensitive eluder dimension}, a novel complexity measure tailored to the logistic structure of preference feedback that yields fine-grained regret guarantees without unfavorable dependence on $κ$. Building on this notion, we propose \textbf{GINOP} (Generic INformative OPtimism), an algorithm that constructs log-loss confidence sets and jointly selects arm pairs to balance optimism and informative exploration. We establish a first-order regret bound that, in contrast with what previous results suggest, demonstrates that learning with preference feedback is as statistically efficient as learning from direct reward observation. Finally, we corroborate our theoretical findings with empirical evaluations against competitive baselines.

</details>


### [205] [Autoresearch in Mixed-Integer Linear and Nonlinear Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39360)
*Yuwei Gu,Yaoxin Wu,Tong Guo,Wen Song,Zhiguang Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoMIP is an autoresearch framework that uses idea pooling and algorithm tree search to solve challenging MILP/MINLP problems more effectively, finding many new best solutions on standard benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autoresearch methods struggle on real-world NP-hard mixed-integer linear and nonlinear programming problems because they cannot easily manage many competing ideas or plan and adapt over long experimental horizons. There is a need for a framework that can systematically explore, refine, and switch between algorithmic ideas over extended research trajectories.

Method: The authors propose AutoMIP, an agent skill that structures autoresearch as two key components: (1) an idea pool that persistently stores diverse, complementary algorithmic ideas and unexplored hypotheses; and (2) an algorithm tree search that organizes experiments into a tree of algorithms, where branches correspond to different methodological directions. The agent uses this structure to run experiments, update the pool, refine promising branches, and revisit or switch directions based on historical performance and states. They evaluate AutoMIP on standard MILP and MINLP benchmark libraries and perform ablation studies to isolate the effects of idea pooling and tree search.

Result: On MILP and MINLP benchmark cohorts, AutoMIP attains the highest final success rates among compared autoresearch systems. On the MIPLib benchmark, it finds new best solutions for 31 out of 60 instances, and on MINLPLib it finds new best solutions for 52 out of 60 instances, outperforming existing autoresearch baselines. Ablation experiments show that removing either idea pooling or algorithm tree search degrades performance, indicating each component’s distinct contribution.

Conclusion: Jointly maintaining a diverse pool of algorithmic ideas and a structured algorithm tree of experimental trajectories enables more effective long-horizon autoresearch in mixed-integer programming. AutoMIP’s design leads to superior performance and discovery of new best solutions on standard MILP and MINLP benchmarks, suggesting that structured idea and experiment management is crucial for scaling autoresearch to complex optimization problems.

Abstract: Despite recent progress in autoresearch, applying it to practical operations research problems, typically formulated as NP-hard mixed-integer linear or nonlinear programs (MILPs or MINLPs), remains challenging because effective research requires systematically managing competing ideas and long-horizon experimental trajectories. We introduce AutoMIP, a reusable agent skill for organizing long-horizon autoresearch in mixed-integer programming through idea pooling and algorithm tree search. AutoMIP maintains a persistent pool of complementary candidate ideas while organizing executable experiments into an algorithm tree, enabling the agent to preserve unexplored hypotheses, refine promising algorithms, and switch to alternative methodological directions based on historical states. On MILP and MINLP benchmark cohorts, AutoMIP achieves the highest final success rates among the evaluated autoresearch frameworks. On MIPLib, AutoMIP discovers new best solutions for 31 of 60 instances, surpassing existing autoresearch frameworks. On MINLPLib, it achieves new best solutions for 52 of 60 instances. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary contributions of idea pooling and algorithm tree search, highlighting the importance of jointly maintaining diverse research ideas and structured experimental trajectories for long-horizon autoresearch.

</details>


### [206] [EHR-RobustGym: Benchmarking and Training Agents for Robust Clinical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39371)
*Yitong Qiao,Yancheng Jin,Lei Liu,Yue Shen,Jian Wang,Jinjie Gu,Zhixuan Chu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EHR-RobustGym is a large-scale interactive benchmark built on MIMIC-IV to evaluate and train clinical LLM agents for robustness to noisy EHR data, showing large robustness gaps and that SFT/RL can substantially improve performance and generalize to external EHR tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical question-answering and decision-support agents rely on EHR data that is inherently noisy or incomplete. Existing benchmarks typically assume clean, curated data and do not stress-test whether models can detect and handle discrepancies between queries and evidence. This leads to plausible but unsupported clinical answers, which is unsafe in practice. The paper aims to create a realistic, large-scale environment to systematically measure and improve the evidence-grounded robustness of clinical agents operating over noisy EHRs.

Method: The authors construct EHR-RobustGym on top of the MIMIC-IV database (365K patients, 31 tables, 500M+ records). They design 5,486 paired clinical questions (Clean vs. Noise) covering six clinical intents and both patient-level and population-level analytics. Noise is injected at three levels: (1) Record-level (e.g., missing or spurious entries), (2) Value-level (e.g., altered lab values), and (3) Query-level (e.g., ambiguous or misleading phrasing). The environment exposes interactive SQL/Python execution with automated outcome verification, enabling collection of agent trajectories and use for supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. They then evaluate several proprietary and open-weight LLM-based agents in this environment and train models with SFT and RL on the collected data.

Result: Across both proprietary and large open-weight LLMs, average task success is 62.2% on Clean questions but drops to 37.9% on Noise questions, indicating major robustness deficits when EHR noise is present. Model consistency is also poor: at k=4 samples per question, pass^k consistency is below 50% for most models, revealing instability in clinical task completion. Applying supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning using the EHR-RobustGym environment leads to significant performance gains, and these gains transfer to five external EHR benchmarks, demonstrating that training on this noisy, interactive testbed improves generalizable robustness.

Conclusion: EHR-RobustGym provides a scalable, realistic, and interactive benchmark for studying and improving how clinical agents reason over noisy EHR data. The observed performance drop and low consistency on noisy queries highlight that current LLM-based clinical agents are far from robust. However, training with SFT and RL in this environment meaningfully enhances robustness and generalizes to other EHR tasks. The authors position EHR-RobustGym as a standard testbed for evaluating and developing evidence-grounded, reliable clinical agents that can better handle the imperfections of real-world hospital data.

Abstract: In hospital workflows, electronic health records (EHRs) are often noisy, and may not contain the evidence needed to confirm events or measurements referenced in a clinical query. Even when database retrieval succeeds, clinical agents can overlook such discrepancies and return plausible but unsupported answers. We introduce EHR-RobustGym, a scalable and interactive environment for evaluating and training robust clinical agents grounded in noisy EHRs. Built on MIMIC-IV hospital records (365K patients, 31 tables, and over 500M records), EHR-RobustGym comprises 5,486 Clean-Noise pairs spanning six clinical intents and both patient-level and population-level queries. The pairs test robustness to Record-level, Value-level, and Query-level noise, while interactive SQL/Python execution and outcome verification support trajectory collection and training. Evaluating multiple LLMs reveals substantial robustness gaps: average task success across proprietary and large-scale open-weight models drops from 62.2% on Clean questions to 37.9% on Noise questions. At k=4, pass^k consistency falls below 50% for most evaluated models, exposing instability in clinical task completion. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in EHR-RobustGym improve performance, with gains generalizing to five external EHR benchmarks. Together, these results position EHR-RobustGym as a testbed for evaluating and improving the evidence-grounded robustness of clinical agents.

</details>


### [207] [SkillFM: Generating Skills for LLM Agents via Latent Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39382)
*Zuming Zhang,Jie He,Yizhe Zhang,Jeff Z. Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SkillFM, a generative framework that learns to synthesize task-conditioned textual skills for LLM agents in a latent space, avoiding manual skill banks and retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent skill systems depend on manually curated skill repositories or reinforcement learning that learns skills indirectly from delayed rewards. Both are costly, brittle, and inefficient, and they do not provide a direct, flexible way to generate textual skills adapted to new tasks. The authors aim to automatically generate reusable, task-specific textual guidance that can plug into existing frozen LLM agents across different domains.

Method: The authors propose SkillFM (Skill Flow Matching), which learns a continuous latent space of textual skills via a codec: a text encoder maps skills to latent representations and a decoder reconstructs them back into natural language. On top of this latent space, they train a conditional flow model using an improved MeanFlow objective to model a velocity field conditioned on the current task. At inference, a single-step sampling in the learned latent space generates a new skill vector, which is then decoded by an LLM into textual guidance. The downstream LLM agent remains frozen and simply consumes the generated textual skill as additional context or instructions.

Result: On embodied environments (ALFWorld), question answering benchmarks (e.g., Search-QA), and web shopping tasks, SkillFM yields higher performance than competing vector-based skill methods. Among the baselines that augment agents with skill vectors or rely on retrieval from a skill bank, SkillFM consistently achieves the best overall results on ALFWorld and Search-QA. Analytical studies confirm that the generative latent skill approach provides competitive or superior gains compared to retrieval-based skill augmentation.

Conclusion: SkillFM demonstrates that directly generating task-conditioned latent skills and decoding them into textual guidance is a powerful alternative to manual or retrieval-based skills for LLM agents. By separating a learned skill generator from a frozen downstream agent, the method improves performance on diverse tasks without requiring test-time skill retrieval or expensive RL training. The results suggest that flow-matching-based latent skill generation is a promising direction for scalable, reusable skill acquisition in LLM-based agents.

Abstract: Textual skills provide reusable guidance for large language model agents, but existing approaches often rely on manually curated skill banks or reinforcement learning with indirect and delayed feedback. We introduce SkillFM (Skill Flow Matching), a generative framework that synthesizes task-conditioned textual skills directly without test-time skill retrieval. Our framework combines a codec for encoding and reconstructing textual skills in a continuous latent space with a conditional flow model trained using improved MeanFlow. At inference time, the learned velocity field enables single-step latent sampling, and an LLM-based decoder converts the sampled representation into textual guidance for a frozen downstream agent. We evaluate the framework on embodied tasks, question answering, and web shopping. On ALFWorld and Search-QA, our method achieves the best overall performance among the compared vector-based skill approaches. Our analyses further demonstrate that latent skill generation is an effective alternative to retrieval-based skill augmentation. Our code and training skill libraries are available at https://github.com/lulushang999/SkillFM.

</details>


### [208] [Experimental Experience Modeling for Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39392)
*Wenda Wei,Yingchen Zhang,Ruqing Zhang,Jiafeng Guo,Daiting Shi,Xueqi Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose Experimental Experience Modeling (EEM), a framework that lets autonomous research agents reuse distilled experience from past experiments, run cheap pilot experiments when prior evidence is lacking, and thereby decide more efficiently which expensive experiments to run, improving performance while reducing computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous research agents can generate hypotheses and run experiments, but experiments are computationally expensive and current systems lack a principled way to decide when an experiment is worth running, especially under uncertainty and limited prior evidence. There is also no systematic method to reuse knowledge from past experimental runs to guide new experimental decisions.

Method: They design EEM, which (1) extracts decision-relevant records from past experimental trajectories, (2) distills them into reusable experiential units, and (3) stores them in an organized experience library. For a new decision about whether to pursue a candidate research direction, EEM retrieves relevant historical experience and evaluates whether it suffices to make a go/no-go decision. If not, EEM runs a targeted, low-cost pilot experiment to acquire the missing decision-relevant experience, then fuses this new experience with retrieved history to decide whether to invest in a full-scale, resource-intensive evaluation. Outcomes from these full runs are again distilled into the experience library, enabling continual accumulation and reuse of experience.

Result: On autonomous research benchmarks, EEM leads to better research outcomes (higher performance on the tasks/benchmarks) while simultaneously lowering model interaction overhead, implying fewer or cheaper experimental calls for comparable or better performance versus baselines without EEM.

Conclusion: EEM provides an effective framework for managing experimental decisions in autonomous research by systematically reusing accumulated experimental experience and acquiring new experience only when needed. This yields improved research performance and lower computational cost, and the experience library becomes richer over time via iterative accumulation of distilled experimental knowledge.

Abstract: Autonomous research agents can generate hypotheses and conduct experiments, but experimentation remains a major source of computational cost. A fundamental challenge is deciding which experiments are worth running, particularly when prior evidence is insufficient to resolve uncertainty. Yet current research agents lack a systematic way to leverage experimental experience when making such decisions. We introduce Experimental Experience Modeling (EEM), a framework for making informed experimental decisions by acquiring, reusing, and accumulating experimental experience. EEM extracts decision-relevant records from earlier experimental trajectories, distills them into reusable experience, and organizes them in an experience library. For a new experimental decision, EEM retrieves relevant historical experience and assesses whether it provides sufficient support for deciding whether a candidate direction warrants further investment. When historical experience is insufficient, EEM conducts a targeted, low-cost pilot experiment to acquire the missing decision-relevant experience on demand. It then combines this newly acquired experience with retrieved historical experience to determine whether the direction warrants full-scale evaluation, which requires substantial resources. The resulting experimental outcomes are further distilled into reusable experience, allowing the library to continually grow through iterative accumulation. Experiments on autonomous research benchmarks show that EEM improves research performance while reducing model interaction overhead, demonstrating the value of reusing accumulated experience and acquiring additional experience only when needed.

</details>


### [209] [Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39394)
*Jipei He,Wenhui Tan,Xiaoyi Yu,Enver Sangineto,Fiorenzo Parascandolo,Rita Cucchiara,Ruihua Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models can reuse computation from earlier conversation turns to improve accuracy on later problems and proposes a lightweight method, STAIR, that leverages attention over stored past activations to boost multi-turn reasoning performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models are typically prompted with conversation history, but it is unclear whether and how the internal computation from earlier turns can reliably help with new problems, especially when those problems are independent but in the same domain. Existing uses of history can sometimes help and sometimes hurt performance. The authors want to understand these effects in a controlled way and design a mechanism that systematically exploits useful past computation while mitigating harmful interference, without retraining or heavily modifying the base model.

Method: (1) They run preliminary experiments where the same current problem is paired with different earlier conversation histories, measuring how retained history affects later-turn accuracy. (2) Using controlled replay, they isolate and analyze the internal state changes (activations) induced by each problem-history pair, examining how representations of the current problem vary across histories. They find that while absolute activations change, relative relationships among current problems are preserved. (3) Based on these insights, they propose STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse), which stores keys and values from earlier response generation in a fixed external bank. During processing of a new query, the model is allowed to attend over this bank. A tiny set of additional parameters (12,288) is trained to learn how to redirect current queries to useful stored representations. The original base LLM weights remain frozen; only the STAIR module is learned.

Result: Experiments on three Qwen models across four benchmarks show that simply keeping history can both improve and degrade later-turn accuracy, confirming the mixed effect of retained computation. When augmented with STAIR, the models achieve consistent gains on later-turn problems, with average accuracy improvements up to 11.67 percentage points compared to the same models using history but no STAIR mechanism.

Conclusion: Retained conversation history in large language models induces internal state changes that affect subsequent problem solving, but these effects are not uniformly beneficial. By explicitly capturing and reusing past keys and values via an external attention bank, STAIR can exploit useful structure in prior computations while keeping the base model frozen and adding only a small number of parameters. This leads to substantial improvements in later-turn reasoning accuracy, demonstrating that structured inter-query reuse is a promising direction for enhancing multi-turn LLM performance.

Abstract: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? To answer this question, we first conduct preliminary experiments showing that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To understand these effects, we use controlled replay to isolate internal state changes specific to each problem-history pairing. Across different histories, these changes preserve similar relationships among current problems. To improve reasoning under retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). STAIR captures keys and values from earlier response generation in a fixed bank. It learns to redirect current queries when they read this bank during prompt processing. The base model remains frozen; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history.

</details>


### [210] [Advancing Entropy-Level Credit Assignment in RLVR via Proximal Entropy Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39402)
*Yun Kim,Nojun Kwak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Proximal Entropy Policy Optimization (PEPO), a method that uses a local, context-relative entropy measure to weight token-level advantages in RL for language models, outperforming GRPO and global-entropy baselines on math reasoning and extending to other RL setups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing value-model-free RLVR methods like GRPO assign the same learning signal (advantage) to all tokens in a generated sequence, even though different tokens contribute differently to final performance. Recent attempts to fix this use token entropy as a proxy for importance, but they compute entropy globally across the batch, which entangles actual token importance with confounders such as prompt difficulty and positional effects. There is a need for a principled, token-level importance measure that is robust to these confounders and better targets learning to influential tokens.

Method: The authors define a new importance metric called proximal entropy, which measures a token’s entropy relative to its local neighborhood in the sequence, rather than across the whole batch. They provide a theoretical analysis showing that this local, relative measure is invariant to confounding factors like global prompt difficulty and systematic positional trends. They then build Proximal Entropy Policy Optimization (PEPO), a policy-gradient RL algorithm that uses proximal entropy to weight per-token advantages in value-model-free RL with verbal rewards (RLVR). They further plug proximal entropy into other existing RL algorithms and evaluate it in both standard multi-token RL and single-stream RL settings.

Result: PEPO consistently outperforms GRPO and global-entropy-based importance weighting methods on math reasoning benchmarks using several language models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). When proximal entropy is substituted into other RL algorithms, those methods also show improved performance, indicating the general utility of the proximal entropy importance signal. In single-stream RL, where global entropy-based methods fail, using proximal entropy leads to successful training, demonstrating robustness of the local importance formulation.

Conclusion: Measuring token importance via a local, context-relative entropy (proximal entropy) provides a more reliable signal than global batch entropy for value-model-free RL with language models. By weighting token-level advantages with proximal entropy, PEPO better focuses learning on influential tokens, leading to superior performance on mathematical reasoning tasks and more stable, effective training across different RL algorithms and settings, including challenging single-stream RL scenarios.

Abstract: Value-model-free RLVR methods such as GRPO assign uniform advantages to all tokens in a rollout, ignoring that tokens contribute unequally. Recent methods use token entropy as an importance proxy but compute it globally across the batch, conflating importance with prompt difficulty and positional trends. We argue that importance should instead be measured relative to the local context of each token. We introduce proximal entropy, a local measure of token importance relative to neighboring tokens, and prove it is invariant to both confounders. Proximal Entropy Policy Optimization (PEPO) uses it to weight per-token advantages and outperforms GRPO and entropy-based baselines on mathematical reasoning across Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. We also show the formulation generalizes to other algorithms where substituting proximal entropy into existing methods improves, and applying it to single-stream RL succeeds where global entropy fails.

</details>


### [211] [Inferring Causal Relations between Two Sequences of Events with Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39406)
*Nishchal Prasad,Eric Gaussier,Emilie Devijver,Alexander Obeid Guzman,Armen Aghasaryan,Gregor Gössler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper explores using Large Language Models to infer causal relations between two event sequences when only single observations are available, outperforming standard causal discovery methods on various time-series datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional causal discovery methods usually require many observations and cannot be applied effectively when only single or very few event sequences are available. However, in many real-world scenarios, such as online monitoring of alarm streams or rare abnormal phenomena, one only observes short, unique sequences that must be analyzed on the fly. There is a need for methods that can extract causal information from such limited data, moving beyond associations to genuine understanding of causal structure. The authors are motivated to see whether the implicit knowledge and predictive power of Large Language Models can be leveraged to fill this gap.

Method: The authors represent causal structure as directed graphs over events or variables and focus on the challenging regime where only a single observed sequence is available for each pair of event streams. They encode pairs of event sequences into a textual or structured prompt suitable for a Large Language Model and query the LLM for judgments about likely causal direction or presence/absence of causality. They then compare the inferred causal relations from the LLM with those from standard causal discovery algorithms that are normally designed for multivariate time-series or multiple observations, applied after converting the time series data into smaller, single-observation sequences. The evaluation is conducted on both synthetic datasets with known ground-truth causal structures and real-world time-series data, measuring accuracy and related metrics for causal edge recovery.

Result: Across several datasets, the LLM-based method is able to infer causal relations between two event sequences more accurately than standard causal discovery algorithms that are forced to operate in the single-observation or reduced-data regime. On synthetic data, the approach better recovers the known causal directions and structures, while on real data it achieves improved performance in identifying likely causal influences in alarm/event streams. The results show that LLMs can successfully exploit their pre-trained world knowledge and pattern recognition capabilities to infer plausible causal links even when classical methods are starved of statistical information.

Conclusion: The study concludes that Large Language Models can be effectively used as causal discovery tools in scenarios where only one or very few observations are available, a setting where traditional causal discovery methods struggle. By leveraging LLMs’ predictive abilities and implicit knowledge, the proposed approach extracts useful causal information from pairs of event sequences and achieves superior performance to standard algorithms on both synthetic and real time-series data. This suggests a promising new direction for integrating LLMs into causal AI pipelines, especially for online monitoring, anomaly detection, and other applications characterized by limited or rare observational data.

Abstract: Causal AI is a branch of Artificial Intelligence which helps understand and reason about cause and effect relationships, not just patterns or correlations. Causal discovery aims to infer elements of the underlying causal structure--often represented as a directed graph--from observational and, when available, interventional data. While causal discovery is the fundamental step for moving beyond mere associations toward genuine understanding, and thus the basic building block of causal AI, it becomes intrinsically difficult when causal relations must be inferred from single observations. In such situations, standard causal discovery methods cannot be used and one has to identify causal relations from limited amount of information. This is typically the case for, e.g., sequences of events produced by different alarms which need to be analyzed on the fly to detect abnormal phenomena, which are usually rare. We show in this study that it is possible to leverage the predictive power of Large Language Models (LLMs) to infer causal relations between only two sequences of events. This approach, which is validated on both synthetic and real data, provides better results than standard causal discovery algorithms on several time series data, even though these data were converted into smaller, single observed sequences.

</details>


### [212] [Beyond the Shadows of Plato's Cave: Evaluating False Memory in Autonomous Agents via Counterfactual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39473)
*Quan M. Tran,Zhuo Huang,Zhen Fang,Jing Zhang,Mingming Gong,Tongliang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces FAME, a training-free framework to detect and evaluate false memory in autonomous agents by tracking how their internal belief representations change under counterfactual interventions, achieving strong performance across multiple reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents increasingly use memory to generalize to new environments, but this makes them vulnerable to false memories—internally held beliefs that are wrong due to spurious correlations, environment shifts, or conflicting knowledge. Existing evaluations struggle to distinguish such false memories from standard generalization errors, especially because they are tied to internal belief states rather than just outputs. There is a need for a principled, practical way to detect and measure false memory in agents without retraining them or relying purely on answer correctness.

Method: The authors formalize false memory as biased internal beliefs arising from memory in unseen environments. They propose FAME, a training-free evaluation framework that uses counterfactual reasoning: they construct counterfactual scenarios that hypothetically intervene on the latent memory-related concept and observe how the agent’s beliefs (captured via hidden states before answer generation) evolve. By estimating latent concepts from hidden states and measuring concept drift under these counterfactual interventions, FAME quantifies whether the underlying memory is faithful or false, without designing rewards or relying on output sampling. They provide counterfactual templates to systematically generate such scenarios.

Result: Empirical experiments show that simply monitoring agents’ answers is often insufficient to detect false memory. FAME attains AUROC scores between 76.2% and 96.7% across various false-memory settings and surpasses the best baseline methods by 3.4%–23.3% on multiple realistic benchmarks, including math reasoning (GSM-Symbolic), code generation (GitChameleon), and complex reasoning (BigBench-Hard).

Conclusion: The paper concludes that internal belief dynamics under counterfactual interventions provide a strong signal for identifying false memories in autonomous agents. FAME offers an effective, training-free mechanism for evaluating false memory that outperforms output-based and other baselines across diverse tasks. The released counterfactual templates and benchmarks are intended to support further research on understanding and mitigating false memory in memory-augmented agents.

Abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on memory to generalize beyond their training environments. However, agents are bounded by what they have seen and believed, and leveraging such memories in unseen environments can introduce biases into their internal beliefs. We formalize this phenomenon as \textit{false memory}, which can arise from spurious correlations, environment shifts, and knowledge conflicts. Despite its importance, false memory is difficult to evaluate because it stems from agent internal beliefs and is easily confounded with ordinary generalization failures. Therefore, we propose FAME, a training-free framework that evaluates false memory through the evolution of agent beliefs under counterfactual reasoning. Specifically, counterfactual scenarios reveal how beliefs change as the latent concept of memory shifts under hypothetical interventions; thus, measuring the resulting concept drift provides a signal for distinguishing faithful versus false memory. Such concepts can be estimated from agent hidden states before answer generation, avoiding the need for reward design or answer sampling. Empirical experiments reveal that simply monitoring answers often fails to detect false memory, while FAME achieves AUROCs of 76.2% - 96.7% across false-memory settings, and outperforms the best baseline by 3.4% - 23.3% across realistic benchmarks, spanning math reasoning (GSM-Symbolic), code generation (GitChameleon), and complex reasoning (BigBench-Hard). We further release corresponding counterfactual templates and facilitate future research on false memory.

</details>


### [213] [Who Owns That? Evaluating Ownership Intuitions in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39483)
*Xizhi Xiao,Yue Wu,Shan Xu,Jia Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines how large language models (LLMs) assign ownership in situations with competing claims, comparing them to humans, and finds that while aggregate similarity is high, models show less diversity and different contextual sensitivities than people.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems increasingly interact with people and their property, they must navigate social norms around ownership, especially in ambiguous or contested cases. Current evaluations mostly look at overall similarity to human judgments, but it is unknown how LLMs behave when multiple, conflicting ownership claims exist and whether they match the variability and context dependence of human reasoning in these situations.

Method: The authors design the Competing Ownership Attribution Task (COAT), a set of 42 scenarios involving competing ownership claims. They collect ownership allocations from 108 human participants and from 24 different LLM configurations. They then compare humans and models on multiple dimensions: similarity of ownership allocations, degree of homogeneity vs. diversity across respondents, how ownership is divided within a single answer, clustering of viewpoints across respondents, and how allocations change with contextual factors such as material value and public recognition of later holders as owners.

Result: Humans and LLMs show similar overall ownership allocations at a coarse level, with human–model similarity approaching human–human similarity. However, LLMs exhibit greater homogeneity in their judgments than humans. Within individual responses, models tend to split ownership more evenly among claimants than humans. Across all configurations, LLMs produce more scenarios with a shared, consensus-like judgment and fewer scenarios with distinct viewpoint clusters than humans. In scenarios where humans diverge into viewpoint groups, LLMs often converge on a single or intermediate perspective. Contextual sensitivity also differs: as material value increases, models reduce allocations to creators less than humans do; when later holders are more publicly recognized as owners, models increase allocations to them whereas humans’ allocations slightly decrease.

Conclusion: LLMs can approximate average human ownership judgments but fail to reflect the full diversity, clustering, and context dependence found in human reasoning about competing ownership claims. This limits their adequacy for socially aware applications that must handle contested or normatively plural cases. The authors argue that future work should go beyond aggregate human-model similarity and explicitly model the range and situational variability of human judgments if AI systems are to interact robustly and fairly with human ownership norms.

Abstract: Ownership establishes rights over the use, control, and transfer of objects. Understanding these relations is essential for AI systems to interact appropriately with people and their resources. Yet how large language models (LLMs) attribute ownership under competing claims remains unclear. We introduce the Competing Ownership Attribution Task (COAT), comprising 42 scenarios, and compare ownership allocations from 24 LLM configurations with those of 108 human participants. Overall, human-model similarity is close to human-human similarity, but models show greater homogeneity in their ownership judgments. Within individual answers, models also divide ownership more evenly among claimants than humans do. Pooling responses across model configurations reveals more scenarios with a shared judgment and fewer with distinct viewpoint groups than in humans. When humans form distinct groups, models may converge on one viewpoint or between competing viewpoints. Further comparisons reveal different contextual sensitivities. As material value increases across scenarios, allocations to creators decline less sharply in models than in humans. Across scenarios differing in public recognition of later holders as owners, allocations to these holders increase in models but decrease slightly in humans. Together, these findings suggest that the evaluated LLM responses do not fully capture the diversity of participants' ownership judgments or how those judgments vary across situations. Developing socially capable AI therefore requires moving beyond overall similarity to capture the diversity and context dependence of human judgments.

</details>


### [214] [Disentangling Self-Distillation: Measuring and Modeling Acquisition and Retention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39494)
*Luis Zuin,Alexis Huet,Dario Rossi,Zied Ben Houidi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper systematically studies self-distillation with privileged context in language model adaptation, providing a unified framework that disentangles three key design axes and empirically characterizes their effects on acquisition-retention trade-offs across tasks and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-distillation methods for language models vary along several design choices—rollout source, teacher coupling, and KL direction—but these factors have usually been explored only in fixed, entangled combinations. This has led to conflicting empirical findings and unclear guidance on how to tune self-distillation for different tasks, especially when new behavior conflicts with pretrained behavior. The authors aim to disentangle and unify these methods, provide a clear taxonomy, and offer principled insights into how each axis affects learning new tasks (acquisition) while preserving prior capabilities (retention).

Method: The authors introduce a unified formal framework (taxonomy) for self-distillation with privileged context that captures three orthogonal axes: (i) rollout source (student vs teacher trajectories), (ii) teacher coupling (frozen teacher vs exponential moving average of the student with varying coupling rates), and (iii) KL divergence direction (reverse vs forward KL). They then instantiate all combinations of these choices and compare them to standard supervised fine-tuning. Using two base models (Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B), they perform around 1,200 adaptation runs across both ordinary and deliberately contradictory tasks, measuring acquisition and retention. Additionally, they construct a controlled theoretical/modeling abstraction of the learning objective to analytically explain the empirical acquisition–retention trade-offs and reproduce the observed trends.

Result: Empirically, they find: (i) The rollout source (teacher vs student) significantly affects performance primarily on tasks that contradict the model’s pretrained behavior: using teacher rollouts leads to much higher acquisition than student rollouts while leaving retention almost unchanged. (ii) Teacher coupling (the EMA rate) is the dominant factor for acquisition across all tasks: acquisition improves as coupling rate increases, up to a task-dependent optimum, beyond which it declines. (iii) The effect of KL direction on retention is model-dependent: changing from reverse to forward KL induces retention losses in one of the evaluated models but not in the other, implying that the most impactful axis to tune can differ between models. Their controlled model reproduces these three patterns, supporting the interpretation of the empirical results.

Conclusion: Self-distillation with privileged context can be organized under a unified framework defined by rollout source, teacher coupling, and KL direction, and each axis has a distinct, interpretable role in the acquisition–retention trade-off. Teacher rollouts are especially beneficial when learning behaviors that contradict pretraining, teacher coupling is the primary lever for controlling acquisition, and the importance of KL direction depends on the base model. The controlled model’s alignment with empirical outcomes suggests these design axes are fundamental levers for systematically optimizing language model adaptation rather than relying on ad hoc or conflicting heuristics.

Abstract: Self-distillation with privileged context adapts a language model from demonstrations by letting the model, once conditioned on a reference response, teach its context-free copy token by token. Our taxonomy reveals existing methods differ along three entangled axes: (i) the rollout source (student or teacher), (ii) the teacher coupling (frozen, or an exponential moving average of the student at some coupling rate) and (iii) the KL direction (reverse or forward), yet these axes are usually studied in fixed combinations and have led to conflicting conclusions. We formalize a unifying framework to encompass all self-distillation methods vs classic supervised fine-tuning: we train every combination of the three axes, on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs, to systematically investigate the impact of the above axes. We propose a controlled model of the same objective to explain the resulting acquisition-retention trade-offs. We find that (i) the rollout source matters mostly where the task contradicts the pretrained behavior: there teacher rollouts raise acquisition well above what student rollouts achieve, with almost no change in retention; (ii) the teacher coupling changes acquisition most, on every task: acquisition rises with the coupling rate, then falls past a task-specific rate; (iii) switching the KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other so which axis to tune first depends on the model. The controlled model reproduces the three trends.

</details>


### [215] [Referential Uncertainty in Human--AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39518)
*Christian Poelitz,Finale Doshi-Velez,Siân Lindley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how AI systems can recognize and communicate uncertainty about which object is being referred to in collaborative tasks, and how that affects human-AI teamwork.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In collaborative tasks, humans and AI must refer to the same objects, but references can be ambiguous due to vague descriptions, similar objects, or different viewpoints. Current AI models are often overconfident and do not communicate uncertainty well, which can mislead human partners. The paper aims to understand and improve how AI represents and externalizes referential uncertainty so that humans can make better decisions when collaborating with AI.

Method: The authors design a collaborative puzzle task where a human Helper instructs an AI Worker (a vision-language model) to place pieces. They compare two ways of measuring the AI’s uncertainty over candidate pieces: (1) raw action-token probabilities and (2) a separately elicited belief distribution over pieces. They evaluate calibration (ECE) and discrimination (AUROC) across three frontier VLMs (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5). They manipulate instruction vagueness and presence of competing referents, and measure how often models ask for clarification. They also run a controlled human-subject experiment (N=210) where humans see either the Worker’s default messages or messages augmented with more precise descriptions or hedged explanations tied to the model’s internal uncertainty, and then decide whether to accept or reject the Worker’s moves.

Result: The elicited belief distribution is substantially better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and better at discriminating correct from incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) than raw action probabilities, which are overconfident (mean confidence 0.97, ECE 0.44). Elicited uncertainty increases with instruction vagueness but not reliably with the presence of competing referents, even though such referents raise error rates. Models rarely externalize their uncertainty, requesting clarification in only 3.5–16.7% of turns. In the human study, participants who only see the Worker’s default message accept 78% of wrong placements and show no ability to distinguish right from wrong moves (AUC 0.50). Providing precise descriptions and especially well-targeted hedges reduces acceptance of wrong moves to 36% while maintaining high acceptance of correct ones. However, when hedges are automatically triggered based on belief entropy, they mirror the underlying uncertainty signal’s weaknesses and can degrade performance.

Conclusion: Referential uncertainty is both common and under-communicated in current vision-language models. A separately elicited belief distribution offers a more reliable internal representation of uncertainty than action-token probabilities, but models rarely leverage this to ask for clarification or hedge appropriately. Human partners are easily misled by confident-sounding AI, yet can benefit significantly when uncertainty is accurately and selectively externalized through precise descriptions and targeted hedges. However, naïve, deployable heuristics (e.g., entropy-based hedging) may harm collaboration if they do not track true error likelihood. Effective human-AI collaboration requires both well-calibrated internal uncertainty representations and carefully targeted communication of that uncertainty.

Abstract: Effective human-AI collaboration requires partners to establish references through interaction, which becomes fragile when descriptions are ambiguous, similar referents compete, or partners see different things. We study referential uncertainty - uncertainty over which candidate object a description refers to - in a collaborative puzzle task where a human Helper instructs an AI Worker to place pieces. The Worker must identify and communicate its uncertainty, and the Helper must recognize and act on it. We show that a separately elicited belief distribution over candidate pieces is better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and better discriminates correct from incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) than raw action-token probabilities, which are severely overconfident (0.97 mean confidence, ECE 0.44). Across three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5), this elicited uncertainty rises predictably with instruction vagueness, but not with competing referents in context, even when those increase errors. The models seldom externalize it, asking for clarification on only 3.5-16.7% of turns. In a controlled human study (N=210), participants given only the Worker's default message accept 78% of wrong placements and cannot tell right from wrong (AUC 0.50). Precise descriptions and, especially, well-targeted hedges cut wrong-move acceptance to 36% while largely preserving correct-move acceptance, compensating for missing shared awareness such as not seeing the Worker's action. But this benefit depends on targeting: a deployable hedge derived from the model's own belief entropy inherits that signal's weakness and can do more harm than good. Externalized uncertainty helps a human partner only when it is accurately targeted.

</details>


### [216] [Growing an Agent/Prover Interface: Evolutionary Tool Design for Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving in Rocq and Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39544)
*Jules Viennot,Guillaume Baudart,Marc Lelarge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They evolve a better machine–computer proof (MCP) server interface for theorem-proving agents, showing it improves success rate and efficiency on Rocq and transfers to Lean.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI theorem-proving agents rely on interfaces to proof assistants (like Rocq/Coq and Lean) that were originally designed for humans. These interfaces control what information the agent sees and how expensive each interaction is, but they are not optimized for performance, cost, or speed of agents. A more suitable, systematically designed interface could significantly boost automated proof search and reduce resource usage.

Method: They introduce an evolutionary optimization framework where a strong “frontier” model proposes modifications or new features for the MCP server interface. Proposed changes are evaluated by measuring how much they help smaller target models on a curated set of math problems. Only changes that improve overall performance (success rate, cost, time) are kept and accumulated, effectively “growing” a specialized MCP server (named rme) for Rocq. They then benchmark agents using rme against baselines: a minimal interface exposing only the Rocq compiler and an existing MCP server. Finally, they port the evolved interface to Lean and test cross-system transfer.

Result: On the held-out test split of the miniF2F-Rocq benchmark, agents using the evolved rme server outperform both the Rocq-compiler-only baseline and an established MCP server. This improvement holds across four different language models from two model families and spans success rate, cost per solved problem, and time per solved problem. When the learned interface is ported to Lean and applied to a subset of PutnamBench, it also reduces cost and time per solve, indicating some degree of transferability, though the abstract doesn’t quantify success-rate changes there.

Conclusion: Automatically evolving the interaction interface between AI agents and proof assistants leads to a more effective MCP server than hand-designed alternatives. The evolved Rocq server rme improves theorem-proving success, reduces compute cost, and accelerates solves, and its design partially transfers to Lean. This suggests that AI–tool interfaces themselves are valuable optimization targets and that evolutionary search guided by a strong frontier model can systematically discover beneficial interaction patterns for automated theorem proving.

Abstract: Recent achievements in AI-assisted mathematics require intensive interaction of agents with proof assistants to generate machine-checked proof certificates. Agents interact with proof assistants such as Rocq or Lean through an interface that controls what the agent receives from the prover and the cost of these interactions. Today, these interfaces are adapted from tools designed for humans and not optimized for agents. We propose an evolutionary method where a frontier model incrementally proposes new features and only keeps the ones that improve the overall performance of smaller models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by growing, on a curated set of mathematical problems, \rme, a new MCP server for the Rocq prover. On the held-out \texttt{test} split of miniF2F-Rocq, an agent equipped with \rme outperforms both the baseline that only exposes the Rocq compiler and an established MCP server, across four models from two families, in success rate, cost per solve, and time per solve. Although evolved for Rocq, the resulting server transfers to Lean, improving cost and time per solve on a subset of PutnamBench. We release \rme and its port to Lean.

</details>


### [217] [RankEvolve: A Reliable Multi-Agent Auto-Research Harness for Evolving Ranking Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39551)
*Zheng Chen,Linfeng Liu,Hong Li,Hong Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RankEvolve is an auto-research framework that uses a runtime-enforced protocol and heterogeneous composition of coding agents to reliably evolve generative ranking models, significantly improving execution accuracy and recommendation quality while tracking knowledge across iterations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Auto-research agents can in principle automate the ML experimentation loop, but in practice they frequently introduce subtle execution errors (data leakage, miswired training/eval flags, missing normalization, broken gradients) that silently invalidate expensive runs, especially over many iterations. There is a need for a systematically controlled execution framework that can orchestrate multiple coding agents, detect and repair errors, and maintain rigorous experimental integrity over long-running research workflows.

Method: The authors design RankEvolve, centered on an Executable Operating Protocol (EOP) that specifies phases, gates, branches, and loops of the experimental process as a state machine, which the runtime strictly enforces. They build a meta-meta-harness that treats entire coding-agent products (e.g., Claude Code, Codex) as black-box nodes in an execution graph, where these heterogeneous agents review and repair each other’s outputs. A knowledge layer records and propagates findings, including negative results, across iterations. They then evaluate execution accuracy using an oracle benchmark (ExecML-HSTU) derived from real incidents, compare heterogeneous composition against single-agent baselines under matched budgets, deploy the system on the HSTU recommender for multiple iterations, and test transfer to a LitGPT split, including ablations on instruction injection strategies.

Result: Heterogeneous composition of coding agents under the RankEvolve framework raises all-oracle execution accuracy from 45.8% (best single-product baseline) to 62.5% (+16.7 percentage points, 95% CI [6.6, 26.7]) while maintaining a 10.4% rate of silent critical defects. In a 12-iteration deployment on the open-source HSTU recommender, RankEvolve improves NDCG@10 to 0.2192 on MovieLens-20M LARGE (+4.48% over the published anchor) and 0.1948 on BASE (+2.80%). On a pre-specified LitGPT transfer split, the heterogeneous-composition effect generalizes, yielding a +12.5 point execution-accuracy gain (95% CI [3.0, 22.0]). Paired ablations separate the contribution of per-step instruction injection from that of the full protocol.

Conclusion: RankEvolve shows that enforcing a structured executable protocol and composing multiple heterogeneous coding agents at runtime can markedly improve execution accuracy in auto-research workflows and lead to measurable performance gains in real ML systems such as recommenders. The results suggest that runtime-controlled agent composition, backed by a knowledge layer and rigorous benchmarks, is an effective strategy for reducing silent execution defects and scaling automated experimentation beyond a single model or domain. The work also clarifies under what conditions such composition is beneficial, informing future designs of auto-research and agentic ML frameworks.

Abstract: Auto-research agents, LLM systems that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes across iterations, promise to automate applied ML's experimental loop. Over long horizons, execution accuracy is a binding constraint: a change can silently leak held-out data, omit normalization, disconnect a gradient, or leave a train/eval flag unwired, invalidating expensive runs and compounding error across iterations. We present RankEvolve, an auto-research framework for evolving generative ranking models. An Executable Operating Protocol (EOP) declares phases, gates, branches, and loops, and the runtime enforces the compiled state machine. A meta-meta-harness composes complete black-box coding-agent products, including Claude Code and Codex, as execution-graph nodes that review and repair one another's work. In a budget-matched evaluation, heterogeneous composition raises all-oracle execution accuracy from the best single-product baseline of 45.8 percent to 62.5 percent (paired +16.7 points, 95 percent CI [6.6, 26.7]) while achieving a 10.4 percent silent critical-defect rate. An implemented knowledge layer carries findings, including negative results, across iterations. In a twelve-iteration deployment on the open-source HSTU recommender, RankEvolve reported NDCG@10 of 0.2192 on MovieLens-20M LARGE (+4.48 percent over the published anchor) and 0.1948 on BASE (+2.80 percent). ExecML-HSTU, seeded by incidents from that deployment, provides the oracle benchmark for the execution-accuracy evaluation. A pre-specified LitGPT transfer split replicates the heterogeneous-composition effect beyond recommendation (+12.5 points, 95 percent CI [3.0, 22.0]), and a paired ablation isolates per-step from full-protocol instruction injection. These results characterize when runtime-controlled composition of coding-agent products improves execution accuracy.

</details>


### [218] [Divide and Collapse: MAPF-Collapse via Exact Decomposition into Independent Sub-Instances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39559)
*Oren Salzman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They optimize existing multi-agent paths by removing redundant moves, decomposing the problem into mostly independent subproblems to solve it much faster than the prior ILP-based Judgelight approach while keeping solution quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern learning-based MAPF solvers often generate feasible but inefficient plans containing redundant moves; improving these plans (MAPFC) is NP-hard and existing ILP-based solutions like Judgelight reason over all agents jointly, making them slow and dependent on commercial ILP solvers. There is a need for a faster, exact post-optimizer that better exploits the problem structure.

Method: They observe that MAPFC instances naturally decompose into largely independent sub-problems, usually involving only a single agent. They (1) analyze the given MAPF plan to detect which agents must coordinate, (2) partition the instance into independent subproblems, (3) solve non-coordinating cases with an ultra-lightweight specialized solver that is about 1,900x faster than Judgelight, and (4) solve coordinating cases with either Judgelight or a new CBS-like solver more efficient on easier coordination problems. They also propose a hybrid, regime-aware planner that selectively falls back to Judgelight in coordination-heavy instances.

Result: Their framework is exact and avoids commercial ILP solvers. On coordination-light instances, it matches Judgelight’s solution quality while being much faster (with the single-agent solver roughly 1,900x faster in its regime). On coordination-heavy instances, their hybrid approach chooses between the CBS-like solver and Judgelight. Across all tested benchmarks, the overall planner yields a median 10.5x per-instance speedup over Judgelight while preserving solution quality.

Conclusion: Exploiting the natural decomposition structure of MAPFC allows most instances to be solved via simple, mostly single-agent reasoning, drastically reducing runtime without sacrificing optimality. A combination of lightweight specialized solvers for independent subproblems and judicious use of heavier joint solvers for the few truly coupled parts yields a practical, exact, and significantly faster alternative to the existing ILP-based Judgelight method.

Abstract: In this work we study the problem of MAPFC, a post-optimization step for Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) plans where we are given a feasible plan produced by a modern MAPF solver and are tasked with removing avoidable moves while preserving feasibility. This NP-hard problem naturally arises when using learning-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) solvers which construct plans that contain redundant moves that can be removed. Recently, Tang et al. presented Judgelight, which uses Integer Linear Programming (ILP) to solve MAPFC. Importantly, the ILP is constructed over all agents jointly, so its cost is governed by the full instance rather than by the small coupled residue that actually requires joint reasoning. Our key insight, motivating this work, is that MAPFC instances naturally decompose into independent sub-problems, most of which involve a single agent and can be solved without any inter-agent reasoning. To this end, we first identify which agents need to coordinate their motion and partition the instance into sub-problems accordingly. For the cases where no coordination is required, we introduce an extremely lightweight solver that is $\approx\!1{,}900\times$ faster than Judgelight. For cases where coordination is required, Judgelight can be used but we introduce an alternative CBS-like solver which is more efficient on easier problems. The resulting framework is exact, uses no commercial ILP solver, and matches Judgelight's quality while running substantially faster on the coordination-light majority of instances; on the coordination-heavy instances we propose a regime-aware hybrid planner that falls back to Judgelight. Over all benchmarks tested, this planner achieves a median $10.5\times$ per-instance speedup over Judgelight.

</details>


### [219] [A2Z GameSpec-Bench: How Faithfully Can Coding Agents Generate Games from Game Design Specifications?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39564)
*Seonho Lee,Wonryeol Jeong,Alberto Cereser,Inha Kang,Hyeonjong Kim,Seungmin Kwak,Dongmin Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces A2Z GameSpec-Bench, a benchmark of 100 long-form Game Design Documents (GDDs) to evaluate how well coding agents can develop full games that faithfully follow complex specifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing game-development benchmarks use short, simple specs and don’t test whether agents can follow long, interdependent requirements across game logic, rendering, and player interaction. As agents are increasingly used for full application development, we need a way to measure if they preserve the intended design, not just generate plausible code.

Method: The authors build a benchmark of 100 long-form GDDs and convert each into a dependency-aware contract with explicit rules, constraints, and prerequisite relations between requirements. They evaluate agents by combining source-code inspection with agent-generated test policies for scenario-based replay and adaptive playtesting, checking whether both the code and actual gameplay satisfy the contracts. The contracts and requirement-level judgments remain fixed across agents and revision rounds, enabling consistent comparison and failure detection. They also compare different feedback strategies, including requirement-specific feedback versus generic self-revision.

Result: Experiments show that current coding agents have difficulty jointly satisfying interdependent requirements that span implementation and gameplay. Providing requirement-specific feedback improves GDD fidelity scores by 10.9% compared to agents doing only self-revision over two rounds.

Conclusion: A2Z GameSpec-Bench offers a more realistic, end-to-end way to evaluate specification-following in game development, going beyond code-only metrics. It reveals current agents’ limitations on complex, interdependent requirements and shows that structured, requirement-level feedback can significantly improve fidelity, making the benchmark useful both for evaluation and for guiding more faithful game development by agents.

Abstract: Delegating complete application development to coding agents requires preserving the intended design rather than simply producing plausible outputs through naive prompting. Game development provides a demanding testbed, as long-form Game Design Documents (GDDs) describe requirements that must work together across game logic, visual rendering, and player interactions. However, existing game-development benchmarks typically use compact specifications and provide limited support for evaluating interdependent requirements across these aspects in long-form GDDs. We introduce A2Z GameSpec-Bench, a benchmark of 100 long-form GDDs for evaluating end-to-end game development by agents. We measure faithfulness by checking whether the game satisfies the GDD requirements and preserves the relationships among them. Each GDD is turned into a dependency-aware contract that contains rules, constraints, and prerequisite relations. Following game-development practices, we combine source-code inspection with agent-generated test policies for scenario-based replay and adaptive playtesting. The contract remains fixed across agents and revision rounds, while judgments and evidence linked to the same requirements support consistent comparison and failure detection. Our evaluations show that current agents struggle to jointly satisfy interdependent requirements across code implementation and actual play. Requirement-specific feedback improves GDD Fidelity by 10.9% relative to self-revision after two rounds. A2Z GameSpec-Bench assesses end-to-end specification-following ability beyond implementation judgments and provides targeted feedback to support more faithful game development. Code and datasets are available at https://a2z-gamespec-bench.github.io.

</details>


### [220] [AVERT-VLN: Abstention-aware Visual Error Recovery and Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39579)
*Minrui Liu,Jingke Wang,Yuehao Huang,Hao Su,Jiajun Lv,Yukai Ma,Yong Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AVERT-VLN is a closed-loop framework for vision-and-language navigation that detects when an agent is lost, requests human help to recover, and then uses those interactions to improve future navigation via preference learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-and-language navigation agents struggle in unseen environments because novel layouts and visual conditions cause them to deviate from instructions, yet continuous human supervision is impractical. The authors aim to enable agents to autonomously detect when they are going off-instruction, selectively ask for human guidance, recover the task, and leverage those corrections to improve later performance.

Method: They introduce AVERT-VLN, which adds a separate vision-language Monitor to existing navigation policies. The Monitor is trained to assess instruction-execution consistency using a new LOSTNAV dataset of 20K counterfactual risk trajectories with rule-based deviation labels, plus 40K normal trajectories. Training is staged: first on normal trajectories to estimate progress along the instruction, then jointly on normal and risk trajectories to detect semantic deviations. At run time, the Monitor acts as an asynchronous sidecar, evaluating each step. When it predicts a LOST state with sufficient confidence, a controller pauses the agent, requests human guidance, and uses that guidance for recovery. For offline learning, they propose Trajectory-Anchored Preference Learning, which converts monitored deviation events into decision-level preference pairs within shared contexts, focusing supervision on the specific decisions that need correction.

Result: With human-assisted monitoring and recovery, AVERT-VLN achieves success rates of 76.2% on R2R-CE and 66.3% on RxR-CE validation-unseen splits. The monitoring and recovery interface is shown to provide consistent gains across three different navigation architectures, demonstrating architecture-agnostic benefits.

Conclusion: Separating monitoring from control and treating deviation detection plus human recovery as a closed loop significantly improves robustness of VLN agents in unseen environments. The LOSTNAV dataset enables effective deviation recognition, and converting deviations into preference-based supervision yields targeted policy improvement. The framework generalizes across navigation models, indicating it is a practical plug-in solution for human-assisted VLN in realistic settings.

Abstract: Deploying vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents in unseen environments remains challenging because unfamiliar layouts and visual conditions can cause execution to go off track. Rather than relying on continuous human supervision, a practical strategy is to selectively request corrective guidance, recover the ongoing task, and reuse corrective interactions to improve subsequent navigation. We propose Abstention-aware Visual Error Recovery and Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation (AVERT-VLN), a closed-loop framework that uses a plug-in vision-language Monitor for online human-assisted recovery and offline preference learning. The Monitor operates separately from navigation decision generation and assesses instruction-execution consistency from the instruction, visual history, and current observation. To train the Monitor for deviation recognition, we construct LOSTNAV DATASET with 20K counterfactual risk trajectories and rule-based deviation labels. The Monitor is first fine-tuned on 40K normal trajectories to assess instruction progress and then jointly fine-tuned on normal and risk trajectories to recognize semantic deviations. At runtime, Asynchronous Sidecar Monitoring evaluates execution alongside the navigation model. When the controller accepts a LOST verdict, it suspends autonomous execution and requests human guidance for recovery. For offline policy improvement, Trajectory-Anchored Preference Learning converts deviation-associated failures into decision-level preference pairs under shared decision contexts, restricting supervision to the decisions targeted for correction. Under human-assisted evaluation, the full AVERT-VLN system achieves success rates of 76.2% and 66.3% on the val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, respectively. The same monitoring and human-assisted recovery interface also improves success rates across the three evaluated navigation architectures.

</details>


### [221] [Why Do Conventional World Models Fail to Learn Cellular Automata?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39604)
*Shaoyang Guo,Ziming Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper tests whether standard world models (Transformers, CNNs, diffusion models) can learn *exact* dynamics, using cellular automata as a testbed, and shows they typically fail at perfect rollouts despite high per-pixel accuracy, but simple information-flow modifications fix this without changing the backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models are often evaluated by average predictive accuracy, but for many scientific or planning tasks we need models that capture the *exact* underlying dynamics, not just surface statistics. Cellular automata provide a controlled setting where the true dynamics are known and fully local, so they are ideal for probing whether modern deep architectures actually learn the correct update rules. The authors want to understand why high-performing models still fail at long-horizon rollouts, and whether this is due to fundamental architectural limits or fixable design choices.

Method: The authors use various cellular automata (including Conway's Game of Life and unseen CA rules), billiards, and a simulated Burgers equation as testbeds. They train standard world models: CNNs, Transformers, and diffusion models (with both joint and ordered sampling). They then identify three failure modes—spatial locality, temporal locality, temporal stability—by analyzing when models fail to produce exact rollouts even though most cells are predicted correctly. For each failure mode they introduce a minimal change to information flow only: (1) 2D rotary positional encodings for better spatial locality in Transformers, (2) augmenting each token with its cell's previous-frame neighborhood to enforce temporal locality, and (3) a “causal freezing” mechanism for diffusion models to enforce temporal stability. They keep the underlying architectures and weights otherwise unchanged and measure rollout completion rates before and after these changes.

Result: Baseline models achieve high per-cell prediction accuracy but low exact-rollout completion: e.g., a CNN attains 96.3% cell accuracy yet completes only 18.9% of rollouts; a joint diffusion model completes none. Introducing the targeted information-flow modifications dramatically improves performance on exact rollouts. For spatial locality, adding 2D rotary positional encodings increases a Transformer's completion rate on Game of Life from 39.1% to 100%. For temporal locality, providing each token with its prior-frame neighborhood boosts performance on unseen CA rules from 25.8% to 99.9%. For temporal stability in diffusion models, causal freezing improves rollout completion from 42.2% to 99.9%. These gains are achieved without changing the backbone architectures, only the way information is routed through them. The authors also report comparative behavior of joint vs ordered sampling on billiards and preliminary results on a Burgers-equation simulator, though details are more exploratory.

Conclusion: Standard deep world-model architectures, even when apparently accurate at the per-pixel level, often fail to learn the exact underlying dynamics, as revealed by their inability to sustain long, perfect rollouts in cellular automata and other physics-inspired domains. The failures can be categorized as breakdowns in spatial locality, temporal locality, and temporal stability. However, these are not fundamental limitations of the backbones themselves: simple, targeted changes that adjust information flow—2D rotary positional encodings, neighborhood-conditioned tokens, and causal freezing for diffusion—are enough to recover nearly perfect rollout completion in the studied settings. This suggests that achieving exact dynamics may be more about respecting locality and stability constraints in the model’s input–output structure than about inventing new large-scale architectures, and it highlights the need to evaluate world models by strict rollout correctness rather than only average predictive accuracy.

Abstract: Although conventional world models - auto-regressive or diffusion models based on transformers or convolutional networks - may learn surface statistics of world dynamics, can they learn the exact world dynamics from its observed history? Leveraging cellular automata as a simple testbed, we find the answer to be no in many cases. Conventional architectures predict most pixels correctly yet rarely complete a rollout: a CNN predicts 96.3% of cells but completes 18.9% of rollouts; a joint diffusion model completes none. We trace the gap to three failure modes of these world models - namely, they fail to exactly capture spatial locality, temporal locality or temporal stability. Simple changes repair each: (1) for spatial locality, two-dimensional rotary positions lift a transformer from 39.1% to 100% on the Game of Life; (2) for temporal locality, handing each token its cell's previous-frame neighbourhood lifts the same transformer from 25.8% to 99.9% on unseen rules; (3) for temporal stability, causal freezing lifts the same diffusion weights from 42.2% to 99.9%. None of the three changes touches the architectural backbone; each only modifies the information flow within it. We also compare joint and ordered sampling on billiards and, in an exploratory study, on a simulated Burgers equation.

</details>
