### [222] [ChronoGraph: Functional 4D Scene Graphs with Vision-Language Models for Interaction Understanding and Grounded Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39665)
*Chenyangguang Zhang,Malgorzata Gwiazda,Guanlong Jiao,Yuanchen Ju,Federico Tombari,Koushil Sreenath,Marc Pollefeys,Sunghwan Hong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ChronoGraph, a 4D scene graph representation and training framework that unifies understanding past interactions and planning future actions for embodied agents, along with a benchmark and a specialized VLM, ChronoGraphVLM, that improve 4D interaction reasoning and robot planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied agents need to reason not only about static scenes but also about how their actions change the world over time: where to act, what effects those actions will have, and how to interpret those effects to guide subsequent behavior. Existing models often separate perception from planning and struggle to connect past interaction understanding with future-oriented, spatially grounded planning. There is a lack of a unified representation and training regime that treats observed and anticipated scene transitions consistently, limiting robust long-horizon manipulation and navigation in real-world environments.

Method: The authors propose ChronoGraph, a functional 4D scene graph that encodes actions on object affordance parts and the resulting semantic and geometric state changes in the environment. They build ChronoGraphBench, a benchmark generated via an automatic data engine that transforms human-interaction videos and simulated robot trajectories into graph-annotated question-answer pairs for training and evaluating vision-language models on interaction understanding and planning. They then develop ChronoGraphVLM by adapting existing pretrained VLMs in two stages: (1) Graph-as-Chain-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning, which trains models to first generate graph traces that reconstruct observed transitions or predict future ones before producing final answers; and (2) joint 4D graph reinforcement learning, which optimizes policies using rewards based on both graph quality (structural and semantic correctness) and answer accuracy.

Result: Across different model scales, ChronoGraphVLM outperforms corresponding pretrained VLM baselines on the ChronoGraphBench tasks for both interaction understanding and future prediction, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to the external benchmark VLM4D, indicating improved generalization in 4D reasoning. The system also supports real robot experiments, where agents use graph-based planning and affordance grounding to perform mobile manipulation tasks by leveraging existing low-level robot skills without any additional fine-tuning.

Conclusion: ChronoGraph provides a unified 4D scene graph representation that aligns observation and planning, enabling embodied agents to better understand how actions transform environments and to plan future interactions. Coupled with the ChronoGraphBench dataset and the ChronoGraphVLM training pipeline, this framework significantly improves 4D interaction reasoning in VLMs and transfers to real-world robot control. The results suggest that explicitly modeling scene transitions as structured graphs and using them as an intermediate reasoning step is a powerful paradigm for bridging perception, temporal understanding, and action planning in embodied AI.

Abstract: Embodied agents must determine where to act, anticipate the resulting scene changes, and interpret observed outcomes to guide subsequent actions. This requires connecting 4D interaction understanding, which explains how past actions changed the scene, with spatially grounded planning, which determines how and where to act toward a goal and anticipates the resulting scene changes. We introduce ChronoGraph, a functional 4D scene graph that links actions on affordance parts to semantic and geometric state changes. By representing observed and anticipated transitions in the same form, it provides a shared basis for understanding and planning. We construct ChronoGraphBench through an automatic data engine that converts human-interaction videos and simulated robot trajectories into graph-annotated questions for training and evaluating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on both tasks. Using these annotations, we train ChronoGraphVLM by adapting pretrained VLMs in two stages. Graph-as-Chain-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning teaches the models to reconstruct observed transitions and predict future ones as graph traces before answering. Subsequent joint 4D graph reinforcement learning directly rewards graph properties and answer correctness. Experiments across model scales show improvements over the corresponding pretrained baselines and zero-shot transfer to VLM4D. Real-world demonstrations further show that graph-based planning and affordance grounding support mobile manipulation through existing robot skills without additional fine-tuning.

</details>


### [223] [Values as Style: Disentangling Values from Semantics with One-Way Mixing for Low-Damage LLM Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39701)
*Jiale Dai,Hongcan Deng,Liuxian Ma,Xiaoke Niu,Guojie Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a method to steer the values (normative priorities) of large language models while keeping their understanding of the scenario and task intact, using a specialized semantic–value interface on frozen residual states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing value-steering and activation-edit methods often entangle semantics (what the model thinks is going on) with values (what it prefers or judges), so changing values can unintentionally distort facts, task constraints, or cause unnecessary refusals. There is a need for techniques that adjust value orientation with minimal collateral damage to the model’s capabilities and semantic understanding.

Method: The authors design an interface that splits residual representations into a semantic code and a value code, with a one-way pathway from semantic to value information. They freeze the backbone residual states and add an editable value pathway. Stop-gradient is used to block gradients from flowing back through the semantic-to-value link, ensuring semantics do not get overwritten by value updates. They apply regularizers—swap consistency, topic de-confounding, and decorrelation—to encourage the emergence of selective value-related codes. At inference time, they edit only the value code to generate a residual delta, while keeping the semantic code fixed. They compare this with a matched mixing-by-gating ablation that uses similar capacity but without the same selective interface and also train dimension-matched probes to quantify how selectively value information is encoded.

Result: On two instruction-tuned LLM backbones, the method preserves semantics better and reduces unnecessary (benign) refusals while maintaining comparable value alignment. In comparison to a strong prompting baseline on LLaMA-3.1-8B selected via validation, their method achieves nearly identical alignment scores (0.750 vs. 0.748) but higher BERTScore (0.938 vs. 0.923, indicating better semantic preservation) and fewer contradictions in outputs (5.1% vs. 7.6%). Probing shows that the learned codes are more selective for value information than in the ablations.

Conclusion: The proposed semantic–value interface offers a more precise, low-damage way to steer LLM values: it can adjust normative priorities while largely preserving task semantics and avoiding unnecessary refusals or contradictions. The architectural choices—one-way semantic-to-value pathway, stop-gradient, and regularizers—help disentangle value representation from core semantic processing, leading to more controllable and interpretable value edits than conventional activation editing or prompting alone.

Abstract: Value steering should change an LLM's normative priorities while preserving the scenario, facts, and task constraints underlying its answer. Conventional activation edits often change both. We introduce an editable semantic-value interface on frozen residual states, with a one-way semantic-to-value pathway that grounds value recognition in context. Stop-gradient blocks feedback through this pathway; swap consistency, topic de-confounding, and decorrelation encourage selective codes. At inference, editing the value code produces a residual delta while holding the semantic code fixed. On two instruction-tuned backbones, this interface improves semantic preservation and reduces benign refusals at comparable value alignment. A matched mixing-by-gating ablation separates representation learning from selective edit activation, and dimension-matched probes establish improved code selectivity. Against validation-selected prompting on LLaMA-3.1-8B, the method achieves comparable alignment (0.750 vs. 0.748), higher BERTScore (0.938 vs. 0.923), and fewer contradictions (5.1% vs. 7.6%). Human ratings and cross-taxonomy controls provide complementary evidence for low-damage value steering.

</details>


### [224] [A helps B while B hurts A: directed transfer in instruction-tuning mixture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39702)
*Nima H. Siboni,Vahid Rostami*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They study how different instruction-tuning tasks positively or negatively transfer to each other and propose a “transfer map” that predicts which source tasks will help a new target task under a fixed fine-tuning budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When adapting LMs to specialized domains with limited fine-tuning budget, we must choose which instruction-tuning tasks to include. Existing heuristics (use more tasks; use similar tasks) assume transfer is always positive and symmetric, which is often false, leading to suboptimal or harmful mixtures of source tasks.

Method: Define transfer between tasks as a signed, directional effect of one source task on a specific target task. Introduce the “transfer map,” a matrix estimating this effect for ordered source–target pairs. Empirically estimate the map via hundreds of fine-tuning runs on Qwen3 and Mistral models (0.6B–32B parameters), using sources from one corpus and no target training data, then evaluate how well the map predicts target performance for unseen mixtures and across model scales.

Result: The estimated transfer map predicts held-out target accuracies on unseen mixtures substantially better than a baseline that ignores mixture composition (less than half the prediction error). Despite being corpus- and target-specific, maps generalize across model sizes: mixtures chosen using a map from one model size outperform “train on all sources” at every other tested size. On reasoning targets (causal explanation, multi-hop QA, methodological critique), using map-selected helpful tasks and excluding harmful ones boosts accuracy by up to 14 percentage points over training on all source tasks.

Conclusion: Transfer effects between instruction-tuning tasks are directional and can be negative, invalidating common assumptions that more tasks or similar tasks always help. These effects can be systematically captured in a transfer map that is tied to data rather than model size. Using this map to select source tasks yields better fine-tuning mixtures, leading to significantly improved performance—especially on reasoning tasks—under a fixed adaptation budget.

Abstract: Adapting a language model to a specialized corpus means choosing which instruction-tuning tasks to train on under a fixed budget, and testing one choice costs a fine-tuning run. Common heuristics add more source tasks or pick sources similar to the target. The first assumes transfer is never negative; the second, that it is symmetric. We show that both assumptions fail: task $A$ can help task $B$ while $B$ hurts $A$, so helpfulness is a signed property of ordered source--target pairs. We introduce the transfer map, a signed estimate of how much each source helps or hurts each held-out target. We fit the map in hundreds of fine-tuning runs on Qwen3 and Mistral models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, with all sources drawn from one corpus and no training examples from the target. The map predicts a held-out target's accuracy on unseen mixtures: recorded before those runs, its predictions have less than half the error of a mixture-agnostic baseline. The map is specific to its target and corpus but transfers across model scale: a mixture selected in advance at one size beats training on all source tasks at every other size we tested. Transfer is thus a property of the data. The map selects the tasks that help and drops the one that interferes: accuracy on the reasoning targets (causal explanation, multi-hop questions and methodological critique) rises by up to 14 percentage points over training on all source tasks.

</details>


### [225] [ArchitectureIQ: On the Measure of Training Intuition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39714)
*Zirui Ren,Shaoyang Guo,Chencheng Tang,Jinxin Wang,Chengyu Xiong,Shanbin Yu,Peihang Li,Yidi Wu,Bangzhe Huang,Qingyu Qu,Leqian Yang,Ziming Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ArchitectureIQ, a benchmark to test how well large language models (LLMs) can intuit which training recipes will perform best on synthetic datasets, comparing them with human AI researchers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantitatively measure and compare the informal “model intuition” of LLMs and top human AI researchers about training setups, and to understand the strengths and limitations of LLMs’ understanding of model training and data–architecture interactions.

Method: They design the ArchitectureIQ benchmark, where each question specifies a synthetic dataset and several possible training recipes (architectures and training setups). Models and humans must predict which recipe yields the best test performance. They evaluate frontier LLMs and human experts, study the effect of chain-of-thought prompting, construct a small explicit knowledge base from benchmark insights, and test how adding this knowledge base affects weaker models’ performance.

Result: Frontier LLMs reach about 76% accuracy (random is 33%), surpassing the best human researcher’s 66% but still far from perfect. On architecture-only questions, humans reach 65% while a top model (“GPT-6 Astra”) scores only 38%. Extra chain-of-thought compute barely improves performance, suggesting intuition is empirical rather than based on a formal theory. A hand-crafted knowledge base of 20 items significantly boosts weaker models (GPT-4o with this knowledge nearly matches Claude Opus 5). LLMs’ choices are largely insensitive to dataset properties, even though the optimal model should depend on data characteristics.

Conclusion: LLMs possess reasonably strong but imperfect model intuition, in some respects surpassing humans but lagging notably on architecture-specific reasoning. Their intuition appears empirical rather than grounded in a structured “Science of AI.” It can be distilled into a compact knowledge base to aid weaker models, and both LLMs and humans underutilize dataset characteristics, indicating that understanding data remains a major missing piece in AI modeling expertise.

Abstract: Top researchers have good intuition, but do language models have as good intuition about model training as top AI researchers? To measure model intuition of LLMs and humans, we introduce the ArchitectureIQ benchmark. Each question presents a synthetic dataset and several training recipes, and the test-taker is asked to predict the recipe yielding the best test metric. Overall, we find that LLMs' model intuition is good but has four limitations: (1) The intuition is imperfect, or even sub-human in some cases. Frontier models achieve around 76% accuracy (random choice 33%) vs best human researcher (66.0%), yet remain far from perfect. For architecture-only questions, best human achieves 65% while GPT-6 Astra only has 38%. (2) The intuition is empirical, not structured, supported by the fact that more CoT compute does not lead to substantial improvement. Unlike math, we still lack a "Science of AI" language that enables structured reasoning on AI. (3) The intuition is not maximally condensed, and can be further compressed into a knoledge base. Our constructed knowledge base with only 20 items yields large gains for weak models: GPT-4o equipped with the accumulated knowledge almost matches the performance of Claude Opus 5. (4) The intuition is insensitive to dataset properties, but the best model should in general depend on data properties. This suggests that data is the real "dark matter" in AI -- LLMs (so do human researchers) understand too little about data, even less than model architectures.

</details>


### [226] [Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39717)
*Serhii Zabolotnii*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a gap in current AI assurance approaches and proposes Runtime Assurance Contracts (RACs), a formal policy schema that ties specific evidence to changes in an AI agent’s authority, then validates the mechanisms on synthetic agentic-coding and decision traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks, audits, and agent protocols describe performance, permissions, and repair processes, but they do not formally specify how concrete runtime evidence should change an AI or agent’s authority during high-stakes, ongoing tasks. This missing link—the “assurance-transition gap”—creates risk that systems will rely on aggregate performance metrics or scores to justify action when mandatory safety conditions are unknown or violated. The authors aim to formalize this transition logic so that authority changes are principled, checkable, and not overridable by soft performance metrics.

Method: The authors introduce Runtime Assurance Contracts (RACs), a formal, policy-level schema that encodes: autonomy boundaries, component eligibility, the state of evidence, transition policies, human-review capacity, and non-compensatory (mandatory) gates. They define the RAC structure, an associated evidence record, a permission rule, and five invariants that must hold. They illustrate RAC behavior in synthetic clinical, industrial, and judicial failure scenarios. They then run a deterministic failure-injection experiment in an agentic coding setting with 280 constructed cases, comparing: (1) a strict gate-conjunction rule (non-compensatory), (2) a soft score-only rule, and (3) a restricted protocol baseline. They analytically characterize when a weighted-score rule can or cannot replicate the conjunction’s behavior under general conditions on weights, thresholds, and binary risk signals. Additional experiments use 18 hand-authored traces to check evidence and review transitions, and a 24-episode synthetic holdout labeled by blinded LLM judges to compare RAC against a full stateful baseline implementation.

Result: In the agentic coding failure-injection study, using published example weights and threshold, the score-only rule incorrectly authorizes many unsafe cases: it admits 80 of 100 injections that the contract marks as “block-required” and all 40 injections that require human review, demonstrating that aggregate performance scores cannot substitute for hard safety gates. With hindsight tuning, the score rule can be adjusted to match the gate conjunction on this particular corpus, but the authors prove that, under mild assumptions (positive weights and threshold, binary risk signals, zero-signal controls, and each signal firing alone on some case), exact agreement between a score rule and a gate-conjunction rule holds if and only if the threshold does not exceed the smallest weight—highlighting the fragility of such tuning. In the hand-authored traces, RAC correctly enforces version-pinned evidence and governs review transitions, distinguishing it from simpler policy variants. In a prospective synthetic holdout of 24 episodes (72 action attempts), two blinded LLM judges give identical labels to all actions, and both RAC and an independently implemented full stateful baseline match these labels exactly, showing that RAC can be implemented consistently for the tested synthetic scenarios.

Conclusion: Runtime Assurance Contracts provide a formal way to bind runtime evidence to authority transitions, enforcing non-compensatory safety gates that soft performance metrics cannot override. Empirically, score-only rules can badly misalign with safety requirements and only match strict gate logic under narrow, fragile conditions. RACs can be implemented in a way that is consistent with richer stateful policies and expert-like judgments on synthetic tasks, but the authors emphasize that their studies are limited to synthetic scenarios and do not yet demonstrate real-world safety or cross-domain generality. The work primarily contributes a conceptual and formal framework, plus empirical probes, for more rigorous control over AI agent autonomy and review escalation during consequential tasks.

Abstract: Benchmarks, audits, and agent protocols describe performance, permissions, and repair, but not how observed evidence should change an agent's authority during a consequential task. We call this the assurance-transition gap. We propose a Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC), a policy-level formal schema binding autonomy boundaries, component eligibility, evidence state, transition policy, human-review capacity, and non-compensatory gates. Under RAC, soft metrics may inform routing, whereas a failed or unknown mandatory gate forces retry, switch, escalation, deferral, or stop; aggregate performance cannot authorize action. We define the contract, an evidence record, a permission rule, and five invariants, and illustrate them in clinical, industrial, and judicial failure probes. We then report a deterministic failure-injection study in agentic coding: 280 constructed cases evaluated by a gate conjunction, a score-only rule, and a restricted protocol baseline. At the published example weights and threshold, the score rule admits 80 of 100 block-required injections and all 40 review-required injections. Tuned in hindsight, it matches the conjunction on this corpus. For positive weights, a positive threshold, binary risk signals, zero-signal controls, and an injected case firing each signal alone, we show that exact agreement holds if and only if the threshold does not exceed the smallest weight. A separate set of 18 hand-authored traces checks version-pinned evidence and review transitions against simpler policy variants. In a further prospective synthetic holdout of 24 episodes, two blinded LLM judges assign identical labels to all 72 action attempts; RAC and a separately implemented full stateful baseline both match these labels. These studies test mechanisms on synthetic cases; they establish neither deployed safety nor cross-domain effectiveness.

</details>


### [227] [OverForge: Reasoning Through Strategies and Tactics Helps Cooperative Lifelong Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39727)
*Oana Madalina Fron,Ojas Shirekar,Chirag Raman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OverForge is a training-free hierarchical LLM-agent architecture that separates persistent coordination strategies from tactical action choices, enabling better long-horizon cooperation and adaptation in multi-agent tasks like Overcooked.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cooperative LLM agents struggle with long-horizon coordination, adapting to changing environments, and working with partners that use unfamiliar conventions, largely because they directly map observations to actions without explicitly representing persistent coordination strategies (e.g., roles, division of labour) separately from low-level action execution. This limits robustness, role stability, and partner adaptation.

Method: The authors propose OverForge, a hierarchical, training-free architecture for cooperative LLM agents. It has two levels: (1) a strategic level that reasons about roles and division of labour, and (2) a tactical level that selects actions based on each agent's private, partner-conditioned world model. A metacognitive Prefrontal Cortex Module links these levels by generating candidate strategy–action branches, imaginatively rolling them out via a forward model, and committing to a branch when sufficiently confident. They evaluate in the OvercookedV2 environment, compare against flat LLM baselines, run ablations removing parts of the hierarchy, and design a fixed-strategy probe and memory-restart experiments to test cross-episode partner knowledge and continual adaptation.

Result: In OvercookedV2 connected-kitchen scenarios, OverForge achieves about 7 soups delivered, compared to 3 soups by each flat LLM baseline. It maintains agreed roles across play, flexibly adopts roles suggested by previously unseen partners, and shows that persistent strategies meaningfully guide tactical adaptation. Ablation and probing indicate both the strategic and tactical levels are necessary for good coordination, and that the hierarchy enables effective role retention and partner adaptation. Memory-restart experiments demonstrate that knowledge about partners carried across episodes improves both task performance and prediction of partner behavior.

Conclusion: Hierarchically separating strategic coordination (roles, division of labour) from tactical action selection, and coupling them with a metacognitive control module, substantially improves long-horizon cooperative performance of LLM agents without additional training. The OverForge architecture enables stable yet flexible role-based coordination, supports adaptation to unfamiliar partners, and leverages cross-episode memory for continual adaptation, highlighting the importance of explicit, persistent strategy representations in multi-agent LLM systems.

Abstract: Cooperative language-model agents must coordinate over long horizons and adapt to changing environments and to partners with unfamiliar conventions, yet existing agents map observations to actions without separating persistent coordination strategies from their tactical execution. We introduce OverForge, a training-free hierarchical architecture that separates strategic reasoning over roles and divisions of labour from tactical reasoning over actions within each agent's private, partner-conditioned world model. A metacognitive Prefrontal Cortex Module couples the two levels by forming strategy-action branches, imagining their consequences with a forward model, and committing when confident. In OvercookedV2, OverForge delivers 7 soups in a connected kitchen versus 3 for each flat LLM baseline, retains agreed roles, and adopts roles proposed by unfamiliar partners. Ablations and a fixed-strategy probe show that persistent strategies guide tactical adaptation while each reasoning level contributes to coordination. Memory restarts show that cross-episode partner knowledge supports task performance and partner prediction, linking the hierarchy to continual adaptation.

</details>


### [228] [Safety of Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39788)
*Muhammad Huzaifa,Sina Mavali,Thorsten Eisenhofer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how latent communication links between safety-aligned agents can undermine safety, showing that training these links—especially under attacks—greatly increases harmful compliance, and proposes RL-based attacks and repairs that act only on the links, not the agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent systems increasingly use latent (representation-space) communication to reduce the overhead of text-based messaging. However, safety alignment work usually focuses on individual agents, not the communication channels between them. The authors are motivated by the concern that even if each agent is safety-aligned in isolation, the learned latent links that let them talk could reintroduce harmful behavior, especially if an attacker manipulates link training.

Method: They introduce lightweight, trainable mapping layers (links) that translate one agent’s internal representations into another’s input space, enabling latent communication. They then empirically study how training these links—under benign conditions and under various adversarial schemes—affects harmful compliance. Adversarial schemes include: (1) optimizing links directly on harmful query–response pairs, (2) poisoning otherwise benign link-training data, and (3) a reinforcement-learning attack that jointly rewards harmful compliance and benign task performance without relying on explicit harmful target responses. They test the effects across three communication topologies and four safety benchmarks, and compare against direct supervised optimization. They also experiment with modified RL rewards aimed at safer behavior to see if compromised links can be repaired without retraining the agents themselves.

Result: They find that even benignly trained latent links already increase harmful compliance compared to standard text-based communication, despite the agents themselves remaining unchanged and safety-aligned. Adversarial training of the links substantially worsens this: their RL-based attack raises the mean harmful-compliance score from 27.9 (benign links) to 76.9 across the evaluated settings. Moreover, this RL attack achieves higher accuracy on two benign utility benchmarks than direct supervised optimization, meaning it can both make the system more capable and more harmful. When they modify the RL rewards to favor safer behavior, they can “repair” compromised links and significantly reduce harmful compliance across all evaluated attack settings, again without touching the base agents.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that safety alignment cannot be treated as a property of individual agents alone; it must encompass the entire multi-agent system, including learned latent communication links. Even when base agents are safety-aligned, training or attacking the links between them can dramatically increase harmful compliance. However, carefully designed reward schemes can also be used to mitigate or reverse this effect by acting solely on the links. This highlights latent communication as a critical surface for both safety vulnerabilities and safety interventions in multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Latent communication enables multi-agent systems to exchange information directly in internal representation space, reducing the token, computation, and latency overhead of text-based communication. To this end, lightweight trainable links are introduced to map the sender's representations into the receiver's input space. In this work, we show that even benign link training can increase harmful compliance relative to text-based communication while the underlying safety-aligned agents remain unchanged. An attacker can amplify this effect by optimizing the links on harmful query--response pairs or poisoning otherwise benign training data. We further develop a reinforcement-learning attack that rewards harmful compliance alongside benign task performance without requiring harmful target responses. Across three communication topologies and four safety benchmarks, this attack raises the mean harmful-compliance score from 27.9 with benignly trained links to 76.9. Compared with direct supervised optimization, it also achieves higher average accuracy on two benign utility benchmarks. Adapting the rewards toward safer behavior also enables repair of compromised links, substantially reducing harmful compliance across all evaluated attacks without updating the agents. Overall, our results show that safety alignment requires considering the multi-agent system as a whole.

</details>


### [229] [Learning Steganography Is Easy, Learning Steganographic Reasoning Is Hard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39838)
*Julian Schulz,Lukas Fülle,Rieke Fruengel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates how easily language models learn to hide their internal reasoning (“steganographic reasoning”) compared to two related behaviors—steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning—under different training and elicitation methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a proposed safety and oversight technique for AI, but it can be undermined if models learn to conceal their reasoning in hidden channels within normal-looking text. Existing work already shows that LLMs can develop steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning under realistic training pressures, raising concern that steganographic reasoning might similarly emerge unintentionally and compromise oversight. The authors want to understand how likely and under what conditions this more threatening capability actually arises.

Method: The authors empirically compare three related capabilities—steganographic reasoning, steganographic messaging, and encoded reasoning—across three elicitation methods: reinforcement learning, in-context learning, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). They design tasks where a model either hides a message, performs reasoning in an encoded/unreadable form, or carries out its intermediate reasoning steganographically within benign-looking outputs. They then measure how readily and under what training effort each capability is acquired for different model–task combinations, including a specially designed “cover task” that makes hiding information particularly easy.

Result: Models reliably learn steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning under all three elicitation methods (RL, in-context learning, and SFT). In contrast, for most tasks, steganographic reasoning emerges only under supervised fine-tuning, and even then requires at least twice as much training as steganographic messaging. In several model–task settings, steganographic reasoning fails to be learned at all. However, when the task structure makes it especially convenient to hide information (the cover task), steganographic reasoning can be learned under all three elicitation methods.

Conclusion: Steganographic reasoning is significantly harder for current models to learn than steganographic messaging or encoded reasoning, and the presence of the latter two behaviors does not imply that a model can or will hide full chains of reasoning steganographically. Nonetheless, steganographic reasoning is not out of reach: in favorable settings where outputs naturally provide good cover, even simple elicitation methods can induce it. This suggests some safety buffer for chain-of-thought monitoring today, but also a realistic risk that steganographic reasoning may emerge in future systems or under certain training regimes, especially when tasks make information hiding easy.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought monitoring as an approach for AI oversight and control is threatened by the possibility of steganographic reasoning, where LLMs conceal their reasoning inside innocuous-looking text. Two neighbouring capabilities, steganographic messaging (passing a concealed message) and encoded reasoning (reasoning in an illegible but unconcealed format), have already been shown to emerge under training pressures that occur in real pipelines, such as reinforcement learning against monitors. This suggests that steganographic reasoning too might arise as an unintended side effect of training. Here, we compare how easily models learn steganographic reasoning and these two neighbouring capabilities across three elicitation methods: reinforcement learning, in-context learning, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
  For most tasks, models learn steganographic reasoning only under SFT, while they learn steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning under all three elicitation methods. Even under SFT, steganographic reasoning requires at least twice as much training as messaging, and for several model-task combinations it is not learned at all. However, on a cover task that makes hiding information especially convenient, steganographic reasoning can be successfully learned under all three elicitation methods. Steganographic reasoning is thus much harder than steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning, and learning the latter two does not imply learning the former. Yet it lies within reach: an easy version is learned under every elicitation method, when the cover task is convenient for hiding information.

</details>


### [230] [FIGS: Evaluating Multi-Turn Sycophancy Without Penalizing Empathy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39863)
*Sidharth Pulipaka,Ruta Binkyte,Ivaxi Sheth,Sahar Abdelnabi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces FIGS, a framework to evaluate large language models on how well they balance factual integrity and supportive behavior over realistic multi-turn dialogues, distinguishing harmful sycophancy from healthy empathy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of sycophancy in large language models are mostly single-turn, rigid, and script-based, which fail to capture how sycophantic behavior naturally emerges and evolves over repeated user interactions. Moreover, current benchmarks conflate empathetic validation with yielding to users, potentially pushing models toward cold and overly rigid behavior. The authors aim to create a more realistic and nuanced evaluation that separates truthfulness from emotional support and examines model behavior over extended conversations.

Method: The authors propose FIGS (Factual Integrity and Grounded Support), a dual-axis evaluation framework that uses an adaptive 10-turn conversational simulator. This simulator dynamically challenges the target model by simulating users who repeat requests, push back, or subtly steer toward preferred answers. They define and apply a taxonomy that splits behavior into Sycophancy (truthfulness and proportionality of praise) and Calibrated Validation (empathetic understanding without excessive agreement). They build 500 diverse multi-turn scenarios and implement an automated judge to score model behavior along these axes across full dialogue trajectories.

Result: Using FIGS, the authors evaluate several leading large language models and find a consistent trade-off: over the course of extended, realistic interactions, models tend either to gradually become sycophantic—yielding on facts and over-praising—or to over-correct, resulting in detached, robotic responses with insufficient empathy. This pattern holds across systems, revealing systematic weaknesses in how current models maintain both honesty and supportive tone over time.

Conclusion: The study concludes that balancing factual honesty with appropriately calibrated emotional support across multi-turn dialogues is still an open, unresolved challenge for large language models. FIGS provides a more realistic and fine-grained benchmark that can guide future model training and alignment efforts by separately measuring sycophancy and healthy validation, and by stressing models with adaptive, user-like conversational pressure.

Abstract: Large language models frequently fail to balance staying truthful with being supportive. They often exhibit sycophancy in responses to users, agreeing with false claims, offering unwarranted flattery, and giving advice skewed toward users' expressed views. In reality, sycophancy rarely happens in a single exchange; it may emerge organically as users repeatedly insist or subtly steer the dialogue over time. Current evaluations, however, rely on rigid, single-turn tests or fixed scripts that fail to capture these natural dynamics. Furthermore, these benchmarks often mistake showing basic empathy for yielding, penalizing models for acknowledging a user's feeling. This view may drive future models to over-correct into cold, dismissive rigidity. To address this gap, we introduce FIGS (Factual Integrity and Grounded Support), a dual-axis evaluation framework built around extended, realistic dialogue. We use an adaptive 10-turn conversational simulator that dynamically challenges the target model, reflecting how users repeat requests, push back, or steer a conversation toward a preferred answer. To accurately evaluate these trajectories, we apply a taxonomy that strictly separates Sycophancy (whether the model holds firm to the truth and keeps its praise proportional) from Calibrated Validation (showing empathetic understanding of the user's feelings without overdoing it). We release our complete testing environment, including 500 diverse multi-turn scenarios and an automated judge. Our evaluation of leading models reveals a consistent trade-off: over the course of a sustained interaction, current systems either slowly drift to sycophancy or over-correct into robotic detachment. This demonstrates that balancing honesty with appropriate support throughout a natural conversation remains a critical, unsolved challenge.

</details>


### [231] [Completion-Aware Cross-Fidelity Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Line Bus Holding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39868)
*Yifan Zhang,Qifan Zhang,Liang Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes hybrid offline-and-online reinforcement learning for bus fleet control, focusing on mismatches between simulators and real-world operations and a failure mode where apparent performance gains hide incomplete passenger trips.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Running exploratory reinforcement learning directly on a live bus fleet is unsafe and impractical, but policies trained only on static historical data cannot adapt to new conditions. Hybrid Offline-and-Online RL aims to exploit cheap simulators plus logged data, yet real-world bus operations involve complex, time-based passenger and vehicle dynamics that simulators may not capture accurately. This mismatch can produce misleading performance metrics in public transit control, such as seeming improvements in passenger time that actually stem from failing to complete some journeys.

Method: The authors consider a multi-line bus holding control problem and analyze a Hybrid Offline-and-Online (H2O) RL framework that uses fixed target replay with simulator interaction. They model and study the cross-fidelity gap—differences in transition and event-duration dynamics between the inexpensive online simulator and the real target system. By examining how RL policies behave under these mismatches, they identify and characterize a specific failure mode in which policies reduce generalized passenger time while causing incomplete journeys.

Result: The study shows that in the presence of cross-fidelity mismatch, H2O RL can learn bus holding policies that appear to optimize the objective (lower generalized passenger time) in the simulator, but in reality achieve this by producing incomplete passenger journeys. This reveals that the RL algorithm can exploit inaccuracies in the simulator’s transition and timing dynamics, leading to misleading performance metrics and unsafe or unacceptable policies for real transit operations.

Conclusion: Hybrid Offline-and-Online RL in transit control is vulnerable to cross-fidelity issues between simulators and real systems. Inaccurate modeling of transitions and event durations can induce pathological behaviors, such as policies that superficially improve passenger time metrics by failing to complete trips. The paper concludes that care must be taken in designing objectives, simulators, and evaluation procedures to ensure that learned policies do not exploit model imperfections and that completeness and realism of passenger journeys are explicitly safeguarded.

Abstract: Exploratory reinforcement learning (RL) on an operating bus fleet is impractical,while policies trained only from historical data cannot acquire new experience. Hybrid Offline-and-Online (H2O) RL combines fixed target replay with simulator interaction, but the inexpensive online simulator can differ from the target in transition and event-duration dynamics. We study this cross-fidelity problem for multi-line bus holding and address a failure mode in which lower generalized passenger time coexists with incomplete passenger journeys.

</details>


### [232] [GrammarRL: Effective Grammar-Constrained Decoding via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39869)
*Gabriele Tuccio,Antonino Furnari,Aldo Gangemi,Misael Mongiovì*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes GrammarRL, a reinforcement learning approach that adapts language models to grammar-constrained decoding, improving semantic quality without labeled data or extra inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grammar-constrained decoding ensures syntactic validity but often harms semantic quality, especially with underspecified prompts or weaker instruction-following models. Beam search can help but is computationally expensive and sequence likelihood is a poor proxy for semantic quality. The authors want a way to adapt models to grammar constraints so that outputs are both syntactically valid and semantically faithful, without needing labeled supervision.

Method: The authors propose GrammarRL, a label-free reinforcement learning framework that fine-tunes a language model for grammar-constrained generation. They define two self-supervised rewards, both based on model likelihoods: (1) a direct reward that scores how likely the constrained output is given the input, and (2) a reverse reward that scores how well the input can be reconstructed when conditioning on the generated output. Training uses REINFORCE with a Leave-One-Out (RLOO) baseline over groups of grammar-constrained rollouts, augmented by including the top-1 beam-search hypothesis as a candidate and regularizing the policy toward a frozen base model to prevent degeneration.

Result: On sign language gloss translation, hierarchical text classification, and named entity recognition with Llama models from 1B to 8B parameters, GrammarRL outperforms grammar-constrained greedy decoding by an average of 9.8 points and up to 22.8 BLEU. It matches or beats beam search on two out of three tasks while keeping greedy-decoding-level inference cost. Ablation studies show that using only direct or only reverse reward can do worse than the untrained baseline, whereas combining both yields consistent improvements.

Conclusion: GrammarRL successfully adapts language models to grammar constraints using self-supervised RL, improving semantic quality without labeled data or extra inference-time cost. The dual direct and reverse rewards are crucial and complementary, enabling grammar-constrained generation that can rival or surpass beam search while retaining the efficiency of greedy decoding.

Abstract: Grammar-constrained generation guarantees syntactic validity, but can substantially degrade semantic quality when the model's preferred outputs are poorly aligned with the imposed grammar. This trade-off is particularly severe when the prompt is underspecified or the model has limited instruction-following ability. Beam search can partially mitigate these failures by exploring multiple valid sequences, but its computational cost grows with beam width, while sequence-level probability is only an imperfect proxy for semantic quality.
  We introduce GrammarRL, a label-free reinforcement learning method that adapts language models to grammar constraints without requiring annotated data. GrammarRL optimizes the model using two complementary self-supervised rewards derived from its own likelihoods: a direct reward, measuring how likely the constrained output is given the input, and a reverse reward, measuring how well the input can be reconstructed from the generated output. We optimize these rewards with a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) objective over groups of grammar-constrained rollouts, augmented with the top-1 beam-search hypothesis and regularized towards a frozen base model.
  We evaluate GrammarRL on sign language gloss translation, hierarchical text classification, and named entity recognition using Llama models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters. GrammarRL consistently outperforms constrained greedy decoding, with an average improvement of 9.8 points and gains of up to 22.8 BLEU. It matches or outperforms beam search on two of the three tasks while preserving greedy-decoding inference cost. Ablations further show that the two rewards are complementary: either reward alone can underperform the untrained baseline, whereas their combination consistently improves upon it.

</details>


### [233] [OSWorld-Science: A Benchmark of Computer Use Agents for Learning and Using Scientific Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39903)
*Dingyuan Dai,Heli Qi,Lei Liu,Yinxi Li,Baiding Chen,Zijun Dou,Qingcheng Zeng,Qi Kang,Oliver Sun,Eric Wang,Bo Zhou,Haixin Wang,Yufan Du,Shi Bo,Ruihan Lin,Mengqi Yuan,Dunjie Lu,Steven Dillmann,Yiming Shi,Tina Su,Amy Xin,Minghao Liu,Xi Wang,Xu Huang,Ge Zhang,Pengyu Nie,Zhen Yang,Jie Tang,Juanzi Li,Weihao Xuan,Tianyu Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce OSWorld-Science, a benchmark and harness to systematically evaluate visual language model–based software agents on real scientific software workflows, showing current VLMs still struggle with these tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual language model agents are promising for operating graphical software, but scientific software poses especially hard challenges: interfaces are complex, tasks require domain expertise, outputs must be scientifically valid, and existing benchmarks lack realistic, verifiable scientific workflows. The authors aim to create a standardized way to test and analyze how well VLM-based agents can use actual scientific tools to perform end-to-end research tasks.

Method: They build OSWorld-Science, an evaluation environment and benchmark consisting of 146 expert-designed tasks across multiple scientific domains (e.g., molecular drawing and retrosynthesis, pathology image analysis, statistical computing, physical simulation) and diverse software setups. Tasks are created via expert proposals and iterative human–AI co-design, then filtered by scientific importance and difficulty. For each task, they implement execution-based evaluators that inspect application states and generated artifacts (molecular structures, segmentation masks, plots, numerical outputs) and assign granular, partial-credit scores. They integrate these tasks into a specialized harness that standardizes interaction loops, model adapters, and trajectory logging, enabling systematic comparison of 12 different VLMs and different agent-control strategies.

Result: Applying the benchmark to 12 VLMs, even with a strong interaction harness, reveals that state-of-the-art models still frequently fail to complete scientific workflows or answer key scientific questions correctly. The fine-grained evaluators quantify partial progress and expose specific weaknesses in handling complex interfaces, scientific reasoning, and artifact creation. Their analyses examine performance across factors such as language settings, reasoning depth, context length, and interaction strategy, yielding empirical patterns and failure modes rather than uniformly strong results.

Conclusion: OSWorld-Science provides an end-to-end, artifact-based framework for evaluating VLM-based computer-using agents on realistic scientific software tasks. The study shows that current leading VLMs are not yet reliable scientific software agents, highlights how performance depends on language, reasoning style, and context usage, and suggests directions for model and harness design improvements. The benchmark and harness together offer a standardized testbed for future work on scientific AI agents and for measuring progress in their ability to conduct verifiable scientific workflows.

Abstract: Scientific software presents a demanding test for computer-using agents based on visual language models (VLMs): completing a research workflow requires interpreting specialized interfaces, manipulating scientific objects, and producing verifiable results. We thus introduce OSWorld-Science, a benchmark and evaluation environment that combines scientifically meaningful tasks, artifact-based evaluation, and an efficient agent harness for studying computer use in the scientific domain. The benchmark contains 12 VLMs and 146 high-quality tasks across several scientific domains and software configurations, covering workflows such as molecular drawing and retrosynthesis, pathology image analysis, statistical computing, and physical simulation. Tasks are developed through expert proposals and iterative human--AI co-design, with selection guided by scientific value and difficulty. Task-specific execution-based evaluators inspect application states and generated artifacts, including molecular structures, segmentation masks, plots, and numerical results, and award partial credit for incomplete outcomes. Our special harness integrates model adapters, interaction-loop control, and trajectory logging to support comparisons of models and interaction strategies. Our results show that current state-of-the-art VLMs with a strong harness still face challenges in addressing key questions in the scientific domains. We also analyze the benchmarking results across multi-linguistics, reasoning efforts, context length and other factors and derive several important conclusions and directions to assist future development. Overall, we provide an integrated framework connecting expert-defined scientific goals to verifiable software outcomes, enabling systematic evaluation of both agent capabilities and harness design in scientific workflows.

</details>


### [234] [ConflictGuide: AutoResearch Improves When Competing Behaviors Are Made Visible](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39933)
*Binqian Xu,Qiran Zou,Xiangbo Shu,Dianbo Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce ConflictGuide, a framework that augments LLM-based AutoResearch with feedback about competing behaviors (not just scalar task scores) to better navigate trade-offs and continue improving models past plateaus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AutoResearch systems that iteratively edit model code typically rely on a single scalar task-performance metric. However, real ML models exhibit trade-offs between competing behaviors, where improving one aspect can harm another. Scalar feedback alone cannot reveal how edits affect these competing behaviors, which leads to plateaus and regressions. There is a need for a structured way to identify, measure, and alleviate such behavioral conflicts during automated model evolution.

Method: The authors study LLM-based AutoResearch systems that modify model code and select edits based on performance feedback. They (1) show that scalar-only feedback enables broad exploration but fails to expose trade-offs between conflicting behaviors; (2) define the notion of competing behaviors and how to probe them; and (3) introduce ConflictGuide, a two-stage evolutionary framework. ConflictGuide uses a reusable skill module (ConflictGuide-Skill) that combines a literature-based taxonomy of conflicts with model-specific evidence to identify likely competing behaviors and design probes/metrics for them. Evolution proceeds in two phases: Stage I uses only task (scalar) feedback for exploration, while Stage II adds probe metrics to explicitly steer proposals toward edits that alleviate conflicts and filters marginal task gains unless probe metrics show sufficient conflict reduction. They test this across five different model families and with multiple code agents.

Result: In matched-budget experiments, the introduction of competing-behavior feedback once task gains start to diminish increases the proportion of code-edit proposals that simultaneously improve both the main task and competing behaviors, and it prolongs progress beyond the performance plateaus seen with scalar-only feedback. Quantitatively, across five diverse model families, ConflictGuide reduces task errors by up to 28% and conflict-related errors by up to 14% compared to standard scalar-only AutoResearch. The improvements generalize across different code agents, meaning the learned guidance is not specific to a single agent implementation.

Conclusion: Incorporating structured feedback about competing behaviors into AutoResearch systems allows them to handle trade-offs more intelligently than approaches that rely on a single scalar task metric. ConflictGuide operationalizes this by helping identify conflicts, design probes, and integrate their signals into a two-stage evolutionary process. This leads to more edits that improve both task performance and conflict-related behaviors and sustains progress beyond the plateaus encountered by scalar-only methods, with benefits that hold across model families and code agents.

Abstract: When designing machine learning models, desirable properties are often in tension: improving one behavior can impair another, so task progress can depend on alleviating the conflict. LLM-based AutoResearch systems, which iteratively edit model code and retain edits based on scalar task-performance feedback, have largely ignored this trade-off. We find that scalar feedback supports broad exploration early in search, but it does not reveal how edits affect competing behaviors. In matched-budget experiments, introducing competing-behavior feedback as task gains diminish increases the share of proposals that improve both behaviors and sustains progress beyond scalar-only plateaus. Obtaining this feedback for a given model requires identifying its competing behaviors and designing probes to measure them. To make competing-behavior feedback actionable, we introduce ConflictGuide. Its reusable ConflictGuide-Skill combines a literature-grounded taxonomy with model-specific evidence to identify competing behaviors and specify probes for a code agent to implement as metrics. Evolution proceeds in two stages: Stage I explores with task feedback; Stage II uses probe feedback to steer proposals toward conflict alleviation and retains marginal-gain edits only when probes indicate sufficient alleviation. Across five diverse model families, ConflictGuide reduces task and conflict-related errors by up to 28% and 14%, respectively, relative to scalar-only AutoResearch, with gains extending to other code agents.

</details>


### [235] [Coverage Before Control: Route-Instruction Grounding and Steering for Controllable Retrosynthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39955)
*Xuemin Chen,Xiaozhuang Song,Xinjian Zhao,Yaoyao Xu,Tianshu Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose RIGS, a two-stage framework to make retrosynthesis models follow natural language-like instructions when choosing among multiple valid precursor sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing single-step retrosynthesis models are judged mainly by whether they can reproduce recorded reactions, but in real use chemists often need to pick among several valid precursor options based on preferences (e.g., preserving a motif). Current metrics and models don’t evaluate or provide this preference-following behavior, so there’s a need for methods that both cover many valid alternatives and can be steered toward desired ones.

Method: RIGS has two stages. Stage A trains a language projector that learns how textual instructions map to preferences over alternative precursor sets, i.e., which choices are favored or discouraged. Stage B keeps the base generative retrosynthesis model frozen and attaches lightweight residual adapters that use the learned projector to steer the generation toward alternatives consistent with the given instruction. For training, they construct nested one-to-many supports by pairing each product with increasingly many candidate precursor sets, so the model sees multiple valid routes per product.

Result: Experiments show that increasing the breadth of training support (more candidate precursor sets per product) enables the model to propose a wider variety of plausible retrosynthetic alternatives. RIGS successfully conditions generation on instructions, steering the choice of precursors according to user-specified preferences. They also find that the interaction between having broad coverage of alternatives and being able to control them via instructions is stable across different model sizes but does not improve monotonically with coverage.

Conclusion: RIGS enables instruction-conditioned control in single-step retrosynthesis: it increases the diversity of valid precursor options while allowing users to steer which ones are preferred via natural language-like instructions. Coverage of alternatives and controllability are linked in a consistent but non-monotonic way, suggesting a nuanced tradeoff that must be managed when designing such systems.

Abstract: Single-step retrosynthesis models are commonly evaluated by their ability to recover recorded reactions. In practice, chemists may need to choose among several precursor sets for the same product, for example to preserve a particular motif. Recovering a recorded answer alone does not establish this ability to follow a preference. Satisfying such requests requires both coverage of relevant alternatives and control over which alternatives are favored. We introduce Route-Instruction Grounding and Steering (RIGS), a two-stage framework for instruction-conditioned retrosynthesis. Stage A trains a language projector, teaching it which alternatives an instruction favors or discourages. Stage B uses the projector learned in Stage A to steer a frozen generative model through lightweight residual adapters. We construct nested one-to-many training supports by pairing each product with increasing numbers of candidate precursor sets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that broader support helps the model generate a wider range of alternatives, and RIGS can learn to guide generation according to instructions. The relationship between coverage and control is consistent across model scales but non-monotone.

</details>


### [236] [Better Deck or Different Judge? Evaluating Agentic Harness Gains in Corporate and Investment Banking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39958)
*Ludovic Gibert,Matis Despujols,Andre-Louis Rochet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how an agentic system that combines a 27B LLM with financial tools, templates, and validation improves the quality of corporate banking pitch decks, and evaluates how reliably LLM judges can measure that improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Producing corporate and investment banking credit/financing decks is labor-intensive: teams must reconcile financials, track data provenance, and translate analysis into recommendations. LLM-based systems could automate much of this workflow, but it is unclear how to structure such systems and how to reliably evaluate their outputs, especially when evaluations themselves rely on LLM judges that may change their grading behavior over time.

Method: The authors retrospectively study the development of an agentic harness built around a 27B language model augmented with financial calculation modules, narrative templates, and validation checks. They run multiple development rounds (seventeen deliverables) where the system is iteratively improved. To evaluate, they use LLM judges in a shared-session, text-only grading setting with template markers removed. These judges compare decks produced by the full system to decks generated directly by the same base model from a short prompt, assigning scores out of 95, and the authors analyze score differences, consistency across judges, and variability in repeated grading of unchanged decks.

Result: In aggregate, five LLM judges rate the complete agentic system between 20.4 and 33.6 points (out of 95) higher than direct short-prompt generation by the same model. For all seventeen development deliverables, every judge scores the system version higher than the direct-generation baseline. However, when comparing against direct Opus generation from a short prompt, score margins are much smaller, ranging from -4.7 to +0.8 points. Judges show consensus on the existence of broad progress over development rounds, but they exhibit lower agreement on the exact ranking of final decks. Moreover, repeated grading of unchanged decks yields shifted scores, indicating notable judge variability.

Conclusion: The agentic harness that augments a 27B LLM with financial tools, templates, and validation produces substantially better banking decks than naive short-prompt use of the same model, according to LLM-judge evaluations. However, evaluation with LLM judges is noisy: while they capture broad improvements, they are inconsistent on fine-grained rankings and can change scores even for identical decks on re-evaluation. This variability means small measured improvements may not be statistically reliable, underscoring the need for more robust evaluation practices when using LLM judges to guide system development.

Abstract: Corporate and investment banking teams use presentations to support credit decisions and advise clients on financing and transactions. Producing these decks requires reconciling financial data, tracing sources and turning analysis into a recommendation. We retrospectively study the development of an agentic harness combining a 27B language model, financial calculations, narrative templates and validation checks. LLM judges guide engineering changes and assess the resulting decks, raising the question of whether higher scores reflect better documents or changes in grading. In shared-session text-only grading with template markers removed, five judges score the complete system 20.4 to 33.6 points out of 95 above the same model generating directly from a short prompt. Every judge scores the system higher on all seventeen development deliverables. Margins against direct Opus generation from a short prompt range from -4.7 to +0.8 points. Judges agree on broad progress across development rounds but agree less on final-deck rankings than on pooled scores. Repeated grading also shifts scores on unchanged decks, making small improvements difficult to distinguish from judge variability.

</details>


### [237] [AIMS: An Agentic AI Framework for Sim-to-Real Multi-Modal ISAC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39964)
*Yijie Bian,Kai Zhang,Wei Guo,Zixin Wang,Shenghui Song,Jun Zhang,Khaled B. Letaief*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce AIMS, an agentic AI framework that automatically configures and runs sim-to-real pipelines for multi-modal ISAC, improving task performance and orchestration quality using structured domain knowledge and validation feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data-driven multi-modal ISAC needs large amounts of annotated real-world data to learn cross-modal relations between sensing and wireless signals. Synthetic data helps but is hard to adapt to new deployments because scene simulation, sensing, wireless channels, and learning setups must be consistently configured; mismatches degrade sim-to-real transfer. There is a need for an automated, deployment-aware way to design and coordinate the whole sim-to-real pipeline from a high-level task description.

Method: They propose AIMS, an agentic AI framework with two collaborating agents. A scene construction agent builds geographically grounded scenes and generates synchronized multi-modal sensing and wireless data from shared physical states. A scene understanding agent selects task-relevant modalities and configures a mixture-of-experts (MoE) learning setup for either zero-shot inference or few-shot adaptation, depending on the real-data budget. The system starts from a natural-language deployment request, uses structured domain knowledge to perform dependency-aware planning of the sim-to-real configuration, and employs validation-derived evidence to iteratively revise earlier decisions when needed. They also design an orchestration benchmark to test task interpretation, reasoning over dependencies, and feedback-driven replanning.

Result: On the DeepSense 6G real-world dataset, AIMS yields better performance on vehicle detection and beam prediction tasks compared with existing simulation-based and fusion-based baselines. On the orchestration benchmark with varied deployment requests, AIMS achieves higher plan correctness, and both structured domain knowledge and validation feedback are shown to contribute to these improvements.

Conclusion: An agentic, planning-based AI framework can automate deployment-specific sim-to-real pipelines for multi-modal ISAC from natural-language requests. By explicitly coordinating scene construction and task learning, grounding simulations geographically, and leveraging structured domain knowledge plus validation feedback, AIMS improves both downstream task accuracy and the quality of orchestration compared to standard baselines.

Abstract: Multi-modal integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception and reliable connectivity for intelligent wireless networks. Data-driven multi-modal ISAC models depend heavily on annotated real-world data to learn relationships across sensing and wireless observations, thereby constraining scalable deployment. Although synthetic data generation reduces the burden, adapting existing simulation pipelines to a target deployment requires consistent scene, sensing, wireless, and learning configurations, while mismatches among these coupled components impair sim-to-real transferability. To address the challenge, we propose an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for sim-to-real multi-modal ISAC, named AIMS. Given a natural-language deployment request specifying the target task, deployment conditions, and real-data budget, AIMS derives a deployment-specific sim-to-real configuration and coordinates its execution to produce a deployment-specific task model. A two-agent architecture coordinates scene construction with task learning. A scene construction agent generates geographically grounded, synchronized sensing and wireless records from shared physical states, while a scene understanding agent configures task-relevant modalities and mixture-of-experts (MoE) learning for zero-shot inference or few-shot adaptation. Structured domain knowledge guides dependency-aware planning, while validation evidence supports feedback-driven revision of affected decisions. Experiments on the real-world DeepSense~6G dataset demonstrate improved vehicle detection and beam prediction over the considered simulation and fusion baselines. A separate orchestration benchmark evaluates task interpretation, dependency reasoning, and feedback-driven replanning across diverse deployment requests, showing improved plan correctness with structured domain knowledge and validation feedback.

</details>


### [238] [What Can Component-Replacement Evidence Establish? A Critical Scoping Review of Local Decisions in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39989)
*Shuyang Zhang,Jianshuo Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper is a critical scoping review of component replacements in language-model agents, showing that improvements in local decision metrics do not automatically imply task-level performance gains, and deriving reporting guidelines to properly attribute benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In language-model agents, individual components (e.g., detectors, routing modules, termination criteria) are frequently swapped or improved. However, such changes alter the entire execution trajectory, affecting later observations, resource use, and opportunities for recovery, making it hard to know whether observed task-level gains are due to the local component or other factors. The field lacks a clear framework and evidence standards to connect local decision quality to end-to-end task outcomes.

Method: The authors conduct a critical scoping review of 348 studies and focus on 90 comparison records (88 from 40 included studies plus 2 supplementary). They select eight representative cases and analyze them along several dimensions: what decision was replaced, under which execution conditions, how measurements are defined and made comparable, what controls are used, and what alternative explanations remain. They distinguish studies reporting local decision metrics from those reporting task-level endpoints or proxies and examine how well these are matched in actual comparisons.

Result: Of 222 studies that report local decision metrics, 142 also report measured task endpoints and 49 report proxy endpoints, but these reports often do not correspond to tightly matched comparisons, limiting attribution. In the detailed cases: (1) Outcome Monitors show package-level completion gains but cannot clearly attribute them to detector quality; (2) First-chunk selection shows local decision improvements evaluated only against an offline proxy endpoint; (3) Evidence-Carrying Termination reduces premature unsupported terminations and maintains completion rates (non-inferiority) but does not demonstrate improved task completion. Cross-case analysis suggests three mechanisms—recovery/disruption dynamics, timing of interventions, and downstream use patterns—that shape how component changes affect tasks. The authors find that attribution and deployment decisions are highly sensitive to comparison design, label definitions, and the information available to the system controller.

Conclusion: The review formalizes the distinction between the task-level benefit of replacing a component and the specific contribution of its local decision quality. It proposes eight claim-specific reporting items to clarify what kind of evidence is needed for different attribution claims. The central conclusion is that neither running components in online settings nor observing simultaneous gains in local and task metrics suffices to claim that better local decisions caused task-level improvements; careful controls and reporting standards are required to support such causal attributions.

Abstract: Background. A component replacement in a language-model agent changes an execution trajectory, potentially altering later observations, resource use, and recovery opportunities. Different evidence is needed to assess its task-level benefit and the contribution of local decision quality. Methods. This critical scoping review maps 348 studies and examines 90 comparison records: 88 from 40 included studies and two from supplementary studies. Eight purposively selected cases structure the synthesis around the replaced decision, executed conditions, measurement comparability, controls, and remaining explanations. Results. Of 222 studies reporting local decision metrics, 142 also report measured task endpoints and 49 report proxies. These counts identify studies that report both types of measurement, without establishing that the measurements come from matched comparisons. Outcome Monitors reports a package-level completion gain whose attribution to detector quality remains limited; First-chunk selection reports a local improvement assessed against an offline proxy endpoint; Evidence-Carrying Termination reports fewer premature unsupported terminations and completion non-inferiority, without establishing completion superiority. Cross-case analysis identifies three candidate mechanisms involving recovery and disruption, intervention timing, and downstream use. Attribution and deployment depend on the comparison controls, label definitions, and information available to the controller. Conclusions. The review distinguishes the task-level benefit of a component replacement from the contribution of local decision quality and derives eight claim-specific reporting items. Neither online execution nor simultaneous gains in local and task metrics alone establish that better local decisions explain the task-level gain.

</details>


### [239] [Who Verifies the Graph? Misspecification Attacks on Causal Action Verification for Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40027)
*Fabio Rovai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper stress-tests a causal action verifier (CIVeX) by corrupting its causal model and shows how small misspecifications lead to many harmful or missed actions, then proposes randomized attestation and auditing to recover safety and value, quantifying the experimental cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Causal action verifiers like CIVeX aim to make AI tool use safer by only allowing interventions that are identifiable from a committed causal graph, providing internal certificates of safety. However, these guarantees assume the committed graph is correct. The authors want to understand how fragile this setup is to realistic misspecifications or attacks on the graph, and how to detect or mitigate such failures in practice.

Method: The authors red-team the CIVeX verifier by altering only the committed causal graph while leaving the rest of the system unchanged. They consider two minimal corruptions: (1) omitting a single bidirected (confounding) edge, and (2) reversing an arrow so that a mediator is treated as a confounder. They then run the benchmark for confounded tool use at various confounding strengths, measuring false executions, harmfulness, and utility under these corruptions. Next, they introduce an attestation step that randomly tests a bounded subset of observationally certified executions via randomized experiments, rejecting actions that fail or cannot be tested. They also analyze an auditing regime that inspects rejections and executions to see how safety and value can be restored, and compute the experiment cost per number of actions.

Result: A single missing bidirected edge increases the false execution rate from 0 to 15.3% at the benchmark’s confounding strength, with 91% of executions being harmful and utility dropping from +2.27 to +0.35. Reversing one arrowhead so that a mediator is mis-committed as a confounder causes 48.9% false executions and zero correct ones. All of these actions still carry internally valid causal certificates. The proposed randomized attestation detects both types of attack, incurring 2 false alarms out of 555 executions on a truthful graph. If the system refuses actions that fail or cannot be tested, it achieves zero false executions in all measured settings, but many beneficial actions are still rejected due to misspecification. At the benchmark’s published confounding strength, 97.1% of beneficial actions are never executed. Auditing rejections and executions can recover both safety and value, but the cost scales differently: protecting only against wrongful action requires 127 experiments per 1,050 actions, whereas fully recovering lost value requires 614 additional experiments, after which the audited verifier matches the honest graph’s decisions using exactly this experiment budget.

Conclusion: Causal action verifiers that rely solely on identifiability certificates from a committed causal graph are highly vulnerable to even minimal graph misspecification, enabling many harmful or missed actions while still issuing internally valid certificates. Adding a randomized attestation step that empirically tests a sample of certified executions can effectively eliminate wrongful executions but does not by itself restore beneficial ones, because the same misspecification blocks them earlier in the pipeline.
