Full recovery of both safety and value requires targeted auditing of rejected actions, at a quantifiable experimental cost that scales with the number of rejections rather than executions. The work highlights that causal certification must be combined with empirical checks and auditing if one wants robustness both to wrongful action and wrongful inaction under imperfect causal models.

Abstract: Causal action verifiers gate an agent's state-changing tool calls by checking whether each proposed intervention is identifiable against a committed action-state graph, and they issue a certificate that carries the identification argument and a one-sided lower confidence bound. One such verifier, CIVeX, reports zero false executions on a confounded tool-use benchmark. We red-team it by corrupting only the committed graph. Omitting a single bidirected edge takes it from zero false executions to 15.3% at the benchmark's published confounding strength, with 91% of its executions harmful and utility falling from +2.27 to +0.35. Reversing one arrowhead, so that a mediator is committed as a confounder, gives 48.9% false executions and no correct ones. Every one of these actions carries an internally valid certificate. An attestation step that tests each observationally certified execution against a bounded randomised sample detected both attacks, with 2 false alarms in 555 executions on a truthful graph; refusing what fails the test, or cannot be tested, gave zero false executions in every setting we measured. It does not restore beneficial execution: at the published strength 97.1% of beneficial actions are still never executed, because the same misspecification rejects them before attestation runs. Those rejections carry certificates too, and auditing them works, but its cost scales with the number of rejections rather than the number of executions. Recovering safety costs 127 experiments per 1,050 actions; recovering the lost value costs 614 more, at which point the audited verifier makes the honest graph's decisions on every instance and spends exactly its experiment budget. An audit that inspects only executions protects against wrongful action. Wrongful inaction has to be paid for separately.

</details>


### [240] [PTNO: Training Neural Operators with Noisy Monte Carlo Estimates for Particle Transport Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40090)
*Yubo Cao,Xi Deng,Mengqi Xia,Vignesh Gopakumar,Ander Gray,Anima Anandkumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce PTNO, a neural operator that learns fast surrogates for particle transport directly from noisy, low-sample Monte Carlo data, handling both label noise and extreme dynamic range while remaining accurate and much cheaper than standard Monte Carlo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations for particle transport in radiative transfer and plasma physics are extremely costly because they must track many particles. Existing learning-based surrogates still rely on expensive, well-converged Monte Carlo solutions as training labels, which limits their practicality. The authors want a surrogate that can be trained from much cheaper, noisy simulations while remaining accurate, and that can handle the high dynamic range of particle transport quantities without numerical or statistical issues.

Method: They propose Particle Transport Neural Operator (PTNO), a neural operator that maps from problem configurations to particle transport solutions. PTNO is trained directly on noisy, low-sample Monte Carlo outputs. The method leverages two ideas: (1) For noise, they show that because Monte Carlo estimates are unbiased, minimizing squared loss on noisy labels has the same minimizer as on converged labels; they then study how to allocate a fixed computational budget across number of scenes M, samples per render N, and independent renders per scene K, concluding that many noisy scenes are better than a few converged scenes. (2) For high dynamic range, they avoid logarithmic transforms that would bias learning with noise; instead, they predict in physical space with a softplus output to enforce positivity and better represent small values. They also introduce or adopt a pointwise relative L2 loss (PRelL2), which normalizes residuals by a stop-gradient prediction rather than the noisy label, improving stability on HDR data. PTNO is evaluated on neutron transport and radiative transfer benchmarks.

Result: On two neutron-transport tasks relevant to fusion reactors, PTNO achieves speedups of 10^4–10^5× over fully converged Monte Carlo on the same CPU, and at a fixed accuracy level it makes predictions that are 10^3–10^5× cheaper than Monte Carlo. On two radiative-transfer tasks in participating media, Monte Carlo methods need 0.8–11× more computational cost than PTNO to reach comparable accuracy, showing PTNO’s advantages also extend beyond neutronics.

Conclusion: PTNO can be trained directly from noisy, low-sample Monte Carlo labels while remaining accurate, thereby dramatically reducing the cost of generating training data and of inference compared to standard Monte Carlo. Its architecture and loss design explicitly address label noise and high dynamic range without resorting to biased transformations, leading to large computational gains in neutron transport and radiative transfer problems. This suggests that neural operators trained on cheap, noisy simulations are a practical path to scalable surrogates for particle transport and related high-dimensional physics problems.

Abstract: Particle transport under multiple scattering is central to radiative transfer and plasma physics, yet high-fidelity Monte Carlo (MC) simulations must trace prohibitively many particles. Learning-based surrogates can amortize this cost, but typically train on expensive, well-converged MC solutions. We propose the Particle Transport Neural Operator (PTNO), a neural operator that learns particle transport surrogates directly from noisy, low-cost MC labels. Such labels pose two challenges: (1) high variance, which destabilizes standard supervised learning, and (2) a high dynamic range (HDR) spanning many orders of magnitude. For the first, we learn the solution operator from noisy labels of many configurations, amortizing MC cost and generalizing to unseen configurations. Because MC labels are unbiased, we show that the squared loss on them shares its minimizer with the loss on converged solutions, and our budget-allocation study over training scenes $M$, MC samples per render $N$, and independent renders per scene $K$ shows that many noisy scenes beat fewer converged ones. For the second, a nonlinear transform such as the logarithm biases noisy supervision. Instead, PTNO keeps labels in physical space and enforces positivity with a softplus output layer that represents small values effectively. We further train with a pointwise relative $L_2$ loss (PRelL2), the stop-gradient relative loss of HDR denoising and neural rendering, which normalizes each residual by the stop-gradient prediction instead of the noisy label. We demonstrate PTNO on neutron transport in fusion reactors and radiative transfer in participating media. On the two neutronics tasks, PTNO is $10^4$-$10^5\times$ faster than converged MC on the same CPU and $10^3$-$10^5\times$ cheaper than MC at matched accuracy; on the two radiative-transfer tasks, MC at matched accuracy costs $0.8$-$11\times$ as much as PTNO.

</details>


### [241] [Agent Error Dataset: Scaling 50,000 Error--Diagnosis Pairs for Failure Analysis and Error-Aware Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40111)
*Kunlun Zhu,Xuyan Ye,Yibo Li,Cheng Qian,Beibin Li,Heng Ji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Agent Error Dataset (AED) and a pipeline to convert failed LLM agent rollouts into supervision signals, improving diagnosis quality and agent performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Typical training for LLM-based agents focuses on final rewards or successful trajectories, ignoring the rich information in failed rollouts. There is a lack of standardized data and methodology for turning these failures into structured supervision for both error diagnosis and policy repair across diverse environments and models.

Method: The authors build the Agent Error Dataset (AED) with over 50k pairs of error diagnoses and corrections derived from failed rollouts of text-based LLM agents across many environments, harnesses, and models. They log complete traces and metadata, then implement a five-stage Agentic Error-to-Training (AET) pipeline: (1) collect natural failures, (2) generate diagnoses and proposed fixes, (3) validate these against recorded evidence, (4) where possible, replay from checkpoints to compare proposed corrections with original actions under matched settings, and (5) construct distinct training views tailored to learning diagnosis and to training the acting policy. They evaluate both the correctness of proposed corrections and their impact when used as training data via fine-tuning and various actor-training recipes.

Result: On 3,062 replayable failures, the first proposed correction increases a verifier's pass rate from 18.4% to 51.1% (+32.7 points). Using a frozen diagnosis model, fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with full-diagnosis signals on 1,656 tasks improves exact-step agreement with internal teacher labels from 47.2% to 63.6% on a 943-case holdout, beating the best prompted baseline at 54.7%. Performance improves monotonically with larger training sets. In a WebShop-lite benchmark, an action-only repair training recipe outperforms success-only training by 6.67 percentage points in a single-seed comparison.

Conclusion: Failed LLM agent trajectories can be systematically mined to produce high-quality supervisory signals for both error diagnosis and policy repair. The AED dataset and AET pipeline show that structured corrections of specific decisions significantly improve agent reliability and alignment with teacher signals, outperforming strong prompting baselines and naive success-only training. This positions failure-centric training as a practical, scalable route to better LLM agents.

Abstract: An unsuccessful LLM agent rollout contains more information than its final reward: the observations available to the agent, the actions it chose, and the environment's responses. Reusing this experience for learning requires identifying a decision to revise and testing a concrete alternative. We introduce the Agent Error Dataset (AED), comprising 50,228 error-diagnosis pairs from 9,961 source tasks across 33 environments, 19 harness families, and 23 policy models in text-based agent systems. We retain source traces and execution metadata to support cross-setting failure analysis and re-diagnosis without repeating the original rollout. Our five-stage Agentic Error-to-Training (AET) pipeline collects natural failures, generates diagnoses and proposed corrections, and checks them against recorded evidence. Where replay is supported, we compare corrections with original-action retries from the same checkpoint under matched execution settings. We then construct separate training views for diagnosis and actor recovery. Across 3,062 matched replay pairs, first-proposal corrections raise verifier pass rates from 18.4% to 51.1%, a gain of 32.7 percentage points. Using a separately frozen diagnosis release, full-diagnosis fine-tuning on 1,656 source tasks raises Qwen3-8B's exact-step agreement with internal teacher labels from 47.2% to 63.6%, averaged over three seeds on a 943-case holdout. The strongest prompted reference in this comparison scores 54.7%, and mean agreement improves at each of four increasing training-set sizes. In a single-seed comparison of actor-training recipes, action-only repair training scores 6.67 percentage points higher on WebShop-lite than success-only training.

</details>


### [242] [Unlearnable, or Unmeasured? On the Reliability of Difficulty Labels in RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40115)
*Chandak Chakma,Syed Nazmus Sakib,Nafiul Haque,Shifat E. Arman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reexamines claims that some prompts in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards are 'unlearnable,' finding instead that they do learn more slowly and that prior difficulty labels and gradient-based explanations are unstable and require better measurement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on RL with verifiable rewards reported an 'unlearnability' phenomenon: some difficult prompts seemed not to improve, even when correct solutions occasionally appeared, raising concerns about fundamental limitations of current post-training methods and their theoretical explanations.

Method: The authors reanalyze the unlearnability phenomenon by (1) measuring learning progress on previously-labeled difficult prompts, (2) studying the stability and reproducibility of difficulty labels that are estimated from limited sampled responses and multiple random seeds, (3) proposing a sampling-based framework to quantify label instability and required evaluation budget, and (4) reexamining gradient-similarity evidence by controlling for the number of correct rollouts used to estimate gradients.

Result: They find that so-called 'unlearnable' prompts do improve, at roughly one third the rate of other prompts; that difficulty-defined prompt sets are much less reproducible than expected because aggregating across seeds changes which prompts are selected; that their sampling-based analysis quantifies how many samples are needed to obtain reproducible difficulty assignments; and that part of the previously-reported gradient separation is explained by difficult prompts having fewer correct rollouts, with the gradient difference reduced but not eliminated when matching sample counts.

Conclusion: The previously-claimed unlearnability is better characterized as slow learning rather than no learning; both the definition of difficult prompts and the gradient-based explanations for their behavior are sensitive to sampling and require more careful measurement, though a genuine slow-learning effect remains.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach for improving reasoning during post-training. Recent work suggests that some difficult prompts remain resistant to learning even when they occasionally produce correct solutions. We revisit this unlearnability phenomenon and find that the affected prompts do improve, at roughly one third of the learnable rate, while the difficulty-defined set used to study them is much less reproducible than expected. These difficulty labels are estimated from a limited number of sampled responses. Combining them across seeds can further change which prompts are selected instead of simply reducing measurement noise. We develop a sampling-based framework for quantifying this instability and determining how much evaluation is required for difficulty assignments to reproduce reliably. We also revisit the gradient-similarity evidence proposed to explain unlearnability and show that part of the observed separation arises because difficult prompts provide fewer correct rollouts from which their gradients can be estimated. Matching this sample count weakens the gradient difference but does not remove it. Overall, the slow-learning phenomenon survives our reanalysis, while both the prompts used to define it and the evidence used to explain it require more careful measurement.

</details>


### [243] [Learning from Research: Toward Lifelong Agent Harness Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40169)
*Jingbo Yang,Kwei-Herng Lai,Xiaowen Wang,Yaar Harari,Evgeniy Gabrilovich,Shiyu Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ScholarEvolve is a framework that automatically improves the software harness around a fixed language model by reading and incorporating ideas from new research papers, leading to better tool use and task performance over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language agents are applied to more complex, evolving tasks, their surrounding harness (tool orchestration, memory, task execution logic) must continually improve. Existing automated harness-evolution methods depend mainly on a meta coding agent that learns only from its own failures and prior knowledge, which limits exploration, makes adaptation reactive, and underuses the fast-growing research literature that contains novel strategies for agent design. The authors want a way to systematically and automatically inject up-to-date research advances into the evolution of agent harnesses.

Method: The authors propose ScholarEvolve, a framework that treats the agent harness as a set of functional modules (e.g., tool use, memory management, task execution). For each module, the system mines the research literature and uses topic modeling to identify distinct improvement strategies reflected in recent papers. It then instantiates these strategies as concrete harness modifications, composes different strategies across modules, and evaluates the resulting harness variants on benchmark tasks. The framework is designed to be recurrently updated: as new papers appear, they are incorporated into the topic models and candidate strategies, enabling continual evolution driven by the state of the art.

Result: In experiments on the AppWorld and Tau2-Bench benchmarks, ScholarEvolve significantly improves the performance of fixed base language models by evolving only their harnesses. Specifically, it boosts Qwen3.5-27B’s task goal completion rate on the AppWorld Challenge from 49.6% to 63.6%, and increases GPT-5.4-mini’s pass@1 on the Tau2-Bench Telecom subset from 72.7% to 81.9%. These results show that literature-guided harness evolution yields substantial gains over the baseline harness design without changing the underlying language model.

Conclusion: ScholarEvolve demonstrates that automatically leveraging the research literature can guide proactive, lifelong evolution of language-agent harnesses, leading to substantial performance improvements on complex tasks while keeping the base language model fixed. By modularizing the harness, using topic modeling to extract diverse strategies from papers, and continually incorporating new publications, the framework turns research progress into concrete harness upgrades. This suggests a scalable path for keeping language agents aligned with the rapidly advancing state of the art without repeatedly retraining the core models.

Abstract: Language agents are expected to solve increasingly complex tasks, creating a growing need for continual improvement. One promising approach is to evolve the agent harness, the software that governs tool use, memory management, and task execution, while keeping the underlying language model fixed. Recent methods automate this process by using a meta coding agent to modify the harness based on execution feedback. However, relying on that agent's existing knowledge and observed failures can restrict exploration and make adaptation reactive. Inspired by how human experts learn from the research literature for new solutions, we introduce ScholarEvolve, a framework that automatically draws on state-of-the-art research to guide harness evolution. ScholarEvolve organizes the harness evolution directions into functional modules and uses topic modeling to identify distinct improvement strategies for each module. It implements these strategies and evaluates their combinations to improve task performance. Moreover, the framework is designed to incorporate new publications over time, allowing research advances to drive proactive lifelong evolution. Experiments demonstrate improvements on AppWorld and Tau2-Bench. ScholarEvolve raises Qwen3.5-27B task goal completion from 49.6% to 63.6% on AppWorld Challenge, and raises GPT-5.4-mini pass@1 from 72.7% to 81.9% on Tau2-Bench Telecom.

</details>


### [244] [Belief-Aware Multi-Agent Path Finding under Map Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40269)
*Viraj Parimi,Shao-Hung Chan,Han Zhang,Jingkai Chen,Brian Williams*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MAGIC, a MAPF framework that exploits spatial correlations in map changes to reduce execution cost by updating a shared probabilistic belief over traversability using Gaussian inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical Multi-Agent Path Finding assumes a fully known static map, which is unrealistic in dynamic environments where local changes (e.g., new obstacles) appear during execution. Existing methods either precompute contingent plans or replan only from directly observed obstacles, ignoring spatial correlations in map changes. This leads to myopic behavior where agents repeatedly discover nearby obstacles and incur costly rerouting. The paper aims to incorporate spatially correlated uncertainty into MAPF so that a single observation can inform belief about nearby unobserved locations, improving robustness and efficiency at scale.

Method: The authors formulate Belief-Aware MAPF with unknown but fixed map discrepancies and spatially informative observations. They propose MAGIC (Multi-Agent Gaussian belief Inference for Coordination), which maintains a shared probabilistic belief about cell traversability modeled as a Gaussian Markov Random Field over the environment. As agents move and observe traversability, MAGIC performs Gaussian Belief Propagation to update this field, inferring likely traversability of both observed and unobserved cells. From this inferred map, MAGIC derives detour-aware edge costs that can be plugged into standard MAPF planners without changing their core algorithms, enabling anticipatory routing that accounts for likely obstacles. The approach is evaluated across different MAPF planner families and varying team sizes.

Result: On standard MAPF benchmarks, MAGIC consistently reduces the realized execution cost (sum of path costs actually traveled) compared to baselines that do not use spatial belief inference. It achieves improvement on 96.3% of test instances. The method scales to large teams with up to 800 agents and is compatible with multiple planner families, indicating that the Gaussian belief layer adds significant performance benefits with manageable computational overhead.

Conclusion: Spatially correlated uncertainty can be efficiently exploited in MAPF via a Gaussian inference layer. MAGIC provides a planner-agnostic framework that converts local observations into a global, detour-aware cost structure, enabling agents to anticipate and avoid likely but unobserved obstacles. This reduces executed path cost and scales to large multi-agent teams, demonstrating the practical value of belief-aware, probabilistic reasoning about traversability in dynamic environments.

Abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) aims to find collision-free paths for multiple agents in a shared environment. Classical MAPF assumes that all static obstacles are known in advance, but real-world environments can change unexpectedly due to fallen objects, spills, or other local disturbances. When such changes are spatially correlated, an observation can inform traversability estimates beyond the observed location. Prior approaches address uncertainty in traversability through contingent plans or replanning based on direct observations, but do not leverage this spatial dependence to infer the traversability of nearby unobserved locations. As a result, they cannot use one observation to anticipate nearby unobserved obstacles that may cause costly rerouting later. We focus on Belief-Aware MAPF, where map discrepancies are fixed during execution but initially unknown, and observations can be informative beyond the observed location. We propose Multi-Agent Gaussian belief Inference for Coordination (MAGIC), a framework that updates a shared belief about traversability online based on agents' observations. MAGIC uses a Gaussian Markov Random Field and Gaussian Belief Propagation to approximately infer traversability and construct detour-aware costs for standard MAPF planners. Our experiments on MAPF benchmarks show that MAGIC reduces the executed sum of costs compared to existing approaches on 96.3% of instances, across several planner families and teams of up to 800 agents, demonstrating its applicability to large-scale MAPF problems.

</details>


### [245] [PivotOPD: Learning to Recover from Pivotal Mistakes in Multi-Turn Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40285)
*Yinghui He,Yapei Chang,Khushi Bhardwaj,Daniele Molinari,Tugrul Konuk,Jan Kautz,Ali Hatamizadeh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PivotOPD is an on-policy distillation framework that identifies pivotal mistakes in multi-turn language agent trajectories and teaches models both to avoid and to recover from them, yielding state-of-the-art performance across several embodied and web-based tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard on-policy distillation trains agents using supervision only on the states they actually visit, but in multi-turn tasks, early mistakes change subsequent states and cause cascading failures. Many failures hinge on a small number of early, pivotal mistakes that could in principle be corrected with brief guidance, yet existing methods neither explicitly detect these mistakes nor train agents to recover from them. The authors aim to exploit this structure in failure modes to improve robustness and task completion rates of language agents, especially for smaller student models distilled from larger teachers.

Method: The authors first empirically analyze rollouts of several Qwen3 models to identify pivotal mistakes—actions that move the agent further from task completion and after which trajectories often fail, despite being recoverable with a few guided steps. They then introduce PivotOPD, which augments on-policy distillation with two components at these pivotal turns. A teacher model labels the correct (gold) action at the pivotal step and provides a short sequence of recovery actions for the subsequent turns. Preventive distillation applies reverse KL between student and teacher at the pivotal step, encouraging the student to choose the gold action instead of the mistaken one. Recovery distillation applies forward KL on the teacher’s recovery actions over the next few steps so that the student learns recovery behaviors that it would rarely sample on its own. This joint training is integrated into the standard on-policy distillation framework so that the student learns both to avoid and to bounce back from pivotal mistakes.

Result: Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA benchmarks, PivotOPD is evaluated against 13 baselines using Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B as students. It achieves the best average performance in both student sizes, including a +5.5% improvement over the strongest prior method on ALFWorld with the 1.7B model. The authors further test transfer to a different model family and domain: a Nemotron-3.5 student on the SWE-Bench Verified software engineering benchmark, where PivotOPD increases the resolve rate by +3.2%, indicating cross-domain and cross-architecture benefits.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that many multi-turn agent failures are driven by a small number of early, pivotal mistakes that are nonetheless recoverable with targeted guidance, and that explicitly modeling these points in training substantially improves robustness. By combining preventive (reverse KL) and recovery (forward KL) distillation around pivotal mistakes, PivotOPD enhances the ability of smaller student models to avoid catastrophic early errors and to recover when they do occur. The framework outperforms a wide range of baselines across several tasks and transfers to different model families and domains, suggesting PivotOPD is a generally useful strategy for training more reliable language agents via on-policy distillation.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a promising approach for training language agents, providing dense teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, in multi-turn interaction, an incorrect action changes the states the student encounters later, so errors compound across turns. In preliminary experiments across three Qwen3 models (8B to 235B), we find that more than half of the failed rollouts contain a pivotal mistake, an action that moves the agent farther from completing the task, and this mistake typically occurs early. These pivotal mistakes often remain recoverable: guiding the model for only a few turns after the pivotal turn can restore task success. We therefore propose PivotOPD, an on-policy distillation framework that jointly trains the student to prevent pivotal mistakes and to recover from the states they create. At each pivotal mistake, a teacher model provides a gold action and then names a recovery action at each of the next few turns. Preventive distillation uses the gold action with reverse KL to steer the student away from the pivotal mistake, while recovery distillation uses the recovery actions with forward KL to transfer recovery behaviors that the student rarely samples. Against 13 baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA, PivotOPD achieves the strongest average performance for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B students, improving over the strongest baseline on ALFWorld by +5.5% with the 1.7B student. The gains also transfer to another model family on the software engineering domain, where PivotOPD raises the resolve rate of a Nemotron-3.5 student on SWE-Bench Verified by +3.2%. Project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/pivotopd/

</details>


### [246] [How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40303)
*Kirill Brilliantov,Alejandro Hernández-Cano,Emmanuel Abbé*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that, given the same strong LLM backbone and time budget, simple coding agents with direct execution access match or outperform complex multi-agent MLE harnesses, implying that backbone quality—not orchestration complexity—drives current benchmark performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous MLE agents have recently done well on public leaderboards, but progress is thought to be limited by long-horizon challenges and constrained LLM tools. As a result, increasingly complex multi-agent and tool-heavy harnesses are being built. The authors question whether such complexity actually adds value when strong LLMs already have direct coding and execution capabilities.

Method: The authors build a minimal-harness coding agent that gives a frontier LLM direct access to code execution via read, write, and shell commands. They then perform controlled comparisons between this baseline and several open-source state-of-the-art multi-agent MLE harnesses, holding constant the LLM backbone and time budget. They complement this with large-scale systematic ablation studies that remove or vary specific machinery layers (e.g., orchestrators, retrieval subagents) to measure their marginal contribution in the coding-agent setting.

Result: Across benchmarks and given equal compute/time and the same underlying LLM, complex open-source MLE harnesses do not outperform a single-session minimal coding agent. Ablation studies indicate that many orchestration layers contribute little or no measurable benefit when the LLM can already read, write, and execute code directly.

Conclusion: Current performance on MLE benchmarks is primarily driven by the strength of the LLM backbone rather than by elaborate multi-agent or tool-heavy harness design. In coding-agent scenarios, additional machinery becomes largely redundant, so investing significant engineering effort into complex orchestrations yields poor returns under present conditions.

Abstract: Recent autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have made significant progress on public leaderboards. Often motivated by progress stagnation over long-horizon cycles and limited Large Language Model (LLM) primitives, modern MLE agents are deployed on top of increasingly elaborate machinery: multi-agent orchestrators, dedicated retrieval subagents, and more. While such harnesses expand, the use of more primitive but improved coding agents - where LLMs have direct access to the execution environment through read, write, and bash primitives - has received little attention in the field. In this paper we find that, under an equal time budget and the same frontier LLM backbone, open-source state-of-the-art harnesses provide no advantages over a single session of a minimal-harness coding agent baseline, pointing to the backbone as the primary driver for performance. Via a series of large-scale systematic ablation studies, we argue that the machinery layers become redundant in the coding agent setting. We conclude that the effort spent elaborating hand-crafted harnesses around strong models yields poor returns for current MLE benchmarks.

</details>


### [247] [Cogentic: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Automated Proof Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40324)
*Yang Cai,Vineet Gupta,Yanchen Jiang,Christopher Liaw,Aranyak Mehta,Grigoris Velegkas,Di Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Cogentic is a multi-agent system that uses iterative prove–verify loops with an orchestrated population of provers and verifiers plus a persistent ledger to solve open research problems in math and theoretical CS, achieving several novel results using Gemini as the base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-shot generations from strong language models can propose good mathematical ideas but are inadequate for hard open problems that require exploring many proof directions, handling subtle obstacles, and preserving partial progress over long reasoning horizons. There is a need for a structured, multi-step, multi-agent approach that coordinates exploration, verification, and memory to push toward research-level automated theorem proving and discovery.

Method: They build Cogentic, a multi-agent “harness” wrapped around a base LLM (Gemini). An orchestrator manages a population of independent prover agents, assigning them to different proof directions. Their outputs are checked by several specialized adversarial verifier components. Proven or highly reliable intermediate lemmas and results are written into a persistent verified ledger. Future rounds of proving use this ledger as shared memory, enabling iterative prove–verify cycles over long horizons and across multiple conjectures and strategies.

Result: With Gemini as the underlying model, Cogentic solved five previously open problems in fields like online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design. The discovered results were strong enough to be written up in separate, full companion papers and were independently verified by human domain experts. A living list of these and future results is maintained on the Cogentic website.

Conclusion: A carefully orchestrated multi-agent prove–verify framework with persistent verified memory can turn a general-purpose LLM into a tool capable of producing bona fide research-level mathematical results, beyond what single-shot prompting can usually achieve. This suggests that structured coordination, verification, and long-term state management are key ingredients in automating advanced theorem proving and open-problem discovery.

Abstract: We present Cogentic, a multi-agent harness for automated proof discovery on open research problems. While frontier language models can generate strong mathematical ideas in a single shot, single-shot generation is often insufficient for open problems that require exploring multiple competing conjectures, overcoming subtle technical obstructions, and retaining intermediate progress over a long horizon. Cogentic addresses these challenges through an iterative prove--verify loop in which an orchestrator allocates a population of independent provers across distinct proof directions, subjects their output to adversarial verification by several specialized components, and promotes confirmed intermediate results into a persistent verified ledger that later rounds build on. The harness is designed to be able to solve research-level math and theoretical computer science problems. Using Gemini as the base model, Cogentic produced novel results on five open problems across online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design. Each result was independently verified by domain experts and is developed in full in companion papers. We list these results, and new ones as they are verified, at https://sites.google.com/view/cogentic .

</details>


### [248] [WorldAuditBench: Interactive 3D World Auditing with Multimodal Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40325)
*Ziyan Jiang,Jingbo Yang,Jiabao Ji,Yujian Liu,Qiucheng Wu,Tommi Jaakkola,Yang Zhang,Shiyu Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorldAuditBench is a benchmark to test how well multimodal agents can find and verify visual anomalies in interactive 3D environments, revealing a large performance gap to humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As 3D simulated worlds are increasingly used to study intelligent behavior, there is a need for scalable, automated methods to detect anomalies like floating objects or inconsistent scene elements. Current multimodal AI systems show promise, but it is unclear whether they can effectively integrate navigation (action) with visual reasoning to audit complex 3D environments, motivating a dedicated benchmark.

Method: The authors build WorldAuditBench, a benchmark consisting of 213 anomaly-finding tasks across 13 interactive 3D environments created with Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js, covering five types of anomalies. They then evaluate five state-of-the-art multimodal models under a fixed exploration budget using two paradigms: (1) a pipeline where a vision-language-action (VLA) model explores and then a vision-language model (VLM) identifies anomalies from collected observations; and (2) an end-to-end VLM agent where the same model performs both visual reasoning and action selection during exploration.

Result: Across both auditing paradigms and all five evaluated models, task success rates lie between 6.6% and 42.3%, which is far below human performance of 83.4%. This demonstrates that, even with strong multimodal models, current systems struggle to reliably find and confirm anomalies in 3D worlds within limited exploration budgets.

Conclusion: WorldAuditBench offers a controlled testbed for analyzing how multimodal agents combine visual reasoning with action in interactive 3D environments. The benchmark exposes substantial limitations in current systems’ ability to strategically explore, gather relevant evidence, and correctly interpret observations for anomaly detection, and can guide future research on tighter integration of perception and control in embodied AI agents.

Abstract: As interactive 3D worlds are increasingly used to study intelligent behavior, it becomes important to develop efficient pipelines for identifying anomalies in these simulated environments, such as floating objects, traversable walls, or objects inconsistent with the surrounding scene. Multimodal AI systems, including vision-language models (VLMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs), have shown potential for automating this task. However, 3D world auditing is complex, requiring the close coupling of two distinct capabilities: action, to navigate the 3D world and search for anomalies systematically and efficiently; and visual reasoning, to understand the environment and identify anomalies from multimodal observations. It remains largely unexplored whether multimodal agents can effectively couple these two capabilities, using visual reasoning to identify potential anomalies while taking actions to validate them. In this paper, we introduce WorldAuditBench, a benchmark for 3D world auditing comprising 213 anomaly tasks across 13 environments built with Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js, spanning five anomaly families. We evaluate five frontier models under a fixed exploration budget using two auditing paradigms: VLA-based exploration followed by VLM-based anomaly identification, and an end-to-end VLM agent in which visual reasoning directly guides action selection. Across the evaluated models and two paradigms, success rates range from 6.6% to 42.3%, substantially below human performance (83.4%). Through the task of world auditing, WorldAuditBench provides a testbed for studying how multimodal agents couple action and visual reasoning in interactive 3D environments, while highlighting current limitations in their ability to gather and interpret evidence during exploration.

</details>


### [249] [Turbo Harness: Instance-Adaptive Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40330)
*Tunyu Zhang,Hao Wang,Kai Xu,Dimitris N. Metaxas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Turbo Harness adapts a globally optimized agent harness to individual task instances using recycled optimization artifacts and a learned editor, improving performance over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global, one-size-fits-all harnesses are not optimal for every task instance in recursive self-improvement of agents; there is a need to efficiently adapt harnesses per instance using prior optimization experience.

Method: Run a standard global harness optimization once, collect and recycle all intermediate artifacts, and summarize them into a structured playbook. Train a harness editor model that, given a new instance plus this playbook, predicts instance-specific patches to the global harness, producing a tailored harness in which the execution model runs.

Result: Across seven benchmarks covering interactive agents, software engineering, and long-horizon terminal tasks, Turbo Harness consistently outperforms existing global harness optimization baselines in numerical experiments.

Conclusion: Reusing artifacts from global harness optimization and learning an editor to produce instance-specific patches is an effective way to move beyond one-size-fits-all harnesses, yielding better performance across diverse benchmarks and bringing agents closer to practical recursive self-improvement.

Abstract: Automating the search for effective harnesses is an important step toward enabling agents to recursively self-improve. Existing harness optimizations typically produce a single global harness that is applied uniformly across task instances. However, a harness that works well on average may not be optimal for every instance. We introduce Turbo Harness, a framework that can adapt a globally optimized harness to each instance by reusing information generated during the original optimization process. Specifically, Turbo Harness recycles artifacts produced during a completed global harness optimization run, and summarizes them into a structured playbook. We train a harness editor to leverage this prior optimization experience to generate instance-specific patches to the global harness. At inference time, the editor uses the instance and the playbook to construct a tailored harness in which the execution model operates. Through numerical experiments, we show that Turbo Harness consistently outperforms existing harness optimization baselines across seven benchmarks spanning interactive agent tasks, software engineering, and long-horizon terminal tasks.
